An SMTP client: connect, connect_starttls and connect_tls, EHLO extensions, AUTH PLAIN, LOGIN, XOAUTH2 and CRAM-MD5 (plaintext authentication is refused unless insecure_auth), send with per-recipient results, dot-stuffing, pipelining when advertised, and errors separating 4xx from 5xx.

SOCKS5 (RFC 1928, with RFC 1929 username and password) and SOCKS4a clients: dial, dial4a, tunnel and tunnel4a over an existing connection, and dialer and dialer4a, which return a net.Dialer. The proxy resolves the target name.

The driver contract: Connection, the droppable owner that closes the driver connection when released; ConnectionHandle, the copyable view of closures that std/orm and std/sql/pool use, held in the owner's public handle field (adopt makes an owner from one); Value, Rows, Error, Options and Dialect. A Dialect is a record that owns everything that differs between databases: the OpenTelemetry system name, default port, placeholder prefix, identifier quotes, generated-key and paging syntax, column types, the conditional CREATE TABLE, the session lock statements and the write-transaction statement. postgres(), sqlserver() and sqlite() build the three; std/orm and std/sql/migrate read the one a connection carries. rolled_back rolls a transaction back after an error and reports the rollback's own error when it fails.

What the drivers share. A Session holds the busy and closed state. Every operation of a connection runs as a call on the session, which fails with Busy or Closed and abandons the connection on an error the driver calls fatal. establish runs the login under it, collect, ignore_columns and ignore_row are the row callbacks, dial opens the socket at the dialect's default port, and traced wraps a handle with otel.instrument_sql. connection guards, traces and adopts a driver's handle, so std/sql/postgres, std/sql/sqlserver and std/sql/sqlite do not import std/otel.

Ordered migrations recorded in a schema_migrations table with a SHA-256 checksum: plan, with_table, status, up, up_to and down, each migration in its own transaction under a lock. from_text and load_dir read -- +up and -- +down files named NNN_name.sql.

A pool of connections made by an opener. open takes a Config (max, max_idle, idle_timeout, max_lifetime, wait_timeout, ping_after, ping, clock). acquire and acquire_until (with a cancel token) park in first-in first-out order while every connection is in use. A droppable Lease returns its connection on release. Also with, discard, prune, stats and shutdown.
A PostgreSQL driver over protocol 3.0, plain or over TLS.

SQLite through libsqlite3, linked only when a program calls it. open and open_with (read-only, create, busy timeout). exec runs scripts. query, each and execute take ? or ?N parameters over cached prepared statements. Also last_insert_id, begin, begin_immediate, commit and rollback, and backup to a file through the online backup API. close and close_on are idempotent; a closed Database fails with sql.Error.Closed. connection and connect present a database as an sql.Connection: the one connection returns leaves closing to the Database, the one connect returns closes it. Calls block their OS thread.
A Microsoft SQL Server driver over TDS 7.4, plain or over TLS.

Mutex with lock, try_lock, unlock and locked. WaitGroup with add, done and wait. Once with run. RwLock, first in first out and writer-fair, with read_lock, read_unlock, write_lock, write_unlock, try_read_lock, try_write_lock, reading and writing. Semaphore with acquire, try_acquire, release and available. Cond with wait_cond, signal and broadcast. Barrier with wait_barrier. OnceValue[T]. ErrorGroup[E], whose go blocks while limit tasks run and whose join returns the first error. All are built on channels, so a waiting green thread parks instead of spinning. lock_thread and unlock_thread pin the calling green thread to its OS thread, for C libraries whose state belongs to one thread; they nest.

The operating system layer: Linux system calls, and kernel32, ws2_32 and the other Win32 libraries on Windows. It is the only standard library module besides the prelude that calls __syscall, and its Windows files call none. It owns every syscall number, flag, errno and structure layout and exposes typed wrappers that repeat an interrupted call and fail with an io.Error, so callers match io.Error variants. Descriptors: FdHandle, a copyable view whose closing is coordinated by an io.Guard, and the droppable Fd that owns one; read, write, write_all, stream and the _on forms on a view park the green thread while a non-blocking descriptor is not ready; pipe, set_nonblocking, try_read, try_write and wait_input. Files: open with an Open mode, stat, fstat, access, chmod, chown, set_times, unlink, rmdir, mkdir, rename, symlink, link, readlink, statfs, lock, seek, fsync, ftruncate, list_dir and random_bytes. Processes: fork_exec, reap, kill, signal dispositions and handlers, identity, working directory, arguments, environment, executable_path, memory mapping and exit_process. Sockets: socket, socketpair, bind, listen, accept, connect, finish_connect, recv, send, write_view, wait_socket, set_option, get_option, interface_index and multicast membership. Terminals: termios, raw_mode, window size and open_pty. inotify_init, inotify_add and inotify_remove.

A text template engine over a Data model (to_data[T] through serde): {{ expr }}, if, for, include, block and extends, let, trim markers, filters (built in and registered), HTML autoescaping, depth and output limits, and errors with line and column. A Set is read-only while rendering, so green threads share it.

is_tty, size and set_size. enter_raw returns a droppable Raw that restores the terminal when released. Key, read_key (a lone escape resolves after 50 ms) and parse_keys. ANSI helpers: fg, bg with 16, 256 and RGB colours, bold, dim, underline, cursor movement, clear_screen, the alternate screen, strip and visible_width. colour_enabled honours NO_COLOR, CLICOLOR_FORCE and TERM=dumb. open_pty.

T, passed to a test fn(*T), with log, error, fatal, skip, require and sub. Assertions equal, not_equal, equal_slice, is_true, is_false, is_some, is_none, contains, contains_item, close_to, unexpected, must and expect_error render values of any type. table and table_of. run and run_with run each test on its own green thread with a timeout, filter with -run, print with -v and exit with status 1 on failure. bench, bench_for and blackhole. golden rewrites its file when Settings.update_golden is set, which -update does. check_property, check_shrunk and check_ints print the seed and shrink integers.

Parsing and formatting: integer parsing in any base from 2 to 36; correctly rounded float parsing, which allocates only to expand a decimal when digits beyond the 19th decide the rounding; parse_bool, radix, hex, hex encoding and digit and hex_digit, the value of one digit byte in a base or in hex; append_hex and parse_hex_at, which write and read a fixed number of hex digits; fixed(x, places), which rounds half to even on the exact binary value. Trimming and splitting: trim and its start, end, prefix and suffix forms; split on a byte; split_str on a string (an empty separator splits into code points); fields; lines (drops a final empty line and \r before \n); chars; join. Searching: index, last_index, contains, count, starts_with, ends_with. Rewriting: repeat, replace, ASCII upper and lower (return their argument when no byte changes), and case-insensitive equal_fold and starts_with_fold (allocate nothing). Widths: char_count, from_char, and pad_left and pad_right to a width in code points. append and append_char onto a []u8; char_len and put_char encode one code point into a buffer, and are the only UTF-8 encoder. Comma-separated token lists. cut and last_cut return a Cut of before, after and found. strip_prefix and strip_suffix return str?. Also split_n, title, quote and unquote (backslash, \x, \u and \U escapes, failing with QuoteError), edit_distance over code points, wrap to a width, is_ascii, is_digits and reverse. is_scalar tells whether a u32 is a Unicode scalar value, lead_len gives the length of the UTF-8 sequence a lead byte starts, and trailing_backslashes counts the backslashes that end a line. parse_u64 and parse_uint parse unsigned digits, digit_char writes one digit, and position(s, at) turns a byte offset into a Position of line and column counted from 1. float32_bits and float32_from_bits convert between an f32 and its bits, float_decimal writes a float in the decimal form that TOML and YAML share, float_diagnostic in the form of CBOR's diagnostic notation, and quote_ascii writes a string as a double-quoted ASCII literal.

Myers line diff: diff, lines, stats, distance, similarity, GNU-compatible unified and hunks, patch and patch_within over a unified diff, and word and character level inline, inline_chars and inline_markup.
words, snake, kebab, dotted, screaming_snake, camel, pascal, title, sentence, the matching is_ predicates, and slug and slug_with (transliterate Latin letters and cut at a word boundary).
format_bytes and parse_bytes in decimal and binary units, grouped, ordinal, percent, compact, si, English words, and roman with parse_roman. Arithmetic is exact.

Table with per-column Align, width limits, truncation and wrapping, and Border styles None, Ascii, Unicode, Markdown and Tabs. Widths use unicode.text_width and ignore ANSI sequences. align and align_tabbed align tab-separated cells like Go's tabwriter.

now (Unix seconds), now_millis and now_nanos (the wall clock at finer resolution), monotonic (nanoseconds), sleep_for (rounds up to whole milliseconds), after, Timer and Ticker (their channels work in select), and Stopwatch. Calendar and zone types live in the submodules below, one module per type, so d.plus(span.days(3)) resolves to date.plus.

The proleptic Gregorian calendar the date types share: leap_year, days_in_month, days_from_civil and civil_from_days from the Unix epoch, weekday_index, and the English month and weekday names, full and short.

Clock, closures for the wall reading, the monotonic reading and a cancellable sleep, with system, fixed and manual. A Manual clock moves with advance and set, and its sleep records the wait in sleeps and advances the clock without waiting, so code that asks for the time and waits is tested without sleeping.

Date with private fields and validated constructors (of, clamped, from_epoch_days, from_ordinal, from_iso_week, from_weekday_in_month). Month, Weekday and IsoWeek. plus and minus by Span with month-end clamping, until and since with a Diff, next_weekday and on_or_next, and range. ISO 8601 to_string and parse (calendar, ordinal and week dates). format and parse_with over a pattern.

DateTime, a civil date and time of day with no zone: plus by Span or Duration, until and since with a Diff, round, truncate, to_string, parse (an offset is rejected), and pattern format and parse_with.

Duration, an exact signed elapsed time with private seconds and nanoseconds. Constructors from nanoseconds to hours, and from_seconds_f64. Arithmetic: plus, minus, times, divide, ratio, negate, abs, with try_ forms returning an optional. Plain forms panic on overflow. Also round and truncate with a Rounding, comparison, to_string (ISO 8601 PT1H30M), friendly (1h 30m) and parse, which reads both forms and fails at the offset of the first bad character.
Fault (OutOfRange, Invalid, Syntax(at), Overflow, UnknownZone, Malformed, Unsupported, Skipped, Ambiguous, OffsetConflict), the error every fallible time function returns, and to_string.
ago, relative, in_words, compact and round_to over a Words value; English by default.
Offset, a UTC offset in whole seconds within ±25:59:59, with utc, hours, hm, to_string, to_string_z, parse, and read, which reads an offset out of the middle of a string and reports where it ended.

Compiled strftime and strptime patterns shared by the types above: compile, Names for other languages, render and scan. Verbs: %Y %y %C %m %d %e %j %b %B %a %A %u %w %U %W %V %G %H %I %M %S %f %N %p %P %z %:z %::z %Z %s %F %T %R %D %% %n %t. Flags: -, _, 0 and ^. Parsing is strict, and every error carries a byte offset.
Rounding (Trunc, Ceil, Floor, Expand and the five Half modes) and the helpers the other time modules share.
Scan, the read position the time parsers share, with more, at_digit, at_byte, accept, expect, digits, take_whole and take_fraction, and the fraction text the formatters share.

Span, a calendar amount of years, months, weeks, days and time units with one sign. Unit, Diff (largest, smallest, increment, mode), to_duration and from_duration, of_calendar (calendar counts and a time duration), of_elapsed and step_of (rounding an exact elapsed time by a Diff), round_fraction (the rounding every difference shares), ISO 8601 to_string (P1Y2M3DT4H), friendly and parse.
TimeOfDay to the nanosecond. plus fails past midnight and plus_wrapping wraps. Also until, round, truncate, to_string, parse, and pattern format and parse_with.

Timestamp, a point on the UTC timeline from 0001-01-01 to 9999-12-31 with nanosecond precision: now, from_unix in seconds, milliseconds or nanoseconds, plus and minus by Duration, until and since, round, truncate, RFC 3339 to_string and parse (offset required, :60 read as :59), and to_http_date and parse_http_date (IMF-fixdate, RFC 850 and asctime).
An embedded copy of the database for hosts without one: source (for zone.load_from), names and version. The data is linked only when source or names is reachable.

IANA zones. Zone is a shared value decoded once, from named (the host database, honouring ZONEINFO), load_from (any fn(str) -> []u8?), local (TZ, /etc/localtime, /etc/timezone, then UTC), from_posix, decode, utc or fixed. fixed_offset returns the offset of a zone fixed made. Queries: info_at, candidates (One, Overlap, Gap for a civil time), next_transition, previous_transition and transitions.

Zoned, a Timestamp seen through a Zone whose offset is always the zone's own. Built from a civil time with a Disambiguation (Compatible, Earlier, Later, Reject) or strict. plus by Span moves calendar units on civil dates and time units by elapsed time; plus_duration is exact. Also until and since with a Diff, start_of_day, hours_in_day, series and round. RFC 9557 to_string (2026-11-11T10:00:00+00:00[Europe/London]), to_rfc3339, to_rfc2822, and parse with an OffsetPolicy for a written offset that disagrees with the zone. Pattern format and parse_with.

TLS 1.2 and 1.3 clients and servers. client, server and dial return a droppable Session that sends close_notify and closes the stream beneath it when released. Its handle is the shared *SessionHandle holding protocol, version, group, suite, cipher_suite and peer_certificates. client_handle and server_handle return the view alone, and read_on, write_on, close_on and stream_on operate on it. quic_client and quic_server run the TLS 1.3 handshake of RFC 9001 through a QuicTransport of callbacks that send and receive handshake bytes per Level and install each QuicSecret, and return a QuicResult. suite_hash, key_size, cipher and expand_label derive keys for a Suite.
TOML 1.0.0: a table tree, an encoder, and serde binding.
TrueType parsing, glyph outlines, the rasteriser and the embedded fallback font.
Point, Size, Rect, Edges, Corners and Color, all in f32.
The Vulkan renderer, its shaders, offscreen targets and swapchains, and the generated Vulkan bindings.
The flexbox engine over a tree of styled nodes.
Windows, input events and the waiting loop: Wayland, xkbcommon and the generated Wayland bindings on Linux, user32 and kernel32 on Windows.
Quads, shadows and sprites with their clip rectangles and draw order, and batching.
Shaping, line breaking, measurement and the glyph atlas.

Normalization (Unicode 16.0.0): nfd, nfkd, nfc and nfkc; combining_class; full case folding with casefold; search_key, which case-folds, applies NFKD and drops combining marks in one pass. Properties: category, is_letter, is_upper, is_lower, is_digit, is_space, is_punct, is_identifier_start and the other predicates; east_asian_width, display_width and text_width; script. Case mapping: to_upper, to_lower and to_title, and upper and lower with SpecialCasing but without final-sigma or locale rules. Segmentation: UAX #29 graphemes, grapheme_count and grapheme_end. UTF-8 helpers: decode_rune, is_invalid, encode_rune, utf8_valid, utf8_to_valid. Order is the byte order of UTF-16 and UTF-32, and bom_order reads the byte order mark of either width. Category, width and identifier data are Unicode 16.0.0; script, grapheme break and case data come from 17.0.0 restricted to characters assigned in 16.0.0. The tables are generated by cmd/tablegen and linked only when a function that reads them is reachable.

RFC 3986 percent coding and references. escape leaves the unreserved bytes, escape_form writes a space as +, escape_target encodes only the bytes a request target cannot hold and keeps existing escapes, and escape_where takes the set to keep. unescape returns str? and is none on a bad escape; unescape_lossy leaves a bad escape in place and unescape_form_lossy also reads + as a space. encode_form writes a list of Fields as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, and parse_query reads one into a [str: str] where the last value of a name wins. scheme_end, without_fragment, remove_dots and resolve follow RFC 3986 section 5, working on strings.
Random v4 and time-ordered v7 UUIDs, format, parse (reports the offset of the first bad character), version, timestamp for v7, equal and nil.

A router with groups, middleware and typed JSON endpoints, problem details (RFC 9457), an OpenAPI 3.1 document built from the types, cookie sessions, CSRF protection, API key, Basic and bearer authentication, CORS and response compression. static and static_with serve a directory. events and event_stream serve server-sent events.
A WebAuthn relying party: registration and authentication options as JSON, registration and authentication verification for ES256, EdDSA and RS256 credentials, and COSE key parsing.
XML 1.0 with namespaces: a pull reader, a tree, a writer, and serde binding.
YAML 1.2.2: events, a node tree, an encoder, and serde binding.
A compiled, garbage-collected language with green threads, enums and typed errors. It builds small static binaries for Linux and Windows.

Low A compiled, garbage-collected language with green threads, enums and typed errors. It builds small static binaries for Linux and Windows. Install Read the docs Browse packages enum Shape { Circle(radius: i64) Rect(w: i64, h: i64) } fn area(s: Shape) -> i64 { match s { Circle(r) => 3 * r * r Rect(w, h) => w * h } } fn main() { print(area(Shape.Rect(3, 4))) }
sections: let name = "lowlang" var count = 0 count += 1 let is immutable, var is mutable. Types are inferred and may be written as let x: i64 = 1. let { x, y } = rect.max var { x: min_x, y: min_y } = cells[0] var { x: max_x, y: max_y } = cells[0] let { min: { x: left }, max, label } = rect A struct pattern { x, y } = value binds each listed field to a local of the same name; { x: name } binds field x to name, as in a struct literal. Entries are separated by commas or newlines. A pattern lists only the fields it wants. A field named twice, two entries binding one name, an empty {}, a field the struct lacks and a value that is not a struct (a pointer included) are errors. A struct with drop cannot be destructured. A field that is a struct nests a pattern: { min: { x, y }, max }. var makes every bound name mutable and let makes them immutable. A pattern takes no type annotation, and using binds one name. The value is evaluated once, then each field is read from it. { after let or var always starts a pattern.

/// The width that stands for no limit. pub const unbounded: f32 = 1.0 / 0.0 const kib = 1 << 10 const mib = kib * kib const greeting = "hello, " + name const name = "low" const ok = 200 fn status(code: i64) -> str { match code { ok => "ok" 404 => "not found" _ => "other" } } const name: T = value declares a constant at the top level of a module. Without a type it takes the type let would infer: an integer literal is i64 and a float literal f64. A constant is a number, a bool or a str. Its value is built from literals, other constants, unary and binary operators and numeric conversions such as u8(x), and is evaluated at compile time with the wrapping, shifts, rounding and conversions of the same expression at run time. Division by zero, a constant that depends on itself and a float out of the range of u64 converted to u64 are errors. Constants of a module may be declared in any order and in any of its files. Each use is the folded value. pub exports a constant, read as module.name. A constant cannot share its name with a function, type or builtin of its module, and a local of the same name hides it. A constant cannot be assigned or passed as mut, and const inside a function body is an error. In a match arm, a constant's name, or module.name, compares the subject with the constant instead of binding a new name.

fn add(a: i64, b: i64) -> i64 { a + b } fn counter() -> fn() -> i64 { var n = 0 fn() -> i64 { n += 1 n } } let twice = fn(x: i64) -> i64 { x * 2 } let ops: [str: fn(i64) -> i64] = ["twice": twice, "negate": negate] let parse: fn(str) -> i64 ! ParseError = parse_int let square: fn(i64) -> i64 = fn(x) { x * x } let cube = fn(x: i64) x * x * x let lengths = words |> slices.map(fn(w) w.len) fn first(s: str) -> u8 { s[0] } "simon".first() items.push(4) let shouted = "hi" |> text.repeat(3) |> first let n = input |> parse()? A function type is written fn(i64, mut str) -> bool, with ! E for a result that can fail. Two function types are the same when their parameters, mut markers and results are. A named function is a value of its function type. fn(params) -> R { body } is a closure, and fn(params) expr is a closure whose body is one expression, which extends as far as an expression can. A closure that writes its result or error type takes a braced body, so ! after the parameters always starts an error type. A closure's parameter and result types may be omitted when the expected function type supplies them. An argument to a generic function is checked after the arguments that are not closures, so its expected type takes the type arguments they bind: slices.map(words, fn(w) w.len) gives w the element type of words. When the expected type leaves the result open, as U in slices.map, or there is no expected type and the body is one expression, the result is the body's type, or the type of the first return's value. ? and fail need a written result. A braced closure with no written result and no expected type returns nothing. Values of function type can be stored in variables, fields, slices and maps, passed and returned, and called like functions. They cannot be compared or printed. A closure captures the variables it names by reference, as Go does: it reads and assigns the variable itself, which lives as long as any closure holding it. Each loop iteration binds fresh variables, so closures made in different iterations see different ones. A mut parameter cannot be captured. A variable that is never assigned after its binding, never passed as mut and never modified by push, pop, truncate or delete cannot be told apart from a copy, so the closure holds its value directly. x.f(args) calls f(x, args), so calls chain left to right: "ab".repeat(3).first(). f is any function callable by its plain name: a function in the current module, a function value in scope, a generic function or a builtin. When no such name exists and x is a struct or enum, or a pointer to one, from another module, f is that module's public function: url.authority() calls http.authority(url). Otherwise f is the public function of that name, in an imported module, whose first parameter accepts x, with a generic first parameter's constraints met by x's type: words.map(fn(w) w.len).sum() calls slices.sum(slices.map(words, ...)), and "banana".count("an") calls text.count. When more than one imported module has such a function, the call is an error naming them. A struct field of function type named f takes precedence, so op.apply(v) calls the stored function. When the first parameter is mut, x is passed as mut and must be a mutable place. x |> f(args) calls f(x, args), and x |> f calls f(x). The right side is a call, a function name, a module function such as text.repeat, a closure, or a struct field holding a function; any other expression is an error. x |> ops.scale calls the stored function, never a function named scale. |> has the lowest precedence of the binary operators and groups left to right: a + b |> f() is f(a + b). A trailing ?, catch or or applies to the call: x |> parse()? is parse(x)?. A mut first parameter receives x as mut, as with x.f(args). A line that starts with |> or . continues the expression on the line before it.

if n > 0 { print(n) } else { print(0) } for i in 0..10 { print(i) } for x in xs { print(x) } for i, x in xs { print(i) } for { x, y } in points { print(x + y) } for i, { x } in points { print(i + x) } for n > 0 { n -= 1 } for { break } rows: for row, cells in grid { for col, cell in cells { if cell == want { break rows } } } for i in a..b counts from a up to but not including b; the bounds are integers of one type. for x in xs visits each element of a slice; for i, x in xs also binds the index as i64. Loop variables are immutable. for { x, y } in points and for i, { x, y } in points destructure each element with a struct pattern, as in ### Bindings, binding immutable names. In for, { starts a pattern only when its closing } is followed by in, so for { break } is still an infinite loop. break, continue, return and fail are expressions of type never, so they can stand wherever a value is expected: after ??, in an arm, or as a branch of if. name: before for labels a loop. break name and continue name act on that loop from inside nested loops and run the deferred statements and drops of every block they leave. A label must be used, cannot repeat the label of an enclosing loop, and is not visible inside closures.

let mask: u32 = 0xFF00 var flags: u8 = 0b0000_0101 let mode = 0o640 flags |= 1 << 4 let shifted = mask >> 8 let ratio: f32 = 0.5 let length = sqrt(3.0 * 3.0 + 4.0 * 4.0) let whole = i64(floor(length)) let byte = u8(300) Integer types are i64, i32, u64, u32, u16 and u8; float types are f64 and f32. Integer literals are decimal, or hexadecimal, binary and octal with 0x, 0b and 0o. Float literals may have an exponent. In any number literal _ may separate two digits, as in 1_000_000.0 or 0xFF_FF; an _ anywhere else is an error. An integer literal takes the type the context expects, including the other operand of a binary operator, and must fit it; otherwise it is i64. A literal above the i64 range is accepted only as a u64. In an if expression with no expected type, an integer literal branch takes the type of the other branch. A float literal is f64 unless an f32 is expected. Integer arithmetic wraps at the type's width. Division by zero panics. Operands of a binary operator have the same type. Conversions are explicit calls such as u8(x), f64(n) and i64(f): integer conversions truncate or extend, float to integer truncates toward zero. &, |, ^, ~, << and >> work on integers. >> is arithmetic on signed types and logical on unsigned ones. The shift count may be any integer type; a count of 64 or more, or a negative one, gives 0, or the sign fill for >> on a negative signed value. Binary operators bind as in Go, from tightest to loosest: *, /, %, <<, >>, &; then +, -, |, ^; then ??; then comparisons; then &&; then ||. So a - b >> 1 is a - (b >> 1) and x | y - z is (x | y) - z. % is integer only. Floats follow IEEE 754: division by zero gives an infinity, and comparisons with NaN are false except !=. sqrt, floor and exp take and return f32 or f64. print accepts any integer or float type.

import std/bits import std/simd fn find(data: []u8, c: u8) -> i64 { let needle: u8x32 = simd.splat(c) var i = 0 for i + 32 <= data.len { let chunk: u8x32 = simd.read(data, i) let hits = simd.mask(chunk == needle) if hits != 0 { return i + bits.trailing_zeros(hits) } i += 32 } -1 } Vector types are 128 or 256 bits of one lane type: u8x16, u8x32, u16x8, u16x16, i32x4, i32x8, u32x4, u32x8, i64x2, i64x4, u64x2, u64x4, f32x4, f32x8, f64x2 and f64x4. +, -, *, &, |, ^, ~ and unary - work lane by lane. / works on float lanes. << and >> work on integer lanes by a scalar count, arithmetic on signed lanes. Compound assignments work the same way. Comparisons work lane by lane and give a vector of the same type whose lanes are all ones or all zeros; unsigned lanes compare unsigned. A scalar operand of the lane type is broadcast, so chunk == '"' compares every lane. u8x32(v) reinterprets a vector of the same width. std/simd provides read and write between a vector and a slice at an element index, read_str, splat, mask (one bit per lane from its top bit), any, blend, min, max, lane, with_lane, shuffle and shuffle16 (a byte table lookup within each 16-byte half, zero where the index has its top bit set), find_byte and find_byte_str. Reads and writes are bounds-checked. Vectors are values: they can be passed, returned, stored in fields and slices, and compared lane by lane. They cannot be compared with == as a whole. They print as <1, 2, 3, 4>.

let xs = [3, 1, 4] var squares: []i64 = [] push(mut squares, 9) let middle = xs[1..3] xs[0] = 10 print(xs.len) []T is a pointer, a length and a capacity over garbage-collected memory. Assigning or passing a slice shares its elements. [a, b] builds a slice; an empty [] needs an expected type. xs[i] reads or writes an element and panics when i is outside 0..xs.len. Any integer type indexes. xs.len is the length as i64. xs[a..b], xs[..b] and xs[a..] share the elements in that range. The result's capacity equals its length, so push onto it always copies and never overwrites the parent. push(mut xs, v) appends, growing the capacity to twice plus four when full. pop(mut xs) removes the last element and returns it as T?, or none when xs is empty. truncate(mut xs, n) sets the length to n and panics unless 0 <= n <= xs.len. pop and truncate keep the capacity, so a later push reuses the freed space. They change only the binding they are given. A slice that shares its elements with another binding sees a later push overwrite the freed elements, as after any push that finds spare capacity. A reslice such as xs = xs[..n] is the form that copies on the next push. Elements past the length stay in the array, and keep what they point to alive, until a push overwrites them. A function in the program named pop or truncate takes precedence over the builtin. A slice literal or map literal whose elements are all constants is built once per program, at its first evaluation, and reused. A literal is used in place when it is bound with let and the binding is only indexed, iterated or asked for .len, or when it is indexed, iterated or measured directly. Any other use gets a copy, because push, a slice of it, an argument, a return value, a field or an assignment through it would otherwise mutate the shared value. A slice literal under 1024 bytes and a map literal under 4 entries are rebuilt for those uses, since copying them costs more than building them. Elements of u8, u16, u32, i32 and f32 are packed at their natural width; other elements take a word each.

let ages = ["ada": 36, "alan": 41] ages["grace"] = 85 print(ages["bob"] ?? -1) var counts: [str: i64] = [:] counts["a"] += 1 delete(mut counts, "a") for name, age in ages { print("{name} {age}") } for name in ages { print(name) } [K: V] maps keys of an integer type, bool, str or a pointer type to values of any type. A map is a pointer to a table on the garbage-collected heap, so assigning or passing it shares the table, and m[k] = v works through any binding. [k: v, ...] builds a map; [:] is an empty one and needs an expected type. m[k] returns V?. m[k] = v inserts or replaces. A compound assignment such as m[k] += 1 starts from a zero value when k is missing. delete(mut m, k) removes a key; removing a missing key does nothing. m.len is the number of entries. for k, v in m and for k in m visit entries in insertion order. An overwritten value keeps its key's position; a deleted and re-inserted key moves to the end. Inserting new keys while iterating may skip or repeat entries. A map literal of constants is built once per program in a release build. A use that only indexes, iterates or measures it shares the built table; any other use gets a copy from the prelude's __map_clone, which copies the entry array and the index. A literal of fewer than 4 entries is rebuilt for those uses, because the copy costs as much as the build. A map is an array of entries in insertion order plus an open-addressed index of one word per slot. A slot is 0 when empty, -1 when its entry was deleted, and otherwise holds the upper 32 bits of the key's 63-bit hash above the entry number plus one. A probe skips empty slots and slots of other keys without reading the entries. Iteration reads the entries, never the index, so the hash function never shows in the order. No program output depends on a hash value. The map code reads the low bits of the hash as the position and the upper 32 bits as the tag. Hashes are seeded per process, so no key set can be built to collide without the seed. Start-up fills rt_hash_seed with 128 random bits and forces the second word odd. On Linux the bits are the 16 bytes at AT_RANDOM, or getrandom when the auxiliary vector has none, or the fallback when that fails. On Windows they come from ProcessPrng, with the same fallback. The fallback derives each word through its own SplitMix64 finalizer: s0 from one RDTSC read, the stack address and one RDRAND word, and s1 from a second RDTSC read taken after a cpuid, a rotated stack address and a second RDRAND word. RDRAND contributes only when CPUID reports it and the instruction succeeds within 10 tries. Hash function, with s0 and s1 the two seed words and mum(a, b) the high 64 bits of the 128-bit product of a and b xor its low 64 bits: An integer, bool or pointer key k hashes to fold(mum(k ^ s0, s1)). A str of 16 bytes or fewer reads two words a and b. 8 to 16 bytes give the first and last eight. 4 to 7 give the first and last four packed into a with b zero. 1 to 3 give the first, middle and last byte. The empty string gives zero. Every str starts from acc = mum(s1 ^ length, s0 | 1), so the length reaches the hash only through a product with seed words. A longer string folds every 16-byte block while more than 16 bytes remain, computing acc = mum(w0 ^ s0, w1 ^ acc), and then reads its last 16 bytes as the two words. A str hashes to fold(mum(a ^ s0, b ^ acc)). fold(h) is x = h ^ h >> 32 followed by (x ^ x >> 16) >> 1, which keeps 63 bits. Two strings of different lengths whose input words differ by a chosen xor do not collide under every seed, because cancelling the length term needs mum(s1 ^ n, s0 | 1) ^ mum(s1 ^ n', s0 | 1), which depends on the seed. Collisions between distinct strings remain possible with probability about 2^-63 per pair, and the hash gives no protection once s0 and s1 are known.

let name = "Ada" let line = "{name} is {age}, ratio {score / 2.0}" let row = "{name,-8}|{age,4:d3}|{score,8:f2}|{age:x4}|{score:#,##0.0#}" let full = name + " Lovelace" for c in "héllo" { print(c) } let first: u8 = name[0] let copy = str(bytes(name)) str is an immutable pointer and length over UTF-8 bytes. s.len is the length in bytes, s[i] reads a byte as u8, and s[a..b] shares a byte range. for c in s visits code points as u32; for i, c in s also binds each code point's byte offset. Invalid UTF-8 yields U+FFFD for one byte. "{expr}" interpolates a value of any type; {{ and }} are literal braces. print(expr) writes the same text followed by a newline. "{expr,width:format}" aligns and formats the value, as in "hello {name,13} your age is {age:##}", "{price,10:f2}", "{id:x8}" and "{n,-6}|". Both parts are optional, and {x,} and {x:} are errors. The expression ends at the first , or : outside brackets, which is where the width starts; the width ends at the next : or at the closing brace; the format is all the text up to the closing brace, so it may contain , and .. A width is a non-zero decimal integer with an optional - and optional surrounding spaces. A positive width right-aligns and a negative one left-aligns, padding with spaces to that many code points. A longer text is never cut. A width applies to every type, including str and the default text of a struct. A format has no spaces and is checked at compile time. It applies to integers and floats, and is either a standard format, one letter with an optional precision of 0 to 99, or a picture. The compiler lowers it to prelude calls with constant parameters, so no format text is parsed at run time. Standard formats, where N is the precision: Format Types Output dN integers decimal with at least N digits, zero-padded after the sign: {-5:d3} is -005 xN, XN integers lower or upper case hex with at least N digits. A negative value is its two's complement at the width of its type: {i32(-1):x} is ffffffff, {-1:x} is ffffffffffffffff bN integers binary, with the rules of x fN integers, floats fixed point with N decimals, 2 by default: {3.14159:f3} is 3.142, {7:f1} is 7.0 eN integers, floats one digit, then N decimals (6 by default) and an exponent written like the default float text: {12345.678:e2} is 1.23e+4 nN integers, floats like f with a , between every three integer digits; N is 0 for an integer and 2 for a float by default: {1234567:n} is 1,234,567 A picture is a format of only 0, #, , and ., with at least one 0 or # and at most one .. In the integer part each 0 is a digit that is always written and each # is a placeholder. A , between two placeholders groups the integer digits in threes. With no 0 in the integer part a zero integer part is omitted: {36:##} is 36, {0:##} is empty and {0.5:#.##} is .5, while {0.5:0.##} is 0.5. In the fraction part the value is rounded to the number of 0s plus #s, then trailing zeros are dropped down to the number of 0s. The . is dropped when no decimals remain: {2.5:0.##} is 2.5, {2:0.##} is 2, {3.14159:0.00} is 3.14, {1234567.891:#,##0.00} is 1,234,567.89 and {5:000} is 005. Rounding is correct for the exact binary value of a float and breaks ties to even, as glibc's printf does: {0.125:f2} is 0.12, {0.375:f2} is 0.38, {2.675:f2} is 2.67 because 2.675 lies just below the tie, and {1e300:f2} writes every digit. An f32 formats its own exact value and integers are exact up to the whole range of u64 and i64. A negative value that rounds to zero keeps its sign, as in -0.00. NaN, inf and -inf ignore the format, and the width still applies. A format on a value of a type other than an integer or float is an error: cannot format a value of type str with "f2". So is d, x, X or b on a float, an unknown letter, a precision above 99 and a picture with other characters, two . or no 0 or #. a + b concatenates, and s += b appends to a place. A chain such as a + b + c + d, with any interpolations inside it, is one operation that allocates the result once. Floats are formatted as the shortest decimal that reads back to the same value: positional for exponents from -6 to 20, otherwise 1.5e-7 or 1e+21. Infinities print as inf and -inf, NaN as NaN. Every type has a default text, generated by the compiler with no annotation or constraint: Integers, floats and bool use the formats above and true/false. A str that is itself printed or interpolated is inserted unchanged; a str inside another value is quoted with ", with ", \, newline and tab escaped. A struct is Point{x: 1, y: 2}: its name without module or type arguments (Stack{items: [1]}) and every field, private ones included. An enum variant is its name, Leaf; with positional fields Node(a, b); with labelled fields Move{x: 1, y: 2}. An optional is none or its value. A slice is [1, 2, 3], a map {k: v, k2: v2} in iteration order with keys rendered like any nested value, and a vector <1, 2, 3, 4>. A []u8 is 0x and lowercase hex digits, 0x6869. A pointer renders its target. A pointer met again while it is being rendered is <cycle>, so shared pointers render in full each time and only a cycle is cut. A function or channel is its type, fn(i64) -> i64 or chan[str]. A ptr[T] is its type and address, ptr[u8](0x7ffd1c2a), and a null one ptr[u8](0x0). 'a' is a code point of type u32, or u8 where one is expected. bytes(s) copies a string into a []u8; str(b) copies one back. == and != compare contents. <, <=, > and >= compare bytes in order, which for UTF-8 is code point order. Equality checks the lengths, then the pointers, then compares eight bytes at a time with an overlapping final load.

struct Point { x: f64 y: f64 } fn len(p: Point) -> f64 { sqrt(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y) } fn shift(mut p: Point, dx: f64) { p.x += dx } var p = Point { x: 3.0, y: 4.0 } p.x += 1.0 shift(mut p, 2.0) let x = 1.0 let q = Point { x, y: 2.0 } print(len(p) + len(q)) struct Div { padding: f64 = 0.0 align: Align = Start on_click: fn() = fn() {} children: []Element = [] } let page = Div { padding: 8.0 } { Label(Text { value: "title" }) Box(Div { align: Center } { button("ok") button("cancel") }) } A declaration's fields are separated by commas or newlines. Literals name their fields, separated by commas or newlines; x alone means x: x. A field declared with = expr may be left out; every other field must be given. A default is any expression. It is checked once against the field's type, in the declaring module's scope, with no access to locals or other fields. It is evaluated at every literal that leaves the field out, after the written fields. A field with a default can be left out of a literal in another module even when it is private. A brace block on the same line after a struct literal holds its children: the entries, one per line or separated by commas, become a slice literal for the struct's children field. A brace block after a call becomes a slice literal passed as the last argument, so fn button(label: str, children: []Element) -> Element takes children the same way. A trailing block is not allowed where a struct literal is not. A struct literal cannot appear directly in an if, for or match condition; wrap it in parentheses. Structs are values: assignment and argument passing copy them. == and != compare structs field by field when every field can be compared: numbers, bool, str, pointers, channels, and structs and enums made of them. Each field uses its own ==, so strings compare by content, floats by value and pointers by identity. Fields are assigned through a var binding or a mut parameter, at any depth: r.max.x = 1. Other parameters are immutable. A struct cannot contain itself by value; it can hold a * pointer to its own type. Fields are laid out in declaration order, one word per scalar, with no padding.

fn swap(mut a: i64, mut b: i64) { let t = a a = b b = t } var x = 1 var y = 2 swap(mut x, mut y) A mut parameter refers to the caller's variable; reads and writes go through to it. The call site writes mut before the argument. A mut argument must be a var binding, a mut parameter, a field or element of either, or a place through a dereferenced pointer. One call cannot pass overlapping places as mut: swap(mut p.x, mut p.x) is rejected, swap(mut p.x, mut p.y) is allowed. Two mut parameters therefore never alias. References exist only as parameters. They cannot be stored, returned or bound with let, so they never outlive the variable they refer to. A mut parameter occupies one word holding the address of the place. A place narrower than a word, such as an element of a packed slice like []u8 or a narrow extern struct field, is copied into a word-sized frame slot before the call and copied back at its own width after it, so the callee's word-sized reads and writes never touch the neighbouring bytes. Code in the callee that reads the same element through another route, such as a pointer to the slice, sees the value from before the call until the callee returns.

enum List { Cons(i64, *List) Nil } var list = List.Nil list = Cons(1, new(list)) let c = new(Counter { hits: 0 }) c.hits += 1 bump(mut *c) let copy = *c new(value) copies a value onto the garbage-collected heap and returns a *T. Pointers are never null. p.field reads and writes through the pointer; *p is the whole value, readable, assignable and passable as mut. The object behind a pointer is mutable through any pointer to it, including one held by let. == and != on pointers compare identity. mut arguments through pointers are not checked for overlap, since two pointers may refer to the same object.

enum Shape { Circle(radius: f64) Rect(w: f64, h: f64) Empty } fn area(s: Shape) -> f64 { match s { Circle(r) => 3.14159 * r * r Rect(w, h) => w * h Empty => 0.0 } } match must cover every variant, or end with _ or a binding arm. Arms after _ or a binding arm, and duplicate arms, are errors. A binding arm is a name starting with a lowercase letter that is not a variant, such as other => describe(other). It matches anything and binds the whole subject. A capitalized name that is not a variant is an error, so a mistyped variant is never taken for a binding. An arm that starts with a literal (4, -1, 'x', "a", true), a parenthesised expression, ! or ~, or a name followed by . (Mode.Fast, limits.max) is a test arm: an expression compared with ==. 4 => ... means == 4 => ... and (base + 1) => ... means == base + 1 => .... A match with a test arm must end with _. A bare name is a variant or a binding, so write (limit) => ... to compare against a variable. An arm that starts with a binary operator tests the subject: % 3 == 0 => ... means subject % 3 == 0, with the subject on the left and ordinary precedence after it. The subject is evaluated once and arms are tried in order. Such tests work on a subject of any type, including enums (== Empty) and the error of a catch. A match that uses one, or whose subject is not an enum, must end with _. Arms are separated by newlines or commas. fn classify(n: i64) -> str { match n { % 15 == 0 => "FizzBuzz", % 3 == 0 => "Fizz", % 5 == 0 => "Buzz", _ => "number" } } Patterns bind fields by position; _ ignores a field, and a bare variant name ignores all of them. An arm body is an expression, or break, continue, return or fail. Variants are constructed as Shape.Circle(2). Where the expected type is known (an annotated let, an argument, an assignment, a return, fail), the bare name works: let s: Shape = Empty. Variants are separated by commas or newlines. enum Colour { Black = 0, Red = 1, Indexed(n: u8) = -1, Rgb(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) = -1, } let index = Colour.Red.index = n after a variant gives it an index: an integer literal, with an optional leading -, that fits in an i64. When one variant has an index, every variant must have one. Variants may share an index. e.index is the i64 index of the variant e holds. It is an error on an enum whose variants have no indexes, an optional included. The index is a value the variant carries, not its tag: layout, == and match are the same with or without indexes. e.index compiles to the tag plus a constant when every variant's index is its tag plus that constant. Otherwise it is a switch on the tag, as for a match, whose default is the index shared by the most variants. Code generation for a match depends on its arms. It applies when the arms before the last are all distinct variants of one enum, or all distinct integer or character literals of one type: With at least 12 such arms whose values span at most 4096 and at most three times the arm count, it compiles to a switch block: the backend emits a bounds check and an indirect jump through a table of 32-bit offsets. Without that density, 48 or more arms compile to a binary search over the values. Fewer arms keep the chain of comparisons. Duplicate values, test arms and arms with other expressions always keep the chain. A switch on a constant folds to its target. An enum whose variants all have no payload is a single word. Otherwise an enum is a tag word followed by the largest variant's fields. An enum cannot contain itself by value; it can hold a * pointer to its own type. == and != compare enums whose variant fields can all be compared: equal values have the same variant and equal fields. Optionals compare the same way, so x == none and x == 5 work on an i64?.

fn find(xs: []i64, target: i64) -> i64? { for i, x in xs { if x == target { return i } } none } let index = find(xs, 7) ?? -1 match find(xs, 4) { some(i) => print("at {i}") none => print("missing") } struct Node { value: i64 next: *Node? } T? holds either some(value) or none. A T is accepted wherever a T? is expected: an annotated let, an assignment, an argument, a field, a return and either branch of an if or match. none and some(v) take their type from that expectation. x ?? fallback gives the value inside x, or evaluates fallback when x is none. The fallback may itself be a T?, making the result a T?. The fallback may leave instead, as in let line = read_line() ?? break. ?? binds tighter than comparisons and looser than arithmetic, and groups to the right: a ?? b ?? 0 tries a, then b. match unwraps an optional with some(v) and none arms and must cover both. ? after a type binds to everything before it: *Node? is an optional pointer and []i64? an optional slice. An optional is an enum with none as tag 0 and some as tag 1, so it takes one word more than its value.

An error type is an enum. A function that can fail declares -> T ! E. enum ParseError { Empty BadDigit(at: i64) } fn parse(s: str) -> i64 ! ParseError { if s.len == 0 { fail Empty } ... } fn total(a: str, b: str) -> i64 ! ParseError { parse(a)? + parse(b)? } fn validate(n: i64) ! ParseError { if n < 0 { fail BadDigit(n) } } enum ConfigError { Port(ParseError) Missing } fn describe(e: ParseError) -> ConfigError { Port(e) } fn port(s: str) -> i64 ! ConfigError { let n = parse(s) catch Port let m = s |> parse() catch describe let k = parse(s) or fail Missing n + m + k } fn main() ! ParseError { let n = parse("42") catch { Empty => 0 BadDigit(at) => at } let m = parse("") or -1 let o: i64? = parse("") or none validate(n)? } fail v returns the error v; v is checked against the function's error type, so bare variant names work. Postfix ? returns the error to the caller, whose error type must be the same enum. catch is for when the error matters: catch { arms } matches the error exhaustively; a binding arm such as e => report(e) receives the whole error. catch M returns the error to the caller after mapping it with M, a variant or a function written as a name or a qualified name. parse(s) catch Port is parse(s) catch { e => fail Port(e) }. M(e) must have the caller's error type, so M is a one-field variant of that enum or a function value of type fn(E) -> F. The mapping runs before the deferred statements. or value is for when it does not: it discards the error and evaluates value in its place. The value may leave instead, as in or fail Missing, or return none or or break. Where an optional T? is expected, or and catch { arms } produce one, so the fallback or an arm may be none. fn f() ! E fails or returns nothing. A result cannot be discarded, bound or passed on without ?, catch or or, except by returning it from a function with the same result type. When main declares ! E and returns an error, the program prints error: <Variant> to stderr and exits with status 1. Panics exit with status 2. A result is a tag word (0 ok, 1 error) followed by the larger of the ok value and the error enum.

let shader = embed("shaders/quad.spv") let font = embed("fonts/fallback.ttf") print(shader.len) embed("path") is the contents of a file as a str, read at compile time. The path must be a string literal and is relative to the directory of the file that calls embed, so a module carries its own assets. The bytes live in the binary's read-only data, aligned to 16 bytes; nothing is copied at run time. Indexing, slicing, .len and bytes(...) work as on any string. A missing file is a compile error. low dev watches embedded files, and a change to one reloads the functions that embed it.

extern "c" { fn malloc(n: i64) -> ptr fn free(p: ptr) fn strtol(s: ptr[u8], mut end: ptr, base: i32) -> i64 fn snprintf(buf: ptr[u8], n: i64, format: ptr[u8], ...) -> i32 pub fn div(a: i32, b: i32) -> DivT } extern struct DivT { quot: i32 rem: i32 } using block = Block[u8] { data: malloc(64) } let buf = block.data snprintf(buf, 64, cstr("%d-%.2f"), 42, 3.14159) print(str(buf)) var end: ptr = null let n = strtol(cstr("123abc"), mut end, 10) let pixels = view(buf, 64) extern "name" { ... } at the top level of a file names a C library and declares its functions without bodies. "c" is the C library itself. A trailing ... makes a function variadic. fn errno_location() -> ptr[i32] = "__errno_location" gives a function a Low name different from its C symbol, for symbols that start with __ or are Low keywords. Declarations are private to their module unless marked pub. A library is linked when code reachable from main calls or takes the address of one of its declared functions, so importing a module that declares C functions costs nothing until one is used. A program that uses no library is a static executable with no libc. A program that uses any is a dynamic executable linked against libc and each used library. C signatures use C types: integers, floats, bool, ptr, ptr[T], and extern structs by value. A mut parameter passes the address of a Low place for the duration of the call, as C# passes ref. C may read and write through it. ptr[T] is a nullable pointer to C memory. ptr is void* and converts to and from any ptr[T]. null takes its type from context. == and != compare addresses. ptr(n) makes an address from an i64 or u64, and i64(p) and u64(p) give a ptr's address as a number, for C values that carry either, such as a Win32 LPARAM. view(p, n) is a []T over n elements at p, bounds-checked like any slice. load(p) and store(p, v) read and write one T. cstr(s) is a NUL-terminated copy of a string. str(p) copies a NUL-terminated ptr[u8] back. extern struct has C layout: fields in order at their natural alignment, size rounded to the largest alignment. Its fields must have C types. It is used like any struct, and its fields are read and written at their own width. Memory may be passed to C for the duration of a call. Memory C keeps after the call must be pinned: pin(x) returns the address of a pointer, slice, map or string's data and keeps it alive until unpin(p). Memory C allocates is never touched by the collector. extern fn(ptr[i64], ptr[i64]) -> i32 is a C function pointer, one word, like C#'s delegate* unmanaged. Its parameters and result must have C types. It is a C type, so it can be a parameter, a result or an extern struct field. A top-level Low function becomes a C callback where an extern fn is expected, if it takes and returns only numbers, bool, ptr or extern fn, with no mut parameters. An extern function used as a value is its C address. Calling an extern fn value makes a C call. A closure reaches C through a ptr user-data argument: pin a pointer to the state it needs and pass a top-level callback that loads it. extern "c" { fn qsort(base: ptr, n: i64, size: i64, compare: extern fn(ptr[i64], ptr[i64]) -> i32) } fn ascending(a: ptr[i64], b: ptr[i64]) -> i32 { i32(load(a) - load(b)) } qsort(data, n, 8, ascending)

let fd = open(path)? defer close(fd) defer { let summary = "closing {path}" log(summary) } defer runs a statement when its enclosing block exits: at the end of the block, on return, fail or a propagated ?, and when break or continue leaves it. Deferred statements of a block run last first. The statement sees variables as they are at exit. It cannot return, fail, use ?, break, continue or contain another defer.

struct File { fd: i32 drop close(fd) } struct Conn { sock: i32 buf: Block[u8] drop { flush(sock) close(sock) } } struct Block[T] { data: ptr[T] drop free(data) } using f = open_file("config.low") using c = connect(addr)? using var current = open_file("a") current = open_file("b") drop <stmt> inside a struct body declares its cleanup, with the struct's fields in scope as borrowed values. Like defer, it takes one statement or a { } block. A struct has at most one drop, and using cannot appear in it. A struct with a drop is droppable, and so is a struct with a droppable field, even without its own drop. Generic instances are droppable per instance: Pair[File, i64] is, Pair[i64, i64] is not. Releasing a value runs its own drop first, then releases its droppable fields in declaration order. using x = expr binds x and releases it when the enclosing block exits by any path: the end of the block, return, fail, ?, break or continue. Releases and defers run together, last first. using var x = expr can be reassigned. Assignment releases the old value, and exit releases the value held then. using cannot appear inside defer. Binding a non-droppable value with using is an error. A droppable value cannot be bound with let or var: "File has drop; bind it with using". Results of droppable types are unwrapped with ?, catch or or straight into a using binding. Droppable values are move-only: return x, or a function body ending in x, moves a using binding out. The caller owns the value and must bind it with using. A struct literal field or an assignment to a field of a droppable value moves the value into it, and the outer value releases it. A field is assigned through a using var binding or a mut parameter, and the field's old value is released first. using y = x moves x into y. Passing a value as an argument borrows it: the callee cannot release it, store it or return it. A freshly produced value, such as a call result or a struct literal, must be bound with using before it is passed. Any other copy is an error: binding it with let, storing it in a slice, map, channel, optional, pointer or enum variant, moving a field out of its struct, discarding a call result, or capturing it in a closure. A struct with a droppable field is itself droppable, so it cannot be built with new or held by a pointer, and spawn cannot take one as an argument: "spawn cannot take File; it has drop". Code that shares a resource across closures, pointers or green threads passes a copyable view of it and binds the owner where the resource has one home (see Resource ownership). Using a binding after it was moved is an error, as is using one that may have been moved on one branch or by an earlier loop iteration. Generic code is checked under these rules for each instance whose type arguments are droppable, so fn same[T](x: T) -> T { x } cannot be instantiated with File. Each using binding has a hidden flag that a move clears. The release at exit runs only while the flag is set, so a value moved on one branch is released exactly once.

import geometry import t = ui/text pub struct Circle { pub radius: f64 cache: f64 } pub fn area(c: Circle) -> f64 { 3.14159 * c.radius * c.radius } fn main() { let c = geometry.circle(2.0) print(geometry.area(c)) let s: geometry.Shape = Square(3) print(t.shout("hi")) } A module is a directory. Every .low file in it shares one namespace, so files of a module need no imports between them. A file whose name ends in _linux.low or _windows.low belongs to the module only when building for that operating system. The standard library uses this to give std/sys and the operating-system parts of std/os, std/process, std/net and std/crypto/x509 one implementation per target; a test requires every target to declare the same public items with the same doc comments. A directory named examples inside a module holds that module's examples: each .low file in it is a whole program that imports the module, with its expected output in a .out file of the same name. An examples directory is never a module, and importing a path with an examples segment is an error. The project root is the nearest directory, starting at the entry, that holds a low.mod file. Without one it is the entry's directory. import ui/text loads <root>/ui/text/. A path starting with std/ names a module of the standard library, which is compiled into low, so a project directory named std cannot be imported. low build dir builds the directory as the entry module. low build file.low builds that one file as the entry module, without the other files beside it. low lint file.low type-checks the program, prints warnings for the program's own modules (not the standard library), and exits with status 1 if there were any. -target picks the operating system whose files are checked and defaults to the host. low build, low run, low asm and low ir print the same warnings to stderr and continue. The language server reports them as warnings. prefer-match flags an if / else if / else chain with at least two conditions in which every condition is == between one side-effect-free subject (a variable, field, index or dereference) and a non-negative integer, character or string literal, a constant or an enum variant. It suggests match subject { 4 => ..., _ => ... }. prefer-loop-label flags a break out of an inner loop that sets a boolean flag to a literal when the statement right after that loop is if flag { break } or if flag { continue } (or if !flag for a flag set to false), with no else. It suggests labelling the loop that if acts on and jumping to it with break name or continue name, reusing the label the if already names. Breaks inside a nested loop, closure, spawn or defer are not counted. prefer-const flags a function with no parameters or type parameters that returns a number, bool or str, is never used as a value, and whose body is one expression that a constant can hold: literals, constants, operators and numeric conversions. It suggests const name: T = ... with the () dropped where the function is called. low doc dir prints, as JSON, every module under the directory with its imports, each with the name it is used through, and its public structs, enums, constants and functions, each with its declaration as written, its file and its line. A struct shows its public fields, and ... stands for its private ones. A function whose first parameter is a public type of its module, or a pointer to one, names that type as its receiver. Each module lists its examples with their name, source and expected output. low doc std documents the standard library, and the website builds its package pages from it with -target linux/amd64. -target picks the operating system whose files are documented and defaults to the host. Imports come before declarations and apply to their file. A module is used through its last path segment, text.shout(...), or through a name given with import t = ui/text. Types are written geometry.Shape and built with geometry.Point { ... }. A variant can be named geometry.Shape.Dot or, where the type is expected, Dot. Declarations and struct fields are private to their module unless marked pub. A pub enum's variants are public. A struct with private fields without defaults cannot be built with a literal outside its module. An import cycle is an error, as is importing two modules under one name.

/// A point on the plane. pub struct Point { /// Distance from the y axis. pub x: i64 pub y: i64 } /// Returns the point mirrored in the y axis. pub fn mirror(p: Point) -> Point { return Point { x: -p.x, y: p.y } } A line starting with /// documents the declaration, struct field or enum variant directly below it. Consecutive /// lines form one doc, written in Markdown; one space after /// is dropped. A /// line anywhere else is an error. //// starts an ordinary comment. The language server shows a doc under the signature on hover, low doc prints it, and the website renders it on the package pages.

struct Stack[T] { items: []T } enum Tree[T: Ord] { Node(*Tree[T], T, *Tree[T]) Leaf } fn max[T: Ord](a: T, b: T) -> T { if a > b { a } else { b } } fn sum[T: Number](xs: []T) -> T { var total: T = 0 for x in xs { total += x } total } fn sort[T](mut xs: []T, less: fn(T, T) -> bool) { ... } print(max(3, 9)) print(max[u8](200, 100)) var s = Stack[str] { items: [] } let p = Pair { first: 1, second: "x" } let t: Tree[i64] = Leaf let pick: fn(i64, i64) -> i64 = max Functions, structs and enums take type parameters in brackets after their name. Generic types are written with arguments: Stack[i64], geometry.Labelled[str]. A constraint lists what a type parameter supports, joined with +: Eq allows == and !=. It is met by numbers, bool, str, pointers, channels, and structs and enums whose fields are all Eq. Ord adds <, <=, > and >=. It is met by numbers and str. Hash adds use as a map key. It is met by integers, bool, str and pointers. Number adds arithmetic, numeric literals, conversion with T(x) and the f, e and n formats and pictures of interpolation. Integer adds bitwise operators and shifts and the d, x, X and b formats, and implies Hash. Float is met by f64 and f32. An unconstrained parameter can only be moved, stored, passed, printed and interpolated, with a width but no format, each instance rendering its own type. Anything else a generic function needs, such as an ordering of its elements, is passed in as a function value. A generic body is checked once against its constraints, so a missing constraint is reported at the definition, not at a use. Each generic function's type parameters are its own. Two functions may both name a parameter T, and a function type mentioning one is distinct from the same text mentioning the other. Type arguments are inferred from the arguments, then from the expected type. They can be written explicitly: max[u8](a, b), Stack[str] { ... }. A generic struct literal or enum variant takes its arguments from the expected type or from its field values. A generic function used as a value takes them from the expected function type. Each distinct set of type arguments compiles to its own copy, max[i64] and max[f64], so generic code runs as fast as code written for one type. Values of different kinds that share behaviour, such as the elements of a UI tree, are structs of function values whose closures capture each kind's state.

fn worker(jobs: chan[i64], results: chan[i64]) { for j in jobs { results <- j * 2 } } let jobs = chan[i64](16) let results = chan[i64](16) spawn worker(jobs, results) jobs <- 21 close(jobs) print((<-results) ?? 0) let next = select { v = <-results => v ?? -1 jobs <- 5 => 0 after(100) => -2 else => -3 } sleep(10) wait_readable(fd) spawn f(args) starts a green thread running the call. The function value and the arguments are evaluated before it starts. mut arguments are not allowed. A function that can fail must have its error handled inside the spawned call. chan[T](n) makes a channel holding up to n values. chan[T]() is unbuffered, so every send waits for a receiver. A channel is a reference: assigning or passing it shares it. c <- v sends, waiting while the buffer is full. <-c receives a T?, waiting while the channel is empty. It gives none once the channel is closed and drained. close(c) wakes every waiter. Sending on or closing a closed channel panics. for v in c receives until the channel is closed and drained. select waits on several operations at once and runs the arm of the first that can proceed. It is an expression like match. Arms are name = <-c, <-c, c <- v, after(ms) and else. after is a contextual keyword: it is an ordinary identifier everywhere except at the start of a select arm followed by (. Channel and value expressions are evaluated first, in order. Ready arms are taken in order. else runs when nothing is ready. Without else the green thread waits. after(ms) fires once ms milliseconds pass. sleep(ms) pauses the green thread. wait_readable(fd) and wait_writable(fd) wait until a file descriptor is ready, using epoll on Linux. On Windows fd is a waitable handle and both wait until it is signalled. One green thread may wait on a descriptor at a time. A program ends when main returns, whatever other green threads are doing. When every green thread is waiting and nothing can wake one, the program panics with every green thread is blocked forever. A green thread that exhausts its stack panics with stack overflow.
bytes(s: str) -> []u8 copies a string's bytes into a new slice.
close(c: chan[T]) closes a channel and wakes every waiter. Sending on or closing a closed channel panics.
cstr(s: str) -> ptr[u8] is a NUL-terminated copy of a string, for passing to C.
delete(mut m: [K: V], key: K) removes a key from a map. Removing a missing key does nothing.
embed(path: str) -> str is the contents of a file, read at compile time. path is a string literal relative to the directory of the file that calls embed.
exp(x: f64) -> f64 is e raised to the power x. It takes and returns f32 too.
floor(x: f64) -> f64 rounds x down to a whole number. It takes and returns f32 too.
e.index is an i64: the index declared with = n on the variant an enum value holds. The enum's variants must have indexes; see ### Enums.
xs.len is an i64: the number of elements in a slice, the number of entries in a map, or the number of bytes in a str.
load(p: ptr[T]) -> T reads one T from C memory. A null pointer traps.
new(value: T) -> *T copies a value onto the garbage-collected heap and returns a pointer to it. A droppable value cannot go on the heap.
pin(value) -> ptr returns the address of a pointer, slice, map or string's data and keeps it alive until unpin. Memory C keeps after a call must be pinned.
pop(mut xs: []T) -> T? removes the last element and returns it, or none when xs is empty. The capacity stays.
print(value) writes a value of any type to standard output, followed by a newline. The text is the default rendering described under ### Strings.
push(mut xs: []T, value: T) appends value, growing the capacity to twice plus four when full.
sleep(ms) pauses the green thread for ms milliseconds. ms is any integer type.
sqrt(x: f64) -> f64 is the square root of x. It takes and returns f32 too.
store(p: ptr[T], value: T) writes one T to C memory.
truncate(mut xs: []T, n) sets the length to n and keeps the capacity. n is any integer type. It panics unless 0 <= n <= xs.len.
unpin(p: ptr) releases an address returned by pin.
view(p: ptr[T], n) -> []T is a slice over n elements at p, bounds-checked like any slice. n is any integer type.

wait_readable(fd) waits until a file descriptor is ready to read, using epoll. On Windows fd is a waitable handle and the wait ends when it is signalled. fd is any integer type. One green thread may wait on a descriptor at a time.

wait_writable(fd) waits until a file descriptor is ready to write, using epoll. On Windows fd is a waitable handle and the wait ends when it is signalled. fd is any integer type. One green thread may wait on a descriptor at a time.

Calling a numeric type converts a number to it, as in u8(x), f64(n) and i64(f). Type Values i64 Signed 64-bit integers. An integer literal with no expected type is an i64. i32 Signed 32-bit integers. u64 Unsigned 64-bit integers. u32 Unsigned 32-bit integers. u16 Unsigned 16-bit integers. u8 Unsigned 8-bit integers, and the bytes of a str. f64 64-bit IEEE 754 floats. A float literal is an f64 unless an f32 is expected. f32 32-bit IEEE 754 floats. bool true and false. str An immutable pointer and length over UTF-8 bytes. str(b) copies a []u8 into a string, and str(p) copies a NUL-terminated ptr[u8]. ptr ptr[T] is a nullable pointer to C memory. ptr alone is void* and converts to and from any ptr[T]. chan chan[T] is a channel of T values. chan[T](n) makes one holding up to n values, and chan[T]() an unbuffered one. u8x16 16 lanes of u8, 128 bits. u8x32 32 lanes of u8, 256 bits. u16x8 8 lanes of u16, 128 bits. u16x16 16 lanes of u16, 256 bits. i32x4 4 lanes of i32, 128 bits. i32x8 8 lanes of i32, 256 bits. u32x4 4 lanes of u32, 128 bits. u32x8 8 lanes of u32, 256 bits. i64x2 2 lanes of i64, 128 bits. i64x4 4 lanes of i64, 256 bits. u64x2 2 lanes of u64, 128 bits. u64x4 4 lanes of u64, 256 bits. f32x4 4 lanes of f32, 128 bits. f32x8 8 lanes of f32, 256 bits. f64x2 2 lanes of f64, 128 bits. f64x4 4 lanes of f64, 256 bits.
Constant Value true The true bool. false The false bool. none The empty optional, typed by its context. null The null ptr, typed by its context.

Every standard library resource that must be disposed of is a droppable owner bound with using. defer is for work that is not disposal: unlocking a lock, signalling a channel, restoring ambient state and logging. An owner keeps the resource's name (file.File, net.Conn, net.Listener, net.Socket, tls.Session, http.Connection, websocket.Socket, process.Child, cancel.Registration, pipe.Reader, pipe.Writer, sqlite.Database, sql.Connection, cdp.Browser, otel.Sdk) and holds its view in a public handle field. Its drop closes through the handle. A view is named <Owner>Handle: FileHandle, ConnHandle, ListenerHandle, SocketHandle, SessionHandle, ChildHandle, RegistrationHandle, ReaderHandle, WriterHandle, DatabaseHandle, ConnectionHandle, BrowserHandle and SdkHandle. SocketHandle names the view in both net and websocket. A view is a copyable struct, or a pointer to the shared state when that state is mutable, so closures capture it, slices, channels, optionals and pointer-held structs store it, and spawn takes it. A view never closes anything on its own. Operations a caller uses directly take the owner and borrow it: net.read(c, buf). Operations that run after ownership has moved elsewhere (green threads, io.Stream closures, pools, callbacks) take the view and end in _on: net.read_on(h, buf), net.stream_on(h), net.close_on(h). A function that returns a view without an owner ends in _handle: net.accept_handle, tls.client_handle, cdp.launch_handle. adopt(h) makes an owner from a view. detach(mut owner) gives up an owner's responsibility so a function that opened a resource and wrapped it can return the wrapper. Closing is explicit and idempotent from the owner, the view and the stream, and the drop after an explicit close does nothing. The closed state lives in the shared view. Descriptor-based views share an io.Guard: every operation enters it, retire marks it closed and wakes blocked operations, and the last operation to leave closes the descriptors. A view used after its owner closed fails with NotConnected and never reaches a reused descriptor. The SQL drivers fail with sql.Error.Closed and cdp with cdp.Error.Closed. io.Stream is a view whose close closes everything beneath it. In tls.client(net.stream(c), config), closing the session closes the connection, and the connection's own drop does nothing. A droppable cannot be stored in a pointer, slice, map, channel, optional or enum variant, captured by a closure or passed to spawn, so long-lived and shared state holds views. The HTTP client's idle connections, its HTTP/2 connections and the reaper's deadlines hold ConnHandle and io.Stream views and close them explicitly with the _on operations. A green thread that should own a resource receives its view and binds the owner itself: http.serve accepts with net.accept_handle, and each spawned connection thread runs using c = net.adopt(h). Pump threads that only use a resource take its view and leave it to its owner. A scope that opens a resource for a wrapper it returns binds it with using var and calls detach, as tls.dial does. A process.Child that was not waited for is killed and reaped when released. A pipe.Reader or pipe.Writer completes when released, so a peer never waits on an abandoned end.

Sockets are non-blocking. An operation that would block waits with sys.wait_socket, so a green thread waiting on the network never holds an OS thread the collector must wait for. Every connection writes through a second descriptor from sys.write_view, so one green thread can wait to read while another waits to write. A timeout spawns a green thread that sleeps and shuts the socket down if the operation is still waiting. The waiting operation then fails with TimedOut. A connection counts the reads and writes in progress. Closing it shuts it down, which wakes any green thread still waiting while the descriptor stays registered. The last operation to finish closes the descriptors, so a descriptor number is never reused under a waiting operation. Reads and writes after close fail with NotConnected, and closing twice does nothing. serve runs each connection on its own green thread. Cancellation is cooperative. A token runs its callbacks and closes its channel once, so code stops blocking work by closing what it waits on: net.close wakes a waiting read or write, process.kill ends a child, and select takes <-cancel.done(t). An HTTP/1.1 handler without an Upgrade header runs on the connection's green thread while one spawned watcher reads ahead into the request reader. End of input or a read error cancels the request's token, and the response is still written. Requests read ahead are served in order afterwards. An HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 stream's token is cancelled when the client resets it or the connection ends. Every request's token is cancelled once its handler returns. A client request with a token arms its deadline even without a timeout. Cancelling the token fires the deadline, which shuts down the connection the request is using and wakes the request from waiting on a pooled connection or an HTTP/2 stream. A server speaks HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 on the same port. A connection that opens with the HTTP/2 preface is served as HTTP/2; any other is HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive, pipelining, chunked bodies and Expect: 100-continue. Over TLS, ALPN offers h2 and http/1.1 and the same detection applies. The h2c upgrade from HTTP/1.1, deprecated by RFC 9113, is not offered. HTTP/2 covers framing, HPACK with its dynamic table and Huffman decoding (std/http/huffman), stream multiplexing, flow control in both directions, SETTINGS, PING, RST_STREAM, GOAWAY and CONTINUATION, and the request validation of RFC 9113 section 8. A reader green thread feeds frames to the connection, each request's handler runs on its own green thread, and the connection selects over frames and finished responses, so every write happens on one green thread. The encoder uses the static table and literals without Huffman coding. It passes h2spec except the test sending a garbage preface, which the shared port reads as an HTTP/1.1 request. A handler's Response.trailers are sent as a final HEADERS frame over HTTP/2; HTTP/1.1 responses carry none. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is served by serve_quic and serve_quic_on over a quic.Listener whose ALPN is h3; a connection that negotiated another protocol is closed with H3_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR. Each connection opens a control stream that carries SETTINGS (QPACK table capacity 4096, 16 blocked streams, field section size 65536) and a QPACK decoder stream, and the encoder is static-only so no encoder stream is opened. A green thread per peer unidirectional stream reads the control, QPACK encoder and QPACK decoder streams, at most 16 at a time; a duplicate or a push stream is H3_STREAM_CREATION_ERROR, a closed critical stream H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM, a first control frame that is not SETTINGS H3_MISSING_SETTINGS, and an unknown stream type is stopped and ignored. A green thread per request stream reads HEADERS, DATA and an optional trailing HEADERS, runs the handler and writes the response; a connection runs at most the listener's max_streams of them at a time and does not accept the next request stream until one has finished, so a client that stops its streams cannot push the handler count past that.
