One qpack.Decoder per connection sits behind a mutex; a section that needs table entries the encoder stream has not delivered waits for them, bounded by the life of the connection, and every decode, cancel_stream and on_encoder_stream writes the decoder stream bytes it owes, taking and writing them under one lock so the instructions reach the peer in the order they were produced. A write to the decoder stream that fails because the peer sent STOP_SENDING closes the connection with H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM. Frame sizes are checked before anything is read or allocated: a HEADERS frame over 64 KiB or a control frame over 16 KiB is H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD, and no buffer is sized from a declared length, since a field section is read into a buffer that grows with the bytes that arrive, unknown frame types are read and discarded in chunks of at most 4 KiB, DATA is read in chunks of at most 16 KiB, each chunk no larger than what is left of the frame, and a body over 64 MiB resets the stream with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD. A frame out of order, such as DATA before HEADERS or HTTP/2-only frame types, is H3_FRAME_UNEXPECTED. A request with an uppercase field name, a connection-specific field, a missing or repeated pseudo-header, a pseudo-header in the trailers or a content-length that differs from the DATA total resets and stops its stream with H3_MESSAGE_ERROR and the handler is not called. A field section over the size limit is answered with 431. A response is HEADERS, DATA, an optional trailing HEADERS for Response.trailers, then FIN; a streaming Response.stream sends one DATA frame per chunk. Request.token is cancelled when the response is complete, when a write of the response fails because the client stopped or reset the stream, and when the connection ends; a stop or reset that arrives while the handler runs is not noticed before the response is written. A client that resets its request stream before it is complete has its response reset with H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED. Server push, extended CONNECT and HTTP datagrams are not supported. A handler that returns status 101 owns the connection: the server writes nothing more and closes it once the handler returns. http.upgrade(req, headers) writes the 101 and returns the connection's reader, and http.upgraded() is the response returned after a WebSocket session. Request.connection is the buffered reader of an HTTP/1.1 connection. websocket.accept writes the handshake to it and reads frames from it. A WebSocket server requires masked client frames, answers pings, reassembles fragments, checks UTF-8 in text messages, limits messages to 16 MB and echoes a close frame. http.client() returns a Builder[Client] value whose with_* functions return updated copies. build makes a *Client that any number of green threads share. c.request(method, url) copies the client's settings into a Builder[Response], so headers, authentication, timeouts, redirects, retries, version and decompression can be overridden per request. The type parameter only selects whether build or send applies. HTTP/1.1 client connections: a request takes an idle keep-alive connection from a pool keyed by scheme, host and port, dials a new one while the host is under its limit, or queues for one. A sweeper green thread expires idle connections. A pooled connection that fails before any response byte is retried once on a fresh one. HTTP/2 client connections: over TLS the client offers h2 and http/1.1 by ALPN and keeps one HTTP/2 connection per host. A reader green thread decodes frames into per-stream queues, request green threads wait on their stream, flow control credits windows as bodies are consumed, and SETTINGS, PING, RST_STREAM, GOAWAY and the peer's stream limit are honoured. with_prior_knowledge(true) speaks HTTP/2 to http:// URLs without negotiation (h2c), keeping one connection per host as over TLS. HTTP/3 client connections: with_version(Http3) sends https requests over QUIC and keeps http requests, requests through a proxy and requests of a client with a dialer on HTTP/1.1. There is no fallback: a QUIC connection that cannot be made fails the request with Connect, Tls or Timeout. The host holds one connection, shared by concurrent requests, next to its HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 state; it is replaced once it has ended or the server sent GOAWAY, and close_idle and the sweeper close it when idle. The TLS options of the client apply with ALPN h3 and the URL host as server name, with_resolver supplies the addresses, which are tried in turn when one times out or is refused, with_connect_timeout becomes quic.Config.handshake_timeout and with_interface fails with Connect(Unsupported). The handshake runs on its own green thread, so a cancelled token abandons it at once. The client shares the connection code of the server: it opens the control stream with SETTINGS and the QPACK decoder stream, reads the server's control, QPACK encoder and decoder streams under the same limits (at most 16 at a time, duplicates and unknown critical streams rejected), and decodes field sections through one mutex-guarded qpack.Decoder that waits for encoder stream instructions. A push stream is H3_ID_ERROR because the client never sends MAX_PUSH_ID, and a MAX_PUSH_ID from the server is H3_FRAME_UNEXPECTED. QUIC is configured with no server-initiated bidirectional streams. A request opens a bidirectional stream, writes HEADERS (:method, :scheme, :authority, :path, then the lowercased request headers without connection-specific ones, host and a te other than trailers), DATA frames for the body, streamed from a body reader in 16 KiB frames, and FIN. The response is up to 16 interim 1xx HEADERS that are discarded, then a final HEADERS checked by valid_h3_response, DATA frames read as the body stream, and an optional trailing HEADERS checked by valid_h3_trailers that fills Response.trailers; Response.version is Http3. A malformed response, which is an invalid section, a content-length that differs from the DATA total, DATA on a bodiless response, or too many interim responses, resets and stops the stream with H3_MESSAGE_ERROR and fails as Protocol(Malformed); a frame out of order closes the connection with H3_FRAME_UNEXPECTED; a section over 64 KiB resets the stream with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD. One green thread per request watches the deadline and the token and, when either fires, resets and stops that stream with H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED and wakes a blocked QPACK wait, leaving the connection open. Opening a stream also races the deadline, because it parks at the peer's stream limit, and so does opening the control and QPACK decoder streams right after the handshake, which parks when the server allows fewer than two unidirectional streams: that setup runs on its own green thread under the deadline, the token and the connect timeout (10 seconds when none is set), and closes the connection when one of them fires, so the host's dial flag is always cleared. A stream the server reset before the response head, a stream the server refused with GOAWAY, a request on a connection that ended, and a request that finds the connection draining count as stale, and a replayable request is sent once more on a new connection, as for HTTP/2. Decompression, redirects, cookies, retries and the 64 MB body limit sit above the transport and apply as for HTTP/2. One reaper green thread per client enforces whole-request deadlines by shutting down an expired HTTP/1.1 exchange. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 waits select on the deadline and reset the stream. Redirects switch 301, 302 and 303 to GET without a body, keep the method and body on 307 and 308, resolve relative locations and drop Authorization and Cookie across origins. Responses are decoded from gzip, deflate (zlib or raw), Brotli and Zstandard as they stream, and chunked bodies are read and sent. An optional RFC 6265 cookie jar is shared by the client. Retries apply to connection failures and, for idempotent methods, to transport errors and 429, 502, 503 and 504, through std/retry with exponential backoff, where Retry-After raises the planned wait. Servers set TCP_NODELAY so separate HEADERS and DATA writes are not held back by delayed acknowledgements. Response.trailers holds the trailer fields of chunked HTTP/1.1 bodies and of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 responses. Request and response bodies are limited to 64 MB.

process.start builds the path, arguments, environment and pipes before fork, so the child runs only straight-line syscalls: setpgid for a new group, dup2 onto descriptors 0 to 2, chdir and execve. Every descriptor the standard library opens is close-on-exec, so the child inherits only its three streams. A child's pipes are streams over guarded descriptors, so closing one twice or using it after it closed fails with NotConnected and never reaches a reused descriptor. A failed chdir or execve writes its errno to a close-on-exec pipe, which the parent reads before returning. The read sees end of file once execve succeeds; otherwise the parent reaps the child and fails with that errno. The parent's pipe ends are non-blocking and wait through the scheduler, as sockets do; the child's ends stay blocking. wait waits for the process's pidfd to become readable, then reaps it with waitid and remembers the result. kill signals through the pidfd, or the whole group when the command asked for one. signal.notify installs a handler with rt_sigaction. The handler is a short block of machine code in a mapped page: it writes the signal number to a non-blocking pipe and returns through rt_sigreturn. The runtime gives every OS thread an alternate signal stack, so the handler runs on whichever thread receives the signal. A forwarding green thread reads the pipe with wait_readable and sends to the signals channel, which holds 16 and drops repeats while full. Another notify for the same signal replaces the handler. Dropping a Watch restores the saved dispositions and unmaps the page, except that a handler another notify has replaced is silenced and its page stays mapped. raise signals the calling thread, so its handler has run when raise returns; send is process-directed and unordered against other threads. watch.next reads every event an inotify read returns and queues them. With recursive set, new and moved-in directories are watched before the batch that reports them is returned. stop wakes a parked next by adding and removing a watch on /, which makes the descriptor readable. The kernel merges identical consecutive events it has not yet delivered.

retry.delay is the capped exponential backoff and jittered applies the chosen jitter to it. reserve plans the wait and stops at the attempt limit, the deadline or a cancelled token; commit calls the observer, waits through the clock's sleep, which a cancelled token ends early, and starts the next attempt; next is reserve then commit. A Bucket keeps its balance as an integer in units of one token over per nanoseconds, so refills are exact and a wait is the ceiling of the deficit over the rate. reserve consumes and returns the wait. wait sleeps that long and refunds if cancelled. Group.do runs the function outside its lock, removes the key and stores the result before waking the waiters. It matches the key by call identity, so a forget followed by a new call is not disturbed.

diff.unified merges hunks whose gap is at most twice the context, omits a count of 1 in a hunk header and writes \ No newline at end of file, as GNU diff -u does. The edit script is minimal. number.format_bytes shows one decimal below 10 and rounds half to even on exact integers. parse_bytes reads k and kb as 1000 and ki and kib as 1024, and fails with OutOfRange on overflow or TooPrecise beyond 18 fraction digits. si rounds on the exact decimal expansion of the f64. naming.words splits at case, acronym and digit boundaries and keeps combining marks attached to their letter, so HTTPServerID2 is http server id 2.

Each concept is its own type: Timestamp is a point on the UTC timeline; Date, TimeOfDay and DateTime are civil values with no zone; Zoned is a timestamp seen through a zone; Duration is exact elapsed time; Span is a calendar amount. Types never convert silently. Fields are private and constructors validate, so a Date cannot hold February 30. Months are 1 to 12, and Month and Weekday are enums. Nothing rolls over: date.of(2026, 2, 30) fails with Invalid, and the clamping forms are named (clamped, plus_months). Calendar arithmetic and elapsed arithmetic are separate. A Duration moves a Timestamp or Zoned by elapsed time. A Span moves a Date, DateTime or Zoned by calendar units: a month after January 31 is the last day of February, and a day after a spring-forward midnight is the next civil day although it is 23 hours long. until and since take a Diff, add whole years, then months, to the start without passing the end, then count the rest. Only zone.local reads the host zone. A civil time in a daylight saving gap or overlap needs a Disambiguation. In an overlap, Compatible and Earlier pick the first occurrence and Later the second. In a gap, Compatible and Later move forward by the gap and Earlier back. Reject fails with Skipped or Ambiguous. zoned.start_of_day is the first instant of the civil day, correct where midnight does not exist. Zones come from TZif versions 1 to 4, using the 64-bit body from version 2, with the footer's POSIX TZ rule applying after the last transition. Before the first transition the first standard-time type applies. The rules cover Jn, zero-based n and Mm.w.d days and transition times from -167 to 167 hours, so negative daylight saving (Dublin, Casablanca), half-hour shifts (Lord Howe) and skipped days (Apia) work. Parsing is strict ISO 8601, RFC 3339 and RFC 9557: T, t or a space separates date and time, a fraction has 1 to 9 digits, :60 reads as :59, and a civil type rejects an offset. A written offset that disagrees with a bracketed zone is OffsetConflict unless an OffsetPolicy says which wins. Every parse error is Syntax(at) with the byte offset of the first bad character, or a value error naming the field. The supported range is 0001-01-01 to 9999-12-31 for a Timestamp and years -9999 to 9999 for a Date. Leap seconds are not modelled. Plain arithmetic panics on overflow; the try_ forms return an optional. Month and weekday names are English. pattern.Names and humanize.Words carry other languages.

cdp.launch finds chromium, chromium-browser, google-chrome-stable or google-chrome on PATH unless given an executable, and creates a profile with file.temp_dir. It starts the browser headless in its own process group with --remote-debugging-port=0, standard input and output discarded and standard error piped. A green thread reads standard error until the DevTools listening on line, which gives the WebSocket address, and keeps draining it so the browser never blocks on a full pipe. Another waits with process.wait_exit_on for the browser to end, so a browser that dies before the line fails the launch at once, as Launch(Aborted), even while a helper it started, such as the crash reporter, keeps standard error open. Standard error closing with the browser still running is Launch(Eof) and the startup deadline Launch(TimedOut). shutdown closes the WebSocket, kills the process group, waits for that thread, reaps the browser and removes the profile. Commands carry an id and, for a session, its sessionId. A pump green thread routes replies to the waiting call and sends every other message to each subscription. A message that is not JSON fails every waiting call with Protocol. Sends are serialised and a call waits at most 30 seconds. Once the socket closes, every waiting call fails with Closed and the subscription channels close. open_page creates a browser context that is disposed on detach, denies downloads in it, and turns on auto-attach with waitForDebuggerOnStart and flat sessions, so every page, frame and worker target pauses on creation. Each page subscribes to the events and acts only on those of its own context and the sessions attached in it. The first page in the context is the opened page; any other page in it, such as a popup, is closed before it runs. Every other target in the context gets Fetch.enable for all URLs, Network.enable, auto-attach for its own children and, for pages, Network.setBypassServiceWorker, and only then resumes, so no request escapes interception; a target that cannot be prepared is closed and, for the opened page, fails open_page. close_page ends the subscription and disposes the context. Each paused request is passed to Handlers.request on its own green thread and continued or failed with its verdict. Responses and failed loads are reported with their URL. Cancellation is the caller's: let h = b.handle and cancel.on_cancel(t, fn() { cdp.shutdown_on(h) }) end everything the browser was doing.

TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246), client and server. Config.min_version and Config.max_version, written with tls12 and tls13, bound the versions and default to 1.2 through 1.3. A client offers its range through supported_versions, and a server answers with the highest version both support. Session.handle.version holds the result. Downgrade protection: a server that supports 1.3 ends a 1.2 ServerHello random with the RFC 8446 downgrade sentinel; a client that offered 1.3 aborts with illegal_parameter when it sees either sentinel; a server refuses TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV below its highest version with inappropriate_fallback. Config.cipher_suites lists suites in preference order, and a server takes the first of its own list that the client offers. Session.handle.cipher_suite holds the IANA code and Session.handle.suite the AEAD and hash. TLS 1.3 has TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. TLS 1.2 has ECDHE with ECDSA or RSA authentication and AES-128-GCM with SHA-256, ChaCha20-Poly1305 with SHA-256 or AES-256-GCM with SHA-384, AEAD only: GCM records carry the 64-bit sequence number as their explicit nonce, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 records use the RFC 7905 nonce. TLS 1.3 key exchange offers the hybrid post-quantum group X25519MLKEM768 first, then X25519, P-256 and P-384. A client sends key shares for X25519MLKEM768 and X25519. A server picks the first group of its own order that the client supports, answering with a HelloRetryRequest when the client sent no share for it, so a client that supports X25519MLKEM768 always gets it. TLS 1.2 uses the first of X25519, P-256 and P-384 in the server's order that the client lists, and a server with an ECDSA certificate also requires the client to list the certificate's curve (RFC 8422). Servers sign with ECDSA P-256 or P-384, RSA-PSS, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 in TLS 1.2, or Ed25519, with keys loaded from PEM (x509.pem_certificates, x509.pem_private_key). std/crypto/x509 owns the one table of signature scheme codes: the client offer, the codes a key signs with and the key exchange authentication of a code all come from it. TLS 1.2 ECDSA signature schemes name only the hash, so either curve signs with SHA-256 or SHA-384 (x509.SignatureRules.Tls12); in TLS 1.3 a code names its curve. Clients verify the chain against Config.roots, or the system roots when that is empty, and check the host name against the certificate's subject alternative names. They verify CertificateVerify or ServerKeyExchange with any offered scheme the certificate allows and, in TLS 1.2, the suite's authentication. TLS 1.2 requires the extended master secret (RFC 7627) on both sides. A client requires the secure renegotiation indication (RFC 5746), a server echoes it when the client sends it, and both refuse renegotiation with a no_renegotiation warning. ALPN, SNI, KeyUpdate in TLS 1.3 and close_notify are supported. Session tickets are ignored, so there is no resumption or 0-RTT. Servers do not request client certificates; a client answers a CertificateRequest with an empty Certificate. Records hold at most 2^14 bytes of plaintext, and a peer's ciphertext may add 256 bytes in TLS 1.3 or 2048 in TLS 1.2. A record or handshake error sends its fatal alert, such as bad_record_mac, record_overflow, unexpected_message or decode_error, and leaves the session unusable. A session's read and write sides are independent, with a write lock, so different green threads can read and write it. QUIC mode (quic_client, quic_server) runs the TLS 1.3 handshake without records: handshake messages go to the transport per level, and the traffic secrets are handed over as the schedule derives them. It offers TLS 1.3 only, carries the transport parameters in extension 0x39, requires ALPN and an empty legacy_session_id, rejects handshake data at the wrong level and bytes left over when a key changes, and caps a handshake message at 64 KiB.

An endpoint is one UDP socket and one reader green thread. A datagram over 1500 bytes is dropped, and the rest are routed by destination connection ID, at most 4096 routes. Each connection is a loop green thread that owns all of its state; the reader, the TLS handshake green thread and user calls reach it through channels, and every send to it also waits on a channel that closes when the loop exits, so nothing blocks on a connection that has ended. A server answers an unsupported version with Version Negotiation only for datagrams of at least 1200 bytes. It holds at most 256 connections whose handshake is incomplete, at most 8 of them per client IP address; an Initial beyond either limit is dropped. From 128 of them, or always when Config.retry is set, a new Initial gets a Retry whose token is an HMAC-SHA256 over the client address, an expiry 10 seconds ahead, the original connection ID and the source connection ID of the Retry, compared in constant time. The token is accepted only on an Initial whose destination connection ID is that source connection ID, so one token starts one connection: later Initials with that ID are routed to it. Before the client address is validated the server sends at most three times the bytes received. A client accepts one Retry and ignores Retry and Version Negotiation once it has processed another packet. A short-header datagram of at least 42 bytes for no connection gets a smaller stateless reset whose token is an HMAC of the connection ID. The handshake runs tls.quic_client or tls.quic_server on its own green thread. Received CRYPTO data is reassembled to at most 64 KiB in at most 64 pieces per level, beyond which the connection fails with CRYPTO_BUFFER_EXCEEDED, and at most 16 packets wait for keys not yet installed. CRYPTO data that arrives after the handshake, such as session tickets, is discarded. Initial keys are discarded when Handshake packets flow and Handshake keys when the handshake is confirmed. Each side checks the peer's transport parameters: the connection IDs they name, including a Retry's, must match the ones seen on the wire, and a client must not send the parameters only a server sends. Packets carry ACKs for at most 32 received ranges, sent within 5 ms or at once after two ack-eliciting packets. Loss recovery is std/quic/recovery. The sender skips a packet number every 128 to 384 packets, and an ACK of a skipped or unsent number is PROTOCOL_VIOLATION; only the first 256 ranges of an ACK frame are processed. Lost frames are sent again from what the packet carried, so stream data, flow control updates and control frames are rebuilt rather than copied. 1-RTT keys are updated after 2^23 packets or when update_keys asks, and a peer's key update is followed. Every change of the sending keys sends a PING, so the acknowledgement that allows the next update arrives even when there is no data to send. A connection closes with AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED once more packets fail authentication than the integrity limit of its AEAD: 2^52, or 2^36 for ChaCha20-Poly1305. Connection IDs: the endpoint issues 8-byte IDs and stores at most 2 of the peer's. RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames owed to the peer are capped at 8, beyond which the connection fails with CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR. Only the latest PATH_CHALLENGE is answered. Connection migration is not supported. Streams: flow control applies per stream and per connection in both directions, and the receive windows are credited as the application reads. A stream reassembles into one receive buffer that spans the read position to the highest offset received and grows by doubling, never past the flow control window, with each byte copied once into place; bytes that were already received are not overwritten by a retransmission. The buffer is described by a sorted list of received ranges, at most 256, beyond which the connection fails with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION, and data past the flow control limit, a changed final size and an offset plus length over 2^62-1 fail the connection with the matching error. A peer opens at most the advertised number of streams of each type, at most 4096 are tracked, and the allowance of a peer-opened stream returns (MAX_STREAMS) only when the stream is complete and the application has accepted it, so streams the application never accepts stay bounded by the advertised number. write parks while the stream's 1 MiB send buffer or the peer's credit is exhausted. Closing: close_on sends CONNECTION_CLOSE and the connection stays closing for three probe timeouts, answering with the same frame. While a stream holds data the peer has not acknowledged, close_on holds the CONNECTION_CLOSE back for at most 5 seconds and never past the idle timeout. close_listener asks every connection to close before it waits for any, so it takes as long as the slowest one, not the sum. A CONNECTION_CLOSE from the peer drains it. The idle timeout, the handshake timeout and a stateless reset end it. A reason phrase is truncated to 1024 bytes and never interpreted. Not supported: 0-RTT, session resumption, connection migration, datagrams (RFC 9221) and versions other than 1.

std/serde defines a Writer and a Reader, structs of closures through which values are written and read. For every concrete type the compiler derives a function that writes a value to a Writer, a function that reads it from a Reader, and a Schema describing it: Booleans, integers, floats and strings map to their primitives; []u8 to binary; slices to sequences; maps to maps with keys written as text; optionals to null or the value; pointers to their target, a shared pointer in full each time. A pointer reached again while its target is being written is a cycle and panics. A struct is a map from field names to values, and every field takes part, private ones included. A reader opens it with begin_map and steps through it with next_field, which a format may spell differently from next_key, the step through the entries of a map. Reading skips unknown fields, uses a field's default when it is missing, treats a missing optional field as none, and fails with Missing otherwise. An enum variant without fields is its name. One with labelled fields is a single-key map from its name to a map of its fields, and one with positional fields maps its name to a sequence. A schema records each type's kind, name, fields with whether they are required, and variants. A struct or enum reached again through a pointer while it is being described becomes a Ref to its name. A Reader reports at in an Error as its position, whose unit is the format's: a byte offset for JSON, a line for YAML, the count of values read for CBOR, MessagePack and TOML, a column index for std/orm and 0 for XML. CBOR, MessagePack, TOML, YAML and std/template build a serde.Tree from a value and read a value from one, so the variant shape, the text of a map key and the range of a u64 are defined once, in std/serde. std/json, std/orm and std/web are built on these. T.field, where T is a struct type, is a serde.Field[T, F] holding the field's name and index, so a function can take a field of a given struct with a given type.

json.Reader tokenizes UTF-8 bytes like .NET's Utf8JsonReader, strictly per RFC 8259, with a depth limit of 64. It returns strings without copying unless they contain escapes. Numbers are parsed as integers or correctly rounded floats. json.serialize_with and json.deserialize_with take Options for indentation, naming (Unchanged, CamelCase, SnakeCase, PascalCase), maximum depth and omit_none. Naming applies to struct field names and to variant names in both directions, and not to the keys of a map; a variant name read back is matched in PascalCase. With omit_none, a field whose value is none is left out instead of written as null. Binary data is base64; non-finite floats are written as null. std/cbor decodes RFC 8949 items into Values: every major type, indefinite-length strings, arrays and maps, tags, simple values, and half, single and double floats, which become f64. Indefinite-length items arrive as their definite equivalents. Text must be valid UTF-8 and map keys must be distinct. These fail with Malformed: truncated input, reserved additional information, a stray break, indefinite integers or tags, mixed or nested string chunks, a two-byte simple value below 32, data after the item, and a declared length that exceeds the remaining input (checked before anything is allocated). Nesting deeper than Options.max_depth, or a string, array or map longer than max_length, fails with TooLarge. decode_first returns the first item and its length so a caller can continue after it. encode writes the deterministic encoding of §4.2.1: shortest heads, definite lengths, map entries sorted by the bytes of their encoded keys, and floats in the shortest of half, single or double that keeps the value, with NaN as f97e00. diagnostic writes the notation of §8. serialize and deserialize bind types through serde with []u8 as byte strings, structs and variants as maps with text keys, and none as null; reading looks through tags and accepts integer map keys as their decimal text. std/webauthn produces options JSON in the shape py_webauthn's options_to_json writes, with base64url challenges, user ids and credential ids, pubKeyCredParams defaulting to supported_algorithms() of the COSE parser (EdDSA, ES256 and RS256), and attestation none. verify_registration takes the credential JSON a browser's PublicKeyCredential gives in base64url, with or without padding. It checks that id is the base64url of rawId, that type is public-key, that clientDataJSON has type webauthn.create, the expected challenge (compared in constant time) and the origin. It then decodes the attestation object and checks the RP ID hash, user presence, user verification when required, and attested credential data. It parses the COSE key, accepts only the none format with an empty statement, and rejects a backup state without backup eligibility. It returns the credential id, the COSE key bytes exactly as the authenticator wrote them, and the sign count. verify_authentication makes the same client data and authenticator data checks for webauthn.get. It rejects a sign count that is not greater than the stored one unless both are zero. It verifies the signature over authenticatorData followed by SHA-256 of clientDataJSON with the stored key: ES256 as DER ECDSA on P-256, EdDSA as Ed25519 and RS256 as PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256. Each failure is its own Error variant. std/orm builds queries from conditions over field references, such as orm.filter(orm.from(users), orm.ge(User.age, 18)), and type-checks them against the field. It renders them for the connection's Dialect, maps rows onto structs, stores nested values as JSON columns, creates tables from types with an identity key named id, and returns generated keys from inserts. sql.Value holds dates as days since 1970-01-01, times as microseconds since midnight, timestamps as microseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, infinite dates and timestamps as the i64 maximum and minimum, and UUIDs as 16 bytes. A connection serves one green thread at a time; a call made while another is running fails with Busy. orm.transaction rolls back on any error from its body and fails with that error, or with the rollback's error when the rollback fails too. std/sql/postgres authenticates with SCRAM-SHA-256, MD5 or cleartext. It uses the simple protocol for statements without parameters and the extended protocol with a 64-entry prepared statement cache otherwise, streams each in batches of 512 rows, reads results as text decoded by type OID, and keeps a connection usable after a server error. A timeout sends a CancelRequest and closes the connection. connect_tls upgrades with SSLRequest and std/tls. std/sql/sqlserver speaks TDS 7.4 with SQL authentication. Prelogin offers no encryption to connect and full encryption to connect_tls. connect_tls runs the std/tls handshake inside PRELOGIN packets and unwraps the packets the server keeps sending around TLS records. LOGIN7 announces UTF-8 support. Statements without parameters go as SQL batches. With parameters they go to sp_executesql as @p1..@pN declared as bigint, float, bit, decimal(38, s), nvarchar, varbinary, uniqueidentifier, date, time(7), datetime2(7) or datetimeoffset(7), with NULL sent as nvarchar(4000). Every request carries the transaction descriptor, and begin, commit and rollback use transaction manager requests. Results decode every fixed, nullable, decimal, money, date and time, GUID, character, binary, long-value, text, image, XML, sql_variant and user-defined type. GUIDs become RFC 4122 byte order. Single-byte text decodes through its collation's UTF-8 flag or as Windows-1252. Row counts sum the DONE and DONEINPROC counts. each streams rows as they arrive, and stopping early sends an ATTENTION and reads until the server acknowledges it. A server error below severity 20 leaves the connection usable. A per-connection watchdog sends an ATTENTION and closes the stream when one read waits longer than the timeout, and the call fails with Timeout. std/toml parses into ordered tables and applies every rule of TOML 1.0.0, including the restrictions on redefining tables through headers, dotted keys, inline tables and arrays of tables. It agrees with Python's tomllib on the toml-test suite. Errors carry a line and column. encode writes plain values first and then [table] and [[array]] sections. serialize and deserialize bind types through serde, reading date-times as RFC 3339 text. std/yaml parses YAML 1.2.2 into ordered node trees and agrees with the yaml-test-suite on every case's event stream and JSON equivalent. A scanner modelled on libyaml tokenizes the whole stream, tracking indentation, implicit keys, JSON-like adjacent values and the YAML 1.2 tab rules, with 32-byte vector scans over plain scalars and simd.find_byte_str for comment and line ends. Token text is a view into the source. A recursive-descent parser turns tokens into Events with resolved tags, and a composer builds Nodes carrying line, column, tag, anchor and style. Plain scalars resolve with the core schema. !!str, !!int, !!float, !!bool, !!null and !!binary are checked against their content; other tags stay on the node. Aliases share their anchored node. Options.max_nodes bounds the tree with every alias expanded, failing with TooManyNodes, and max_depth bounds nesting. Duplicate scalar keys are an error. encode writes block style, quotes a scalar only when it would read back differently (including YAML 1.1 booleans, numbers and dates), writes multi-line text as literal blocks, and anchors any node reached more than once. serialize and deserialize bind types through serde, with []u8 as !!binary. std/otel keeps the provider in the green thread's context slot as an immutable Context of the active span, baggage, a suppression flag and the SDK. spawn copies the slot, so a child green thread's spans parent to the spawning span. install and setup_from_env return a droppable Sdk that shuts down when released and put the SdkHandle into the calling green thread's slot, reaching the green threads it spawns afterwards. Programs install at the top of main. Every API call checks the slot first and returns a no-op value without allocating when no SDK is present. Timestamps and durations come from time.now_nanos and time.monotonic. Span and trace ids come from a std/rand generator behind a lock. Samplers are always on, always off, trace-id ratio on the low 63 bits, and parent-based. Batch processors for spans and logs queue to a bounded channel with a non-blocking send that counts drops. A worker green thread exports when a batch fills, when the delay passes, and on flush or shutdown. Periodic metric readers use the same control worker for flush and shutdown. Metric instruments aggregate per attribute set, keyed by a canonical encoding of the sorted attributes, in one stream per reader, capped at 2000 series plus an otel.metric.overflow series. Readers collect cumulatively or as deltas, periodically or on demand. Exporters encode OTLP once through a writer that emits protobuf through std/protobuf or the OTLP JSON mapping, and send with the context suppressed. OTLP/HTTP posts, optionally gzipped, retrying 429, 502, 503 and 504 through std/retry with equal-jitter exponential backoff, where Retry-After raises the wait. OTLP/gRPC makes unary Export calls on opentelemetry.proto.collector.{trace,metrics,logs}.v1 over the pooled client's HTTP/2 connection, with h2c prior knowledge for http://. The message carries the 5-byte gRPC prefix, optionally gzipped under grpc-encoding, with te: trailers and grpc-timeout. The result is grpc-status from the trailers or, in a trailers-only response, the headers. CANCELLED, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, ABORTED, OUT_OF_RANGE, UNAVAILABLE and DATA_LOSS are retried. RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED is retried only when grpc-status-details-bin carries a RetryInfo, whose delay replaces the backoff. setup_from_env reads the standard OTEL_* variables. OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc selects gRPC, defaulting to http://localhost:4317. std/http sits below std/otel in the import graph, so the hook runs through the context slot. otel.Context declares an http.Ambient as its first field, and std/http reads the slot as *http.Ambient, which relies on struct fields being laid out in declaration order. One constructor builds every Context and derives the ambient Observer from it: the observer is set exactly when an SDK is installed and the context is not suppressed, and std/http does nothing when it is absent. Processors and metric readers call exporters through quietly, so no exporter has to suppress its own telemetry. http.serve and serve_tls open a server span per request over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, with the parent extracted from traceparent and client.address from Request.remote, and record http.server.request.duration. std/web adopts that span, adds http.route and renames it to the method and route; it opens its own span only when its handler runs outside http.serve. The client opens a CLIENT span named after the method for each attempt sent, redirects and retries included. Each span is under the caller's span, with http.request.resend_count from the second attempt. The client injects traceparent, tracestate and baggage into that attempt, sets url.full without userinfo, and ends the span when the body is delivered or the attempt fails, with error.type the status from 400 or the http.Error variant. It records http.client.request.duration. std/sql/driver wraps every connection that std/sql/postgres, std/sql/sqlserver and std/sql/sqlite return with instrument_sql, reading the db.system.name from the connection's Dialect. std/orm opens client spans with the operation and table; a nested database span merges into the outer one, so an ORM query produces one span. std/protobuf writes and reads the protobuf wire format without code generation. An Encoder appends into a buffer that doubles as needed. Signed integers sign-extend to ten bytes and sint64 zigzag-encodes. begin_message returns a mark and end_message measures the body, shifts it right by the size of its length varint and writes the length, so nested messages need neither a second buffer nor padded lengths. Output matches protoc --encode byte for byte. A Decoder walks fields in order as number, wire type, integer value and a view of the payload. It rejects truncated or overlong varints, lengths past the end, field 0 and wire types 6 and 7 with Malformed, and groups with Unsupported. The as_* readers check the wire type and the unpack_* readers accept packed and single encodings. std/xml reads XML 1.0 (fifth edition) with Namespaces from UTF-8, UTF-16 with a byte order mark, or any encoding std/charset knows by its declared label, converting to UTF-8 and normalising line endings first. xml.Reader is a pull reader: next returns one token and position its line and column. Names arrive with namespaces resolved and are interned in a per-reader table. Text, CDATA, comments and attribute values are views into the input unless a reference or normalisation forces a copy, and 32-byte vector scans find the bytes that end them. The reader enforces well-formedness and the namespace constraints and agrees with libxml2 on what it accepts. The internal subset is parsed. General entities expand, including markup, with recursion detection, a nesting limit of 40 and a total of 1 MiB plus eight times the input. Attribute-list declarations supply defaults and normalise tokenised types. External entities are never fetched and parameter entities are not expanded. xml.parse builds an Element tree of owned strings with attribute, child, children, text and find. xml.Writer escapes text and attributes, splits CDATA around ]]>, writes namespace declarations and indents element-only content. serialize_value and deserialize bind types through serde, mapping fields to attributes or child elements by local name, repeated elements to slices, and xsi:nil to none. Pipes block through channels. A writer flushing more than the pause threshold waits until the reader brings the unconsumed bytes below the resume threshold, or until the reader itself waits for more data, so a message larger than the thresholds cannot deadlock the pipe. pool.open stores ConnectionHandle views, so one connection serves a lease at a time and the pool, not the owner, closes it. Idle and lifetime limits are checked on acquire, release and prune against clock.monotonic, and a release hands the connection to the oldest waiter. A lease marks its connection broken on Connect, Authentication, Closed, Timeout or Protocol errors, and the pool closes it. A transaction left open at release is rolled back. migrate.up refuses any applied migration whose checksum differs (Drift), a pending version below the highest applied one (OutOfOrder) and duplicate or non-ascending versions. The lock is BEGIN IMMEDIATE on SQLite, pg_advisory_lock on PostgreSQL and sp_getapplock on SQL Server, and each migration re-checks inside its transaction that it is not yet recorded. A migration that fails reports its own error, or the rollback's error when the rollback fails too; a lock that cannot be released fails with Sql unless a migration error is reported first. In a text migration a statement ends at a line ending in ;, and -- +begin to -- +end keeps a block with several ; as one statement.

std/unicode reads tables generated by cmd/tablegen unicode from UnicodeData.txt, CaseFolding.txt and DerivedNormalizationProps.txt of Unicode 16.0.0, the version Python's unicodedata reports, and agrees with it on every code point. cmd/tablegen unicode and cmd/tablegen properties also write normalization_layout.low and property_layout.low: constants for the record sizes, field offsets, trie shifts and masks, Hangul constants and packed property bit fields, and one <table>_table() accessor per .bin file that embeds it. The module sources read these instead of literals, and TestLayoutFilesMatchGenerator fails when a committed layout file differs from the generator. The tables are embedded binary files. A two-level trie of 64-entry blocks covers code points below U+2FA40 and gives 0 above. It maps each code point to a 16-bit record id. Each record holds the canonical combining class and 16-bit offsets and lengths into a pool of u32 code points for the full canonical decomposition, the full compatibility decomposition and the C and F case folding. Hangul syllables decompose and compose algorithmically. Decomposition is followed by a stable canonical reordering by combining class. Composition binary-searches a sorted table of primary composites, leaving out Full_Composition_Exclusion. ASCII input returns at once, or lowercased by casefold and search_key. search_key(s) equals Python's ''.join(c for c in unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', s.casefold()) if not unicodedata.combining(c)). It skips reordering, since every reordered character is dropped.

std/html tokenizes UTF-8 HTML following the WHATWG tokenization states. It builds no tree and never fails. Tag and attribute names are lowercased in ASCII, attribute values may be double-quoted, single-quoted or unquoted, a repeated attribute keeps its first value, and a tag cut off by the end of input is dropped. A start tag for script, style, xmp, iframe, noembed or noframes switches to raw text, and one for title or textarea to escapable raw text, until the matching end tag in any case. plaintext takes the rest of the input. The script-data double-escape states are not implemented, and noscript is tokenized as when scripting is disabled. Comments end at --> or --!>, with <!--> and <!---> empty. <?...>, <!...> other than comments and doctypes, <![CDATA[...]]> and </ followed by a non-letter become comments, and </> is skipped. Doctype carries the lowercased name and the optional public and system identifiers. Character references are decoded in text, escapable raw text and attribute values. Named references match the longest name against the full WHATWG table of 2,231 names, including the names valid without a semicolon. cmd/tablegen entities generates the table and also writes entity_layout.low with the index entry layout, the name length limit and the table accessors. Decimal and hexadecimal references work with or without a semicolon. Zero, surrogates and values above U+10FFFF become U+FFFD, and 0x80 to 0x9F map through Windows-1252. Inside an attribute, a match without a semicolon that is followed by = or a letter or digit stays literal. Text without references is a view into the input. The tokens match Python's html.parser except where it departs from WHATWG: duplicate attributes, processing instructions and CDATA as comments, raw text after <script/>, and control-character references.

std/regex compiles a pattern once into a program for a Pike VM, a Thompson NFA simulation that carries capture slots per thread, so matching takes time linear in the input times the program size and never backtracks. A Regex keeps two pools of idle machines: one without capture slots for is_match, one with them for find, full_match and the scans. Each machine owns its thread queues, capture slots and scratch. A call takes an idle machine under a lock, builds one when none is idle, and puts it back when it finishes. A compiled value is therefore shared freely between green threads, and a callback that matches with the same Regex during replace_all gets its own machine. A Match copies its slots out of the machine. Syntax: literals; escapes 
 	    \v \a, \xhh, \uhhhh, \Uhhhhhhhh and escaped punctuation; .; classes with ranges, negation and \d \w \s \D \W \S inside; \d \w \s \D \W \S   \B \A \Z \z; ^ and $; capturing groups, (?:...), inline flags (?i), (?m), (?s), (?-i) and scoped (?i:...); alternation; *, +, ?, {m}, {m,}, {,n} and {m,n} with lazy forms. A { that does not form a valid count is a literal. Inline flags apply to the rest of the enclosing group. Input is UTF-8 matched by code point; offsets are bytes. \d, \w, \s,   and case folding are ASCII. . excludes only 
 unless dot_all is set. Without multiline, $ matches at the end or before a final 
; with it, ^ and $ match at every line boundary. Matching is leftmost-first, as in Python and RE2, and results agree with Python's re under re.ASCII. find_all, replace_all and split follow Python 3.7: an empty match is allowed right after a non-empty one, and after an empty match the next one may start at the same offset only if it is not empty. split does not include group text. split_n splits at most max times; a negative max splits everywhere. Repeat counts are limited to 10000 and programs to 100,000 instructions. Invalid patterns fail with Invalid(at, message), at the byte offset Python reports. Backreferences, lookaround, named groups and possessive quantifiers are rejected. regex.generated("pattern") is a Regex built at compile time, like .NET's [GeneratedRegex]. The pattern must be a string literal; flags are written inline. An invalid pattern is a compile error at the literal, invalid regex at byte N: message, with the offset and message compile would fail with. The result is used through the same functions as a compiled Regex and matches identically. internal/regex holds a Go copy of the parser and assembler, held to the Low one by running the std_regex_errors fixture's patterns through it. The checker turns each distinct literal into Low functions named __regex_ and the FNV-1a hash of the pattern, parsed with the prelude's privileges and added to std/regex, so they reach its private types. A Regex carries an Engine of thread-start, step and skip functions with the queue size. compile fills it with the Pike VM. The generated engine keeps the VM's queues, priorities and capture slots but replaces interpretation with code per instruction: One function per instruction that starts a thread, follows a consumed character or joins two epsilon paths, each guarded by the queue's sparse set. The remaining jumps, splits, saves and assertions are inlined into it. Characters and classes of up to four ranges compare inline in the step, which dispatches on the program counter by binary search. Larger classes get a binary-search function. When no empty match is possible from the start, a skip function moves past ASCII bytes that cannot begin a match before a thread starts. Programs over 2000 instructions are compiled at run time by compile instead, so call depth stays bounded.

std/compress/codec holds what the codecs share. Buffer is a growable byte buffer with an LSB bit packer, and every write to it is infallible. Each encoder is a core that writes into a Buffer; the shared Encoder runs the core's feed, sync and close steps, drains the buffer to its sink and rejects every call after finish with Invalid, so one-shot compress has no error to handle. BitReader reads LSB-first bits from a slice or an io.Reader and fails with Malformed on short input. Tables builds two-level lookup tables for canonical Huffman codes, and Builder computes length-limited code lengths. Chain is a hash-chain match finder and History the sliding window that zstd and LZ4 index with it, decompress runs the one-shot decode of a codec under an output limit, copy_match copies an LZ77 match, and read_varint and write_varint code LEB128 integers, which std/protobuf and xz also use. Deflate, brotli, WebP lossless, zstd, LZ4, snappy, xz and bzip2 build on it where their formats agree. DEFLATE, zlib and gzip decode stored, fixed and dynamic blocks with two-level lookup tables, check Adler-32, CRC-32, ISIZE and the gzip header CRC, and read concatenated gzip members. The encoder uses greedy matching at levels 1 to 3 and lazy matching at 4 to 9 over a hash chain on a 32 KB window, choosing dynamic, fixed or stored encoding per block. flush emits a sync flush so streamed output is decodable as it arrives. xz decodes multiple blocks and streams, the none, CRC32, CRC64 and SHA-256 checks, LZMA2 chunks with their resets, and the delta filter; other filters fail with Unsupported. The encoder writes LZMA2 with a hash-chain match finder and lazy parsing, a dictionary from 256 KiB to 64 MiB by level, and raw chunks where compression does not pay. std/compress/zstd and std/compress/lz4 each offer compress(data, level), decompress(data, limit), a streaming decode(reader, sink, limit) that passes output to the sink one block at a time, and a streaming Encoder with encode, flush and finish. The zstd decoder handles every block and literal type, 1- and 4-stream Huffman literals, all four FSE table modes, repeat offsets, skippable and concatenated frames, and the content checksum. Its history grows with real output up to the smaller of the window and the remaining limit, so large windows never allocate what the header claims up front. The zstd encoder finds matches with two hash chains keyed on 8-byte and 4- or 5-byte prefixes, with depth and lazy evaluation set by the level. It Huffman-codes literals, picks predefined, RLE or custom FSE tables per block by estimated cost, and falls back to raw or RLE blocks. The LZ4 decoder accepts linked and independent blocks, block and content checksums, content sizes and skippable frames. The encoder writes linked 64 KB blocks with a content checksum. Dictionaries and LZ4 frames with magic number 0x184C2102 fail with Unsupported. std/compress/brotli has the same API as zstd and LZ4. The decoder handles compressed, uncompressed and metadata meta-blocks, block switching for literals, commands and distances, all four literal context modes, context maps with run-length coding and inverse move-to-front, distance postfix and direct parameters, the static dictionary with all 121 transforms, and windows of 10 to 24 bits. Output collects in a ring buffer that starts at 64 KB and doubles up to the window, and reaches the sink at the end of each meta-block, when the ring wraps, and before each blocking read. The 122,784-byte dictionary is embedded from dictionary.bin. The encoder writes uncompressed meta-blocks at level 0. Levels 1 to 11 run hash chains of depth 2^(level-1) with lazy matching from level 4 and checks against the four recent distances and their neighbours, writing 256 KB meta-blocks with Huffman-coded commands and distances. From level 5 they model literals in UTF-8 context mode with up to 3·level-11 clustered trees. A block that would grow is stored. flush ends the meta-block and pads with an empty metadata block so everything sent decodes. std/bits holds a growable Set over []u64 words. Counts use a SWAR popcount, and scans (next_set, next_clear, min, max, rank, select_at, members) step a word at a time. std/bits/roaring holds Roaring, a set of u32 split into 65536-value chunks keyed by the high 16 bits. Each chunk is a sorted []u16 array of up to 4096 values, a 1024-word bitmap, or a list of runs. Arrays and bitmaps convert at 4096 values; ranges create runs, and unions and intersections of runs stay runs. Every container tracks its cardinality, so cardinality is constant time. Set operations come as new-set and in-place _with forms, working word by word on bitmaps and by galloping merge on arrays. run_optimize picks the smallest form per container by the Go library's rule. serialize and deserialize implement the portable Roaring format byte for byte as Go roaring/v2 writes it, rejecting any inconsistent length, ordering or cardinality with Malformed. std/image holds an Image of width, height, Format (Gray8, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8, Gray16, Rgba16, 16-bit samples big-endian), stride and pixel bytes. Pixels read and write as 8-bit Rgba, with operations converting through 16-bit intermediates. get outside the image is transparent black and set there does nothing. Operations convert formats, crop, flip, rotate, apply EXIF orientation, fill rectangles, composite straight alpha, premultiply and unpremultiply, and resize separably on premultiplied values with nearest, bilinear, Catmull-Rom bicubic or Lanczos-3 filters. decode picks a codec by signature and rejects images over 2^26 pixels; decode_limited takes another limit. PNG decodes every colour type, bit depth and Adam7, checks every CRC, and encodes with per-row adaptive filtering. The result is Gray16 for 16-bit gray without transparency, Rgba16 for other 16-bit images, Gray8 or GrayAlpha8 for gray, Rgba8 for colour with alpha or tRNS, and Rgb8 otherwise. JPEG decodes baseline and progressive scans with restart markers, any sampling, grayscale and Adobe CMYK/YCCK, with libjpeg's integer IDCT and fancy upsampling, so output matches libjpeg byte for byte. It encodes baseline 4:2:0 with the standard tables scaled by quality. GIF decodes 87a and 89a and composites every frame by disposal method in decode_gif_frames. It encodes one frame with a given or median-cut palette. BMP covers 1 to 32 bits, RLE, bitfields and every header version, and encodes 24 or 32 bits. QOI decodes and encodes; the result is Rgb8 or Rgba8 by channel count. WebP decodes lossless VP8L with every transform, the colour cache and meta prefix codes. Lossy VP8, alpha chunks and animation fail with Unsupported. Every codec has buffer functions, a streaming decoder that pulls from an io.Reader, pushes output to a sink and fails with TooLarge past a caller's limit, and a streaming encoder.

web.app() holds routes and middleware. get, post, put, patch, del and route add handlers for paths with :name parameters and a trailing *. group makes a sub-application with a prefix and more middleware that registers its routes on the same router. An unknown path is a 404. A known path with another method runs the middleware of the first route with that path, then answers 405 with Allow, so cors answers a preflight for any route. endpoint[Req, Res] and query_endpoint[Res] read a JSON body into Req, call a handler returning Res ! web.Problem, and write the result as JSON or the problem as application/problem+json. Their schemas describe the operation in the OpenAPI document that openapi serves, along with path parameters and each route's security schemes. Middleware is a struct of a run closure and an optional security scheme. api_key, basic and bearer authenticate requests and set Context.user. sessions keeps a map in a cookie sealed with AES-256-GCM, with the cookie name as associated data and an expiry inside. csrf requires the session's token in X-CSRF-Token on unsafe methods. require_session, cors (with the request headers it allows), logger and compress complete the set; compress picks Zstandard, Brotli or gzip, in that order, from what Accept-Encoding allows. jwt verifies bearer tokens against a key set with std/crypto/jose. oidc does the same for an OpenID Connect issuer: it reads the discovery document and the JWKS, refreshes them hourly, and refreshes early, at most once a minute, when a token names a key it does not know. oidc_login adds a sign-in route that redirects to the issuer with state, nonce and a PKCE S256 challenge kept in the session, and a callback route that checks the state, exchanges the code, verifies the ID token and its nonce, and hands the claims to the application. A handler streams a body by returning a Response with stream set to a chan[[]u8] and closing it at the end. The server writes each chunk as it arrives, cancels req.token when the stream ends, the client disconnects or a write fails, and drops the stream for HEAD and bodiless statuses. Response compression skips streamed responses. sse.stream sets text/event-stream, no-cache and x-accel-buffering: no, flushes every event, sends a : keepalive comment every 15 seconds unless keepalive is 0, and stops when req.token is cancelled. Emitter.send returns false after the client has gone. sse.format removes CR and LF from id and event and NUL from id. web.static decodes each path segment and answers 400 for .., an embedded separator, NUL or a bad escape, and 404 for dotfiles, non-regular files and any file whose real path leaves the root. A directory without a trailing slash is redirected, and a directory serves index.html or an optional listing. precompressed picks .br then .gz by Accept-Encoding. A multi-range or malformed Range gives the whole file. Files stream in 64 KiB chunks.

Green threads run on OS threads, one per CPU in the process's affinity mask. Threads start as work appears, with clone in a static program and pthread_create in a dynamic one. A thread whose green thread is in a C call does not count against the limit, so another starts while C blocks. Run queues: Each OS thread keeps a 256-entry run queue. A full queue spills to a global queue, and spawn queues on the global queue when its own thread already holds 16. A thread takes work in this order: expired timers; the global queue every 61st schedule; its own runnext and queue; a batch from the global queue (its length divided by the thread count, plus one, at most 128); ready descriptors; stealing. A thief takes half of the victim's queue into its own. It tries the victim's runnext only in the last of 4 rounds, and takes it at once when the victim is in a C call or stopped (asleep on a runtime lock or held by a collection), or when the running victim's runnext sequence has stayed unchanged for 2,000 timestamp-counter ticks. At most half of the running threads spin looking for work. With nothing to do, a thread sleeps on a futex or becomes the single poller that blocks in epoll_wait until the next timer. Every 32nd schedule on an OS thread moves runnext to the tail of its run queue and takes the queue's head, so green threads that keep readying each other cannot starve the rest of the queue. A green thread reserves 1 MB of stack with a guard page below it. Pages are committed as they are touched, and finished green threads are reused. Its context is its saved registers on its own stack. A fault in the guard page panics with stack overflow; any other fault panics with invalid memory access. Per-thread state lives in a 24-byte .tbss block directly below the thread pointer: the thread record at fs:-24, the running green thread at fs:-16 and the preemption flag at fs:-8. A static program sets fs with arch_prctl and CLONE_SETTLS; a dynamic program uses the block glibc allocates for every thread. Generated code uses the fixed offsets, so hot reload patches need no TLS relocations. Preemption: Every loop back-edge tests the preemption flag. A monitor thread sets the flag every 10 ms on a thread whose green thread has run since the last check, and the collector sets it everywhere. A set flag calls rt_poll, which saves every general register and xmm2 to xmm15 and yields or stops for the collector. Code that holds a channel lock does not yield. Recursion without loops is not preempted. park and ready hand a green thread off with a per-thread lock and a wake token, so a wakeup that arrives before the green thread has finished parking is not lost. Wakeups: ready puts the green thread in its OS thread's runnext slot, so it runs as soon as the current one parks, and bumps a per-thread runnext sequence. A green thread pushed out of that slot goes to the stealable run queue. ready then calls wakep, which acts only when its OS thread has not woken anyone in the last 100,000 timestamp-counter ticks or has not scheduled since it last did. A pair of green threads that hand work to each other therefore stays on one OS thread, while a sender that keeps computing after ready always has an idle thread woken to steal its runnext within the 2,000-tick delay. wakep does nothing while an OS thread is already spinning. Otherwise it wakes one idle thread, or starts a new one below the CPU limit, and the woken thread counts as spinning until it finds work or gives up. A spinner that finds work while more is queued wakes a successor. spawn always wakes a thread without the interval. The monitor thread moves the runnext and wakes a thread for the queue of an OS thread that sits in a C call or a blocking system call. In-call threads: An OS thread in a C call, or in a system call that can block, is marked in-call, which the collector treats as stopped. rt_world_stop does not wait for it, and on return from the call the thread parks in rt_m_running while a collection is in progress. The code generator emits __syscall inline only when its number is a constant on a short list of calls that never block on external events: close, lseek, memory mapping, signals, pipe, dup, socket creation and configuration, process creation and exit, time, identity, limits, epoll_ctl, eventfd and getrandom. Every other number, and every non-constant number, calls rt_sysblock. It saves the argument registers on the green thread's scanned stack, marks the thread in-call, makes the call and leaves the in-call state through the same path as a C call. The monitor counts in-call threads that have not scheduled since its previous visit, and wakep does not count them against the CPU limit, so work queued behind one finds a running thread. A green thread blocked in read on a pipe therefore does not delay a collection started by another. Timers are a locked array of deadlines. sleep and select's after arms add to it, and the poller wakes through an eventfd when an earlier timer arrives. Descriptors are registered with EPOLLONESHOT. Channels and select are generic prelude code over __Chan[T]: a lock word, a ring buffer and ring queues of waiters that keep their capacity. A waiter is claimed with compare-and-swap before it is woken, so a select waiting on several channels and timers fires exactly once. Queued entries whose waiter has been claimed are skipped and dropped lazily. An operation that completes at once allocates nothing. A buffered send or receive that needs no waiter runs inline in __chan_send and __chan_recv. An operation that must wait allocates the waiter and value box under the lock it already holds, queues them, releases the lock and parks, so each blocking send or receive takes the lock once. Green threads to wake are readied after the lock is released. select locks its channels in address order and tries each arm with a probe that returns the green thread to wake, using a stack slot as the receive box. A ready arm allocates nothing. When no arm is ready and there is no else, select allocates one waiter, queues it on every channel with the stack slots as boxes, releases the locks, adds the after timers and parks. When woken it deletes the timers and clears the slots. Channel lock word: 0 when free, 1 when held, 2 when held with sleepers. rt_lock takes a free lock with one compare-and-swap. A contender that finds the lock held makes 4 polling rounds. Each round is a pause loop that waits 8,000 timestamp-counter ticks, doubling every round, before it reads the word, so contenders do not bounce the cache line that holds the channel's fields. The contender checks the stop flag each round and takes the lock with a compare-and-swap when it reads 0. After the rounds it yields its OS thread once, then exchanges 2 into the word. Reading 0 means it holds the lock; otherwise it waits on a futex until woken and exchanges again. While it sleeps its OS thread counts as stopped, so a collection can proceed. rt_unlock exchanges 0 into the word and wakes one sleeper only when the old value was 2. C calls run on the OS thread's system stack (8 MB in a static program). Around a C call the generated code pushes the callee-saved registers on the green thread's stack, records where the green thread stopped, marks the thread as in C and switches stacks. On return it marks the thread running again, waiting if a collection is under way. A C callback runs on the green thread's stack. Its thunk marks the thread running, switches back to the green thread's stack below the C call's saved registers, and locks the green thread to the OS thread until it returns, because the C frames live on that OS thread's system stack: if the callback waits, the OS thread waits with it. Callbacks must arrive on the thread that made the C call. A green thread locked to its OS thread, by a callback or by sync.lock_thread, keeps a lock count. When it parks, its OS thread is marked in-call, hands its runnext to the global queue, wakes another thread if work is queued or a timer or descriptor wait has no poller, and sleeps on the green thread's status word. ready wakes that OS thread instead of queuing the green thread, and the OS thread marks itself running before resuming it.

The in-process assembler and linker reproduce GNU as and ld and clang and lld-link output byte for byte: internal/asm matches the object bytes of as for Linux and clang for Windows, and internal/link matches the segments, sections, symbols and loaded bytes of ld for ELF and the whole image of lld-link for PE. Layout choices that look arbitrary, such as clang's padding and jump sizes or the XXH3 timestamp, are there to match. The oracle tests in internal/asm and internal/link check this against the pinned tool versions. A static program is assembled by internal/asm and linked in process by internal/link, which writes the executable without running as or ld. It starts at the generated _start. The image is based at 0x400000, below the hot-reload region, and has the layout of ld -static with separate code: a read-only header segment, then read-execute .text, read-only .rodata, and read-write .data and .bss, each page-aligned in memory and congruent with its file offset. .tbss has a PT_TLS segment and the stack is non-executable. Symbols resolve across the sections of the one object. PC32 and PLT32 resolve alike, and Abs32 and Abs32S fail when the value does not fit. An undefined symbol fails the link and names the symbol. The file carries section headers and a symbol table of the object's non-.L symbols plus __bss_start, _edata and _end, so debug/elf, readelf and gdb read it, and low dev reads it to link patches against it. _start initialises the heap and the scheduler, starts main on the first green thread and enters the scheduler on the process stack. A program that declares C libraries is assembled and linked in process too, by link.Dynamic, as a non-PIE executable that asks /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 to load its libraries. No C start files are linked. The layout follows ld: PT_PHDR, PT_INTERP, a read-only PT_LOAD holding the headers and the dynamic tables, a read-execute PT_LOAD for .plt, .plt.got and .text, a read-only PT_LOAD for .rodata, a read-write PT_LOAD for .dynamic, .got, .got.plt, .data and .bss, then PT_DYNAMIC, PT_TLS, PT_GNU_STACK and PT_GNU_RELRO over everything the loader may write before it starts the program. Each library's -l<name> is the first lib<name>.so in /usr/lib, /usr/lib64, /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, /lib64, /lib and /usr/local/lib, with symlinks followed. DT_NEEDED carries the library's DT_SONAME. c and m name libc.so.6 and libm.so.6. Libraries appear in declaration order, then libc. A library that is missing, or is not a shared object, fails the link and names the library. Every symbol a program calls or takes the address of is checked against the libraries' dynamic symbols, and one that no library exports fails the link. .dynsym records each import with its GLIBC_* version in .gnu.version and .gnu.version_r, and both .hash and .gnu.hash are written. PLT32 calls go through a lazy .plt entry with a JUMP_SLOT, or through a .plt.got entry when the symbol also has a GOT slot. GOTPCREL, GOTPCRELX and REX_GOTPCRELX resolve to a .got slot with one GLOB_DAT for each imported symbol, and a slot for a symbol the program defines holds its address. A direct reference to an imported data symbol would need a copy relocation and fails the link. The generated _start calls __libc_start_main(main, argc, argv, 0, 0, rtld_fini, stack_end) with no init or fini functions, which is all glibc needs: stdio buffers flush and atexit handlers run when the program exits. atexit and at_quick_exit exist only in libc_nonshared.a, so a program that declares them gets shims that tail-call __cxa_atexit and __cxa_at_quick_exit. glibc's start-up code calls the generated C main, which does the same work as _start. When Low's main returns, the program calls exit(0), letting libc run its exit handlers. An error from main prints and exits with status 1. A Windows program is assembled in process with the padding and jump sizes of clang, and linked by link.PE into a PE32+ console executable that starts at start. No import library is read. The image is based at 0x140000000 with 4 KiB section alignment and 512-byte file alignment. It reserves 8 MB of stack and 1 MB of heap, and sets DYNAMICBASE, HIGH_ENTROPY_VA and NX_COMPAT. Sections merge by the name before $, .bss joins .data after its initialised bytes, and .idata joins .rdata. The order is .text, .rdata, .data, the rest by name, then .reloc. Code padding is int3. .rodata is writable. .rdata starts with a debug directory holding one REPRO entry. The header timestamp and that entry carry the low 32 bits of the XXH3-64 hash of the image taken with both zero, so a program always links to the same bytes. The code generator writes the import tables as .idata$2 to .idata$7 with __imp_ labels. The import directory covers the .idata$2 descriptors and a null descriptor the linker adds after them, which is followed by the code generator's .idata$3 terminator, as lld-link lays out the same object, and the import address table directory covers .idata$5. extern "c" imports from msvcrt.dll, extern "m" from the UCRT maths set api-ms-win-crt-math-l1-1-0.dll, which has the C99 functions such as round and cbrt that msvcrt.dll lacks, and any other extern "name" from name.dll. Every Abs64 fixup gets a DIR64 entry in .reloc, one block for each 4 KiB page, so the loader can rebase the image. ImgRel32 resolves to an RVA, and PC32 and PLT32 to rip-relative values. 32-bit absolute, GOT and thread-local references fail the link, and so does an undefined symbol, which the error names. .incbin paths are written with octal escapes for every byte outside printable ASCII, and \ and " escaped, so drive letters, backslashes and non-ASCII names assemble unchanged. Prelude: internal/compiler/prelude.low is Low source compiled ahead of every program. It holds: UTF-8 decoding. The string builder behind interpolation and concatenation. The generic map table. Integer formatting. Float formatting by unrounded scaling against a table of 128-bit powers of ten from 1e-348 to 1e347, which finds the shortest digits that read back to the same value without allocating. Formats and widths for interpolation. A float's exact decimal expansion is its mantissa times 2^e, built in base 10^9 limbs by repeated multiplication by 2 for a positive e and by 5 for a negative one, with the decimal point moved by -e places. An integer's digits are its magnitude. Rounding to the requested decimals or significant digits then works on those digits, using the exact remainder to break ties to even, so f, e, n and pictures need no approximation. NaN and infinities take the default text. cmd/tablegen pow10 generates the table twice: as the __pow10_hi and __pow10_lo functions the prelude holds, and as std/text/pow10.bin, which std/text embeds for float parsing because standard library modules see only the prelude's generic functions and types, not its other functions. Prelude names start with __, which user code cannot use. Four intrinsics are privileged names that the prelude and the standard library can use: __bits gives a float's bit pattern. __str_view turns a []u8 into a str without copying. __hash hashes any Hash value. __zero is the all-zero value of its expected type. A function's IR is built only when main reaches it through a call or a function address, so a program that formats no floats neither builds nor carries any of this code. Reachable functions are built in call order and emitted in declaration order. Standard library: It lives in internal/compiler/std and is embedded in low with go:embed. An import whose path is std or starts with std/ is read from there, never from the project root. Its files are lexed like the prelude, so they may use __ names and intrinsics, and they are left out of the sources low dev watches. embed in a standard library file reads from the embedded tree. Every embedded file, standard or not, is held by its path in the unit, and the assembler resolves .incbin from that map before it reads the disk. Standard library intrinsics: __argc(), __argv(i) and __envv(i) read the argument count, argument i and environment entry i (null past the end) as NUL-terminated ptr[u8]s. The start code saves them from the initial stack in a static program and from main's arguments in a dynamic one. __syscall(n, args...) makes Linux syscall n with up to six integer, bool or ptr arguments and returns rax as i64, a negative errno on failure. It lowers to a syscall instruction, which the code generator emits inline for a constant number on the non-blocking list and as a call to rt_sysblock otherwise (see the Scheduler section). The code generator emits syscall inline: it moves the arguments into rax, rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9 with the parallel move and executes syscall. Being a call, it keeps no value in a caller-saved register across it, which covers the rcx and r11 the kernel clobbers. __slice_ptr(x) gives the data address of a slice or str as a ptr[T]. __mulhi(a, b) is the high 64 bits of the 128-bit product of two u64. It is an IR instruction that becomes one mul. __hash_seed(i) is word i, a literal 0 or 1, of the process's 128-bit hash seed. It is an IR instruction that becomes one load from rt_hash_seed. __extend_by(mut b, n) grows a []u8 by n bytes with at most one allocation and returns the index of the first new byte, whose contents the caller overwrites. __make(n) is a zeroed slice of n elements of the expected slice type, allocated through the runtime's grow routine. __memmove(dst, src) copies min(dst.len, src.len) elements with the runtime's overlap-safe rt_memmove and returns the count. It takes a str source for a []u8 destination. rt_memmove loads up to 64 bytes into registers before storing them and uses rep movsb beyond that. __clock_nanos(id) returns clock_gettime(id) in nanoseconds, or 0 on failure, through rt_clock_nanos. rt_clock_nanos calls __vdso_clock_gettime when start-up found it from AT_SYSINFO_EHDR and the vDSO's dynamic symbol table (DT_HASH or DT_GNU_HASH), and makes the syscall otherwise. __context() reads the current green thread's context slot as the expected pointer type, __set_context(p) replaces it and __has_context() tells whether it is set. spawn copies the parent's slot into the child, and the collector marks every live green thread's slot. __serialize, __deserialize and __schema are the derivations described below, allowed only in std/serde. The garbage collector is a non-moving mark-sweep collector in the runtime: The heap is a 16 GB reservation made with mmap and MAP_NORESERVE. Pages are committed as they are touched. Object layout: Each object has a one-word header. Bits 3 and up hold the object's size in words, header included, so the word is the size in bytes with its low three bits used as flags: bit 0 is always zero, bit 1 marks a free chunk and bit 2 marks an object with no pointers to scan. A bitmap records the first word of every object and free chunk, which resolves pointers into the middle of an object, such as a mut parameter aimed at a heap field. Two summary bitmaps above it hold one bit per non-empty bitmap word and one per non-empty summary word. Finding the start behind an interior pointer skips empty spans 32 KB and 2 MB at a time instead of reading every bitmap word between the pointer and its object's header. A second bitmap of the same shape holds the mark bit of each object. It is zero outside a collection. The start bitmap, the mark bitmap, the first summary bitmap and the mark stack are touched sparsely or in small steps, so they are excluded from transparent huge pages on Linux; one touched byte would otherwise make a 2 MB page resident.
