Allocation buffers: Each OS thread allocates objects of up to 255 words from its own buffer of up to 4096 words without taking the heap lock: it bumps a pointer, writes the header and sets the object's start bit. Only the start-bitmap words at the buffer's unaligned edges are set atomically, with lock or; the other words are updated with a plain or. The summary bits are tested first and set atomically only when clear, and each thread remembers the last bitmap word whose summary bits it set, so allocation skips the summary update while it stays in that word. The memory is reset whenever the thread takes a new buffer. A thread whose buffer is full takes the heap lock and refills it from, in order: the smallest free chunk large enough in the size-class bins below, the exact-size free lists from the largest down, then the end of the heap. It zeroes the buffer's dirty pages in one pass after releasing the lock. A collection turns every thread's unused buffer tail into a free chunk before marking, and an allocation that would leave a single word in a buffer takes that word too, so the sweep finds a header at every object boundary. Free chunks: Free chunks of 64 words or more sit in 256 size-class bins, four per power of two, and a 256-bit bitmap marks the non-empty ones. Bins 0 to 127 hold chunks whose pages may be non-zero (dirty) and bins 128 to 255 hold chunks known to be zero (clean). An allocation scans up to eight chunks of its own bin for the smallest that fits, then takes the first chunk of the lowest non-empty bin above it, preferring a dirty bin to a clean one of the same class, and splits off the remainder. Chunks under 64 words sit in exact-size free lists that only buffer refills read. Objects over 255 words take the heap lock and allocate from the bins, then from the end of the heap, and are zeroed after the lock is released. Dirty pages: A bitmap with one bit per 4096-byte heap page records which pages may hold non-zero words. Pages never handed out are zero from the operating system and are clean. An allocation zeroes only the dirty pages of its range and then marks the whole range dirty, so a large zeroed object that is never written costs no resident memory. Every free chunk of 1 MB or more whose interior pages are all clean is filed in a clean bin. Returning memory: Before the heap end moves for an allocation, every dirty free chunk of at least 1 MB returns its whole interior pages to the operating system on Linux with madvise(MADV_DONTNEED), clears their dirty bits and moves to a clean bin. The walk starts at the first bin that can hold such a chunk and visits dirty bins only, so a chunk is advised once and not again until it is reused and freed. Resident memory holds the live objects and the new one rather than also the chunks that were too small. On Windows the pages stay committed and chunks stay dirty. Collection runs when the words allocated since the last one exceed the words that survived it, with a 4 MB floor. A thread's allocation buffer counts by the size of the chunk it receives, so refilling from small free chunks after a sweep counts no more than the memory handed out. LOW_GCTRACE=1 prints one line per collection to stderr: gc N pause_us= mark_us= sweep_us= live_kb= heap_kb= slow_allocs= refills=, from timestamps around the stop, mark, sweep and restart and from per-thread counters of buffer refills. LOW_GC=off never collects. LOW_GC=stress collects after every 8192 words allocated. An allocation whose type holds no pointers is noscan: new of a pointer-free value, and the backing arrays of slices whose elements hold none, such as []u8, []i64 and []f32. A noscan object is marked but its contents are never read. Other objects are scanned word by word. Allocation and pinning take a heap lock. A collection stops the world: it sets a stop flag and every thread's preemption flag, then waits until each other thread is stopped at a safepoint, idle in the scheduler or in a C call, and holds those threads there until it finishes. Threads waiting for a lock stop for the collector while they wait. Roots come from stack maps. At every call the code generator records the frame words that may hold a heap pointer at that point: the saved callee-saved registers, spill slots of values that may be pointers and are live across the call, and every frame slot. The maps form a table sorted by return address. The words of rt_cells, one per hoisted literal, are scanned as roots in every collection. Green-thread stacks: Every green thread records where it stopped: the return address, stack pointer and frame pointer of the Low code that entered the runtime, and the lowest stack word holding registers it saved. The collector scans each live green thread's saved registers conservatively, then follows its rbp chain, looking up each frame's return address and scanning only its mapped words, and scans the green thread's first frame conservatively. Frames without a map, such as code patched in by hot reload or a loop interrupted by a preemption check, are scanned whole. A green thread that has not started is scanned whole. Values in callee-saved registers are found in the save slots of whichever later frame saved them, or among the registers saved when the green thread stopped. A callback thunk crosses C frames by segment. Its frame record holds the Low caller's frame pointer and return address, so the rbp chain leads from the thunk straight back to the caller. Its frame keeps the bounds of the C frames on the system stack and of the registers the C call saved. The thunk's call site has a map of count -1, which tells the collector to scan both regions conservatively before following the chain. Every candidate word, mapped or not, is checked against the heap before it is followed, so a map that names a word holding an integer is harmless. A ptr counts as a possible heap pointer, so a cstr copy or a pinned object stays alive while Low holds its address. pin records the address in a table of 65536 roots that every collection scans; unpin removes it. Marking resolves a candidate word first by testing the start bit of the word before it, which is the header when the candidate is an object's first field address, and falls back to the summary walk otherwise. Candidates are prefetched through a ring of pending headers before they are marked, so cache misses overlap. Marking sets the object's bit in the mark bitmap and adds its size to the live word count. Newly marked noscan objects are not pushed on the mark stack. Sweeping walks the start bitmap, jumping over empty words with the summary bitmaps, so its cost follows the number of objects and not the address span of the heap. It rebuilds the free lists and bins from empty. Within a word, the start bits without a mark bit are dead and the rest are live. Sweeping jumps between the two kinds of run to coalesce adjacent dead objects into free chunks. A chunk keeps only its first start bit, and the word's mark bits are cleared once it is done. A trailing free run returns to the end of the heap. The derivations are generated as source: When the checker meets __serialize(v, w), __deserialize[T](r) or __schema[T]() with a concrete type, or a print or interpolation of a type other than a number, bool or str, it writes a function for that type in Low text, binding the type and each type it mentions to names like __X0. It parses the text with the prelude's privileges, marks it trusted so it may read and build private fields, and checks it like a generic instance. Calls inside it to the same intrinsics derive the types they reach. Each derived function is cached by type. The serialization of a type is fn(w: Writer, mut path: []i64, v: T). path holds the addresses of the pointers being written, pushed before a pointer's target is written and popped after it; a pointer already on it panics with serde: cycle through *T. __serialize(v, w) starts with an empty path, and the derived code recurses through __serialize_into(w, mut path, x). The rendering of a type is fn(mut b: []u8, mut path: []i64, v: T), which appends to b through the prelude's __append_* functions. path holds the addresses of the pointers being rendered, pushed before a pointer's target is rendered and popped after it. A print or interpolation creates an empty buffer and path, calls it, and uses the buffer as the text; an interpolation appends into the buffer it is composing. A number, bool or str is rendered by the same __append_* functions, so print has one text path: it builds the text and writes it with rt_print_str. __render(v) gives the text of any value with a str quoted, for std/testing's format. Bound names resolve in type positions, struct literals and variant selectors. A field reference T.field is checked as serde.Field[T, F] and lowered to the field's name and index as constants.

Generic templates never reach the IR. The checker keeps an untouched copy of each generic function's syntax tree, clones it for each distinct set of type arguments and checks the clone with those types bound. The result is an ordinary function named like max[i64]; generic structs and enums become ordinary types named like Stack[str]. Instances are made on demand, checked from a work list, and limited to 1000 per template. Symbols escape every character outside A-Za-z0-9_. as . and its hex code, so max[i64] is fn_max.5bi64.5d. SSA is built directly from the checked tree with Braun et al.'s algorithm: variables are read and written per block, phis are created lazily and sealed once a block's predecessors are known, and trivial phis are removed. Every value is one 64-bit word. A struct, enum or result of n words is n SSA values, so aggregates live in registers with no frame temporaries. Narrow integers are kept sign-extended (i32) or zero-extended (u32, u16, u8) in their word. Floats are kept as their bit pattern, f32 zero-extended. Arithmetic, conversion and comparison values carry their type. Frame slots and SSA variables: A variable passed as mut to a function, captured by a closure, or of a C or vector type lives in a frame slot (or a heap box when captured) and is accessed with loads and stores. Every other variable is pure SSA. push, __extend, __extend_by and delete take their mut operand in place. On an SSA variable they read and write its words (a slice's pointer, length and capacity) as SSA values, so a slice that is only pushed to, indexed and passed by value stays in registers. Lengths and capacities these builtins compute are typed integers and never count as pointers. Integer division carries its zero and overflow checks inside the instruction. A constant divisor other than 0 and -1 needs neither check. A call to a C function becomes a ccall carrying its C signature: the symbol, the type of each argument, which arguments are mut places, and the result type. internal/amd64 classifies the signature for the target. On Linux the System V AMD64 rules classify each argument word: Integers, bool and pointers take rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8 and r9. Floats take xmm0 to xmm7. An extern struct of at most 16 bytes is split into eightbytes that go to vector registers when every field in them is a float and to integer registers otherwise. A larger struct, or one that does not fit in the registers still free, goes on the stack. Variadic f32 arguments are widened to f64, and al holds the number of vector registers used. A struct result of at most 16 bytes comes back in rax, rdx, xmm0 and xmm1 by class. A larger one is written to a buffer whose address goes in rdi. Narrow integer, bool and f32 results are re-extended, and so are narrow places passed as mut once the call returns. On Windows the Win64 rules apply. Every argument takes one of four slots, rcx, rdx, r8 and r9, and a float also takes the matching xmm0 to xmm3; a variadic float is passed in both. The slots after the fourth go on the stack above 32 bytes of shadow space. An extern struct of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes passes in its slot. Any other struct is copied into the caller's outgoing area and passed by address, and a struct result of another size is written to a buffer whose address goes in the first slot. Results come back in rax or xmm0. Every frame keeps rsp 16-byte aligned at its calls, as C requires: frames are rounded to 16 bytes, and _start rounds the space it reserves for main's result. An extern struct value is its C bytes, one word per eightbyte. Its locals and parameters live in frame slots. A field is loaded or stored at its own width, and a struct literal or a field of a computed value goes through a temporary slot. A struct whose size is not a multiple of 8 is stored and loaded up to its last byte, with 4-, 2- and 1-byte accesses for the final partial word, so writing a nested field or an element of a view never touches the bytes after it. defer keeps a stack of deferred statements per block and lowers them again at every exit from that block. Drop and using: A struct's drop becomes a function T..drop whose parameters are the struct's fields. Every droppable type gets a generated T..release that calls T..drop and then the releases of its droppable fields. A using binding adds a deferred if flag { T..release(x) } to its block. A move reads the value and clears the flag. Moves are found by a flow-sensitive pass over each checked function body, which joins moved states across branches and runs a loop body a second time when an iteration moves a binding. == on a struct is the conjunction of its fields' comparisons. On an enum it compares tags, then branches on the tag to compare only that variant's fields, since the other payload words are undefined. An extern struct is stored in two frame slots and compared field by field at each field's offset and width, so padding is ignored. Function values and closures: A Low function value is two words: a code address and an environment pointer. Code reached through a function value takes the environment as parameter word 0. A closure is checked in place and becomes a function named after its parent, such as counter..c1. Its environment is a heap array, or 0 when it captures none. Environment words follow the order of the closure's captures. A captured variable that is assigned after its binding, passed as mut, a C struct or a vector lives in a heap box allocated when it is bound. Every access, in its own function and in closures, loads and stores through the box, and the environment holds the box pointer in one word. Any other captured variable stays an SSA variable of its function and the environment holds its words inline. The closure reads them into SSA variables on entry. spawn binds its callee and arguments to such variables, so a spawn allocates the environment and nothing else. A named function used as a value goes through an adapter, name..value, which drops the environment and calls it. A call through a function value moves the code address to r10 and calls it, passing the environment and the arguments like any call. A call through an extern fn value is a ccall with the same plan as a named C function. A C callback is a thunk, cb_name, emitted once per program for every function used as one. It saves the C argument registers, re-extends narrow integers and bool from them and from the C stack, calls the function with Low's convention on the green thread's stack and moves a float result to xmm0. On Windows it also saves and restores xmm6 to xmm15, which C treats as callee-saved. Every loop's back-edge block is marked. The code generator ends it with the poll check described under Code generation. spawn f(a, b) becomes a block that binds the callee and the arguments to fresh locals and passes a closure calling f with them to rt_spawn. Sends, receives, close and channel loops call the prelude's instances for the element type. select calls the prelude's per-arm helpers and the runtime's rt_lock_all, rt_timer_add and rt_park. funcaddr gives a function's code address, its thunk, or an extern function's address through the GOT. Functions reached only through funcaddr are kept. In dev builds every C function gets a global trampoline, cfn_name: jmp name, and calls go through it, so a patch can link against the running binary. An embed becomes an address and a length. The data is emitted with .incbin under a label named by the file's content hash, so a changed file changes the code of every function that embeds it. Every value records whether it may hold a heap pointer. Loads, parameters and call results take this from their type's word layout, where an enum word counts as a pointer if any variant puts one there. Constants, typed arithmetic, string literals and frame addresses never hold pointers. Untyped address arithmetic and anything unclassified count as pointers. A phi holds a pointer if any input may. A str is two words and a slice three. An element access computes pointer + index * stride after a check instruction, which compares unsigned and jumps to the index panic. Packed elements load with movzx, movsxd or a 32-bit mov and store at their width. Maps: A map [K: V] is a pointer to the prelude's generic __Map[K, V], whose entries slice holds __Entry[K, V] records of a live flag, the key and the value. An open-addressing index of entry numbers with linear probing finds them. Deleted entries leave tombstones until the next rebuild, which compacts the entries in order and resizes the index to keep it at most three quarters full. Integer, bool and pointer keys hash their word and str keys their bytes, both with the seeded multiply of the Maps section. Every concrete map type instantiates __map_new, __map_get, __map_set, __map_delete, __map_len, __map_next, __map_key and __map_value for its key and value types. Map literals, lookups, assignments, delete, .len and loops become calls to them. A compound assignment such as m[k] += v is a get, the operation on the value or zero, and a set. push and the formatting helpers call the runtime's grow routine and the prelude. The buffer behind an interpolation lives in a frame slot passed as a mut argument. A push that finds the slice full grows it to twice the capacity plus 4. Counted push loops: A counted loop for i in a..b whose whole body is push(mut xs, v) becomes one reservation instead of a push per iteration. xs must be an SSA variable. v must be made only of literals, other variables, field reads, conversions, unary operators and non-trapping arithmetic or comparison on numbers. The trip count is b - a as an unsigned word when a < b; the loop is skipped otherwise. A trip count above 2^40 bytes of elements calls the grow routine with an impossible size so the program stops with the out-of-memory panic. The slice grows once to exactly its length plus the trip count, or not at all when the capacity already suffices, and its length becomes that sum. When xs is known to be empty the growth is unconditional. A value that is zero in every word (a zero constant or a conversion of one) needs no stores in a freshly grown buffer, since the runtime returns zeroed memory. Otherwise, and in the no-growth case for a zero value, the elements are written with a counted loop. A value that calls a function, can trap or reads the slice itself keeps the push loop. String building: The prelude appends a whole string to a []u8 with __extend, which grows the buffer at most once and copies the bytes with the runtime's rt_memmove, so concatenation, interpolation, bytes and str(b) copy in bulk. An integer is formatted by counting its digits against powers of ten, growing the buffer once with __extend_by and writing the digits from the end. A concatenation chain and an interpolation, including interpolations and chains nested inside either, are flattened into one list of pieces. Adjacent literal pieces merge. Every piece is evaluated first, in order. The result buffer is allocated once with the grow routine at the sum of the literal bytes, the lengths of the str pieces and the widest rendering of each number (20 for an integer, 25 for a float, 5 for a bool), which no rendering exceeds: the longest float is a negative value with exponent -6 and 17 significant digits, -0.0000012345678901234567. A chain with no number pieces copies each piece with rt_memmove at a running offset. With number pieces the buffer lives in a frame slot, str pieces are copied at its length and numbers go through the prelude's __append_*. A piece with a width adds the width's size to the estimate, is appended into the buffer and then padded in place by __align, which counts code points from the byte offset where the piece started. A literal piece with a width is kept as a piece rather than merged into the text around it. A piece with a format calls __append_decimal (d), __append_radix (x, X, b, which masks a signed value to its type's width), or __append_int_layout or __append_float_layout (f, e, n and pictures) with the format's digits, decimals, grouping and mode as constants. An f32 is widened to f64 first, which is exact. A piece with a format or a derived rendering can write more than its estimate. A composition containing one appends its literal and str pieces with __append_str, which grows the buffer when needed, instead of copying at a running offset. String ordering calls the prelude's __str_cmp. Unreachable blocks are pruned after construction. Frame-slot promotion: A frame slot is promoted to SSA values by the optimiser when its address is used only by word-sized loads and stores at word offsets inside it, and is never passed to a call, stored, compared with another address or reached through arithmetic with a variable. Its stores disappear, each load becomes the value stored on every path that reaches it, and phis join the paths. A slot read before any store reads an undefined value. A slot of a C or vector type, a select box, a lock array and a slot with more than one address value stay in memory. After inlining, a mut argument whose callee is inlined therefore lives in registers. Loads and stores carry the flags raw (a narrow or tail access of a C struct, or load and store) and trap (load, which is never discarded). Optimiser: An optimiser runs over each function's SSA before phis are classified. It keeps each value's type, float width and may-hold-a-pointer flag. A value that replaces another holds a pointer if either did. A pass leaves the control-flow graph alone, so phi inputs and predecessor lists stay valid while it runs. Between passes a branch on a constant becomes a jump to the taken successor, blocks left unreachable are pruned together with their predecessor entries and phi inputs, and trivial phis are removed. The pass runs again until no branch folds. The optimiser builds a dominator tree with the Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy algorithm and walks it from the entry, so each value sees only facts established by its dominators. The tree is generic over its node type and the code generator builds it over machine blocks. Predecessors that the entry cannot reach are ignored. Constant folding and simplification: Copies are propagated, and integer operations, comparisons and not on constants are folded at their own type: i32 results are sign-extended and u8, u16 and u32 results zero-extended exactly as the generated code would leave them. Division and remainder of constants by zero or by -1 are never folded, so the runtime panic and the overflow case stay in the instruction. Adding, subtracting, or-ing, xor-ing or shifting by zero, multiplying by one, and multiplying or and-ing by zero reduce to an operand or a constant. Multiplication by a power of two becomes a shift. Division and remainder by a constant other than 0 and -1 become arithmetic on the 64-bit word, which is exact for narrow operands because they are kept extended. A divisor of 1 is the operand or zero. Unsigned powers of two are a shift or a mask. Signed powers of two add (x >> 63) >>> (64 - k) before the arithmetic shift so the result truncates toward zero. A negative divisor negates the quotient. Any other divisor multiplies by a magic number with the high-multiply instruction, signed (imul) or unsigned (mul), adds the operand back or halves and re-adds it when the magic number needs 65 bits, shifts, and for signed values adds the dividend's sign bit. A remainder is the dividend minus the quotient times the divisor. Signed division by the minimum 64-bit value stays an instruction with no checks. Common subexpressions are removed within the dominator tree for add, subtract, multiply, and, or, xor, shifts, conversions, function addresses and check. Comparisons, constants and loads are not merged: a load may observe a store, and a comparison that stays single-use can fuse into its branch. Bounds-check elimination: A check [i, n] is removed when an identical check dominates it, or when i < n is known on the path and i is known to be non-negative. A branch on a single-predecessor block's comparison of integers establishes i < n on the true edge of i < n, on the true edge of n > i, on the false edge of i >= n and on the false edge of n <= i. i is non-negative when it is one of: a non-negative constant; an unsigned value; a value a dominating signed comparison bounds below by a constant of at least 0 (or by -1 strictly); a product of non-negative values that cannot overflow; an induction variable that starts non-negative and only grows by a non-negative step without overflowing. A variable stepping by one cannot overflow below a bound it is compared against. Any other step cannot overflow when the upper bounds of the variable and the step, added, stay within the type's range. An upper bound is derived for a value from a constant, from the width of a narrow unsigned type, from a dominating signed comparison against a value that has an upper bound (strict comparisons subtract one), and for a sum or product of two non-negative values from their upper bounds when the result stays within the type's range. Only comparisons whose block dominates the use contribute. A check [i, n] with a constant n is removed when i is non-negative and its upper bound is below n. Branch facts also record i <= n on the false edge of i < n and the true edge of i >= n. These never remove a check and never prove a step cannot overflow. A length that is a phi satisfies n >= L when every input satisfies it on its incoming edge, by being L, a constant at least L, a phi that does, or a value that a fact on the input's dominators bounds below by L. When i < L is known and n >= L holds, i non-negative removes the check, and otherwise the check compares against L instead of n, which keeps the same panics. A slice filled by a counted push loop from 0 to L has length L when L > 0 and 0 otherwise, so indexing it by a counter below L needs no check. Dead-value removal: Values nothing reads are removed, together with groups of values that only read each other, such as a phi and the add feeding it. Only these operations are removed: constants, strings, embeds, undefined values, phis, add, subtract, multiply, and, or, xor, shifts, negation, not, complement, conversions, sqrt, floor, comparisons, function addresses, high multiplies, trailing-zero counts, loads, float division, and integer division or remainder by a constant other than 0 and -1. Every other instruction stays, including calls, stores, checks, vector instructions, frame slots and divisions that can panic. An unread load through a reference, a slice element or a frame slot is removed, since *T values are never null and an index is checked before its element is loaded. A load through a ptr[T] stays, so a null raw pointer traps even when the value is unused. Float arithmetic, negation, sqrt, floor and conversions between integers, f32 and f64 are folded on constants with the result the SSE instruction produces. f32 operations round to single precision. A float to integer conversion of a NaN or an out-of-range value gives the minimum 64-bit value. Unsigned 64-bit conversions are left to the instruction. A result that is NaN is never folded, so the sign and payload of a NaN come from the hardware. Loop-invariant code motion: It works on natural loops found from back edges whose header dominates the latch, innermost first, in loops with a single outside predecessor that ends in a plain jump. That predecessor is the preheader. Only values whose operands are defined outside the loop or already hoisted move: multiply, and, or, xor, shifts, negation, not, complement, conversions, sqrt, floor, function addresses, high multiplies, trailing-zero counts, float division, and add, subtract or shift that is not the constant-offset address arithmetic an addressing mode absorbs. Loads, checks, calls, stores and integer division stay where they are, so a loop that runs zero times executes nothing it would not have executed. A constant a hoisted value reads is copied into the preheader, because the code generator defines a constant that is not an immediate at its first use. Strength reduction replaces i * c by an add induction variable when i is a basic induction variable of a loop with a constant step, and replaces i * c + d derived from it the same way. The new variable starts at the start value multiplied by c in the preheader and steps by step * c on the back edge, with 64-bit wrapping arithmetic, so the result equals the product for every start, step and trip count, including overflow and negative steps. Devirtualisation and specialisation: A call through a function value whose code address is a function address becomes a direct call that keeps the environment argument. Before inlining, a function loses its function-address and environment parameter words when it is never called through a function value, is not main or a callback, and receives the same function address and the same constant environment from every direct call site. The parameters become the constants, the arguments leave every call site, and the function and its callers are simplified again. Calls from the function to itself that pass its own parameters unchanged count as agreeing. This runs for up to four rounds, so a function value handed down through several calls reaches the call that uses it. A function of at most 150 values that calls a function-value parameter, or hands it to another call, is cloned per function address when its direct call sites pass two or more different function addresses for that parameter, or one function address with different environments. Each clone takes the call sites of one function address and is named name..withN.target, where N is the first parameter word. The clone has that word as the constant, drops the environment word too when every one of those call sites passes the same constant, and is simplified, so its call through the function value becomes direct. Calls from the clone to the original that pass the parameters unchanged call the clone. The original stays for the remaining call sites. A function gets at most 4 clones, and clones add at most 4000 values to the program. The same conditions let an integer parameter that receives one and the same constant from every direct call site become that constant, but only when it pays: the function is simplified as a copy with the constants substituted and as a copy without, and the substitution is kept when the copy with it has fewer checks, blocks or values besides constants and parameters. Inlining: Release builds inline direct calls bottom-up over the strongly connected components of the call graph. A callee is eligible when it: is not part of a cycle; is not a callback; has at most 48 values besides constants, parameters and results; has at most one loop and an entry block no jump returns to; uses no vector instruction. Frame slots, ccalls and runtime calls are cloned with the body, and the callee's slots are appended to the caller's. A callee of at most 6 values is free. Any other site is charged to the caller, which grows by at most 240 values, and to the program, whose budget is a fifth of its value count before inlining, at least 6000 and at most 40000. The last quarter of the program budget is kept for call sites inside loops. A caller inlines up to four rounds. Each round takes its sites inside the deepest loops first, then the smaller callees, then the earlier values; splits the call's block; clones the callee's blocks with parameters bound to the arguments; forwards a single return's values or joins several returns in phis; and simplifies the caller. Calls that an inlined body or a devirtualised call exposes are inlined in the next round. Loop back edges keep their marks, and checks and divisions keep their panics. Dev builds do not inline, specialise or hoist literals, so hot reload patches see every function and every literal's data. A compiler.Profile chooses the target, whether the IR is optimised and whether code generation is hot-reloadable. Release(target) optimises and generates plain code. Dev skips the optimiser, generates fn_table code and is Linux-only. Literal hoisting: A release build hoists a non-empty slice or map literal whose elements are all constants: integer, float, bool and str literals, negated numbers, none, enum variants without payload and non-C struct literals of constants. The checker marks a literal read-only when it is the operand of an index, a for or .len, or is bound by a let whose every use is such an operand. An assignment, a mut argument or any other use anywhere in the target path of an element or field makes the binding non-read-only. Each hoisted literal owns a word of rt_cells. The code loads the word, and when it is 0 builds the literal as usual and stores the pointer, so the first evaluation builds it and a racing thread at most builds a second equal copy. A read-only literal uses the cell's pointer, as a slice of its length for a slice. Any other use copies it: a slice with one grow call that moves the template's bytes, a map with the prelude's __map_clone, which copies the entry array and the index. A literal below the copy thresholds of the Slices and Maps sections is built each time in that case. Block merging and jump threading: A block that ends in a jump to a block with no other predecessor and no phis is merged into it. A block that holds a phi and at most one more value and branches on that phi, or on its negation, is skipped by a predecessor that passes a constant: the predecessor jumps to the successor the constant selects.

Phis and layout: Critical edges are split and each phi becomes a parallel copy at the end of every predecessor, emitted with cycles broken through r11. An argument whose live range ends at that copy prefers the phi's register, and the phi prefers the registers of its arguments, so a loop-carried value usually needs no move. Block layout: Blocks are laid out in reverse post-order, visiting the false successor first so the true successor follows its branch. Inside a loop, the true arm of an integer == comparison against a constant is treated as rare when it holds a loop, a call, a return or an unreachable end. The blocks between the branch and its false successor move after the last block of the innermost loop, so the common path falls through to the back edge. A light arm stays in line, because the extra taken branches would cost more than the arm when it is the common path. A jump or branch to an empty block goes to that block's final target, a jump to the next block in layout is omitted, and a conditional branch whose true target is next is inverted. A block holding phi copies is never empty. Loop latches: A loop's latch whose header holds only a fused compare and branch ends with that compare and a conditional branch to the body, after the poll check when the block has one, instead of a jump to the header. A header with up to 12 instructions, calls included, is copied after the latch instead, so the back edge tests the condition without a jump and the first test still runs at the original header. A comparison used only by the branch that ends its block is fused into a cmp and conditional jump. Addressing: A load or store addresses [base + index*scale + disp] at every width. A 64-bit add read only by addresses folds into them, as does a shl or mul by 1, 2, 4 or 8 feeding the index. A constant operand becomes the displacement. Other strides keep one multiply and fold the add and the displacement. The folded base and index are uses of the load or store, so they stay live to it, across blocks where the definition dominates. A base or index in a spilled slot is reloaded into r10 or r11 immediately before the instruction. An instruction with a memory operand takes any other temporary from rax. Load folding: A load is folded into its only consumer as a memory operand when both are in one block and no store, call, runtime call, vector operation or poll lies between them. Integer arithmetic, logic, bounds checks and compares fold a 64-bit load. A narrow load is never folded into a 64-bit operation. It folds only into a compare of the same type against a constant the type holds, as cmp of a sized memory operand with an immediate. Scalar SSE arithmetic and compares fold a load of the operation's own width, f64 or f32. A float multiplication by 2.0 is an addition of the operand to itself, which is exact for every input including NaN, infinities and signed zeros. Other float constants keep their multiply. Boolean branches: A branch on not x swaps its successors instead of computing the complement, which is exact for float comparisons as well. A comparison read only by not is emitted with the inverted condition. A block that only branches on a boolean phi is threaded: a predecessor that passes a constant jumps to the successor the constant selects, a predecessor that passes the condition of its own branch jumps to the matching successor, and any other predecessor branches on the value it passes. Evaluation order and short-circuiting of && and || operands are unchanged. A branch on the result of a not or a comparison defined in its own block uses that operand directly, so the not and the materialised boolean are not emitted. Spilling: A value's spill weight is the sum over its uses and definitions of 8 raised to the block's loop depth, capped at depth 4. Loop depth counts the natural loops containing the block, found with the dominator tree the optimiser also uses; a cycle with more than one entry is not a loop. When no register is free the allocator spills the conflicting value with the lowest spill cost, breaking ties by the later end of its live range. The allocator runs three times per function, with the spill cost set to the weight, to the weight divided by the length of the live range and to the weight divided by its square root. It keeps the assignment whose spilled values have the lowest total weight plus 2 for each callee-saved register it uses. The weight alone wins ties. Constants that fit in 32 bits are used as immediates and take no register. An undefined value used as an operand or stored to memory is the immediate 0, so a variant's unused payload words never hold stale pointers. Narrow integer results: Results of narrow integer operations that can leave the type's range are re-extended with movsxd, movzx or a 32-bit mov. A u32 add, subtract, multiply, negation, complement and constant left shift uses the 32-bit form of the instruction, whose write zero-extends and needs no re-extension. A conversion to an integer type that holds every value of the source type is a register copy. A right shift of an extended value needs no re-extension. Unsigned comparisons and branches use the unsigned condition codes, and unsigned division uses div. A division by a constant other than 0 and -1 that reaches the code generator, which is signed division by the minimum 64-bit value, emits no zero or -1 test. Float registers: Float values live in xmm2 to xmm15; xmm0 and xmm1 are scratch. A value is a float register value when it is produced or consumed by float arithmetic, a float comparison, a conversion, sqrt or floor. A float that only passes through moves, calls, stores and phis stays in a general register. Scalar SSE instructions (addsd, subss, sqrtsd, roundsd, cvttsd2si and so on) work on registers directly, with a spilled operand as a memory operand. An f32 in an xmm register keeps bits 32 to 63 zero, so movq moves it to a general register or the frame unchanged. movq is used only where a float meets an integer word: call, return and parameter words, stores and loads, bit casts, and C argument registers. A float constant that does not fit in 32 bits is a .rodata quadword, shared by value and used as a memory operand. Zero is xorps. A float comparison used only by the branch that ends its block is fused into ucomisd or ucomiss and a conditional jump. < and <= swap their operands and use ja and jae, so an unordered result is false. == and != also test the parity flag. Shifts and rotates: Variable shift counts go through cl, with rcx saved in r11 around the shift. Counts above 63 take a separate path. The pair (x << k) | (x >> (w - k)) is one rol when it meets all of these: both shifts act on one u32 or u64 value x of width w, k is a constant between 1 and w - 1, the shifts are read only by the or, and they appear in either order. No other combination is a rotate. exp is a runtime routine: range reduction by ln 2 split into high and low parts, a degree-13 polynomial, and scaling by two powers of two so subnormal results stay in range. A comparison of a str against a literal of up to 16 bytes is inline: a length compare, then one compare of the bytes at the pointer against an immediate of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, or two when the length is none of these, ending in sete. The literal's address and length are never materialised and the comparison is not a call. Any other str equality moves the arguments into the argument registers, returns 0 without calling rt_str_eq when the lengths differ and calls it otherwise. Register allocation: Registers are assigned by linear scan over each value's live segments, so a value does not occupy a register where it is dead and a register's holes hold other values. rcx, rsi, rdi, r8 and r9 hold values that are not live across a call. rbx and r12 to r15 hold values that are, and are saved in the function's frame when used. Values that find no register are spilled to the frame. rax, rdx, r10 and r11 are scratch. A growth call, rt_grow_scan or rt_grow_noscan according to whether the new buffer may hold pointers, takes the old pointer, the used bytes and the new size in rax, rdx and r10 and returns the new pointer in rax. It preserves every other general register, so a value that cannot hold a pointer stays in rcx, rsi, rdi, r8 or r9 across it. A value that may hold a pointer is treated as live across a call: the routine saves the preserved registers below the scanned part of the stack, where the collector does not read them. The routine records the caller's return address and frame pointer like any runtime entry, and the old buffer stays reachable through the words it keeps in the scanned region. Float register values are allocated from xmm2 to xmm15 by the same scan. No xmm register survives a call, so a float live across a call is spilled, and spilled floats are not in the stack maps. A function that uses vectors gets no float registers, so its float operations go through xmm0 and xmm1. Register preferences: A value used as a call argument prefers that argument's register, a parameter prefers the register it arrives in, and a copy and its source prefer each other's registers. The result of a two-operand add, subtract, multiply, and, or, xor, shift or float divide prefers the register of its first operand, and for a commutative operation of its second, so the instruction can work in place. Where it cannot share, it avoids the register of the operand it still has to read. Wrapped saves: A function whose calls all lie below one block, the nearest common dominator of its call blocks, saves the callee-saved registers it uses at the head of that block instead of in the prologue and restores them only on returns reached through it. The paths that skip the block use no callee-saved register, have no calls or polls and are at most 8 instructions, copies included, where they rejoin the shared tail, which is duplicated for them. A value defined on a skipping path and live into the block is copied at the end of that path into a fresh value, and the block's head copies it into the original. The original lives only below the block, so a loop counter initialised on the light path stays in a caller-saved register. A value defined in the region below the block and live into it that crosses a call is given a fresh value there. Save slots keep their frame positions, and the stack maps name every save slot at every safepoint. A vector function is not wrapped. The block and the tail are found with the same dominator tree that the optimiser uses. Frame modes: a function has one of three. A full frame is built in the prologue. A function with a wrapped region builds its frame, push rbp, mov rbp, rsp and sub rsp, at the head of the block that holds the saves, and the paths that skip the block return with a bare ret. This needs every skipping block to be free of anything that reads or writes the frame: no spilled value, frame address, slot access, parameter beyond the sixth, poll, panic or return wider than two words. A function with no calls, polls, panicking checks, frame slots or spilled values and no callee-saved register has no frame at all and contains no safepoint. A frame slot's address is not held in a register: a load or store through it addresses [rbp+offset] directly and any other use computes the address with lea into a temporary where it is needed. A spilled value copied from another value whose live range it does not overlap shares that value's slot, so splitting a value at the wrapped block adds no slot-to-slot copy. A call result in rax or rdx that is read once, by the instruction directly after the call, stays there and is not moved. The immediate consumers are integer arithmetic and logic, a store of the value, call arguments, the return, a branch condition and a phi copy. A result word nothing reads is not moved at all. A block that only returns, with at most four predecessors that end in a jump, is copied into them, so each returns without a jump. A return restores with leave, or pop rbp in a frame of size 0. The last instruction of a returning block writes rax directly when it defines the first result and nothing else reads it. Up to two results are placed with a parallel move. Instruction selection: An add or subtract of a constant or a register into a different register is lea. A multiply by a constant is the three-operand imul. A commutative operation takes whichever operand already sits in the destination. A compare with 0 is test. A compare of a memory operand with an immediate reads the memory directly. The constant 0 is xor r32, r32 where the flags are dead. A 32-bit add or subtract into a different register is a lea with a 32-bit destination and 64-bit address registers. A move that undoes the move before it is dropped. The poll check is the TLS_POLL macro, which compares the thread's preemption flag with 0, and jne to an out-of-line stub that calls rt_poll and jumps back to a label placed directly after the jne. On Linux TLS_POLL is cmp byte ptr fs:[-8], 0; on Windows it reads the flag through rt_tls_slot and gs. Alignment: Every function and every C callback thunk starts on a 32-byte boundary. A program for Linux is assembled with branch alignment, which pads so that no jump, and no fused compare and jump, crosses or ends at a 32-byte boundary. Hot patches are assembled without it. A loop that is a single back-edge block, ends in its own conditional jump and has at most four instructions and phi copies besides the poll, if any, and the compare starts on a 32-byte boundary, so the whole loop sits in one window and needs no padding inside. Calling convention: The first six argument words go in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8 and r9. The rest go in an outgoing area at the bottom of the caller's frame, so rsp does not move inside a function. Up to two result words return in rax and rdx. Wider results are written to the outgoing area after the stack arguments. Argument and parameter registers, general and xmm, are filled with a parallel move that breaks cycles through r11.

A vector local lives in a frame slot, like a variable passed as mut, and a vector expression evaluates to the address of a slot holding its result. A vector operation is one IR instruction, vector, taking the destination and operand addresses, or vectorscalar for mask. At calls, returns, fields and other aggregates a vector is its words, loaded from or stored to a slot. A let of a computed vector adopts the slot of the result instead of copying it. A function containing vector instructions is compiled twice. Its symbol is a stub that jumps to the AVX2 version when the CPU and the operating system support AVX2, and to the SSE2 version otherwise. rt_cpu_init checks cpuid and xgetbv at startup. LOW_SIMD=sse2 in the environment selects the SSE2 versions, which the fixture runner uses to test both. The AVX2 version uses three-operand VEX instructions on ymm registers. A slot written once and read only by vector instructions later in the same block, with no call in between, is kept in ymm8 to ymm15 instead of memory. vzeroupper runs before every call and return of such a function. The SSE2 version splits 256-bit operations into two 128-bit halves and keeps every vector in memory. An operation without an instruction in the version being generated runs as a scalar loop over the lanes in a scratch area of the frame. These operations are pshufb on SSE2, 64-bit multiplication, minimum, maximum and comparison where unavailable, byte shifts and arithmetic 64-bit shifts. Unsigned comparisons flip the sign bit of both operands and compare signed.

Module Contents std/ui/geometry Point, Size, Rect, Edges, Corners and Color, all in f32. std/ui/layout The flexbox engine over a tree of styled nodes. std/ui/font TrueType parsing, glyph outlines, the rasteriser and the embedded fallback font. std/ui/text Shaping, line breaking, measurement and the glyph atlas. std/ui/scene Quads, shadows and sprites with their clip rectangles and draw order, and batching. std/ui/gpu The Vulkan renderer, its shaders, offscreen targets and swapchains, and the generated Vulkan bindings. std/ui/platform Windows, input events and the waiting loop: Wayland, xkbcommon and the generated Wayland bindings on Linux, user32 and kernel32 on Windows. std/ui/geometry, std/ui/layout, std/ui/font, std/ui/text and std/ui/scene only compute, so they run on both targets with no library. std/ui/gpu and std/ui/platform hold one file per target for what differs, surface_linux.low and surface_windows.low, wayland_linux.low and win32_windows.low, behind one API (see Modules under Syntax). The generated bindings are private to the module that uses them. std/ui/gpu/vulkan.low holds the types and constants, and vulkan_linux.low and vulkan_windows.low the commands, linked from libvulkan.so and vulkan-1.dll. std/ui/platform/wayland_linux.low holds the Wayland bindings. A Linux program that opens a window links libvulkan.so.1, libwayland-client.so.0, libxkbcommon.so.0 and libc. A Windows one imports vulkan-1.dll, user32.dll and kernel32.dll.

internal/wlgen/protocols holds the Wayland protocol XML, wayland.xml and xdg-shell.xml. go run ./cmd/wlgen -o internal/compiler/std/ui/platform/wayland_linux.low internal/wlgen/protocols/wayland.xml internal/wlgen/protocols/xdg-shell.xml generates the Wayland bindings. Every interface given in one run shares an Interfaces record of wl_interface tables that interfaces() builds in C memory. The record keeps every block it allocates, listener copies included, and release_interfaces(ifs) frees them once the connection is closed. A reference to an interface that no given protocol declares is an error. A request becomes interface_request(...) over wl_proxy_marshal_flags, taking the Interfaces record when it creates an object of a known interface. wl_registry_bind takes the interface table and version. Destructor requests pass WL_MARSHAL_FLAG_DESTROY, and an interface without a destroy request gets one that calls wl_proxy_destroy. Objects are ptr, strings ptr[u8], fixed an i32. Events become an extern struct listener of extern fn fields, each defaulting to a generated function that ignores the event, so a listener names only the events it handles. interface_add_listener(ifs, proxy, listener, data) copies it into the record's C memory. Callbacks receive the listener's data pointer, a pinned Low object. Enum entries are constants such as wl_shm_format_argb8888: u32. Names that clash with Low keywords or builtins gain a trailing _. internal/vkgen/registry holds the Vulkan registry, vk.xml.gz from Vulkan-Docs v1.4.363, and vulkan.list, which selects extensions, commands, extra types such as pNext structures, and the library each target loads. go run ./cmd/vkgen -registry internal/vkgen/registry/vk.xml.gz -select internal/vkgen/registry/vulkan.list -o internal/compiler/std/ui/gpu writes vulkan.low and one vulkan_<os>.low per target. A command line that ends with a target name, such as command vkCreateWaylandSurfaceKHR linux, goes only to that target's file, and library windows vulkan-1 names the library its extern block links. Commands and every type they reach are generated, skipping Vulkan SC variants. Enum values come from the core enums, every Vulkan feature level and the selected extensions. A handle is a one-field extern struct, ptr for dispatchable handles and i64 for the others, so VkBuffer {} is the null handle and handles of different kinds do not mix. Structures and unions become extern structs whose fields all have defaults: zero, null, the empty handle, or for sType the structure's own value, so a literal names only what it sets. A union takes the layout of its widest member. A fixed C array becomes numbered fields, name_0 to name_N, with an accessor Struct_name(s) that returns them as a slice, or as a str for a character array. Vulkan types map to u32 (uint32_t, VkBool32, VkFlags, 32-bit flag bits), i32 (int32_t, enums), i64 (uint64_t, VkDeviceSize, VkFlags64, size_t), u16, u8, f32 and f64. Platform types such as HWND and wl_display* are ptr. Pointers to known types become ptr[T]; void*, function pointers and pointers to pointers become ptr. A command's single input or output through a pointer is a mut parameter; an array or optional pointer is a ptr[T]. Enum entries and API constants are constants such as VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM: i32, and vk_make_api_version builds version numbers. Both generators emit declarations without pub. internal/vkgen and internal/wlgen fail when the checked-in files differ from what the generators produce. std/ui/gpu/shaders holds the GLSL and its SPIR-V. go run ./cmd/shadergen internal/compiler/std/ui/gpu/shaders compiles each stage with glslc to a .spv and records the SHA-256 sums of the sources and the .spv files in shaders.sum.

std/ui/platform gives both targets one API: open(Options) -> Window ! Error creates a window of a logical size with a title. Window is droppable; releasing it destroys the window and closes the connection. A window belongs to the green thread that opened it. next(w, timeout_ms) -> []Event ! Error returns the events that arrived, waiting until at least one arrives, a Waker fires or the timeout passes. A negative timeout waits without limit. The first next after open returns a Resized. waker(w) -> Waker is a copyable handle; wake(k) makes the waiting next, or the next one, return a Woken. Each wake gives one Woken. native(w) -> Native gives the handles Vulkan needs to make a surface: the wl_display and wl_surface on Linux, the HINSTANCE and HWND on Windows. Error is NoDisplay(detail) when there is no compositor or no desktop, Unsupported(detail) when the windowing system lacks something the window needs, Failed(call, code) with the call's error code, and Disconnected. Event is Resized(width, height, scale) in logical pixels, CloseRequested, PointerMoved(x, y), PointerLeft, PointerDown(button, x, y), PointerUp(button, x, y), Scrolled(dx, dy), Key(KeyEvent), FocusChanged(bool) and Woken. Pointer positions are logical pixels from the top left of the window. A KeyEvent carries a Key (Named(NamedKey) for Enter, Escape, Tab, Backspace, Delete, the arrows, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down and F1 to F12, or Character(str), the key's text with at most Shift applied), the text it produces with the modifiers held, the Modifiers (shift, control, alt, super), whether it is a press or a release, and whether it repeats. Control+A is Character("a") with empty text. Modifier keys, and keys with neither a name nor text, give no event. The scale is a whole number: the Wayland surface's preferred buffer scale, or the window's DPI plus 48 divided by 96 on Windows. A Gpu made with gpu.open_for draws into the window, so it is released before the Window. Wayland: open connects to the display, binds wl_compositor, xdg_wm_base and wl_seat from the registry, and makes a surface with an xdg_toplevel. It returns once the first configure has been acknowledged, failing with Unsupported when none arrives within five seconds. The window has no decorations and sets no cursor. Listener callbacks run during wl_display_dispatch_pending on the green thread that called next and append to the window's event queue, a pinned Low object. A failure inside a callback is kept and returned by the next next. xdg_wm_base.ping is answered inside the callback, xdg_toplevel.close becomes CloseRequested, a configure with a non-zero size becomes Resized, and wl_surface.preferred_buffer_scale sets the scale. The keymap arrives as a file descriptor, which is read with std/sys and compiled with xkb_keymap_new_from_string. Keys are translated with xkb_state_key_get_one_sym and xkb_state_key_get_utf8, and modifiers follow xkb_state_update_mask. libxkbcommon is bound by hand in xkb_linux.low. Key repeat follows the compositor's repeat_info: a held key that produces text or is a named key repeats from a timer inside next. next waits on the display's file descriptor without blocking an OS thread. A green thread started by open waits with wait_readable(fd) each time next arms it and reports readiness on a channel; next prepares the read, then selects on that channel, the waker's channel and an after arm for the timeout, the next key repeat or 60 seconds, cancelling the read when anything else wins. Only one green thread may wait on a descriptor, so a flush that would block retries every millisecond for up to five seconds. A broken or reset connection gives Disconnected. The generated bindings' C memory is freed when the window is released. Win32: open locks the green thread to its OS thread with sync.lock_thread, because a window's messages reach only the thread that created it. It sets per-monitor DPI awareness, registers the LowWindow class once per process, and creates the window with CreateWindowExW, its title converted to UTF-16. A creation error of 0 or access denied gives NoDisplay. The window procedure is a Low callback. It reaches the window's state through GWLP_USERDATA, set from lpCreateParams in WM_NCCREATE, and appends events for WM_SIZE, WM_DPICHANGED, WM_CLOSE, WM_MOUSEMOVE, WM_MOUSELEAVE, the button messages, WM_MOUSEWHEEL, WM_MOUSEHWHEEL, WM_KEYDOWN, WM_KEYUP, WM_SYSKEYDOWN, WM_SYSKEYUP, WM_CHAR, WM_SYSCHAR, WM_SETFOCUS and WM_KILLFOCUS. A failed call inside it is kept and returned by the next next. open queues a Resized for the first next, and a WM_SIZE that repeats the last size or minimises the window gives none. Pointer leave is requested with TrackMouseEvent on the first move, and PointerLeft comes only when it was requested. A press captures the pointer until every button is up. The extra buttons are Other(4) and Other(5). One wheel notch scrolls 48 logical pixels. Virtual-key codes map to Key, with ToUnicode giving the character with only Shift applied. The text of a press comes from the WM_CHAR or WM_SYSCHAR that follows it in the same drain, with surrogate pairs joined. next drains the queue with PeekMessageW, and when nothing is pending waits in MsgWaitForMultipleObjectsEx with the timeout. The OS thread is in a C call while it waits, so other green threads keep running. A Waker posts WM_APP to the window; releasing the window detaches its wakers.

gpu.open() -> Gpu ! Error creates a Vulkan 1.3 instance and device on the first physical device that offers dynamic rendering, synchronization2 and a graphics queue. gpu.open_for(Surface) -> Gpu ! Error also needs VK_KHR_swapchain and a queue that presents to the window, and owns the VkSurfaceKHR it makes from the Surface's display and window handles. Gpu is droppable: it waits for the device to go idle and destroys everything it made. A Target made from it is droppable too and must be released first, which using does when it is bound after the Gpu. gpu.Error is NoDevice, Vulkan(call, result) for a failed call and its VkResult, NoMemoryType(allowed, flags) when no memory type matches, InvalidSize(width, height) for a target smaller than one pixel, and NoSurface for present on a Gpu without a window. describe(e) gives it as text. A Gpu keeps one atlas texture that mirrors the scene.Atlas it was last given, so one Gpu draws with one atlas. It holds three pipelines, one per primitive kind, sharing one descriptor set layout (the instance storage buffer at binding 0, the glyph atlas and its sampler at binding 1) and one pipeline layout whose push constant is the target size in pixels. Each frame in flight, two of them, owns a command buffer, a fence, its semaphores and one host-visible instance buffer per kind that grows by doubling. Drawing a scene writes each kind's instances into its buffer in draw order, uploads the glyph atlas's dirty rows through a staging buffer, and records one vkCmdDraw of six vertices per batch, with firstInstance at the batch's first instance, inside one dynamic rendering pass that clears to the scene's background. target(g, width, height) makes an offscreen Target, an R8G8B8A8_UNORM image. render(g, t, scene, mut atlas) submits a frame and returns, and read(g, t) waits for the queue to go idle and returns the pixels as RGBA bytes. present(g, scene, mut atlas) draws into the next image of the Gpu's swapchain and queues it. The swapchain has a B8G8R8A8_UNORM or R8G8B8A8_UNORM format and FIFO presentation. It is made on the first call at the scene's size in device pixels, or at the surface's current extent when the surface fixes one, and made again when that size changes or acquiring or presenting reports VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DATE_KHR or VK_SUBOPTIMAL_KHR. Each frame in flight has its own acquire semaphore and each image its own render-finished semaphore. A scene of no pixels, or a minimised window, presents nothing. Colours are sRGB-encoded and blended in that space with premultiplied-free SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA blending. C structures that Vulkan reads through a pointer are pinned heap values kept by a droppable Pins list for the duration of the call or the frame. The shaders: Quads have per-corner radii and per-edge border widths. The fragment shader computes the signed distance to the outer and inner rounded rectangles and covers one pixel of anti-aliasing. Shadows are a rounded rectangle blurred by a Gaussian of the given sigma, integrated in closed form along x and sampled four times along y, and drawn over the rectangle grown by three sigma. Sprites sample the R8 atlas as coverage for a monochrome glyph tinted with the sprite's colour. Every instance carries a clip rectangle, and fragments outside it are discarded by alpha.

A Scene holds Quad, Shadow and Sprite instances in device pixels, each with its clip rectangle and its draw order, a counter that increases with every primitive pushed. push_clip and pop_clip keep a stack of clip rectangles; each primitive takes the intersection of the stack. batches walks the three lists, each already in draw order, and merges them into runs of one kind, so primitives of different kinds that overlap draw in the order they were pushed.

A layout.Tree holds nodes in a slice; node(mut t, style, children) and leaf(mut t, style, measure) add one and return its index, and compute(mut t, root, available) places every node. rect(t, node) is its border box in logical pixels relative to the window and content(t, node) its content box. A Style has: display (Flex, or None for a node that takes no space), position (Relative, or Absolute with an Inset of one Dimension per side); direction (Row or Column), justify (Start, End, Center, SpaceBetween, SpaceAround, SpaceEvenly), align_items (Start, End, Center, Stretch) and align_self (those or Auto, which follows align_items); grow, shrink and basis; width, height and their minimums and maximums as Auto, Px(f32) or Percent(f32), where Percent(50.0) is half of the parent's inner size, or of its padding box for an absolute node; margin, padding and border edges in pixels, and gap between children. Sizes, minimums, maximums and basis are border-box lengths, and a box is never smaller than its padding and border. An Auto minimum is zero. The algorithm is CSS flexbox for a single line: Each child's flex basis is its basis, else its main size, else its content size: the measure function's answer for a leaf, the sum or maximum of its children for a container. Free space is distributed by grow when positive and taken by shrink weighted by basis when negative, freezing children that hit their minimum or maximum and repeating until none does. A child's cross size is its own, or the container's inner cross size when it stretches. justify places children on the main axis and align on the cross axis. Auto margins are not supported. Absolute children are placed against the padding box by their insets and do not take part in the flow. One with no inset on an axis is placed on it by the parent's justify or align_items. A leaf's measure function takes the width available to it, unbounded when unconstrained (is_bounded tells them apart), and returns its size.

font.parse(data) -> Font ! Error reads a TrueType font with glyf outlines from the head, hhea, maxp, cmap, hmtx, loca and glyf tables and the optional kern table. It uses a cmap subtable of format 12 or 4, preferring a Unicode one that covers every plane, and the first horizontal kern subtable of format 0. It fails with Unsupported(table) for a CFF font and with Malformed(table) for a table directory entry or loca offset that runs past the data. Glyph data and lookup tables are read when used, and a malformed one gives glyph 0, an empty outline or a zero metric. Font metrics (units_per_em, ascent, descent, line_gap, glyph_count) are i64 font units with y up. scale(f, px) converts them to pixels, and glyph_index, advance and kern look up one glyph or pair. font.fallback() is Go Regular, embedded, under the Go fonts' BSD licence in std/ui/font/LICENSE. outline(f, glyph) gives a glyph's contours of on- and off-curve points, with composite glyphs expanded through their offsets and scales, at most 6 deep and 64 components in all. rasterize(f, glyph, px) gives a Bitmap of coverage bytes with its offset from the pen. The rasteriser scales the outline to pixels, flattens each quadratic curve into lines whose count grows with the curve's size, and accumulates each line's signed area and cover into an f32 buffer. A running sum along each row gives the coverage, clamped to 0..1 and stored as one byte per pixel. text.System holds the fonts, in order of preference, the glyph atlas and the caches. system(fonts) makes one, default_system() one with only the fallback font, and system_with_atlas(fonts, size) one with a smaller atlas. A code point is drawn with the first font that maps it, else with the first font's missing glyph. Shaping maps each code point to one glyph and places glyphs by their advances plus the kern pair adjustment when both come from one font. There are no ligatures, no GPOS, no bidirectional reordering and no complex scripts. text.wrap(mut sys, s, size, width) -> Layout breaks lines after spaces and at \n, and breaks a word longer than the width between glyphs; spaces at the end of a line hang past it. Every line has the first font's ascent, descent and line gap. measure gives a layout's size. Layouts of the same string, size and width are kept until end_frame(mut sys), and cached(sys) counts them. paint(mut sys, mut scene, layout, origin, color, scale) pushes one sprite per visible glyph. Glyph origins are snapped to whole device pixels. The atlas is a 1024 by 1024 R8 image packed in shelves. A glyph is rasterised at its pixel size, rounded to 1/64 pixel, the first time it is drawn, with a one-pixel border. A glyph that does not fit is left out, and so is every glyph after it in the frame; end_frame then clears the atlas so the next frame packs its own text.

std/ui/geometry, std/ui/layout, std/ui/font, std/ui/text and std/ui/scene are tested by testdata/run/ui_* programs, which need no library and so run on Linux and, through TestRunWindows, on Windows. They check layouts against hand-computed rectangles, glyph metrics and rasterised coverage of the fallback font, line breaking, atlas packing and scene batching. internal/uitest builds Low programs that import the std/ui modules and runs them: offscreen renders of every primitive kind, clipping, draw order, frames in flight, instance buffer growth and atlas updates, compared by pixels; they skip without libvulkan or a Vulkan 1.3 device; the Wayland listener callbacks and key translation, driven directly by a program built from the platform's sources; key translation skips without libxkbcommon; a Wayland window that opens, opens again after closing, and presents frames through open_for and present; these skip without a running compositor; every program also built for Windows, and the Win32 platform run under wine with posted and sent messages standing in for input, on windows disabled so the desktop's own pointer does not reach them: opening, pairs of windows, pointer, keys, resizing and waking. internal/vkgen and internal/wlgen check that the checked-in bindings match their generators. Both find their libraries through link.SystemDirs. internal/wlgen tests the generated signatures and checks, then builds a registry client from the vendored protocols and, when a Wayland compositor is running, runs it. internal/vkgen tests declaration parsing, extension enum values and the selection format, checks the shape of the generated bindings, and renders a rounded, bordered quad offscreen with the quad shaders through the bindings and dynamic rendering, comparing pixels. It skips without libvulkan or a Vulkan 1.3 device. internal/shaders checks that the sources and the SPIR-V match the sums recorded in shaders.sum and validates the SPIR-V with spirv-val when installed.

A fixture program is a .low file or a directory with a main.low. Its expectations sit beside it in sidecar files named after it: name.low and name/ both take name.out. internal/fixture reads and writes the sidecars; internal/fuzz/corpus writes fixtures through it and internal/fixture/fixturetest lists programs for the tests. testdata/run holds programs that run on Linux: .out is the expected stdout, empty when absent. .err is the expected stderr. A program has one exactly when it exits with a panic status. .maxrss is a limit on peak memory in KB. .maxtime is a limit on the wall-clock time of one run, as a Go duration such as 1s. Only programs whose point is speed have one. A program with a .maxtime or .maxrss runs on its own, not alongside the others. .needed lists the shared libraries the binary must link, one per line in sorted order. Without it the binary must be static with no interpreter. A program with one has no Windows build. .tags declares what the runner cannot learn from the program: simd marks a program that compiles to vector code and runs a second time with LOW_SIMD=sse2, and linux-only marks a program that uses operating system services the Windows standard library lacks, such as signals, pseudo-terminals, inotify, Unix sockets, file modes or /proc, or relies on a kernel guarantee wine does not keep, such as appends from concurrent threads landing whole, and has no Windows build. The runner fails when simd and the compiled code disagree. testdata/windows holds programs that only run on Windows, with .out and .err. internal/compiler/std/<module>/examples holds the module's examples, with .out and, for an example with no Windows build, a .tags of linux-only. The runner does not check simd for them. testdata/fail holds programs that must fail to compile with the message in .err, with file paths shown relative to the fixture. testdata/lint holds programs whose low lint warnings must equal .warn, one per line with relative paths. A program without a .warn file has none. bench/<name>/main.low are the benchmark programs; the compile benchmark and the determinism test use them.

go test ./... compiles every testdata/run program and std example for Linux, runs it with a one-minute limit, compares stdout with .out and stderr with .err, and applies .maxrss, .maxtime, .needed and .tags. These tests skip on a Windows host, as do the internal/hot tests. TestRunWindows builds every testdata/run program and std example that has a Windows build, and every testdata/windows program, for Windows and compares the same way. It runs them directly on a Windows host and under wine on Linux, where lines wine itself writes to stderr, starting wine client error:, are dropped before the comparison. Every testdata/fail and testdata/lint program is checked against its sidecar. The time zone programs read zone rules from the embedded std/time/tzdata, because host databases differ by release and by build (Debian's includes backzone). They read the host database only for the behaviour of zone.named and zone.local, through zones whose rules every build agrees on. The std/cdp programs print launch failed when no browser starts. CI turns off Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on unprivileged user namespaces so Chromium can create its sandbox. cmd/low compiles each program twice in one process and requires identical SSA form and assembly: every testdata/run program for Linux release, every benchmark for Linux release, Linux dev and Windows, and every testdata/windows program for Windows. internal/compiler compiles inline programs, benchmarks and fixtures and checks what the optimiser and code generator did with them: inlining, specialisation, bounds checks, register use, string comparison, switch lowering and allocation. TestBuiltinsDocumented in internal/check requires each public builtin in internal/check/builtins.go to have an entry in ## Builtins with the same name, parameters and mut markers, and each entry to name a builtin. internal/lsp starts the server over its protocol and checks diagnostics, hover, go-to-definition, references, rename, completion, signature help, inlay hints and symbols. go test ./editors/ compares the keyword, contextual keyword, builtin function, type, constant and constraint lists of the editor grammars and site/highlight.mjs with the lexer and the checker, requires the copied editor files to match their sources, and requires the Zed rev to name a commit whose editors/tree-sitter-low/src equals the current one. The rev check skips outside a git checkout. The UI tests are listed under UI tests. internal/hot tests reload against running programs: state kept across a code swap; functions added; compile errors leaving the program running; heap data surviving a reload while the collector runs; stored function values, closures and callbacks running patched code; instances of an edited generic function patched; restarts on layout, signature and capture changes. cmd/lowfuzz generates well-typed, terminating programs from a choice stream (internal/fuzz/gen), predicts their output with a reference interpreter (internal/fuzz/model), builds each with the release profile and the dev profile, the same optimisation and hot-reload code generation as low build and low dev, runs both, and reports any of these (internal/fuzz/oracle): compiler panic; rejected program; link failure; timeout; release/dev difference; difference from the prediction. The generator covers every integer width, f32 and f64, shifts, conversions, if expressions, functions, and for loops with labelled break and continue. Float values are observed through clamped integer conversions and NaN comparisons. internal/fuzz/reduce minimises each new signature. It removes functions, parameters and statements, unwraps if and loop bodies, replaces expressions with literals or their operands, and shrinks literals, keeping only candidates that still produce the signature. -reduce-tests bounds the compiler runs. The minimised program is saved under -out, one per distinct signature. With -fixtures it is also written there as a testdata/run fixture (.low with the predicted .out and .err, named by content hash) that fails until the bug is fixed. internal/asm tests assemble every program with as or clang and require the same object bytes. internal/link tests link programs with ld or lld-link and require the same segments, sections, symbols and loaded bytes for ELF and the same bytes for PE. LOW_LINK_FULL=1 covers every testdata/run program and benchmark. The padding and relaxation choices these tests compare differ between tool releases, so internal/oracletool pins GNU binutils 2.47 and LLVM 23.1.4. The tests skip when a tool is missing or reports another version.

cd editors/tree-sitter-low npm install npx tree-sitter generate npx tree-sitter test src/ is committed because Zed and Neovim compile src/parser.c and src/scanner.c directly. generate writes every file in src/ except scanner.c, which is the hand-written external scanner behind externals: [$._newline]; regenerate after every change to grammar.js. queries/highlights.scm is the highlight query; zed/languages/low/highlights.scm and nvim/queries/low/highlights.scm are copies of it. The repository holds no symlinks, because Windows checks them out as text. Files shared between editors are plain copies, listed in copies in keywords_test.go, and go test ./editors/ fails when a copy differs from its source.

cd editors/vscode npm install npm run package code --install-extension lowlang-0.1.0.vsix The lowlang.server.path setting overrides the low binary. The Low: Restart Language Server command restarts it.

Run zed: install dev extension and choose editors/zed. Zed builds the Rust extension and compiles the grammar at the commit named by rev in extension.toml, so rev must name a commit that contains the current editors/tree-sitter-low/src; go test ./editors/ fails when src/ differs from rev.

Requires Neovim 0.11 or later. With lazy.nvim: { dir = "~/path/to/lowlang/editors/nvim", build = "nvim -l build.lua" } Without a plugin manager, add editors/nvim to runtimepath and run nvim -l editors/nvim/build.lua once. The build compiles the parser to editors/nvim/parser/low.so with cc. The plugin enables the low language server unless vim.g.low_lsp = false. Indentation uses nvim-treesitter's indentexpr when nvim-treesitter is installed, and cindent otherwise.
struct Input { pub source: *io.Reader pub scratch: []u8 ... }
A source of archive bytes that counts what it takes against a budget. The stream the bytes come from. A buffer for discarding data.
struct Item { pub name: str pub full: str pub info: file.Info }
