An object below a directory found by walk. The path relative to the walked directory, with / separators. The path of the object, joined to the walked directory. What lstat reports for the object.
A file opened exclusively for writing by create. Dropping it closes the file descriptor.
struct Stamp { pub path: str pub mtime: i64 }
A modification time to apply to the path path once an extraction has placed every entry. The filesystem path to stamp. The modification time in seconds since the Unix epoch.
Counts n bytes against the budget of the input. Fails with TooLarge when they would exceed it.
Reads and discards n bytes from budget. Fails with Eof when the source ends first.
Writes all of data to o. Partial and interrupted writes are repeated until every byte is written. Fails with the error of the first write that fails.
Sets the modification time of every stamp with set_mtime, last stamp first, so a directory is stamped after the entries below it.

Returns name normalised with path.clean, or fails when an archive entry of that name is not safe to extract. Fails with Malformed for an empty name, and with Denied for an absolute name, a name containing a NUL byte or a name with a .. segment.
fn create(target: str, mode: i64) -> Output ! io.Error

Creates target exclusively for writing and returns the open Output. An existing file or symbolic link at target is removed first and an existing directory fails with IsDir. The file is created with O_EXCL and O_NOFOLLOW, so a link that appears in between is never followed. mode is masked to 0o777, which drops the setuid, setgid and sticky bits, and the process umask applies. An interrupted open is retried.
fn hardlink(target: str, source: str) ! io.Error
Creates target as a hard link to the existing file source. An existing file or symbolic link at target is removed first and an existing directory fails with IsDir.
Returns an Input over source that accepts at most total bytes through charge.
fn make_dir(target: str, mode: i64) ! io.Error

Creates the directory target with the permission bits mode. An existing directory is kept and its mode is not changed. Any other existing object, including a symbolic link, is removed first. mode is masked to 0o777 and always includes 0o700 so extraction can write into the directory; the process umask applies.

Prepares root as the destination of an extraction. A missing root is created together with its missing parents, each by make_dir with mode 0o755. An existing directory or symbolic link is accepted as it is. Any other existing object fails with NotDir.
fn resolve(root: str, name: str) -> str ! io.Error

Returns the filesystem path of the archive entry name below root. name is checked with clean_name, and a name that cleans to . resolves to root. Each missing parent directory below root is created with mode 0o755, filtered by the process umask. A parent that is a symbolic link fails with Denied and one that is any other non-directory fails with NotDir, so a path never passes through a link below root. The final component is neither created nor checked.
fn set_mtime(target: str, seconds: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the modification time of target to seconds since the Unix epoch and leaves the access time unchanged. A final symbolic link is not followed; the link itself is stamped.
fn symlink(target: str, to: str) ! io.Error

Creates a symbolic link at target that points to to. An existing file or symbolic link at target is removed first and an existing directory fails with IsDir. to is stored as given and is not validated.

Returns every object below root in sorted depth-first order, each directory before its children. root itself is not an item and symbolic links are not followed. Fails with the error of the filesystem call that failed.
fn write_file(target: str, data: []u8, mode: i64) ! io.Error
Creates target as create does, writes data to it and closes it.
fn write_from(target: str, mode: i64, read: fn([]u8) -> i64 ! io.Error) ! io.Error
Creates target as create does and fills it with the chunks read produces until it returns 0. read fills a buffer it is given and returns the count. Fails with the error of read or of the filesystem.

struct Entry { pub name: str pub size: i64 pub mode: i64 pub uid: i64 pub gid: i64 pub mtime: i64 pub kind: Kind pub link: str pub ino: i64 pub nlink: i64 pub dev_major: i64 pub dev_minor: i64 pub rdev_major: i64 pub rdev_minor: i64 }

A cpio archive member: its name and metadata, and for a symbolic link its target. The defaults describe an empty regular file with mode 0o644 owned by id 0. When an entry is written, a value that does not fit its header field fails with TooLarge: 8 hexadecimal digits in Newc and Crc, and 6 or 11 octal digits in Odc. The path of the member inside the archive, as stored. The reader does not check it; extract does. The writer rejects an empty name, TRAILER!!! and a name with a NUL byte. The length of the file data in bytes. A reader reports 0 for a symbolic link, whose target is in link. A writer ignores it and uses the length of the data it is given. The permission bits, including setuid, setgid and sticky; the file type is in kind. The numeric id of the owning user. The numeric id of the owning group. The modification time in seconds since the Unix epoch. The type of object the entry stores. The target of a symbolic link; empty for every other kind. The inode number. Entries with the same ino, dev_major and dev_minor and an nlink above 1 are hard links to one file. A writer assigns the next unused number, starting at 1, when this is negative, which is the default. The number of links to the file. A value above 1 marks the entry as one name of a hard-linked file; extract recreates the links. In Newc and Crc only the last link of a file carries its data. The major number of the device that holds the file. The minor number of the device that holds the file. The major number of the device a Char or Block entry stands for. The minor number of the device a Char or Block entry stands for.

The header layout of a cpio archive. A Reader detects the layout of each entry from its magic number. A Writer writes every entry in the format it was made with. The SVR4 newc format, magic 070701: hexadecimal header fields and names and data aligned to 4 bytes. The SVR4 format with a checksum, magic 070702: Newc plus the byte sum of each regular file's data. The POSIX portable odc format, magic 070707: octal header fields and no alignment.
enum Kind { File Dir Symlink Char Block Fifo Socket }

The type of object a cpio entry stores, taken from the file type bits of its mode. A regular file. A directory. A symbolic link; its target is in Entry.link. A character device. A block device. A named pipe. A socket.
struct Limits { pub name: i64 pub entry: i64 pub total: i64 }

Bounds a Reader applies to the input, so a hostile archive fails with TooLarge instead of exhausting memory. The largest accepted name field in bytes, including its terminating NUL, and the largest accepted symbolic link target. The default is 65536. The largest accepted data size of one entry in bytes. The default is 1 << 30. The most bytes the reader accepts from the source across headers, names, data and padding. The default is 1 << 30.
A streaming cpio reader made by reader, reader_with or bytes_reader. Call next for each entry and read its data with read_body or read_entry before calling next again.
A cpio writer made by writer or stream_writer. Add entries in order and call finish to write the trailer.
Returns a Writer that collects an archive in format in memory; output returns the bytes.

Extracts the entries of r below dir, creating dir and its missing parents. Each name goes through archive.resolve, so an absolute name, a .. segment, a NUL byte or a path through a symbolic link below dir fails with Denied. Files are created exclusively and without following links, and an existing file or link at the target is replaced. Permission bits are masked to 0o777, so setuid, setgid and sticky bits are dropped, and the process umask applies. Modification times are applied to files as they are written and to directories once all entries are placed. Symbolic links are created with their stored target, which is not validated. Character, block, fifo and socket entries are skipped. Hard links are recreated: files that share dev_major, dev_minor and ino with an nlink above 1 are linked to the one entry that carries data. A group with no data becomes an empty file with the other names linked to it. Fails with the errors of next and of the filesystem.

Returns the next entry, or none at the TRAILER!!! entry. Every later call returns none. Data of the previous entry that was not read is read and discarded, which still checks the checksum of a Crc entry. The target of a symbolic link is read into link and its size is 0. Fails with Eof when the input ends before the trailer, with Malformed for an unknown magic number, a non-digit in a header field, an empty or unterminated name or an unknown file type, with Unsupported for the binary cpio format, and with TooLarge when a limit is exceeded.

Reads up to dst.len bytes of the current entry's data into dst and returns the count, or 0 once the data is exhausted. Fails with Eof when the source ends first. For a regular file in the Crc format the byte sum is checked when the last byte is read, and a mismatch fails with Malformed. A directory has no data and a symbolic link's data was already read by next, so both return 0.
Returns the rest of the current entry's data in a new slice. Errors are those of read_body. The slice is empty for a directory and a symbolic link.

Writes the entry e with data as its contents. data is used for a File only; a Symlink stores e.link and every other kind stores nothing. e.size is ignored. A negative e.ino is replaced by the next unused inode number. A Crc entry carries the byte sum of its data. Fails with Invalid after finish, for an empty name, for TRAILER!!! and for a name or link with a NUL byte, with TooLarge when a value does not fit its header field, and with the error of the sink.

Writes a directory name with the permission bits mode, owned by id 0 with a modification time of 0.

Writes a regular file name with data and the permission bits mode, owned by id 0 with a modification time of 0.

Writes names as hard links to one file whose metadata is e. Every name gets e with name replaced and an nlink of names.len, and all share one inode number. In Newc and Crc only the last name carries data; in Odc every name does. e.name and e.nlink are ignored. Fails with Invalid when names is empty or e.kind is not File, and otherwise as add.

Writes a symbolic link name that points to target, with mode 0o777, owned by id 0 with a modification time of 0.

Directories, symbolic links, which are not followed, and regular files are archived with the mode, owner and modification time that lstat reports. Other objects are skipped. Regular files that share a device and inode are written with add_links. The archive is built in memory and ends with the trailer. Fails with the error of the filesystem call that failed.
Extracts the cpio archive in data below dir, as extract_from does.

import std/archive/tar import std/io /// Builds an archive in memory, compresses it, then reads every entry back. fn main() ! io.Error { let w = tar.writer() w.add_dir("notes", 0o755)? w.add_file("notes/todo.txt", bytes("water the plants"), 0o644)? w.add_symlink("notes/latest", "todo.txt")? let compressed = w.write_gzip(6)? let r = tar.read_gzip(compressed)? for { let entry = r.next()? ?? break match entry.kind { Dir => print("{entry.name} directory") Symlink => print("{entry.name} -> {entry.link}") _ => { let data = r.read_entry()? print("{entry.name} {entry.size} bytes: {str(data)}") } } } }
struct Entry { pub name: str pub size: i64 pub mode: i64 pub uid: i64 pub gid: i64 pub mtime: i64 pub kind: Kind pub link: str }

A tar archive member: its name, metadata and, for a link, its target. The defaults describe an empty regular file with mode 0o644 owned by id 0. A writer stores values that do not fit a ustar header field, such as a long name or a large size, in a pax extended header. The path of the member inside the archive. A reader joins a ustar prefix to the name and applies pax and GNU long names. It does not check the result; extract does. A directory written by a Writer gets a trailing /. The length of the entry's data in bytes. It is 0 for a directory, symbolic link or hard link. A writer ignores it and uses the length of the data it is given. The permission bits as the header stores them, which can include setuid, setgid and sticky. The numeric id of the owning user. The numeric id of the owning group. The modification time in seconds since the Unix epoch. A pax mtime record replaces the header value and drops any fractional part. The type of object the entry stores. The target of a Symlink or Hardlink; empty for other kinds.
enum Kind { File Dir Symlink Hardlink Other }

The type of object a tar entry stores, taken from its type flag. A regular file. A directory. A symbolic link; its target is in Entry.link. A hard link to an earlier entry named by Entry.link. Any other type flag, such as a device or a FIFO. The reader returns it with its data. extract skips it and the writer rejects it with Unsupported.
struct Limits { pub header: i64 pub entry: i64 pub total: i64 }

Bounds a Reader applies to the input, so a hostile archive fails with TooLarge instead of exhausting memory. The most bytes of extended header records, pax and GNU long name and link, accepted for one entry. The default is 1 << 20. The largest accepted data size of one entry in bytes. The default is 1 << 30. The most bytes the reader accepts from the source across headers, data and padding. For read_gzip it also bounds the decompressed size. The default is 1 << 30.
A streaming tar reader made by reader, reader_with, bytes_reader or read_gzip. Call next for each entry and read its data with read_body or read_entry before calling next again.

A tar writer made by writer or stream_writer. Add entries in order and call finish to end the archive. Headers are ustar. A name over 100 bytes that cannot be split at a / into a name and a prefix of up to 155 bytes, a non-ASCII name or link target, a link target over 100 bytes, and a size, id or modification time that does not fit its header field are written in a pax extended header.

Extracts the entries of r below dir, creating dir and its missing parents. Each name goes through archive.resolve, so an absolute name, a .. segment, a NUL byte or a path through a symbolic link below dir fails with Denied. Files are created exclusively and without following links, and an existing file or link at the target is replaced. Permission bits are masked to 0o777, so setuid, setgid and sticky bits are dropped, and the process umask applies. Modification times are applied to files as they are written and to directories once all entries are placed. Symbolic links are created with their stored target, which is not validated. A hard link is created to the path its target resolves to below dir, so the target must already exist. Entries of kind Other are skipped. Fails with the errors of next and of the filesystem.

Returns the next entry, or none at the end of the archive. The end is a zero block or the end of the input at a block boundary, and every later call returns none. Data of the previous entry that was not read is skipped. Pax extended headers (path, linkpath, size, mtime, uid, gid) and GNU long name and link records apply to the entry that follows; pax global headers are skipped. Numbers are read as octal or base-256. Fails with Malformed for a bad checksum, a bad number or an entry with an empty name, with Eof when the input ends inside a block or an entry, with TooLarge when a limit is exceeded, and with Unsupported for a sparse file.
Reads up to dst.len bytes of the current entry's data into dst and returns the count, or 0 once the data is exhausted. Fails with Eof when the source ends first.
Returns the rest of the current entry's data in a new slice. Errors are those of read_body. The slice is empty for a directory, symbolic link and hard link.
fn add(w: *Writer, e: Entry, data: []u8) ! io.Error

Writes the entry e with data as its contents. data is used for a File only; every other kind stores nothing. The size recorded is data.len for a File and 0 otherwise. A directory name gets a trailing / when it lacks one. Only the low 12 bits of e.mode are stored. Fails with Invalid after finish, for an empty name and for a name with a NUL byte, with Unsupported for Other, and with the error of the sink.

Writes a directory name with the permission bits mode, owned by id 0 with a modification time of 0.

Writes a regular file name with data and the permission bits mode, owned by id 0 with a modification time of 0.

Writes name as a hard link to the entry target that was added earlier, with mode 0o644, owned by id 0 with a modification time of 0. target is not checked against the entries already written.
fn add_symlink(w: *Writer, name: str, target: str) ! io.Error
Writes a symbolic link name that points to target, with mode 0o777, owned by id 0 with a modification time of 0.
Ends the archive with two zero blocks of 512 bytes. A second call does nothing. After finish, add fails with Invalid.
Returns the bytes collected by a Writer made with writer. Call it after finish for a complete archive. It is empty for a stream writer.
Finishes the archive and returns it compressed as gzip at deflate level. Fails with Unsupported for a stream writer. The compressed bytes are only returned; output still returns the plain tar.
Returns a Reader over the archive in data with the default Limits.

Returns a tar archive of the tree below dir. Names are relative to dir, which is not an entry itself, and come in sorted depth-first order. Directories, symbolic links, which are not followed, and regular files are archived with the mode, owner and modification time that lstat reports. Other objects are skipped, and hard-linked files are stored as separate copies. Each file is read fully into memory. Fails with the error of the filesystem call that failed.

Returns the archive create builds, compressed as gzip at deflate level. Fails as create and write_gzip do.
Extracts the tar archive in data below dir, as extract_from does.
Extracts the gzip-compressed tar archive in data below dir. Fails as read_gzip and extract_from do.
Returns the entries of the archive in data without their data. Fails as next does.

Decompresses the gzip data and returns a Reader over the tar archive in it, with the default Limits. The whole archive is decompressed in memory before this returns. Fails when the data is not valid gzip or decompresses to more than Limits.total bytes.
Decompresses the gzip data and returns a Reader over the tar archive in it that applies limits. Fails as read_gzip does, with limits.total as the decompressed size limit.

Returns a Reader over source that applies limits.

An opened zip archive: its entries and comment, together with the bytes they are read from. Made by open or open_with. The entries in central directory order. The archive comment; empty when there is none.

A zip archive member, as listed in the central directory or given to Writer.add. A writer uses only name, mtime, mode, kind and method; the other fields are computed. The defaults describe a deflated regular file with mode 0o644. The path of the member inside the archive, as stored. A directory name ends in /. A reader does not check it; extract_archive does. The uncompressed size in bytes. The compressed size in bytes as stored in the archive. The compression method. A writer stores a Deflate file uncompressed when deflate would not make it smaller, and stores any other method uncompressed. The CRC-32 of the uncompressed data. The modification time in seconds since the Unix epoch. A reader takes the extended timestamp field when present and otherwise the MS-DOS date and time, which has two-second resolution, or 0 when the date is unset. A writer stores both; dates before 1980 are stored in the MS-DOS fields as 1980-01-01. The permission bits, including setuid, setgid and sticky. A reader takes them from the Unix attributes of an entry made on Unix, and uses 0o755 for a directory and 0o644 for anything else when none are set. The type of object the entry stores. A reader reports a symbolic link from the Unix attributes, and a directory from them, the DOS directory attribute or a trailing / in the name. The offset of the entry's local header from the start of the archive. The general purpose bit flags of the entry. Bit 0 marks an encrypted entry and bit 11 (0x800) marks a UTF-8 name.
The type of object a zip entry stores. A regular file. A directory. A symbolic link; the entry's data is the target path.
struct Limits { pub entries: i64 pub entry: i64 pub total: i64 pub ratio: i64 }

Bounds applied to an archive when it is opened and when an entry is read, so a hostile archive fails with TooLarge instead of exhausting memory. The largest accepted number of entries. The default is 1 << 20. The largest accepted uncompressed size of one entry in bytes. The default is 1 << 30. The largest accepted sum of the uncompressed sizes of all entries in bytes. The default is 1 << 30. The largest accepted ratio of uncompressed to compressed size, for each entry and for the whole archive against its length. The default is 1100.

The compression method of a zip entry. The data is stored without compression. The data is compressed with deflate. A method this module cannot read, with its zip method number in code. Reading such an entry fails with Unsupported, and a writer stores it uncompressed.
A zip writer made by writer or stream_writer. Each entry is written as add is called, compressed in memory, and finish writes the central directory. Entries are written without data descriptors.
fn extract_archive(a: Archive, dir: str) ! io.Error

Extracts every entry of a below dir, creating dir and its missing parents. Every name is checked with archive.clean_name before anything is written, so an unsafe name fails with Denied or Malformed and leaves the filesystem unchanged. Then each entry goes through archive.resolve, which also rejects a path through a symbolic link below dir. Directories are created with their mode. Files are created exclusively and without following links, replacing an existing file or link, with permission bits masked to 0o777 and the modification time applied; the process umask applies. A symbolic link is created with its entry data as the target, which is not validated. Directory modification times are not applied. Fails with the errors of read and of the filesystem.
fn find(a: Archive, name: str) -> Entry?
Returns the first entry whose name equals name, or none.
fn read(a: Archive, e: Entry) -> []u8 ! io.Error

Returns the uncompressed data of the entry e of a in a new slice. Fails with Unsupported for an encrypted entry or a method other than stored or deflate, with TooLarge when e.size exceeds Limits.entry, and with Malformed when the local header is missing or out of range, the stored sizes disagree, the deflate data is invalid, or the length or CRC-32 of the result does not match the entry.

Returns the uncompressed data of the entry named name. Fails with NotFound when there is no such entry, and otherwise as read does.
fn add(w: *Writer, e: Entry, data: []u8) ! io.Error

Writes the entry e with data as its contents. A File is compressed per e.method. A Symlink stores data as the link target. A Dir stores no data and gets a trailing / when it lacks one. The type and the low 12 bits of e.mode are recorded as Unix attributes, e.mtime as an MS-DOS timestamp and as an extended timestamp when it is between 0 and 0xFFFFFFFF, and a non-ASCII name sets the UTF-8 flag. Sizes or offsets of 0xFFFFFFFF or more are written as zip64 extra fields. Fails with Invalid after finish, for an empty name, a name longer than 65535 bytes and a name with a NUL byte, and with the error of the sink.
Writes a directory name with mode 0o755 and a modification time of 0.
fn add_file(w: *Writer, name: str, data: []u8, method: Method) ! io.Error
Writes a regular file name with data compressed with method, with mode 0o644 and a modification time of 0.
fn add_symlink(w: *Writer, name: str, target: str) ! io.Error
Writes a symbolic link name that points to target, with mode 0o777 and a modification time of 0.

Writes the central directory and the end of central directory record. zip64 end records are added when the writer is forced, when the entry count reaches 0xFFFF or when the directory size or offset reaches 0xFFFFFFFF. A second call does nothing. After finish, add fails with Invalid.
Makes the writer use zip64 records for every entry added after the call and for the end of the archive, even when no size or count needs them.
Returns the bytes collected by a Writer made with writer. Call it after finish for a complete archive. It is empty for a stream writer.
Opens the zip archive in data with the default Limits and extracts it below dir as extract_archive does.
Opens the zip archive in data with the default Limits. See open_with.
fn open_with(data: []u8, limits: Limits) -> Archive ! io.Error

Opens the zip archive in data by reading its central directory, applying limits. zip64 archives are supported. Entry data is neither decompressed nor checked until it is read. Fails with Malformed when no end of central directory record is found in the last 64 KiB or the records are inconsistent, with Unsupported for an archive split over several disks, and with TooLarge when the entry count, an entry size, the total size or the compression ratio exceeds a limit.
Returns a Writer that writes the archive to sink. The writer does not close sink, and output stays empty.
Returns a Writer that collects the archive in memory; output returns the bytes.
enum Error { BadCharacter(i64) BadLength BadFrame Overflow(i64) }

Why an Ascii85 or Z85 operation failed. A byte is not valid in the alphabet. at is its index in the input. The input length is not valid: a final group of one character for decode, a length that is not a multiple of 4 for encode_z85 or of 5 for decode_z85. The <~ and ~> delimiters are not both present, or nothing is left between them for the frame to hold. A group of five characters encodes a value above 0xFFFFFFFF. at is the index of the group's last character for decode, and of its first for decode_z85.

Decodes Ascii85 text, with or without the Adobe <~ and ~> delimiters. Whitespace is ignored, including around the delimiters. z stands for four zero bytes and is valid only between groups. A final partial group of 2 to 4 characters yields one byte fewer than its length. Fails with BadFrame when only one delimiter is present, with BadCharacter at the index in s of a byte outside ! to u, with BadLength when the final group has one character, and with Overflow when a group exceeds 0xFFFFFFFF.

Decodes Z85 text. The length must be a multiple of 5 and whitespace is not skipped. Fails with BadLength otherwise, with BadCharacter at the index of the first byte outside the alphabet, and with Overflow when a group exceeds 0xFFFFFFFF.

Returns data encoded as Ascii85 without delimiters. Each group of four bytes becomes five characters in ! to u, and a group of four zero bytes becomes z. A final group of n bytes gives n + 1 characters.
Returns data encoded as Ascii85 inside the Adobe <~ and ~> delimiters.
Returns data encoded as Z85 (ZeroMQ), which uses the 85-character alphabet 0-9a-zA-Z.-:+=^!/*?&<>()[]{}@%$#. Fails with BadLength when data.len is not a multiple of 4.
An atomic boolean, stored in an Int. Copies of a Bool refer to the same cell.
An atomic boolean that starts cleared and is switched with set and clear. Copies of a Flag refer to the same cell.
A 64-bit integer cell that is read and updated atomically. Copies of an Int refer to the same cell. No operation parks the green thread.

An atomic cell holding a value of any type T. Each store_value and swap_value allocates a copy of the new value and replaces a pointer to it, so a pointer from snapshot_value stays valid and unchanged while the cell moves on. Copies of a Value refer to the same cell. An internal lock is held only for the pointer exchange, so no operation parks the green thread.

Sets b to v if it currently equals old, and returns whether it did.
Returns the current value of b.
fn swap_bool(b: Bool, v: bool) -> bool
Sets b to v and returns the value it held before.
Clears f and returns whether this call was the one that changed it from set to cleared.
Sets f and returns whether this call was the one that changed it from cleared to set. Exactly one of several concurrent callers sees true, which makes set suitable for running something once.
fn add_int(i: Int, n: i64) -> i64
Adds n to i and returns the new value. n can be negative.
fn compare_and_swap_int(i: Int, old: i64, n: i64) -> bool
Sets i to n if it currently equals old, and returns whether it did.
Returns the current value of i.
fn swap_int(i: Int, n: i64) -> i64
Sets i to n and returns the value it held before.
fn update_int(i: Int, f: fn(i64) -> i64) -> i64

Replaces the value of i with f applied to it, and returns the stored result. If another green thread changes i while f runs, f runs again on the new value, so f can run more than once and should not have side effects.
fn compare_and_swap_value[T](v: Value[T], seen: *T, next: T) -> bool

Replaces the value of v with next if it still holds the version seen, and returns whether it did. seen is a pointer from snapshot_value. The comparison is by pointer identity, not by equality of the values, so a cell that was stored with an equal value since the snapshot does not match.
Returns a copy of the value currently stored in v.

Returns a pointer to the value currently stored in v, without copying it. The pointed-to value is never modified; later stores make the cell point elsewhere. The pointer identifies a version of the cell for compare_and_swap_value.
Replaces the value of v with next.
fn swap_value[T](v: Value[T], next: T) -> T
Replaces the value of v with next and returns the value it held before.
fn update_value[T](v: Value[T], f: fn(T) -> T) -> T

Replaces the value of v with f applied to it, and returns the stored result. If another green thread stores to v while f runs, f runs again on the new value, so f can run more than once and should not have side effects.
Returns a Value holding a copy of initial.
Why a Base32 decode failed. A byte of the input is not in the alphabet. at is its index in the input. The length of the input, ignoring trailing =, cannot come from a whole number of bytes.

Decodes RFC 4648 Base32 text, with or without = padding. Lowercase letters are accepted. Any number of trailing = is stripped before decoding, so an = anywhere else is a BadCharacter. Fails with BadLength when the unpadded length leaves a remainder of 1, 3 or 6 characters modulo 8, and with BadCharacter at the index of the first byte outside the alphabet. Bits left over in the last character are ignored.
Decodes Base32 text written with the extended hex alphabet 0-9A-V, with or without = padding. The failure cases, trailing padding and case handling are those of decode.
Returns data encoded as Base32 with the RFC 4648 alphabet A-Z2-7, padded with = to a multiple of 8 characters.
Returns data encoded as Base32 with the extended hex alphabet 0-9A-V, padded with = to a multiple of 8 characters.
Returns data encoded as Base32 with the RFC 4648 alphabet A-Z2-7 and no = padding.

Why a Base58 decode failed. A byte of the input is not in the alphabet. at is its index in the input. The four checksum bytes of decode_check do not match the payload. The decoded data of decode_check is shorter than the four checksum bytes.

Decodes Base58 text written with the Bitcoin alphabet. Each leading 1 becomes one leading zero byte, and an empty string gives empty data. Fails with BadCharacter at the index of the first byte outside the alphabet.

Decodes Base58Check text and returns the payload without its checksum. Fails with BadCharacter as decode does, with TooShort when fewer than four bytes decode, and with BadChecksum when the last four bytes are not the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of the rest.
Decodes Base58 text written with the Flickr alphabet. Failure cases and leading-character handling are those of decode.

Returns data encoded as Base58 with the Bitcoin alphabet, which omits 0, O, I and l. Each leading zero byte becomes one leading 1, and empty input gives an empty string. The cost is quadratic in the length of data.
Returns data followed by the first four bytes of its double SHA-256, encoded as Base58 with the Bitcoin alphabet (Base58Check).
Returns data encoded as Base58 with the Flickr alphabet, which is the Bitcoin alphabet with lowercase letters ordered before uppercase. Leading zero bytes become leading 1 characters, as in encode.

Why a Base64 decode failed. The input length is not valid for the padding: not a multiple of 4 when padding is required, or 1 modulo 4 once any optional padding is removed. A byte is not in the alphabet, = is misplaced or not allowed, or the bits left over in the last character are not zero. at is the index in the input.

Whether the = padding to a multiple of 4 characters is written and read. The input is a multiple of 4 characters, ending in zero, one or two =. The input has no =. The input ends in at most two =, or in none.
The standard alphabet of RFC 4648 section 4, whose last two characters are + and /.
The URL-safe alphabet of RFC 4648 section 5, whose last two characters are - and _.
Decodes padded standard Base64. The length must be a multiple of 4, so unpadded input fails with BadLength. = is accepted only as the last one or two characters. Fails as decode_with does.
Decodes unpadded standard Base64. = is rejected. Fails as decode_with does.
Decodes unpadded URL-safe Base64. =, + and / are rejected. Fails as decode_with does.
fn decode_with(s: str, alphabet: str, padding: Padding) -> []u8 ! DecodeError

Decodes s written with the 64 characters of alphabet and the given padding. Fails with BadLength when the length does not suit the padding, and with BadByte at the index of the first byte outside the alphabet, of a misplaced or disallowed =, or, at the final index, when the bits left over in the last character are not zero. Empty input gives empty data.
Returns data encoded as standard Base64 (RFC 4648 section 4), padded with = to a multiple of 4 characters.
Returns data encoded as standard Base64 without padding.
Returns data encoded as URL-safe Base64 (RFC 4648 section 5) without padding. The alphabet uses - and _ in place of + and /.
fn encode_with(data: []u8, alphabet: str, padded: bool) -> str
Returns data encoded with the 64 characters of alphabet, padded with = to a multiple of 4 characters when padded is true.
struct DivMod { pub quotient: Int pub remainder: Int }

The quotient and remainder of a division. The quotient. Its rounding depends on the division that produced it. The remainder, satisfying quotient * divisor + remainder == dividend. Its sign depends on the division that produced it.
enum Error { Empty BadDigit(i64) BadBase DivideByZero Overflow NoInverse Negative NotPositive }

The error type of the fallible big functions. The input contains no digits. The input has a character at byte offset at that is not a digit of the base, or a misplaced _ separator. The base is outside the range 2 to 36. The divisor or modulus is zero. The value does not fit the requested type or size. The value has no modular inverse because it shares a factor with the modulus. The operation is undefined for a negative value. The operation requires a value greater than zero.

An arbitrary-precision signed integer. Stored as a sign and a magnitude of 32-bit limbs. Zero is never negative. An Int is a value: every operation returns a new Int and leaves its arguments unchanged. Operations are not constant time.
Returns the absolute value of a.
fn add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns a + b. Costs time linear in the number of limbs.
fn bit(a: Int, i: i64) -> bool
Returns bit i of a, counting from the least significant bit. A negative a is read in two's complement, so its bits above bit_len are all set. Returns false when i is negative.
fn bit_and(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns the bitwise and of a and b with two's complement semantics for negative values.
Returns the number of bits in the magnitude of a, or 0 for zero.
Returns the bitwise complement of a, which is -a - 1.
fn bit_or(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns the bitwise or of a and b with two's complement semantics for negative values.
fn bit_xor(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns the bitwise exclusive or of a and b with two's complement semantics for negative values.
fn cmp(a: Int, b: Int) -> i64
Compares a with b and returns -1 when a < b, 0 when they are equal and 1 when a > b.
fn divmod(a: Int, b: Int) -> DivMod ! Error

Divides a by b, truncating the quotient toward zero. The remainder takes the sign of a. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero. Costs time proportional to the product of the quotient and divisor limb counts.

Divides a by b so the remainder is never negative. The remainder is in 0..|b|. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero.

Divides a by b, rounding the quotient toward negative infinity. A non-zero remainder takes the sign of b. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero.
fn equal(a: Int, b: Int) -> bool
Returns true when a and b are the same integer.
fn gcd(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns the greatest common divisor of a and b, which is never negative. gcd(0, 0) is zero.
Returns true when a is even. Zero is even.
Returns true when a is less than zero.
Returns true when a is odd, whatever its sign.
fn is_probable_prime(n: Int, rounds: i64) -> bool

Returns true when n is probably prime. Negative numbers, zero and one are not prime. Trial division by the primes below 1000 comes first, then Miller-Rabin. The test is deterministic for n below 2^81. Above that it uses base 2 plus rounds random bases drawn from the operating system's random source.
Returns true when a is zero.
Returns the integer square root of a: the largest r with r * r <= a. Fails with Negative when a is negative.
fn lcm(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns the least common multiple of a and b, which is never negative. Returns zero when either argument is zero.
fn mod_inverse(a: Int, modulus: Int) -> Int ! Error
Returns the inverse of a modulo |modulus|: the x in 0..|modulus| with a * x congruent to 1. Fails with DivideByZero when modulus is zero and with NoInverse when a and modulus are not coprime.
fn modpow(base: Int, exp: Int, modulus: Int) -> Int ! Error

Returns base raised to exp modulo |modulus|, as a value in 0..|modulus|. Uses Montgomery multiplication with a sliding window for an odd modulus and plain square-and-multiply for an even one. A negative exp raises the modular inverse of base to -exp. A modulus of 1 or -1 gives zero. Fails with DivideByZero when modulus is zero and with NoInverse when exp is negative and base has no inverse. Not constant time.
fn modulo(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int ! Error
Returns a modulo b as a value in 0..|b|. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero.
fn mul(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns a * b. Uses schoolbook multiplication for small operands and Karatsuba once the shorter operand reaches 32 limbs.
Returns -a. The negation of zero is zero.
Returns the smallest probable prime greater than n. Candidates are tested with is_probable_prime using 24 rounds. Any n below 2 gives 2.
fn pow(a: Int, e: u64) -> Int
Returns a raised to the power e by repeated squaring. pow(a, 0) is 1 for every a, including zero.
fn quo(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int ! Error
Returns the quotient of a divided by b, truncated toward zero. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero.
Returns a uniformly random integer in 0..n from the operating system's random source. Fails with NotPositive when n is zero or negative.
fn rem(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int ! Error
Returns the remainder of a divided by b, which takes the sign of a. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero.
fn shl(a: Int, n: i64) -> Int
Returns a shifted left by n bits, which multiplies it by 2^n. A negative n shifts right.
fn shr(a: Int, n: i64) -> Int
Returns a shifted right by n bits. The shift is arithmetic: the result is a / 2^n rounded toward negative infinity, so shr(-1, n) is -1. A negative n shifts left.
Returns -1, 0 or 1 for a negative, zero or positive a.
fn sub(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
Returns a - b. Costs time linear in the number of limbs.
Returns the big-endian bytes of the magnitude of a, without leading zeros. Zero gives an empty slice. The sign is not encoded.
fn to_bytes_sized(a: Int, size: i64) -> []u8 ! Error
Returns the big-endian bytes of a left-padded with zeros to exactly size bytes. Fails with Overflow when a is negative or needs more than size bytes.
Returns a as the nearest f64, rounding ties to even. Values beyond the f64 range give an infinity of the same sign.
fn to_f64_scaled(a: Int, exp2: i64, sticky: bool) -> f64

Returns (a + e) * 2^exp2 as an f64 rounded to nearest, ties to even, where e is a fraction below one unit of a that is non-zero exactly when sticky is true. sticky lets a caller that has already discarded low bits of an exact quotient keep rounding correct. Results below the normal range round to subnormals or to zero, and results beyond the f64 range are infinite.
Returns a as an i64. Fails with Overflow when a is outside the range of i64.
fn to_str(a: Int, base: i64) -> str

Returns a written in base using lowercase digits 0-9a-z, with a leading - for a negative number. Zero is "0". Panics when base is outside 2 to 36. Bases 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 take time linear in the limb count; other bases take quadratic time.
Returns a as a u64. Fails with Overflow when a is negative or larger than u64 can hold.
Returns the number of trailing zero bits in the magnitude of a, or 0 for zero.
fn binomial(n: u64, k: u64) -> Int
Returns the binomial coefficient n choose k, or zero when k > n.
Returns n!, the product of the integers from 1 to n. factorial(0) is 1. The product is built by splitting the range in halves so that the large multiplications use Karatsuba.
Returns the Fibonacci number F(n) with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1. Uses fast doubling, so it needs a number of multiplications proportional to the bit count of n.
Returns the non-negative integer whose big-endian bytes are data. Leading zero bytes are ignored and empty input gives zero.
Returns v as an Int, including i64 minimum.
fn parse(s: str, base: i64) -> Int ! Error

Parses an integer written in base. The text may start with + or -, and digits may be separated by single _ characters. Letters are accepted in either case. With base 0 the base is taken from a 0x, 0b or 0o prefix after the sign and is 10 without one; with any other base a prefix is not recognised. Fails with Empty when there are no digits, with BadBase when base is not 0 or in 2 to 36, and with BadDigit carrying the byte offset of a character that is not a digit of the base or of a _ that does not follow a digit.

An exact decimal number coefficient * 10^exponent, with an arbitrary-precision coefficient and an i32 exponent. The representation is not normalised: 1.0 and 1.00 have different exponents and compare equal. strip removes the trailing zeros of the coefficient.
enum Rounding { HalfEven HalfUp Down Up Floor Ceiling }

The rule that picks a neighbour when a result has to be rounded to fewer digits. Rounds to the nearest value and, on a tie, to the one with an even last digit. Rounds to the nearest value and, on a tie, away from zero. Rounds toward zero, discarding the excess digits. Rounds away from zero whenever any discarded digit is non-zero. Rounds toward negative infinity. Rounds toward positive infinity.
Returns the absolute value of d with the same exponent.
fn add(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> Decimal
Returns the exact sum of a and b. The result has the smaller of the two exponents.
fn cmp(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> i64
Compares the values of a and b and returns -1 when a < b, 0 when they are equal and 1 when a > b. Exponents do not matter: 1.0 and 1.00 are equal.
Returns the coefficient of d, which carries its sign.
fn div(a: Decimal, b: Decimal, exponent: i32, mode: Rounding) -> Decimal ! big.Error
Returns a / b with the given exponent, rounded according to mode. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero.
fn equal(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> bool
Returns true when a and b have the same value, whatever their exponents.
Returns true when d is zero, whatever its exponent.
fn mul(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> Decimal ! big.Error
Returns the exact product of a and b. The result's exponent is the sum of the two exponents. Fails with Overflow when that sum does not fit an i32.
fn rescale(d: Decimal, exponent: i32, mode: Rounding) -> Decimal
Returns d expressed with the given exponent. When exponent is at most the exponent of d the result is exact. A larger exponent drops digits and rounds the result according to mode.
Returns -1, 0 or 1 for a negative, zero or positive d.
Returns d with the trailing zeros removed from its coefficient and added to its exponent. Zero becomes exponent 0.
fn sub(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> Decimal
Returns the exact difference of a and b. The result has the smaller of the two exponents.

Returns d in plain notation, never in scientific notation. A negative exponent places the decimal point, so from_i64(5, -2) is "0.05", and a positive exponent writes out trailing zeros. A zero with a non-negative exponent is "0".
fn from_i64(v: i64, exponent: i32) -> Decimal
fn from_parts(coefficient: big.Int, exponent: i32) -> Decimal

Parses a decimal number. The text is an optional + or -, digits with an optional . and fraction, and an optional e or E exponent with its own optional sign. Either the whole part or the fraction may be empty, but one of them needs a digit: .5 and 5. are valid. The exponent of the result is the parsed exponent minus the number of fractional digits, and trailing zeros are kept. Fails with Empty when there are no digits, with BadDigit carrying the byte offset of the first unexpected character, and with Overflow when the exponent does not fit an i32.
An exact rational number num / den over big.Int. A Rat is always in lowest terms and its denominator is positive, so equal values have identical parts.
Returns the absolute value of r.
fn add(a: Rat, b: Rat) -> Rat
Returns a + b in lowest terms.
fn cmp(a: Rat, b: Rat) -> i64
Compares a with b and returns -1 when a < b, 0 when they are equal and 1 when a > b.
Returns the denominator of r, which is always positive.
fn div(a: Rat, b: Rat) -> Rat ! big.Error
Returns a / b in lowest terms. Fails with DivideByZero when b is zero.
fn equal(a: Rat, b: Rat) -> bool
Returns true when a and b are the same rational.
Returns 1 / a. Fails with DivideByZero when a is zero.
Returns true when the denominator of r is 1.
Returns true when r is zero.
fn mul(a: Rat, b: Rat) -> Rat
Returns a * b in lowest terms.
Returns the numerator of r, which carries its sign.
Returns -1, 0 or 1 for a negative, zero or positive r.
fn sub(a: Rat, b: Rat) -> Rat
Returns a - b in lowest terms.
fn to_decimal(r: Rat, exponent: i32, mode: decimal.Rounding) -> decimal.Decimal
Returns r as a decimal with the given exponent, rounded according to mode. The result is r divided by 10^exponent rounded to an integer coefficient, so an exponent of -2 keeps two fractional digits.
Returns the f64 nearest to r, rounding ties to even. Values beyond the f64 range give an infinity of the same sign.
fn to_fixed(r: Rat, places: i64) -> str
Returns r as a decimal string with exactly places fractional digits, rounding half to even. A negative places rounds to a power of ten and writes the zeros out.
Returns r as "n/d", or as "n" when r is an integer.
Returns the exact rational value of d.
Returns the integer n as a rational with denominator 1.
Returns the integer n as a rational with denominator 1.

Parses a rational written as a/b or as a decimal. In the a/b form both sides are base 10 integers with an optional sign. Otherwise the text is a decimal with an optional sign, fraction and e exponent, as accepted by decimal.parse. Fails with Empty when a part has no digits, with BadDigit carrying the byte offset in s of the first offending character, with DivideByZero when the denominator is zero and with Overflow when a decimal exponent does not fit an i32.
fn ratio(n: big.Int, d: big.Int) -> Rat ! big.Error
Returns the rational n / d reduced to lowest terms with a positive denominator. Fails with DivideByZero when d is zero.

A growable set of non-negative integers stored as one bit per member in u64 words. Create one with set. A Set is used through a pointer and grows when a member beyond its capacity is added. Membership operations take constant time; whole-set operations, count and the scans take time proportional to the number of words, and scans skip empty words 64 members at a time. Members must not be negative.
Adds x to s, growing the set when x is beyond its capacity. Adding a member that is present changes nothing.
Removes every member from s, keeping its capacity.
Returns a new set with the same members as s.
Returns true when x is a member of s. Returns false for a negative x and for one beyond the capacity.
Returns the number of members of s.
Returns a new set of the members of a that are not in b. Neither argument changes.
Removes from a every member that is in b.
Returns true when a and b have the same members. Capacity is not compared, so sets of different capacity can be equal.
Calls f with each member of s in increasing order. Stops early when f returns false.
Returns a new set of the members that are in both a and b. Neither argument changes.
Removes from a every member that is not in b.
Returns the largest member of s, or none when it is empty.
Returns the members of s in increasing order.
Returns the smallest member of s, or none when it is empty.

Returns the smallest non-member of s that is at least from. A negative from starts at zero. Every value beyond the capacity is a non-member, so the result is never none and is at most the capacity rounded up to a multiple of 64.
Returns the smallest member of s that is at least from, or none when there is none. A negative from starts at zero.
Returns the number of members of s that are at most x. Returns 0 for a negative x and the total count for an x beyond the capacity.
Removes x from s. Does nothing when x is not a member, including when it is negative or beyond the capacity.
Returns the member of s with zero-based position k in increasing order, or none when k is negative or at least count(s). This is the inverse of rank: rank(s, x) - 1 is the position of the member x.
Returns true when every member of a is also in b. An empty set is a subset of every set.
Adds x to s when it is absent and removes it when it is present. Grows the set when x is beyond its capacity.
Returns a new set of the members that are in a or b. Neither argument changes.
Adds every member of b to a, growing a when b is larger.
Returns a new set of the members that are in exactly one of a and b. Neither argument changes.
Makes a the symmetric difference of a and b: members in exactly one of the two. Grows a when b is larger.
Returns the number of bits needed to write x, which is 0 for zero and 1 for one.
Returns the number of zero bits above the highest set bit of x. Returns 64 when x is zero.
Returns the number of bits set in x.
fn rotl32(x: u32, n: i64) -> u32
Returns x rotated left by n bits, with the bits shifted out of the top re-entering at the bottom. n runs from 0 to 32.
fn rotl64(x: u64, n: i64) -> u64
Returns x rotated left by n bits, with the bits shifted out of the top re-entering at the bottom. n runs from 0 to 64.
fn rotr32(x: u32, n: i64) -> u32
Returns x rotated right by n bits, with the bits shifted out of the bottom re-entering at the top. n runs from 0 to 32.
fn rotr64(x: u64, n: i64) -> u64
Returns x rotated right by n bits, with the bits shifted out of the bottom re-entering at the top. n runs from 0 to 64.
fn select_in_word(x: u64, k: i64) -> i64
Returns the position of the kth set bit of x, counting from zero at the least significant bit. Returns 64 when x has k or fewer set bits.
Returns an empty set with room for members below capacity without growing.
Returns the number of zero bits below the lowest set bit of x. Returns 64 when x is zero. Uses the processor's bit scan instruction.

A compressed bitmap of u32 values in the Roaring format. Values are grouped by their high 16 bits into containers, each stored as a sorted array of up to 4096 values, a bitmap of 65536 bits or a list of runs. Create one with roaring. A Roaring is used through a pointer. Locating a container costs a binary search over the container keys, so single-value operations take time logarithmic in the number of containers plus the cost inside one container.
Adds x to r. Adding a value that is present changes nothing.
fn add_range(r: *Roaring, lo: i64, hi: i64)

Adds every value in the half-open range lo to hi, excluding hi, to r. The range is clamped to 0 through 2^32. Does nothing when the clamped range is empty. Whole containers inside the range are made from a single run, so the cost depends on the number of containers touched, not on the number of values.
Returns the number of values in r in constant time.
Returns a new bitmap with the same values as r, sharing no storage with it.
Returns true when x is in r.
Returns a new bitmap of the values of a that are not in b. Neither argument changes.
Removes from a every value that is in b. b does not change. Containers of a are reused where possible, which avoids copying them.
Returns true when a and b hold the same values. The container representations do not need to match.
Calls f with each value of r in increasing order. Stops early when f returns false.
Returns a new bitmap of the values that are in both a and b. Neither argument changes.
Replaces a with the values that are in both a and b. b does not change. Containers of a are reused where possible, which avoids copying them.
Returns true when r holds no values.
Returns true when every value of a is also in b. An empty bitmap is a subset of every bitmap.
Returns the largest value in r, or none when it is empty.
Returns the values of r in increasing order.
Returns the smallest value in r, or none when it is empty.
Returns the number of values in r that are at most x. x does not need to be in r. Costs time linear in the number of containers before x.
Removes x from r. Does nothing when x is absent. A container that becomes empty is dropped.
fn remove_range(r: *Roaring, lo: i64, hi: i64)
Removes every value in the half-open range lo to hi, excluding hi, from r. The range is clamped to 0 through 2^32. Does nothing when the clamped range is empty.

Converts every container of r to the representation that takes the least space, which can be a list of runs. The values do not change. Runs shrink long consecutive ranges, and serialize writes the runs it finds.
Returns the value of r at zero-based position k in increasing order, or none when k is negative or at least cardinality(r). This is the inverse of rank.

Returns r in the portable Roaring serialization format. The format starts with a cookie that says whether run containers are present, then the container keys and counts, then each container: sorted u16 values for up to 4096 values, a 1024-word bitmap above that, or a list of runs. All integers are little-endian. Call run_optimize first to get run containers.
Returns the number of bytes serialize writes for r.
Returns a new bitmap of the values that are in a or b. Neither argument changes.
Adds every value of b to a. b does not change. Containers of a are reused where possible, which avoids copying them.
Returns a new bitmap of the values that are in exactly one of a and b. Neither argument changes.
Replaces a with the values that are in exactly one of a and b. b does not change. Containers of a are reused where possible, which avoids copying them.

Reads a bitmap in the portable Roaring serialization format. Fails with Malformed when the data is truncated, the cookie is unknown, the container keys are not increasing, an offset does not match the container's position, or a container's values are unsorted, overlapping or disagree with its stated count. Bytes after the last container are ignored.
enum Error { Truncated(i64) BadLength(i64) BadType(i64, u8) BadUtf8(i64) BadString(i64) BadBool(i64) TooDeep(i64) TooLong(i64) Trailing(i64) BadName BadObjectId BadDecimal }

The error returned when decoding or encoding BSON fails. Decoding errors carry the byte offset from the start of the input; offset reads it back and message formats it. The input ends before a value is complete. at is the offset where the missing bytes were expected; for a top-level document whose declared size exceeds the input it is the input length. A document, string or binary length is impossible, or a document does not end where its length says. at is the offset of the length. The element type byte kind is not supported. at is the offset of the type byte. Supported types are the ones in Value; the deprecated types undefined, DBPointer, JavaScript, Symbol and JavaScript with scope are rejected. A string or field name is not valid UTF-8. at is the offset of the string, which for a string value is its length prefix. A string's last byte is not the NUL terminator. at is the offset of its length. A boolean byte is neither 0 nor 1. at is its offset. Documents nest deeper than Options.max_depth. at is the offset of the offending document. A document declares a size over Options.max_length. at is the offset of the document. Bytes remain after the document. at is the offset where they start, which is the length of the document. A field name, regular expression pattern or options string contains a NUL byte, which encode cannot represent. An ObjectId does not hold 12 bytes, or parse_object_id was given something other than 24 hex digits. A Decimal128 does not hold 16 bytes.
struct Field { pub name: str pub value: Value }
A named element of a document. The field name. It cannot contain a NUL byte when encoded. The field value.
struct Item { pub fields: []Field pub length: i64 }
A decoded document together with the number of bytes it occupied. The fields of the document in order. The number of bytes of the input that the document used.
struct Options { pub max_depth: i64 pub max_length: i64 }

Limits for decoding. The deepest document nesting accepted, counting the top-level document as depth 1. Defaults to 64. Arrays count as documents. The largest size, in bytes, that any one document, nested or not, may declare. Defaults to 16777216.

enum Value { Double(f64) Str(str) Document([]Field) Array([]Value) Binary(u8, []u8) ObjectId([]u8) Bool(bool) DateTime(i64) Null Regex(str, str) Int32(i32) Timestamp(u64) Int64(i64) Decimal128([]u8) MinKey MaxKey }

A BSON element value (bsonspec.org, version 1.1). A 64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating point number (type 0x01). A UTF-8 string (type 0x02). It may contain NUL bytes. An embedded document (type 0x03): an ordered list of named fields. Names may repeat. An array (type 0x04). It is stored as a document whose field names are the decimal indexes 0, 1, and so on; decoding ignores the names and keeps the values in order. Binary data (type 0x05) with a subtype byte that says how to interpret data. A 12-byte ObjectId (type 0x07), made of a 4-byte big-endian timestamp in seconds followed by 8 bytes that identify the value. bytes must hold exactly 12 bytes to be encoded. A boolean (type 0x08). A UTC datetime (type 0x09) as signed milliseconds since the Unix epoch. The null value (type 0x0A). A regular expression (type 0x0B) with its pattern and options. Neither string may contain a NUL byte, and neither is validated or reordered. A signed 32-bit integer (type 0x10). An internal MongoDB timestamp (type 0x11): the increment in the low 32 bits and the seconds in the high 32 bits. A signed 64-bit integer (type 0x12). A 128-bit IEEE 754-2008 decimal (type 0x13), held as its 16 little-endian bytes without interpretation. bytes must hold exactly 16 bytes to be encoded. The key that sorts before every other value (type 0xFF). The key that sorts after every other value (type 0x7F).
Returns a one-line description of the error, including the byte offset when it has one.
Returns the byte offset a decoding error refers to, or -1 for BadName, BadObjectId and BadDecimal, which are not tied to a position.
Decodes data, which must hold exactly one BSON document, into its fields, with default Options. Fails with Trailing when bytes follow the document. See decode_with.
fn decode_first(data: []u8, options: Options) -> Item ! Error

Decodes the document at the start of data and reports its size, ignoring any bytes after it. Use it to read a stream of back-to-back documents by advancing data by Item.length. Fails like decode_with except that it never returns Trailing.

Decodes data, which must hold exactly one BSON document, into its fields. The document's declared size must match data exactly: a longer input fails with Trailing, and a shorter one with Truncated. Fails with BadLength, BadType, BadUtf8, BadString, BadBool, TooDeep or TooLong for malformed or over-limit input. Strings, binary data and ids are copied, so the result does not alias data.

Returns a one-line text description of a document, in a notation like JSON with type markers, for logs and tests. Fields print as "name": value in braces, arrays in brackets. Strings are quoted with \" and \\, and every character outside printable ASCII is written as \uXXXX, using a surrogate pair above U+FFFF. Doubles print as NaN, Infinity, -Infinity or a decimal that always contains a ., such as 1.0. An Int32 prints plainly and an Int64 with an L suffix. Other values print as bin(subtype, h'hex'), oid("hex"), date(millis), /pattern/options, timestamp(n), decimal128(h'hex'), true, false, null, minkey and maxkey.

Encodes fields as one BSON document. Returns the bytes with the 4-byte little-endian size prefix and the trailing NUL. Arrays are written with the field names "0", "1", and so on. Fields keep their order and repeated names are kept. Fails with BadName when a field name, regex pattern or regex option contains a NUL byte, BadObjectId when an ObjectId does not hold 12 bytes, and BadDecimal when a Decimal128 does not hold 16 bytes.
Returns the value of the first field called name, or none when there is none. Only the given level is searched; nested documents are not.
Returns a new ObjectId value. The first four bytes are the current time in seconds since the Unix epoch, big-endian, and the other eight come from std/crypto's random bytes.
Returns the lowercase hex text of the bytes of id, two digits per byte.
Returns the creation time in seconds since the Unix epoch stored in the first four bytes of id, read big-endian. id must hold at least 4 bytes.
Returns the ObjectId for 24 hex digits, in either case. Fails with BadObjectId when hex is not exactly 24 hex digits.

A growable byte buffer for assembling text and binary data without the cost of repeated string concatenation. A Builder is passed as mut. The buffer doubles when it fills. Obtain one from builder or with_capacity.
Returns the number of bytes allocated, which is at least len.
Returns the number of bytes written.
fn reserve(mut b: Builder, n: i64)
Ensures b can take n more bytes without growing, leaving its length unchanged.
Empties b and keeps its allocation.
Returns the written bytes as a []u8 that shares storage with b. The slice is not a copy: writes made after reset or truncate overwrite the bytes it holds.
Returns a copy of the written bytes as a str.
fn truncate(mut b: Builder, n: i64)
Shortens b to n bytes and keeps its allocation. Nothing happens when n is negative or not below the current length.
fn write(mut b: Builder, s: str)
fn write_byte(mut b: Builder, c: u8)
fn write_char(mut b: Builder, c: u32)
Appends the UTF-8 encoding of the code point c, one to four bytes. The value is not validated: surrogates are encoded as they stand and a value above 0x1FFFFF gives a malformed byte sequence.
fn write_f64(mut b: Builder, x: f64)
Appends x in the text form string interpolation gives an f64.
fn write_i64(mut b: Builder, n: i64)
Appends n in decimal, with a leading - when negative.
fn write_join(mut b: Builder, parts: []str, sep: str)
Appends the strings in parts with sep between consecutive ones.
fn write_line(mut b: Builder, s: str)
Appends s followed by a newline byte.
fn write_repeat(mut b: Builder, s: str, n: i64)
Appends s n times. Nothing is appended when n is 0 or negative.
Returns an empty Builder with no storage allocated.
Returns an empty Builder with room for n bytes allocated.
The owner of a callback registered with on_cancel. Dropping it removes the callback if the token has not been cancelled yet. The copyable reference to the registered callback.
A copyable reference to one callback registered on a token, which release_on removes. Dropping or copying a handle does not remove the callback.

A cancellation signal shared by pointer between the code that cancels and the code that watches. Cancelling a token once closes its done channel and runs the callbacks registered with on_cancel and on_cancel_handle. A token never becomes uncancelled.
Removes the callback registered by on_cancel without running it. Does nothing if the callback has already run or been removed.
Removes the callback behind h without running it. Does nothing if the callback has already run or been removed.
Cancels t. Closes the done channel and runs the registered callbacks on the calling green thread, in no particular order, after releasing the token's lock. Later calls do nothing.
Returns whether t has been cancelled.
Fails with Aborted if t has been cancelled, and returns otherwise.

Returns a token that is cancelled when parent is cancelled. Cancelling the child does not cancel parent, and it removes the child's link to the parent. If parent is already cancelled, the returned token is cancelled.
Returns a channel that is closed when t is cancelled and never carries a value. Receiving from it parks until cancellation, so it works as an arm of select, for example <-cancel.done(t).

Registers f to run when t is cancelled, and returns the Registration that removes it when dropped. If t is already cancelled, f runs immediately on the calling green thread and the returned registration does nothing. Otherwise f runs on the green thread that calls cancel, so it should not block.

Registers f to run when t is cancelled, and returns a copyable handle to the registration. The callback stays registered until t is cancelled or release_on is called with the handle. If t is already cancelled, f runs immediately on the calling green thread and the handle does nothing.
Sleeps for millis milliseconds and returns true, or returns false as soon as t is cancelled. Parks the green thread while it waits.
Returns a new token that is not cancelled.
struct Entry { pub key: Value pub value: Value }
A key and value pair of a Map. The key. It can be any Value. The value for the key.
struct Item { pub value: Value pub length: i64 }
A decoded value together with the number of bytes it occupied. The decoded value. The number of bytes of the input that the value used.
struct Options { pub max_depth: i64 pub max_length: i64 }

Limits for decoding. The deepest nesting accepted, counting a top-level array, map or tag as depth 1. Defaults to 64. A tag counts as a level. The largest length that any one string, array or map may declare, and the largest total length of an indefinite-length string, array or map. Defaults to 16777216. It bounds memory before anything is allocated.
enum Value { Unsigned(u64) Negative(u64) Bytes([]u8) Text(str) Array([]Value) Map([]Entry) Tag(u64, *Value) Simple(u8) Bool(bool) Null Undefined Float(f64) }

A CBOR data item (RFC 8949). Decoding resolves indefinite-length strings, arrays and maps into their definite equivalents, and encode always writes definite lengths. An unsigned integer (major type 0), 0 to 2^64 - 1. A negative integer (major type 1). The integer is -1 - value, so value 0 is -1 and the smallest integer is -2^64. A byte string (major type 2). A UTF-8 text string (major type 3). The decoder rejects invalid UTF-8. An array (major type 4). A map (major type 5), kept as entries in order. Keys can be any value; the decoder rejects a map with two keys that encode to the same bytes. A tagged item (major type 6): the tag number and the item it applies to. Tags are kept as they are and given no meaning by std/cbor. A simple value (major type 7) other than false, true, null and undefined. Valid numbers are 0 to 19 and 32 to 255. The simple values false and true (0xF4, 0xF5). The simple value null (0xF6). The simple value undefined (0xF7). A floating point number. The decoder turns half, single and double precision floats into an f64; encode writes the shortest of the three that holds the value exactly.
Returns the value of an Unsigned or Negative that fits an i64, and none for any other value, including integers outside that range.

Returns the diagnostic notation of v (RFC 8949, section 8) on one line, for logs and tests. Maps print as {key: value}, arrays as [...], a tag as number(content), byte strings as h'hex', simple values as simple(n) and the others as true, false, null and undefined. Text is quoted with \" and \\ escaped and every character outside printable ASCII written as \uXXXX, using a surrogate pair above U+FFFF. Floats print as NaN, Infinity, -Infinity or a decimal that always contains a .. Integers print in decimal, including Negative down to -18446744073709551616.

Encodes v as deterministic CBOR (RFC 8949, section 4.2). Integers, lengths and tag numbers use the shortest head. Strings, arrays and maps have definite lengths. Map entries are sorted by the bytes of their encoded keys, so the same map encodes to the same bytes whatever its order; entries with the same key are not removed. A float is written in the shortest of half, single and double precision that holds its value exactly, and every NaN is written as the half precision quiet NaN 0xF97E00. A Simple value is written with its number as the argument. It cannot fail.
fn get(v: Value, key: Value) -> Value?

Returns the value of the first entry of the map v whose key equals key, or none when v is not a Map or has no such entry. Keys are equal when their deterministic encodings are the same bytes, so an Unsigned and a Float with the same number are different keys.
Decodes data, which must hold exactly one data item, with default Options. Fails with Malformed when bytes follow the item. See decode_with.
fn decode_first(data: []u8, options: Options) -> Item ! io.Error

Decodes the data item at the start of data and reports its size, ignoring any bytes after it. Use it to read a sequence of back-to-back items by advancing data by Item.length. Fails like decode_with except that trailing bytes are not an error.
fn decode_with(data: []u8, options: Options) -> Value ! io.Error

Decodes data, which must hold exactly one CBOR data item. Every major type is read, including indefinite-length strings, arrays and maps, which arrive as their definite equivalents, tags, simple values and half, single and double floats. Fails with Malformed for truncated input, additional information 28 to 30, a stray break, an indefinite length on an integer or tag, a chunk of an indefinite-length string that is not a definite string of the same type, a simple value 24 to 31 written in two bytes, text that is not valid UTF-8, a map with a repeated key, and bytes after the item. Fails with TooLarge when nesting is deeper than Options.max_depth or a length is over Options.max_length. Strings and byte strings are copied, so the result does not alias data.

Decodes CBOR data into a T through std/serde. Decoding uses the default Options. A tag is ignored and its content is read in its place. null and undefined both read as an absent optional. A float is read from a float or an integer, and an integer from Unsigned or Negative when it fits, failing with serde.Error.Range when it does not. Map keys may be text, integers or booleans, the latter two read as text. A decoding failure becomes serde.Error.Syntax with position 0, except that TooLarge stays serde.Error.TooLarge. Fails with Mismatch when a value has another type and with Missing and UnknownVariant as serde.read describes. In errors, at counts the values consumed so far.
Returns the integer n as an Unsigned or a Negative value.

Encodes v as CBOR bytes through std/serde. Structs and maps become maps with text keys, slices become arrays, []u8 becomes a byte string, optionals become null or the value, floats become floats of the shortest exact precision, and integers become Unsigned or Negative. An enum variant without fields becomes text and a variant with fields a one-entry map from its name to a map of its labelled fields or an array of its positional ones. The output is deterministic, as encode makes it.
An owned running browser. Dropping a Browser calls shutdown_on on its handle. The shared handle of the browser.

A shared reference to a running browser, for use from several tasks. Owns the browser process and its temporary profile directory. shutdown_on stops the process and removes the directory. The DevTools connection to the browser.

A WebSocket connection to the DevTools endpoint of a browser. A background task reads every message, delivers command replies to the waiting call and sends every event to each Subscription. When the socket closes, pending calls fail with Closed and the event channels are closed. A message that is not JSON fails every pending call with Protocol.
enum Error { Launch(io.Error) Protocol(str) Closed Timeout }

The error type of the DevTools protocol modules. The browser could not be started or connected to. cause is the underlying I/O error. The browser answered a command with an error, or a navigation failed. message is the text reported by the browser. The connection to the browser is closed. The browser did not answer in time.
struct Event { pub method: str pub session: str pub params: json.Value }

A DevTools event sent by the browser. The event name, for example Network.responseReceived. The id of the session the event belongs to, or an empty string for browser-level events. The event parameters. Null when the event carries none.
struct Handlers { pub request: fn(Request) -> Verdict pub response: fn(str, i64) pub failure: fn(str, str) }

Callbacks invoked for the network activity of a page. request runs on its own task for every request, so calls can overlap. response and failure run on the page's event task, in the order the browser reports events, and delay the following events while they run. Called before a request is sent, including requests of frames and workers of the page. The page waits for the returned Verdict. Called with the URL and HTTP status code when response headers arrive. Called with the URL and the browser's error text when a request fails. The URL is empty when the request was not seen being sent.
struct Options { pub executable: str pub proxy: str pub args: []str pub startup: i64 }

Settings for launching a headless Chromium-based browser. Path of the browser binary. When empty, launch searches PATH for chromium, chromium-browser, google-chrome-stable and google-chrome, in that order. Proxy server passed to the browser as --proxy-server. Empty means no proxy. Extra command line arguments, appended after the built-in headless flags and before the initial about:blank page. Milliseconds to wait for the browser to announce its DevTools endpoint. Defaults to 20000.
struct Page { pub browser: *BrowserHandle pub context: str pub target: str pub session: str ... }

A page in its own isolated browser context. The context is disposed when the browser connection closes. Frames, workers and other targets that the page opens are intercepted through the same Handlers. The browser the page lives in. The id of the browser context created for the page. The id of the page target. The id of the session attached to the page, used as the session argument of call.
struct Request { pub url: str pub method: str pub resource: str }
A request the page is about to make. The absolute URL of the request. The HTTP method, for example GET. The DevTools resource type, for example Document, Script, Image, XHR or Fetch.

A stream of the events of a connection, made by subscribe. Receives every event of every session on the connection from the moment of the subscription, in the order the browser sent them. It holds up to 1024 queued events; while it is full, reading of further replies and events waits. It is closed when the connection closes.
The decision a request handler makes about a paused request. Let the request go to the network. Abort the request with a generic failure. The page sees a network error.
fn open_page(b: Browser, handlers: Handlers) -> Page ! Error
Opens a blank page in b. See open_page_on.
Shuts the browser down. See shutdown_on.
Wraps a handle in a Browser that shuts the browser down when dropped.
fn open_page_on(b: *BrowserHandle, handlers: Handlers) -> Page ! Error

Creates an isolated browser context with downloads denied, opens a blank page in it and starts routing its network activity to handlers. Every page receives only the events of its own context. Fails with Timeout when the page does not attach within 10000 milliseconds, and with the error of the first failing command, or of the command that prepares the page for interception, otherwise; a failed open disposes the context. Further pages that the page itself opens, such as popups, are closed as soon as they attach. A target of the page that cannot be prepared for interception is closed instead of resumed.

Closes the DevTools connection, kills the browser process, waits for it to exit and removes the profile directory. Safe to call more than once and from several tasks; only the first call has an effect. Errors while stopping the process or removing files are ignored.
fn call(c: *Connection, session: str, method: str, params: []json.Member) -> json.Value ! Error

Sends the command method with params and waits for the reply, returning its result. An empty session addresses the browser itself; otherwise the command goes to that session. A reply without a result gives Null. Fails with Closed when the connection is closed before or while the command is sent or while waiting, Protocol(message) when the browser reports an error, and Timeout when there is no reply within 30000 milliseconds. Blocks the calling task until then. Safe to call from several tasks.

Returns a new Subscription to the events of c. Every subscription receives every event, so tasks that read different subscriptions do not take events from each other. A subscription made on a closed connection has a closed channel. End it with unsubscribe when no longer read.
Ends the subscription s: no further events are sent to it and the channel of ended is closed. Safe to call more than once.

Starts a headless browser and connects to it. Returns once the browser has announced its DevTools endpoint and the connection is open.
