Encapsulates a shared secret to the encapsulation key ek using the 32-byte message m (ML-KEM.Encaps_internal, FIPS 203). Intended for known-answer tests; use encapsulate otherwise. Fails with Invalid when ek has the wrong length for level, when any of its 12-bit coefficients is not below 3329 (the modulus check of FIPS 203), or when m is not 32 bytes.
Returns a new key pair for level, with d and z drawn from crypto.random (ML-KEM.KeyGen, FIPS 203).
fn generate_seeded(level: Level, d: []u8, z: []u8) -> Keys

Returns a key pair derived deterministically from the 32-byte seeds d and z (ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal, FIPS 203). d seeds the lattice key and z is the implicit rejection value stored in the decapsulation key. Intended for known-answer tests; use generate otherwise. Both seeds must be exactly 32 bytes; other lengths are not checked.

The HMAC hash function behind a one-time password. HMAC-SHA-1, the default of RFC 4226 and the one every authenticator app supports. HMAC-SHA-256 as specified for TOTP by RFC 6238. HMAC-SHA-512 as specified for TOTP by RFC 6238.
enum Error { BadDigits BadPeriod BadTime BadSecret BadAlgorithm BadUri }

The error type of the otp functions. The digit count is outside 6..=8. The time step is not positive. The Unix time is negative. The secret is not valid Base32, or a key URI carries no secret parameter. The algorithm name is not SHA1, SHA256 or SHA512. The text is not a well-formed otpauth:// URI.
struct Key { pub kind: Kind pub account: str pub issuer: str pub secret: []u8 pub algorithm: Algorithm pub digits: i64 pub period: i64 pub counter: i64 }

The parameters of an authenticator key, as carried by an otpauth:// URI. uri writes one and parse_uri reads one, following the Google Authenticator Key URI format. Whether the key is time-based or counter-based. The account the key belongs to, such as an email address. The service that issued the key, or the empty string when there is none. The shared secret as raw bytes. The HMAC hash function. Defaults to Sha1. The number of digits in a code. Defaults to 6. The seconds each code is valid, used by Totp keys. Defaults to 30. The initial counter, used by Hotp keys. Defaults to 0.
The counter scheme of a key URI. Time-based codes (RFC 6238) that advance every period seconds. Counter-based codes (RFC 4226) that advance on each use.

Returns the otpauth:// URI for key, suitable for a QR code. The label is issuer:account (or the account alone when the issuer is empty), percent-encoded, followed by the secret (unpadded Base32), issuer, algorithm, digits and either period for a Totp key or counter for a Hotp key.
Returns length random bytes from the system random source for use as a shared secret. RFC 4226 recommends at least 16 bytes and 20 bytes for HMAC-SHA-1.
fn hotp(secret: []u8, counter: i64, digits: i64, algorithm: Algorithm) -> str ! Error

Returns the HOTP code (RFC 4226) for counter as a string of digits decimal digits. The code is the dynamic truncation of HMAC(secret, counter), with the counter encoded as 8 big-endian bytes, reduced modulo 10^digits and left-padded with zeros. Fails with BadDigits when digits is not in 6..=8.

Parses an otpauth:// URI into a Key. The issuer is taken from the label prefix; the label separator may be : or its percent-encoded form. An issuer query parameter overrides the label prefix. Parameters other than secret, issuer, algorithm, digits, period and counter are ignored, and fields not given keep the defaults of Key. Fails with BadUri when the scheme or type is not recognised, the percent-encoding is invalid or an hotp URI has no counter. Fails with BadSecret when secret is missing or not Base32, BadAlgorithm for an unknown algorithm, BadDigits when digits is not a number in 6..=8 and BadPeriod when period is not a positive number.
Returns the bytes of the RFC 4648 Base32 text. Spaces and hyphens are ignored so a secret grouped for reading decodes unchanged. Fails with BadSecret when the remaining text is not valid Base32.
Returns secret as unpadded RFC 4648 Base32, the form authenticator apps expect.
fn totp(secret: []u8, time: i64, period: i64, digits: i64, algorithm: Algorithm) -> str ! Error

Returns the TOTP code (RFC 6238) for the Unix time in seconds as a string of digits decimal digits. The counter is time / period, so a code is valid for period seconds; authenticator apps use 30. Fails with BadPeriod when period is not positive, BadTime when time is negative and BadDigits when digits is not in 6..=8.
fn verify_hotp(secret: []u8, code: str, counter: i64, window: i64, digits: i64, algorithm: Algorithm) -> i64? ! Error

Checks code against the HOTP codes for counter up to counter + window inclusive and returns the counter to store next, or none when no code matches. The returned value is one past the matching counter, so a code cannot be accepted twice. Every counter in the window is computed regardless of where a match occurs, and each comparison is constant-time. Fails with BadDigits when digits is not in 6..=8.
fn verify_totp(secret: []u8, code: str, time: i64, period: i64, digits: i64, algorithm: Algorithm, window: i64) -> bool ! Error

Returns whether code is the TOTP code for any step from window steps before to window steps after the one containing time. window counts steps of period seconds; 1 tolerates one step of clock drift either way and 0 accepts only the current step. Steps below zero are skipped. Every step is computed and each comparison is constant-time. Fails with BadPeriod, BadTime or BadDigits as totp does. The function does not remember used codes, so a caller that must reject replays records the accepted step itself.
enum Error { InvalidParameters MemoryLimit InvalidCost InvalidSalt PasswordTooLong }

An error from the password hashing functions. A cost parameter is outside the range the algorithm accepts. The memory an operation would need exceeds the given limit. The bcrypt cost is not between 4 and 31. The bcrypt salt is not 16 bytes. The bcrypt password is longer than 72 bytes.
fn argon2id(password: []u8, salt: []u8, t: i64, m: i64, p: i64, length: i64) -> []u8

Computes Argon2id version 0x13 (RFC 9106) of password with salt and returns length bytes. Equivalent to argon2id_keyed with an empty secret and no associated data, including its parameter limits and the empty slice returned for invalid parameters.
fn argon2id_keyed(password: []u8, salt: []u8, secret: []u8, associated: []u8, t: i64, m: i64, p: i64, length: i64) -> []u8

Computes Argon2id version 0x13 (RFC 9106) with an optional secret value and associated data, and returns length bytes. t is the number of passes, m the memory in KiB and p the number of lanes. salt must be at least 8 bytes. secret and associated may be empty. The memory used is m rounded down to a multiple of 4 * p KiB. Returns an empty slice when p is outside [1, 16777215], t is below 1, m is below 8 * p or above 4294967295, length is below 4, or salt is shorter than 8 bytes. Allocates about m KiB, with no limit applied here.
fn bcrypt(password: []u8, salt: []u8, cost: i64) -> []u8 ! Error

Computes the bcrypt hash of password and returns the 23 raw digest bytes. salt must be exactly 16 bytes and cost is the base-2 logarithm of the number of rounds, from 4 to 31. The password is used with a trailing NUL byte, as in $2b$. The digest is not encoded and carries no cost or salt; see hash_bcrypt for the string form. Fails with InvalidCost for a cost outside [4, 31], with InvalidSalt for a salt that is not 16 bytes, and with PasswordTooLong for a password over 72 bytes.

Computes BLAKE2b (RFC 7693) of data and returns length bytes. length is the digest size, from 1 to 64. key is an optional MAC key of at most 64 bytes; an empty key gives the unkeyed hash. Returns an empty slice when length is outside [1, 64] or key is longer than 64 bytes. The whole input is processed in one call.

Hashes password with Argon2id and returns a PHC string. The parameters are fixed at 19456 KiB of memory, 2 passes, 1 lane, a random 16-byte salt from crypto.random and a 32-byte tag. The result has the form $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$<salt>$<tag>, with salt and tag in unpadded standard base64.
fn hash_bcrypt(password: str, cost: i64) -> str ! Error

Hashes password with bcrypt and returns a $2b$ string. The salt is 16 random bytes from crypto.random. The result has the form $2b$<cost, two digits>$<salt, 22 characters><digest, 31 characters>, using the bcrypt base64 alphabet. Fails with the errors of bcrypt: InvalidCost, or PasswordTooLong for a password over 72 bytes.
fn hash_pbkdf2(password: str, iterations: i64) -> str

Hashes password with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 8018) and returns a PHC string. iterations is clamped to [1, 10000000]. The salt is 16 random bytes from crypto.random and the tag is 32 bytes. The result has the form $pbkdf2-sha256$i=<iterations>$<salt>$<tag>, with salt and tag in unpadded standard base64.
fn hash_scrypt(password: str, log_n: i64, r: i64, p: i64) -> str ! Error

Hashes password with scrypt and returns a PHC string. The cost is N = 2^log_n with log_n in [1, 32]. r and p follow the limits of scrypt, with a memory limit of 512 MiB. The salt is 16 random bytes from crypto.random and the tag is 32 bytes. The result has the form $scrypt$ln=,r=,p=

$$, with salt and tag in unpadded standard base64. Fails with InvalidParameters for log_n outside [1, 32] or invalid r or p, and with MemoryLimit when the memory needed exceeds 512 MiB.
fn pbkdf2(algorithm: hash.Algorithm, password: []u8, salt: []u8, iterations: i64, length: i64) -> []u8

Derives length bytes from password and salt with PBKDF2 (RFC 8018) using HMAC over algorithm. iterations is the iteration count; a value below 1 runs one iteration. Output longer than the digest size of algorithm is built from successive blocks, so length is not limited to one digest. A length of 0 returns an empty slice. The password may be any length; one longer than the block size of algorithm is hashed first, as HMAC specifies. No parameter limits are enforced.
fn scrypt(password: []u8, salt: []u8, n: i64, r: i64, p: i64, length: i64, max_memory: i64) -> []u8 ! Error

Derives length bytes from password and salt with scrypt (RFC 7914). n is the CPU and memory cost, a power of two from 2 to 2^32, r the block size and p the parallelism, both at least 1 with r * p below 2^30. length is from 1 to 137438953440 ((2^32 - 1) * 32). max_memory is the memory limit in bytes and is checked, with scrypt_memory, before anything is allocated. Fails with InvalidParameters when a parameter is outside those ranges, and with MemoryLimit when scrypt_memory(n, r, p) exceeds max_memory.
fn scrypt_memory(n: i64, r: i64, p: i64) -> i64
Returns the bytes of memory scrypt allocates for the cost parameters n, r and p, computed as 128 * r * (n + p + 1). The result is not range-checked.
fn verify(password: str, encoded: str) -> bool

Reports whether password matches the hash string encoded. Accepts $argon2id$v=19$..., $pbkdf2-sha256$..., $scrypt$... and bcrypt $2a$, $2b$ and $2y$ strings. The recomputed tag is compared without an early exit. Returns false, never an error, for an unrecognised format, malformed fields, parameters outside the limits below, a bcrypt password over 72 bytes, or a mismatch. Argon2id requires p in [1, 255], t in [1, 100], m in [8 * p, 1048576] KiB, a salt of 8 to 256 bytes and a tag of 4 to 256 bytes. PBKDF2 requires i in [1, 10000000], a salt of 1 to 256 bytes and a tag of 4 to 64 bytes. scrypt requires ln in [1, 32], a salt of 8 to 256 bytes, a tag of 4 to 256 bytes and at most 512 MiB of memory.
struct PrivateKey { pub n: []u8 pub e: []u8 pub d: []u8 pub p: []u8 pub q: []u8 pub dp: []u8 pub dq: []u8 pub qinv: []u8 }

An RSA private key in the form of PKCS#1 RSAPrivateKey (RFC 8017), with the Chinese remainder theorem parameters. All integers are big-endian with no leading zero byte. The modulus, 2048 to 8192 bits. The public exponent, odd and greater than 1. The private exponent. The first prime factor of n. The second prime factor of n. The exponent d mod (p - 1). The exponent d mod (q - 1). The coefficient q^-1 mod p.
struct PublicKey { pub n: []u8 pub e: []u8 }
An RSA public key. Both integers are big-endian with no leading zero byte. The modulus, 2048 to 8192 bits. The public exponent, odd and greater than 1.
Returns the public key of key, sharing its n and e.
fn sign_pkcs1v15(key: PrivateKey, a: hash.Algorithm, digest: []u8) -> []u8 ! io.Error

Signs the hash digest with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (RFC 8017) and returns a signature as long as the modulus. a must be sha256, sha384 or sha512 and digest must be exactly a.size bytes, the hash of the message. The result is checked with the public key before it is returned. Fails with Invalid when a is another algorithm, when digest has the wrong length, when the modulus is too short for the encoded digest, or when the signature fails that check.
fn sign_pss(key: PrivateKey, a: hash.Algorithm, digest: []u8) -> []u8 ! io.Error

Signs the hash digest with RSASSA-PSS (RFC 8017) and returns a signature as long as the modulus. MGF1 uses the same hash as a, and the salt is a.size random bytes from crypto.random, so signing the same digest twice gives different signatures. digest must be exactly a.size bytes, the hash of the message. The result is checked with the public key before it is returned. Fails with Invalid when digest has the wrong length, when the modulus is too short for the hash and salt, or when the signature fails that check.
fn verify_pkcs1v15(key: PublicKey, a: hash.Algorithm, digest: []u8, signature: []u8) -> bool

Reports whether signature is a valid RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature (RFC 8017) of the hash digest under key. a must be sha256, sha384 or sha512. Returns false, never an error, for an unusable key, an unsupported algorithm, a digest of the wrong length, a signature that is not exactly as long as the modulus or is not below it, and a mismatch. The padding comparison does not exit early.
fn verify_pss(key: PublicKey, a: hash.Algorithm, digest: []u8, signature: []u8) -> bool

Reports whether signature is a valid RSASSA-PSS signature (RFC 8017) of the hash digest under key. MGF1 uses the same hash as a, and the salt length is taken from the signature. Returns false, never an error, for an unusable key, a digest that is not a.size bytes, a signature that is not exactly as long as the modulus or is not below it, and any padding or hash mismatch.

Returns the big-endian integer magnitude without its leading zero bytes, the form every integer of PublicKey and PrivateKey takes. Returns an empty slice when magnitude is empty or all zero. The result shares the memory of magnitude.

Parses a DER PKCS#1 RSAPrivateKey (RFC 8017) with eight integers after the version. The version must be 0 (two-prime); otherwise the call fails with Unsupported, as it does when the modulus or exponent fails the limits of parse_public. Fails with Malformed for DER that is not minimal or has trailing bytes, and when the key is inconsistent: p or q is even, qinv is not below p, p * q is not n, or a test signature does not verify under the public key.

Parses a DER PKCS#1 RSAPublicKey (RFC 8017), SEQUENCE { n INTEGER, e INTEGER }. The DER must be minimal, with no trailing bytes; otherwise the call fails with Malformed. Fails with Unsupported when the modulus is not 2048 to 8192 bits and odd, when the exponent is even, 1 or longer than the modulus.
A SHAKE extendable-output sponge (FIPS 202). Input is absorbed with absorb; the first squeeze ends absorption and returns output of any length.
Feeds data into the sponge. A call after the first squeeze has no effect.
Returns the next n bytes of output. The first call ends absorption. Successive calls continue the same output stream. An n of 0 or less returns an empty slice.
Returns the hash.Algorithm for SHA3-256 (FIPS 202). The name is sha3-256, the digest is 32 bytes and the block size is the 136-byte rate.
Returns the hash.Algorithm for SHA3-384 (FIPS 202). The name is sha3-384, the digest is 48 bytes and the block size is the 104-byte rate.
Returns the hash.Algorithm for SHA3-512 (FIPS 202). The name is sha3-512, the digest is 64 bytes and the block size is the 72-byte rate.
Returns a SHAKE128 sponge (FIPS 202) with a 168-byte rate and 128-bit security.
Returns a SHAKE256 sponge (FIPS 202) with a 136-byte rate and 256-bit security.
Returns a new 32-byte X25519 private key from random in std/crypto.
Returns the 32-byte X25519 public key for the 32-byte private key (RFC 7748). Multiplies the base point with u of 9 by the clamped private key. The length of private is not validated.

Returns the 32-byte X25519 shared secret of private and the peer's public key peer (RFC 7748). Fails with io.Error.Invalid when either argument is not 32 bytes or when the result is all zeros, which a low-order peer point produces. The secret is not uniformly random; derive keys from it with a KDF such as hkdf_extract.
The key exchange authentication that a signature scheme serves. RSA, for the PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS schemes. ECDSA, for the ECDSA and Ed25519 schemes.

struct Certificate { pub raw: []u8 pub tbs: []u8 pub version: i64 pub serial: []u8 pub issuer: []u8 pub subject: []u8 pub common_name: str pub not_before: i64 pub not_after: i64 pub signature_algorithm: str pub signature_parameters: []u8 pub signature: []u8 pub public_key: PublicKeyInfo pub dns_names: []str pub ip_addresses: [][]u8 pub ca: bool pub path_length: i64? pub key_usage: i64? pub ext_key_usage: []str pub unhandled_critical: []str }

A parsed X.509 certificate (RFC 5280). parse produces it and keeps slices of the input, so the DER buffer must stay alive and unmodified for as long as the certificate is used. The complete DER encoding of the certificate. The DER encoding of the tbsCertificate, the bytes the issuer signed. The version as encoded: 0 for v1, 1 for v2 and 2 for v3. The content bytes of the serial number integer. The DER encoding of the issuer Name, comparable byte for byte with the subject of the issuing certificate. The DER encoding of the subject Name. The first common name (2.5.4.3) in the subject as UTF-8, or the empty string when there is none. BMP and universal strings are converted to UTF-8; other string types are taken as they are. The start of the validity period in Unix seconds. The end of the validity period in Unix seconds, inclusive. The object identifier of the signature algorithm in dotted form. The DER encoding of the signature algorithm parameters, or an empty slice when there are none. The signature bytes, with the bit string's unused-bits octet removed. The subject public key. The dNSName entries of the subject alternative name extension, in order. Empty when the extension is absent. The iPAddress entries of the subject alternative name extension as 4 or 16 raw bytes. Empty when the extension is absent. Whether the basic constraints extension marks the certificate as a certificate authority. false when the extension is absent. The pathLenConstraint of the basic constraints extension, or none when it is absent. The key usage extension as a bit set, or none when the extension is absent. Bit n is set when the nth named bit of RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.3 is, counting from the most significant bit of the first byte: bit 0 is digitalSignature and bit 5 is keyCertSign. The object identifiers, in dotted form, of the extended key usage extension. Empty when the extension is absent. The object identifiers of critical extensions the parser does not interpret. Basic constraints, key usage, extended key usage and subject alternative name are interpreted. verify_chain rejects a certificate that lists any other critical extension.
A private key for signing. An RSA private key. An ECDSA private key on P-256 or P-384. An Ed25519 private key as its 32-byte seed (RFC 8032).
struct PublicKeyInfo { pub algorithm: str pub parameters: str pub key: []u8 }

The SubjectPublicKeyInfo of a certificate (RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.7): the key algorithm and the encoded key. The algorithm object identifier in dotted form, such as 1.2.840.113549.1.1.1 for RSA, 1.2.840.10045.2.1 for elliptic curve keys and 1.3.101.112 for Ed25519. The object identifier in the algorithm parameters, such as the named curve of an elliptic curve key (1.2.840.10045.3.1.7 for P-256), or the empty string when the parameters are absent or not an object identifier. The bytes of the subjectPublicKey bit string: a DER RSAPublicKey, an uncompressed SEC 1 point or the 32 raw Ed25519 bytes, depending on algorithm.

How a TLS version applies the SignatureScheme codes. TLS 1.2: an ECDSA code names only the hash, so either curve signs and verifies with it, and RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 may sign. TLS 1.3: an ECDSA code names its curve, and RSA signs with PSS only.
fn check_signature(issuer: Certificate, subject: Certificate) -> bool

Returns whether subject carries a valid signature by the key of issuer. The scheme comes from the signature algorithm of subject: RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 (MGF1 with the same hash and a salt as long as the hash), ECDSA with SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, or Ed25519. Returns false for any other scheme, when the type of the issuer key does not fit, or when verification fails. Names and validity are not checked.
fn verify_chain(leaf: Certificate, intermediates: []Certificate, roots: []Certificate, host: str, now: i64) -> []Certificate ! io.Error

Builds and verifies a certification path from leaf to one of roots and returns it, leaf first and root last. now is Unix seconds and host is a DNS name or IP address literal the leaf must be valid for; an empty host skips that check. A DNS name is matched case-insensitively against the dns_names of the leaf only, never its common name. A wildcard such as *.example.com stands for exactly one label in the leftmost position. An IP address is matched against ip_addresses. Every certificate must be within its validity period and carry no unhandled critical extension. The leaf must allow digitalSignature (when it has key usage) and server authentication (when it has extended key usage; anyExtendedKeyUsage also counts). Each issuer must be a certificate authority (basic constraints, or a v1 root), allow keyCertSign, respect its path_length, allow server authentication, have a subject equal to the issuer of the certificate below it and verify that certificate's signature. At most 8 intermediates are used and none appears twice. Signature algorithms are those of check_signature. A leaf that is itself in roots returns a path of one certificate. Fails with Denied when host does not match the leaf and with Invalid when the leaf is unusable or no path exists. Revocation is not checked.
fn sign(key: PrivateKey, scheme: i64, message: []u8, rules: SignatureRules) -> []u8 ! io.Error

Returns the signature of message under key for the TLS SignatureScheme code scheme. The supported codes and the use of rules are those of verify_signature. An ECDSA signature is DER encoded. Fails with Unsupported when scheme is not supported or the key type or curve does not fit it, and with the error of the signing function otherwise.

Returns the TLS SignatureScheme codes key can sign with under rules, in order of preference. An RSA key signs with PSS and, in TLS 1.2, PKCS#1 v1.5. An ECDSA key signs with the scheme of its own curve first and, in TLS 1.2, then the scheme of the other curve. An Ed25519 key signs with 0x0807.
fn verify_signature(key: PublicKeyInfo, scheme: i64, message: []u8, signature: []u8, rules: SignatureRules) -> bool

Returns whether signature is a valid signature of message under key, for the TLS SignatureScheme code scheme. The supported codes are 0x0401, 0x0501 and 0x0601 (RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512), 0x0804, 0x0805 and 0x0806 (RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512), 0x0403 and 0x0503 (ECDSA with SHA-256 and SHA-384) and 0x0807 (Ed25519). Under Tls13 an ECDSA code requires the curve it names, P-256 for 0x0403 and P-384 for 0x0503; under Tls12 the key's curve is not checked against the code. An ECDSA signature is DER encoded. Returns false for any other code or when the key does not fit the scheme.
Returns the key exchange authentication that the TLS SignatureScheme code scheme serves, or none for an unsupported code.

Parses a DER encoded X.509 certificate. Parsing is strict DER. Fails with Malformed for bad encodings, trailing bytes, an empty serial number, a signature algorithm that differs between the outer and the signed part, a repeated extension, or extensions or unique identifiers in a version that does not allow them. Fails with Unsupported for a version above v3. The signature is not verified; see check_signature and verify_chain.

Parses a DER encoded private key. Accepts PKCS#8 PrivateKeyInfo (RFC 5208) holding an RSA, a P-256 or P-384 ECDSA or an Ed25519 key (RFC 8410), a PKCS#1 RSAPrivateKey (RFC 8017) and a SEC 1 ECPrivateKey (RFC 5915). Use pem_blocks to extract the DER from a PEM file. Fails with Malformed for bad encodings and with Unsupported for an unknown algorithm, curve or PKCS#8 version.

Returns the decoded bodies of every PEM block (RFC 7468) in pem whose label is label, in order. Text outside the -----BEGIN label----- and -----END label----- lines is ignored. A block whose body is not valid Base64, or that has header lines (contains a :), is skipped. An unterminated block ends the search. Returns an empty list when there is no match.

Returns the DER encodings of every CERTIFICATE block in pem, in order, for tls.Config.certificates. The leaf certificate must come first, followed by its intermediates. Blocks that are not valid Base64 are skipped.

Returns the private key in the first PEM block of pem labelled PRIVATE KEY, EC PRIVATE KEY or RSA PRIVATE KEY, tried in that order. The block is parsed with parse_private_key, so PKCS#8, SEC 1 and PKCS#1 are accepted whatever the label. Fails with Invalid when pem has none of these blocks and with the parse error otherwise.
Returns the TLS SignatureScheme codes that verify_signature supports, in the order a client offers them.

Returns the trusted root certificates of the system. On Linux reads the first file that exists among /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt and /etc/ssl/cert.pem as PEM, and on Windows takes the certificates of the ROOT system store. Entries that do not parse are skipped. Returns an empty list when no source can be read.

The error returned when CSV text is malformed (RFC 4180). A quoted field is never closed before the end of the input. line is the line on which the field's opening quote appears, counting from 1. A " appears inside an unquoted field, or a closed quoted field is followed by something other than the separator or a line end. line is the line on which the offending field ends, counting from 1.
fn append_record(mut out: []u8, fields: []str, separator: u8)

Appends one record to out, with fields joined by separator and a \r\n line end. A field is quoted when it contains the separator, ", \r or \n, or starts or ends with a space; inside quotes each " is doubled. Other fields are written as they are. An empty fields slice appends only the line end.
Formats records as comma separated CSV text. Equivalent to format_with(records, ',').
Formats records as CSV text with fields separated by separator. Each record is written by append_record, so every record, including the last, ends with \r\n. Empty records gives an empty string.
Parses src as comma separated records. Equivalent to parse_with(src, ',').
fn parse_with(src: str, separator: u8) -> [][]str ! Error

Parses src into records of fields split on separator. Records end at \n, \r\n or a lone \r; the final line end is optional. Empty lines are skipped, so they produce no record, while a line holding only spaces is a record with one field. Fields are not trimmed. A field that starts with " is quoted: it may hold the separator and line ends, and "" stands for one ". Records may have different numbers of fields, and a trailing separator yields a final empty field. Empty input gives no records. Fails with UnterminatedQuote or BareQuote, each carrying a line number.
enum Error { Read(io.Error) MissingEquals(i64) BadName(i64) UnterminatedQuote(i64) }

The error returned when reading or parsing a .env file. The file could not be read; cause is the I/O error from std/file. A line that is neither blank, a comment nor a NAME=value assignment has no =. line is that line, counting from 1. The name before = is empty or contains a character other than ASCII letters, digits, _, . and -, or starts with a digit, . or -. line is that line, counting from 1. A quoted value is not closed before the end of the input. line is the line on which the opening quote appears, counting from 1.

Parses .env text into a map from variable name to value. Each line is blank, a # comment, or NAME=value with an optional leading export . Whitespace around the name and before the value is ignored. An unquoted value runs to the end of the line, stops at a # that starts the value or follows a space or tab, and is trimmed. A value in single quotes is taken literally. A value in double quotes processes \n, \t and \r; any other backslash pair becomes the character after the backslash. Quoted values may span lines, and text after the closing quote on its line is ignored. A name defined twice keeps its last value. Variables are not expanded. Fails with MissingEquals, BadName or UnterminatedQuote, each carrying a line number.
Reads the file at path and parses it as .env text. Fails with Read when the file cannot be read as text, and otherwise with the errors of parse.
struct Entry { pub name: str pub dir: bool pub link: bool pub regular: bool }

A directory entry returned by read_dir_info. The kind flags describe the entry itself without following symbolic links. An entry that is none of dir, link and regular is another kind, such as a socket or device. The entry's name within its directory. Whether the entry is a directory. Whether the entry is a symbolic link, even when it points to a directory. Whether the entry is a regular file.
An open file that closes itself when dropped. handle is the copyable view for passing the file to other green threads, and close or close_on closes it early. The copyable view of the open file.

A copyable view of an open file, made of its descriptor and the guard that coordinates its closing. Copies of a FileHandle refer to the same descriptor. Once any copy is closed, every operation on the handle fails with NotConnected, so a closed descriptor is never reached after the kernel reuses its number. The operating system file descriptor.
struct Info { pub size: i64 pub mode: i64 pub dir: bool pub modified: i64 pub regular: bool pub link: bool pub accessed: i64 pub uid: i64 pub gid: i64 pub device: i64 pub inode: i64 }

Metadata about a file, as returned by stat, lstat and info. The size in bytes. The permission bits, including setuid, setgid and sticky, without the file type bits. Whether the file is a directory. The modification time in whole seconds since the Unix epoch. Whether the file is a regular file. Whether the file is a symbolic link. Only lstat reports true, because stat and info follow links. The access time in whole seconds since the Unix epoch. The numeric ID of the owning user. The numeric ID of the owning group. The ID of the device that holds the file. The inode number. Together with device it identifies a file.

What walk does after a visit callback returns. Carries on, descending into the entry when it is a directory. Does not descend into the entry; the walk carries on with its siblings. Ends the walk; walk returns without an error.
struct TempFile { pub file: File pub path: str ... }
A temporary file that is closed and removed when dropped, unless keep was called. The open file, readable and writable. The path of the file.
struct Usage { pub total: i64 pub free: i64 pub available: i64 pub files: i64 pub files_free: i64 }

Capacity figures of a file system, in bytes and inodes, as returned by disk_usage. The size of the file system in bytes. The unused space in bytes, including space reserved for the superuser. The unused space in bytes that an unprivileged process can use. The total number of inodes. The number of unused inodes.
struct Visit { pub path: str pub name: str pub depth: i64 pub dir: bool pub link: bool pub regular: bool }

An entry reached by walk. The path, made of the walk's root and the names down to this entry. The name within the parent directory; for the root it is the last component of the root path. The number of directories between the root and this entry, 0 for the root. Whether the entry is a directory. Whether the entry is a symbolic link; walk does not follow it. Whether the entry is a regular file.
The position an offset given to seek is measured from. The beginning of the file. The current position. The end of the file.

Closes the file. Equivalent to close_on(f.handle). Later operations on the file or any copy of its handle fail with NotConnected. The descriptor is released immediately, or when the last operation in flight returns.
Returns the metadata of the open file. Fails with NotConnected when the file has been closed.
fn read(f: File, buf: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error

Reads up to buf.len bytes from the current position into buf and returns the count, or 0 at end of file. Blocks until data is available and can return fewer bytes than requested. The position advances by the count.
fn seek(f: File, offset: i64, from: Whence) -> i64 ! io.Error

Moves the position by offset bytes relative to from and returns the new position measured from the start of the file. offset can be negative. A position past the end is allowed; a later write extends the file with zeros. Fails with Invalid when the resulting position would be negative.
Returns an io.Stream over the file. Closing the stream closes the file.
Flushes the file's data and metadata to the storage device and returns once the device has accepted them.
fn truncate(f: File, size: i64) ! io.Error

Sets the file's size to size bytes. A smaller size discards the tail and a larger one extends the file with zeros. The position does not change. Fails with Invalid when the file was not opened for writing.
fn try_lock(f: File, exclusive: bool) -> bool ! io.Error

Tries to take an advisory flock lock on the file, exclusive when exclusive is true and shared otherwise. Returns false without waiting when another descriptor holds a conflicting lock. The lock is released by unlock or when the file is closed.
Releases the advisory flock lock that this file holds.
fn write(f: File, data: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Writes a prefix of data at the current position and returns how many bytes were written, which can be fewer than data.len. The position advances by the count. Use write_all to write everything.
Writes all of data at the current position, repeating write until nothing remains. Fails with the first error a write returns, after which part of data may have been written.
fn write_str(f: File, text: str) ! io.Error
Writes the bytes of text to the file. Fails as write_all does.

Closes the file that h views. Later operations on h or its copies fail with NotConnected. The descriptor is released immediately, or when the last operation in flight returns. Closing twice does nothing.
fn read_on(h: FileHandle, buf: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Reads up to buf.len bytes from the current position of the file that h views into buf and returns the count, or 0 at end of file. Fails with NotConnected when the file has been closed.
Returns an io.Stream over the file that h views. Closing the stream closes the file. The stream is safe to copy and use from other green threads.
Writes all of data to the file that h views, repeating write_on until nothing remains. Fails with the first error a write returns, after which part of data may have been written.
fn write_on(h: FileHandle, data: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error

Writes a prefix of data at the current position of the file that h views and returns how many bytes were written, which can be fewer than data.len. Fails with NotConnected when the file has been closed.
Stops t from removing its file when dropped and returns the file's path. The file is still closed when t is dropped.

Opens the file at path for appending, creating it with mode 0o644 if it does not exist. Every write goes to the end of the file regardless of seek. The file is write-only and existing content is kept.
fn child_path(dir: str, name: str) -> str

Returns the path of the entry name inside the directory dir, without cleaning either part. A single / separates them, and none is added when dir already ends with one. An empty dir gives name and an empty name gives dir.
fn chmod(path: str, mode: i64) ! io.Error

Sets the permission bits of the file at path to mode. Follows symbolic links. Unlike the creating functions, the umask does not filter mode. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist and Denied when the caller does not own the file.
fn chown(path: str, uid: i64, gid: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the owner and group of the file at path to uid and gid, following symbolic links. Fails with Denied when the caller lacks the privilege.
fn copy(from: str, to: str) ! io.Error

Copies the contents of the file from to to. Follows symbolic links on both paths. to is created or truncated and ends with the permission bits of from. Fails with IsDir when from is a directory and Invalid when both paths name the same file. A failure part way leaves a partial to. See copy_dir for directories.
fn copy_dir(from: str, to: str) ! io.Error

Copies the directory tree from to to. Creates to when it does not exist; its parent must exist. Regular files are copied as copy does, symbolic links are recreated as links instead of followed, and directories are copied recursively. Directory and file modes are kept. Fails with NotDir when from is not a directory, Invalid when to is from or inside it, and Unsupported for an entry that is not a file, link or directory.

Creates the file at path for writing, or truncates it to zero length if it exists. A new file gets mode 0o644, filtered by the process umask. The file is opened write-only, so read fails. See create_mode to choose the mode.
fn create_mode(path: str, mode: i64) -> File ! io.Error

Creates the file at path for writing with permission bits mode, or truncates it to zero length if it exists. mode is filtered by the process umask and applies only when the file is created; an existing file keeps its mode.
Returns the capacity figures of the file system that holds path. Space is in bytes. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist.
Returns whether path exists. Follows symbolic links, so a dangling link gives false. Any error, including a denied lookup, gives false.

Returns the paths that match the glob pattern, sorted and without duplicates. Each /-separated segment is matched against directory entry names with path.matches, so *, ?, [...] and \ work and no segment treats a leading . specially. A segment ** matches any number of nested directories, none included, and as the last segment matches every entry below. Symbolic links are not descended through **. A relative pattern gives relative paths and an absolute one gives absolute paths. Unreadable directories contribute nothing, so a pattern with no match gives an empty slice, not an error.
Returns whether path is a directory, following symbolic links. Any error, including a missing path, gives false.
Returns whether path is a regular file, following symbolic links. Any error, including a missing path, gives false.
Returns whether path is a symbolic link, without following it. Any error, including a missing path, gives false.
fn lchown(path: str, uid: i64, gid: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the owner and group of path to uid and gid, changing a symbolic link itself instead of its target. Fails with Denied when the caller lacks the privilege.
fn link(existing: str, new_path: str) ! io.Error

Creates new_path as a hard link to the file existing. Both names refer to the same inode. Fails with Exists when new_path exists, Denied when existing is a directory and an Os error when the paths are on different file systems.

Returns the names of the entries in the directory path, without . and ... The names are in the order the file system returns them, not sorted. See read_dir_info for entry kinds and walk for a sorted traversal.
Returns the metadata of path without following a final symbolic link. For a link, the result describes the link itself and link is true. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist.
Creates the directory path with mode 0o755, filtered by the process umask. Fails with Exists when path exists and NotFound when its parent does not.
Creates the directory path and every missing parent, with mode 0o755 filtered by the process umask.
fn mkdir_all_mode(path: str, mode: i64) ! io.Error

Creates the directory path and every missing parent, with permission bits mode filtered by the process umask. Succeeds when a component already exists; the existing entry at path is not checked to be a directory. Fails with NotDir when a parent component is a file.
fn mkdir_mode(path: str, mode: i64) ! io.Error
Creates the directory path with permission bits mode, filtered by the process umask. Fails with Exists when path exists and NotFound when its parent does not.

Opens the file at path for reading. Fails with NotFound when the file does not exist. Opening a directory succeeds and the first read fails with IsDir. The descriptor is closed when the returned File is dropped or closed.

Returns the entries of the directory path, without . and ... The entries are in the order the file system returns them, not sorted. The kind comes from the directory record, or from lstat when the file system does not provide one. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist and NotDir when it is not a directory.

Returns the entire contents of the file at path. The buffer is sized from the file's size. A file that reports no size, such as one under /proc, is read into a 64 KB buffer that doubles when full. Fails with NotFound when the file does not exist and IsDir when path is a directory.
Returns the entire contents of the file at path as text. The bytes are viewed as a str without validating them as UTF-8. Fails as read_file does.

Returns the target text of the symbolic link path. The text is returned as stored, relative or absolute. Fails with Invalid when path is not a symbolic link and TooLarge when the target is 1 MiB or longer.
Returns the absolute path of path with every symbolic link resolved and no . or .. components. Requires /proc to be mounted on Linux. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist.
Removes the file or symbolic link at path. A symbolic link is removed, not its target. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist and IsDir when it is a directory; see remove_dir and remove_all.
Removes the file, symbolic link or directory tree at path. Succeeds when path does not exist. Directory contents are removed recursively and symbolic links are removed without being followed.

Removes the empty directory at path. Fails with NotEmpty when the directory has entries, NotDir when path is not a directory and NotFound when it does not exist. On Windows a removed file stays an entry until its last open handle closes, so the directory is NotEmpty until then.
fn rename(from: str, to: str) ! io.Error

Renames the entry from to to. An existing to is replaced atomically, except that a directory can only replace an empty directory. Fails with an Os error when the two paths are on different file systems.
fn set_times(path: str, accessed: i64, modified: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the access and modification times of the file at path, in whole seconds since the Unix epoch. Follows symbolic links. The nanosecond parts are set to zero.
Returns the metadata of the file at path, following symbolic links. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist, including when it is a dangling link. See lstat to inspect a link itself.
fn symlink(target: str, link_path: str) ! io.Error
Creates the symbolic link link_path that holds the text target. target is stored as given and need not exist. Fails with Exists when link_path exists.

Creates a private directory under os.temp_dir_path() and returns its path. The name is prefix followed by ten random characters from 0-9a-z and the mode is 0o700. Fails with Invalid when prefix contains / and Exists after 64 name collisions. The caller removes the directory; see temp_dir_pattern to choose the parent.
fn temp_dir_pattern(dir: str, pattern: str) -> str ! io.Error
Creates a uniquely named temporary directory with mode 0o700 and returns its path. dir, pattern and the failures are as for temp_file. The caller removes the directory.
fn temp_file(dir: str, pattern: str) -> TempFile ! io.Error

Creates a uniquely named temporary file and returns it. The file is created in dir, or in os.temp_dir_path() when dir is empty; dir must already exist. pattern is the file name: its last * is replaced by ten random characters from 0-9a-z, and the characters are appended when there is no *. The file is opened read-write with O_EXCL and mode 0o600. Fails with Invalid when pattern contains / and Exists after 64 name collisions.
Opens the file at path for reading and writing, creating it with mode 0o644 if it does not exist. Existing content is kept and the position starts at the beginning.
fn walk(root: str, visit: fn(Visit) -> Step) ! io.Error

Calls visit for root and everything below it, depth first, with the entries of each directory in name order. visit runs for a directory before its entries and its result decides whether to continue, skip the directory or stop; see Step. Symbolic links are reported and never followed, including a link at root. Fails with the error of lstat on root or of reading a directory.
Writes data to the file at path, creating it with mode 0o644 or truncating it first if it exists. The write is not atomic; a failure part way leaves a partial file.
fn write_file_mode(path: str, data: []u8, mode: i64) ! io.Error

Writes data to the file at path, creating it with permission bits mode or truncating it first if it exists. mode is filtered by the process umask and applies only when the file is created. The write is not atomic.
fn write_text(path: str, text: str) ! io.Error
Writes the bytes of text to the file at path, creating it with mode 0o644 or truncating it first if it exists.
fn write_text_mode(path: str, text: str, mode: i64) ! io.Error

Writes the bytes of text to the file at path, creating it with permission bits mode or truncating it first if it exists. mode is filtered by the process umask and applies only when the file is created.
struct Event { pub watched: str pub name: str pub path: str pub kind: Kind pub dir: bool pub cookie: i64 }

A change to a watched path. The watched path the event arose on, as it was passed to add or, for a recursive watch, the path of the watched subdirectory. The name of the affected entry inside the watched directory, empty when the event is about the watched path itself. The path of the affected entry: watched joined with name, or watched when name is empty. The kind of change. Whether the affected entry is a directory. Links a MovedFrom event to its MovedTo event, which share a non-zero value; 0 for other kinds.
enum Kind { Created Modified Deleted MovedFrom MovedTo Attrib Closed ClosedUnmodified Opened Accessed SelfDeleted SelfMoved Overflow }

The kind of change an Event reports. An entry was created in a watched directory. The contents of a file were written. An entry was removed from a watched directory. An entry was moved out of a watched directory; the matching MovedTo event has the same cookie. An entry was moved into a watched directory. Metadata such as permissions, ownership or timestamps changed. A file that was open for writing was closed. A file that was open only for reading was closed. Reported only with Options.access. A file was opened. Reported only with Options.access. A file was read. Reported only with Options.access. A path passed to add was deleted. A path passed to add was moved. The kernel dropped events because its queue overflowed. watched, name and path are empty.
struct Options { pub recursive: bool pub access: bool }

Settings for a Watcher. Whether to also watch every subdirectory, including those created or moved in later. Symbolic links are not followed. Defaults to false. Whether to also report Opened, Accessed and ClosedUnmodified. Defaults to false.
Watches files and directories for changes through inotify. Dropping a watcher stops it, unless detach was called. The copyable view of the watcher.

A copyable view of a Watcher, made of its inotify descriptor and the state shared with the watcher. Once the watcher is stopped, operations on the handle fail with NotConnected. The inotify file descriptor.
Returns a watcher that watches nothing yet, configured by options. Use add to choose the paths.
fn add(w: Watcher, path: str) ! io.Error
Starts watching path. With Options.recursive and a directory, every existing subdirectory is watched too. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist.
Returns the handle of w and releases w, so that dropping w no longer stops the watcher. The caller stops it with stop_on or by adopting the handle.

Returns a channel that receives the watcher's events. A green thread forwards events into a channel with capacity 64. The channel closes when the watcher stops or reading fails. Competing with next or another channel for events splits them between the readers.

Returns the next event, waiting for one when none is queued. The green thread parks while it waits. Events come in the order the kernel reports them. A change to a path that is no longer watched is dropped, and SelfDeleted and SelfMoved are reported only for paths given to add. Fails with NotConnected once the watcher is stopped.
fn remove(w: Watcher, path: str) ! io.Error
Stops watching path and every watched path below it. Fails with NotFound when path is not watched.
Stops the watcher. A next call that is waiting fails with NotConnected, as do later calls, and a channel from events closes. Stopping twice does nothing.
fn add_on(h: WatcherHandle, path: str) ! io.Error
Starts watching path through the handle h, as add does.
Returns a Watcher that owns the watcher viewed by h, so that dropping it stops the watcher.
Returns a channel that receives the events of the watcher that h views, as events does.
Returns the next event through the handle h, as next does.
fn remove_on(h: WatcherHandle, path: str) ! io.Error
Stops watching path and every watched path below it through the handle h, as remove does.
Stops the watcher that h views, as stop does.
Returns a watcher over paths with default Options. Fails with the error of the first path that cannot be watched, such as NotFound; the watcher is stopped.
fn watch_with(paths: []str, options: Options) -> Watcher ! io.Error
Returns a watcher over paths configured by options. Fails with the error of the first path that cannot be watched, such as NotFound; the watcher is stopped.
enum Error { Unknown(str) Missing(str) Invalid(str, str) }

A command-line parsing failure, naming the flag involved. The argument names a flag that is not in the specs. A flag that takes a value is the last argument and has none. The value is not valid for the flag: a boolean flag given something other than true or false, or a value that number cannot parse as an integer.
The values and positional arguments found by parse. The arguments that are not flags, in order, followed by everything after a -- argument.
struct Spec { pub name: str pub help: str pub boolean: bool pub fallback: str }

The definition of one flag. The flag name without leading dashes, used as --name or -name. A short description shown by usage. Whether the flag is a switch that takes no separate value. A switch is true when given as --name and can be set explicitly as --name=true or --name=false. The value reported when the flag is not given.
fn enabled(p: Parsed, name: str) -> bool
Returns whether the value of the flag name is true.
fn get(p: Parsed, name: str) -> str
Returns the value of the flag name as a string. Returns the flag's fallback if it was not given, and an empty string if name is not in the specs.
fn number(p: Parsed, name: str) -> i64 ! Error
Returns the value of the flag name parsed as an integer. Fails with Invalid if the value, including an empty fallback, is not an integer.

Parses args against specs. args does not include the program name. A flag is written --name or -name, with the value either joined as --name=value or as the next argument; a switch takes no next argument. An argument that does not start with -, and a lone -, is positional. -- ends flag parsing and every later argument is positional. Flags and positional arguments can be interleaved, and a flag given more than once keeps its last value. Fails with Unknown, Missing or Invalid for the first problem found.

Returns help text for specs, one line per flag in the order given. Each line has the form --name value help (default fallback): switches omit value, the help part is omitted when empty, and the default part appears only for non-switch flags with a non-empty fallback.
An incremental CRC-32 checksum state. Made by crc32_new or crc32c_new. The state is mutated in place by crc32_update.
An incremental CRC-64 checksum state. Made by crc64_new and mutated in place by crc64_update.
The error type of the SipHash functions. The key is not exactly 16 bytes long.
An incremental 32-bit FNV hash state, in either the FNV-1 or the FNV-1a order.
An incremental 64-bit FNV hash state, in either the FNV-1 or the FNV-1a order.
struct Hash128 { pub lo: u64 pub hi: u64 }

A 128-bit hash value held as two 64-bit halves. hash128_bytes serialises it to 16 bytes. The low 64 bits, serialised first by hash128_bytes in little-endian order. The high 64 bits, serialised after lo by hash128_bytes in little-endian order.

An incremental SipHash state. Made by one of the siphash*_new functions, which fix the number of compression and finalisation rounds and the output width. siphash_sum needs a 64-bit state and siphash_sum128 a 128-bit one.
Returns the CRC-32 of everything fed to c so far. The state is not consumed; more data can be fed afterwards.
Feeds data into the CRC-32 state c. Updating with several slices in turn gives the same sum as updating with their concatenation. An empty slice leaves the state unchanged.
Returns the CRC-64 of everything fed to c so far. The state is not consumed; more data can be fed afterwards.
Feeds data into the CRC-64 state c. Updating with several slices in turn gives the same sum as updating with their concatenation.
Returns the 32-bit FNV hash of everything fed to f so far. The state is not consumed. The hash of empty input is the offset basis.
Feeds data into the 32-bit FNV state f, using the order the state was made with. Updating with several slices in turn gives the same hash as updating with their concatenation.
Returns the 64-bit FNV hash of everything fed to f so far. The state is not consumed. The hash of empty input is the offset basis.
Feeds data into the 64-bit FNV state f, using the order the state was made with. Updating with several slices in turn gives the same hash as updating with their concatenation.
Returns the 16 bytes of h: lo then hi, each in little-endian order.
Returns the MurmurHash3 x64_128 hash of everything fed to m so far. The state is not consumed. lo holds the first 64 bits (h1) and hi the second (h2).
Feeds data into the state m. Input is processed in little-endian 16-byte blocks and a partial block is held until more data arrives, so splitting the input across calls does not change the hash.
Returns the MurmurHash3 x86_32 hash of everything fed to m so far. The state is not consumed; more data can be fed afterwards.
Feeds data into the state m. Input is processed in little-endian 4-byte blocks and a partial block is held until more data arrives, so splitting the input across calls does not change the hash.
Returns the 64-bit SipHash of everything fed to s so far. The state is not consumed. Panics when s was made by a 128-bit constructor.
Returns the 128-bit SipHash of everything fed to s so far. The state is not consumed. Panics when s was made by a 64-bit constructor.

Feeds data into the SipHash state s. Input is processed in little-endian 8-byte blocks and a partial block is held until more data arrives, so splitting the input across calls does not change the hash.
Returns the xxHash32 of everything fed to x so far. The state is not consumed; more data can be fed afterwards.
Feeds data into the state x. Input is processed in 16-byte stripes and the remainder is held until more data arrives, so splitting the input across calls does not change the hash.
Returns the xxHash64 of everything fed to x so far. The state is not consumed; more data can be fed afterwards.
Feeds data into the state x. Input is processed in 32-byte stripes and the remainder is held until more data arrives, so splitting the input across calls does not change the hash.
Returns the Adler-32 checksum (RFC 1950) of data. The checksum of empty input is 1.

Returns the Adler-32 checksum (RFC 1950) after appending data to input whose checksum was adler. Pass 1 as adler to start a new checksum. The result carries the second sum in the high 16 bits and the first in the low 16 bits, both reduced modulo 65521.
Returns the IEEE CRC-32 of data. The CRC-32 of empty input is 0.
Returns a CRC-32 state using the IEEE 802.3 polynomial (0xEDB88320 reflected), the checksum used by zlib, gzip, PNG and Ethernet. The initial value is 0xFFFFFFFF and crc32_sum inverts the result.
Returns a CRC-32C state using the Castagnoli polynomial (0x82F63B78 reflected), the checksum used by iSCSI, ext4 and SCTP. The initial value is 0xFFFFFFFF and crc32_sum inverts the result.
Returns a CRC-64 state using the ECMA-182 polynomial in its reflected form (0xC96C5795D7870F42), the CRC-64/XZ variant. The initial value is all ones and crc64_sum inverts the result.
Returns the 32-bit FNV-1 hash of data.
Returns the 64-bit FNV-1 hash of data.
Returns the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of data.
Returns the 64-bit FNV-1a hash of data.
Returns a 32-bit FNV-1 state (multiply, then XOR each byte) with the offset basis 0x811C9DC5 and prime 0x01000193.
Returns a 32-bit FNV-1a state (XOR each byte, then multiply) with the offset basis 0x811C9DC5 and prime 0x01000193.
Returns a 64-bit FNV-1 state (multiply, then XOR each byte) with the offset basis 0xCBF29CE484222325 and prime 0x00000100000001B3.
Returns a 64-bit FNV-1a state (XOR each byte, then multiply) with the offset basis 0xCBF29CE484222325 and prime 0x00000100000001B3.
fn jump(key: u64, buckets: i64) -> i64

Returns the bucket in 0..buckets that key maps to under jump consistent hashing (Lamping and Veach, 2014). When buckets grows from n to n + 1, only about 1 / (n + 1) of the keys move, and each moves to the new bucket. Buckets can only be added or removed at the end; the function carries no per-bucket state. Returns -1 when buckets is not positive.
Returns a MurmurHash3 x64_128 state with the given 32-bit seed.
Returns a MurmurHash3 x86_32 state with the given seed.
Returns the MurmurHash3 x64_128 hash of data with the given 32-bit seed. MurmurHash3 is not cryptographic and is not keyed against adversarial input.
Returns the MurmurHash3 x86_32 hash of data with the given seed. MurmurHash3 is not cryptographic and is not keyed against adversarial input.

Returns the index in nodes that key maps to under rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing, or none when nodes is empty. Each node id is scored by mixing it with key through the 64-bit murmur finaliser, and the highest score wins; ties go to the lowest index. Removing a node moves only the keys it owned. Node ids are not required to be sorted, and the result depends on the ids, not on their positions.

Returns the index in nodes that key maps to under rendezvous hashing, or none when nodes is empty. The bytes of each node name are hashed with xxh64, seeded by the xxh64 of key, and the highest hash wins; ties go to the lowest index.
Returns the SipHash-1-3 of data under the 16-byte key as a 64-bit value. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes.
Returns the 128-bit SipHash-1-3 of data under the 16-byte key. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes.
Returns a SipHash-1-3 state with a 128-bit output keyed by the 16-byte key. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes. Finish it with siphash_sum128.

Returns a SipHash-1-3 state with a 64-bit output keyed by the 16-byte key. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes. Finish it with siphash_sum. SipHash-1-3 is faster than SipHash-2-4 with a smaller security margin.

Returns the SipHash-2-4 of data under the 16-byte key as a 64-bit value. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes. SipHash is a keyed pseudorandom function suited to hash tables that must resist collision flooding.
Returns the 128-bit SipHash-2-4 of data under the 16-byte key. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes.
Returns a SipHash-2-4 state with a 128-bit output keyed by the 16-byte key. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes. Finish it with siphash_sum128.
Returns a SipHash-2-4 state with a 64-bit output keyed by the 16-byte key. Fails with BadKey when key is not 16 bytes. Finish it with siphash_sum.
Returns the 64-bit wyhash (final version 4 constants) of data with the given seed. wyhash is fast and non-cryptographic and the seed is not a secret key.
Returns the xxHash32 of data with the given seed. xxHash is not cryptographic.
Returns an xxHash32 state with the given seed.
Returns the xxHash64 of data with the given seed. xxHash is not cryptographic.
Returns an xxHash64 state with the given seed.
struct Header { pub name: str pub value: str }

A header field of an HTTP request or response, of a multipart part, or of a mail message. The field name. Names read from the network are lowercase; names set by a program are sent as written. The field value. Values read from the network have surrounding whitespace removed. A value containing \r, \n or a zero byte is rejected when written.
struct Value { pub main: str pub params: []Header }
A header value with parameters, such as form-data; name="a". The text before the first ;, trimmed. The parameters in order, with names in lower case and values decoded.
Returns true when the name of h is a token and its value passes valid_value.
fn param(v: Value, name: str) -> str?
Returns the value of the parameter name, or none when it is absent. The name is matched without regard to case.
fn add(mut headers: []Header, name: str, value: str)
Appends a header to headers, keeping any existing headers of the same name.
Returns the value of the first header in headers whose name equals name, ignoring case, or none when there is none.
Returns true when headers has a header named name, ignoring case.

Parses a header value into its main part and parameters. A parameter value may be a quoted string, in which \" and \\ are unescaped. Parameters in the RFC 2231 forms are resolved: name*=charset'language'text is percent-decoded, and the pieces name*0, name*1 and so on are joined in order. A value in ISO-8859-1, latin1 or US-ASCII is converted to UTF-8, and any other charset is taken as UTF-8. The extended form wins over the plain one, and when a name is repeated the first occurrence wins.

Returns value as a quoted string for a header parameter. " and \ are escaped with a backslash, and a carriage return, line feed or zero byte becomes %0D, %0A or %00, so the result always passes valid_value.
Returns the headers of headers whose name differs from name, ignoring case, in a new slice.
fn set(mut headers: []Header, name: str, value: str)

Replaces the value of the first header in headers named name, ignoring case, using the spelling of name given here, or appends the header when there is none. Further headers of the same name are left alone.
Returns true when s is not empty and every byte is a token byte.
Returns true when c may appear in an RFC 9110 token: a letter, a digit, the grave accent or one of !#$%&'*+-.^_|~.
Returns true when value has no \r, \n or zero byte.
Returns the values of every header in headers whose name equals name, ignoring case, in order. The slice is empty when there are none.
struct Attribute { pub name: str pub value: str }
An attribute of a start tag. The attribute name, lowercased. The attribute value with character references decoded. Empty for an attribute written without a value.
enum Token { StartTag(str, []Attribute, bool) EndTag(str) Text(str) Comment(str) Doctype(str, str?, str?) End }

One lexical unit of an HTML document. The tokenizer does not build a tree and does not repair markup: it reports tags, text, comments and doctypes in source order. An opening tag. name is lowercased. attributes lists the attributes in source order; when a name repeats, the first occurrence is kept. self_closing is true when the tag ends in />. After script, style, xmp, iframe, noembed and noframes the content up to the matching end tag is one raw Text token. After title and textarea it is one Text token with character references decoded. After plaintext the rest of the input is one Text token. A closing tag. name is lowercased and any attributes are discarded. Character data. In ordinary content and in title and textarea, content has character references decoded; inside raw text elements it is verbatim. A < that does not begin a tag, comment, declaration or processing instruction is part of the text. A comment. content excludes the delimiters. Processing instructions (<?...>), unknown declarations (<!...>) and malformed end tags (</ ...>) are reported as comments holding the text up to the next >. A document type declaration. name is lowercased. public_id and system_id are none when absent. The end of the input. Every call to next after the last token returns it again.
A cursor over an HTML document held in memory. Create one with tokenizer and read tokens with next.
Returns the next token. Returns End once the input is exhausted, and on every later call. A tag that is not closed before the end of the input is dropped, as is an empty end tag </>.
Returns the value of the first attribute called name, or none when there is none. The comparison is exact; the tokenizer lowercases names, so pass name in lowercase.
Escapes s for HTML text and attribute values. &, <, >, " and ' become &, <, >, " and '. A string with none of them is returned as it is.
Returns a tokenizer positioned at the start of input.

Decodes the HTML character references in s: named references, decimal references such as A and hexadecimal references such as A. Named references without a closing ; are decoded when they are one of the historic names. Numeric references to zero, surrogates and values above U+10FFFF become U+FFFD, and values from 0x80 to 0x9F are read as Windows-1252. An unknown reference is left as written.

The value at the start of a task's context slot that the HTTP server and client read to find an Observer. __context() reads the running green thread's context slot as an *Ambient, and spawn copies it to child tasks. A task whose slot is not set, or whose observer is none, is not observed. A program that sets the slot must make its context type begin with an Ambient. The observer that receives the server and client events of this task, or none for no observation.

A configuration under construction: a client when K is Client, a single request when K is Response. client() returns a Builder[Client] and build turns it into a Client. request returns a Builder[Response] that send, stream_to or download runs. Each with_* function returns an updated copy and leaves its argument unchanged. The functions that are generic in K apply to either kind; the rest apply to one. A request starts with the client's headers, timeout, connect timeout, redirect limit, retry count, version, prior knowledge and decompression settings. The fields are private. let client = http.client().with_timeout(5000).with_retries(2).build() let resp = client.request("POST", "https://example.com/items").with_text("hello").send() or return

A pooled HTTP client, made by build. It keeps HTTP/1.1 connections alive and reuses them after a response has been read in full, and sends concurrent requests to an HTTPS host, or to any host with with_prior_knowledge, over one multiplexed HTTP/2 connection when the server accepts it. With with_version(Http3) it sends concurrent https requests to a host over one QUIC connection. It is safe to use from several tasks. It holds no drop: idle connections are closed after the idle timeout or by close_idle. Its fields are private.
struct Connection { pub stream: io.Stream pub protocol: str pub secure: bool ... }

An open connection returned by connect, either plain TCP or TLS. Releasing a Connection closes its stream unless detach was called. The stream to read from and write to the connection. Closing it closes the connection. The ALPN protocol the server selected, for example h2 or http/1.1. Empty for a plain connection and when TLS negotiated none. true for a TLS connection, from an https or wss URL.

struct Cookie { pub name: str pub value: str pub domain: str pub host_only: bool pub path: str pub expires: i64 pub max_age: i64 pub secure: bool pub http_only: bool pub same_site: SameSite pub created: i64 pub accessed: i64 }

A cookie: the form a CookieJar stores, request_cookies returns and set_cookie and format_set_cookie write. A response cookie needs only name and value; the other fields default to a session cookie for / that is HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax. The cookie name, trimmed of surrounding whitespace and never empty. The cookie value, trimmed of surrounding whitespace and otherwise as sent. It is written as given, with no escaping. The host the cookie belongs to: the host of the request that set it, or the lowercased Domain attribute without its leading dot. Empty on a cookie written without a Domain attribute, which format_set_cookie then omits. true when the cookie had no Domain attribute and is sent only to exactly domain; false when it is also sent to subdomains of domain, except when the request host is an IP address. format_set_cookie writes Domain only when this is false and domain is not empty. The Path attribute when it starts with /; otherwise the default path, which is the request target up to its last /, or /. The expiry time in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. A cookie with neither Max-Age nor Expires is a session cookie and holds 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, so it never expires on its own. Max-Age takes precedence over Expires. The Max-Age attribute in seconds as parsed from or written to a Set-Cookie header. A negative value, the default, means the attribute is absent and makes a session cookie; 0 deletes the cookie. true when the cookie has the Secure attribute and is sent only to https and wss URLs. true when the cookie has the HttpOnly attribute. The jar records it and does not otherwise act on it. The SameSite attribute of the cookie. Unset omits it when written. A logical timestamp from the jar's internal counter, set when the cookie is first stored and kept when a later Set-Cookie replaces the cookie. It orders cookies of equal path length in a Cookie header and is not a time of day. A logical timestamp from the jar's internal counter, updated whenever the cookie is stored or included in a header. The jar evicts the lowest value first when it is full.

An in-memory store of cookies that follows the Set-Cookie and Cookie rules of RFC 6265. Copies of a CookieJar share one store, and the store is safe to use from several tasks. The jar holds at most 4096 bytes of name and value per cookie, 1024 bytes per attribute value, 50 cookies per domain and 3000 cookies in total; storing past a limit evicts the least recently accessed cookie. Expired cookies are discarded on the next read or write. A client uses a jar through with_cookie_jar, or a private one through with_cookies.
enum Error { InvalidUrl(str) Connect(io.Error) Tls(io.Error) Timeout TooManyRedirects(i64) Protocol(io.Error) Decode(io.Error) Json(serde.Error) Status(i64) Io(io.Error) }

The failure of a client request or of a response helper. A response with any status is a success for send; ensure_success turns a non-2xx status into Status. Whatever stage a request has reached, it fails with Io(Aborted) when the token given to with_cancel has been cancelled. A URL could not be used. url holds the text at fault: the request URL when it does not parse or its scheme is not http or https, a Location header that does not parse or has another scheme, or the configured proxy URL when it is not valid. Opening the connection failed, including a failed name lookup, a refused or unreachable peer and a failed proxy handshake. cause is the underlying error. A connection attempt that runs out of time is Timeout. The TLS handshake failed, including a server certificate that does not verify. cause is the underlying error. The request ran out of time: the limit from with_timeout passed, a connection attempt took longer than with_connect_timeout, or a read or write on the connection timed out. The response was a redirect after the limit from with_redirects was used up. count is the number of redirects followed. The peer sent a response that is not valid HTTP, or one the client does not support. cause is Malformed, TooLarge or Unsupported. The body could not be decompressed according to its content-encoding. cause is the decoder's error. It only occurs while decompression is on. The body did not deserialize into the requested type, as returned by json. cause is the serde.Error. The status was outside 200 to 299, as returned by ensure_success. code is the status. Any other failure while sending the request or receiving the response, such as a connection that resets or closes early, a request header that is not valid, a request body reader that fails, or the sink given to stream_to failing. cause is the underlying error.
struct Observer { pub serve: fn(Request, fn(Request) -> Response) -> Response pub send: fn(Sending) -> Sent }

A pair of hooks that watch every request the HTTP server handles and every attempt the HTTP client makes. Handles one request received by serve, serve_tls, serve_conn or serve_stream, over HTTP/1 or HTTP/2. It is called with the request and the handler that would otherwise run, and returns the response to send. It calls the handler, typically inside a context of its own, and returns the response to send. Called before each attempt the client makes to send a request, with a Sending that describes it, and returns the Sent for that attempt. A request that is redirected or retried makes one call per attempt. The attempt's request headers are replaced by Sent.headers, and Sent.done is called once when the attempt ends.
struct Part { pub name: str pub filename: str pub content_type: str pub data: []u8 }

One part of a multipart/form-data body, as taken by with_multipart. Make one with text_part or file_part. The form field name. It is quoted as header.quote does, so a " or \ is escaped with a backslash and a carriage return or line feed is percent-encoded. The file name sent with the part. When empty, the default, the part is sent as a plain field without a filename. Quoted like name. The media type of the part. When empty, the default, a plain field has no content-type line and a file part has application/octet-stream. A value with a carriage return, line feed or zero byte fails the request with Io(Invalid). The content of the part, sent as it is.

struct Request { pub method: str pub target: str pub path: str pub query: str pub authority: str pub headers: []header.Header pub body: []u8 pub version: Version pub http10: bool pub connection: *io.Reader? pub token: *cancel.Token pub remote: str }

An HTTP request, as received by a handler or as written by write_request. Build one with new_request and set the remaining fields directly. The request method, for example GET. The request target exactly as received, including the query string. The part of target before the first ?. The part of target after the first ?, without the ?, or an empty string when there is none. It is not decoded. The host and optional port the request is for: the :authority pseudo-header on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, falling back to host, or the host header on HTTP/1. Empty when neither was sent. The header fields in the order received. Names are lowercase, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 pseudo-headers are not included. The complete request body, read before the handler runs; empty when the request has none. A body, including a chunked one, larger than 64 MiB is rejected with status 413 on HTTP/1 and by resetting the stream on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. The protocol version the request arrived on. true for an HTTP/1 request whose request line says HTTP/1.0. Its connection closes after the response unless the request has connection: keep-alive. The buffered reader of the underlying connection on HTTP/1, which a handler can take over to speak another protocol; websocket.accept does so. none on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and on a request made by new_request. A cancellation token for the request. On a server it is cancelled once the handler's response is complete or, for a streaming response, once its last chunk is sent. It is also cancelled when the peer disconnects or the connection fails, so a long-running handler or a streaming producer can watch cancel.done to stop early. The IP address of the peer as text, without a port. Empty when the connection has no address, as with serve_stream.
struct Response { pub status: i64 pub headers: []header.Header pub body: []u8 pub url: str pub version: Version pub trailers: []header.Header pub stream: chan[[]u8]? }

An HTTP response, as returned by a handler or by the client. Build one with response or a struct literal. On a server a response is either whole, with the content in body, or streaming, with the content delivered through stream. The status code, for example 200. The header fields. A server adds content-length to a response that is not streaming when it is absent, except on HTTP/1 for 1xx, 204 and 304. A header with an invalid name or value makes writing the response fail. The complete body. Empty for a streaming response and for a response to HEAD, 1xx, 204 and 304, where it is not sent. The final URL after following redirects, for a response returned by the client. Empty on a response built by a handler. The protocol version the client received the response on. A server ignores it. The trailer fields. The client fills them from the trailers it receives. A server sends them over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3; HTTP/1 responses carry none. A channel of body chunks that a server writes to the peer as they arrive, or none. Closing the channel ends the body. If content-length is set the chunks must add up to exactly that length or the connection fails; otherwise the body is chunked, or delimited by closing the connection on HTTP/1.0. The server drops the stream and cancels the request token for HEAD requests and for 1xx, 204 and 304 responses. Responses returned by the client never have a stream.
enum SameSite { Unset NoRestriction Lax Strict }

The SameSite attribute of a cookie. The jar records the value and returns it from jar_cookies; it does not use it to withhold cookies from requests. The cookie has no SameSite attribute, or its value is not Strict, Lax or None. SameSite=None. SameSite=Lax. SameSite=Strict.
