struct Sending { pub method: str pub url: Url pub resend: i64 pub headers: []header.Header }

The description of a client request attempt that is about to be sent, passed to Observer.send. The request method of the attempt, for example GET. The URL the attempt is for. After a redirect it is the redirect's target. The number of attempts that this request has already made, so 0 for the first attempt and one more for each redirect or retry. The headers the attempt would send, including those the client added, such as user-agent and accept, and the cookie header from the client's cookie jar.
struct Sent { pub headers: []header.Header pub done: fn(i64, str, str) }

The answer an Observer gives for a client request attempt: the headers to send and the callback that reports the outcome. The headers to send in place of Sending.headers. An observer that adds nothing returns the headers it was given. Called once when the attempt ends, with the response status, the protocol version and the error type. The status is 0 when no response head arrived. The version is "1.1", "2" or "3", and is an empty string when no response head arrived. The error type is the name of the Error variant that ended the attempt, for example "Timeout", or an empty string when the attempt received a response that the client accepted, including a redirect or a retried status. A failure while reading the body is reported with the status of the response.
struct Url { pub scheme: str pub host: str pub port: i64 pub target: str pub user: str pub password: str }

A parsed absolute URL. Produced by parse_url and resolve. The fragment is never kept. The lowercase scheme, for example https. The lowercase host. An IPv6 address is held without its brackets. The port number: the one in the URL, or 443 for https and wss and 80 for any other scheme. The path and query, beginning with /. Dot segments are resolved and bytes that are not allowed in a request target are percent-encoded. / when the URL has no path. The user name from the userinfo, percent-decoded. Empty when there is none. The password from the userinfo, percent-decoded. Empty when there is none.
The HTTP protocol version a message travelled over. HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/1.0. Request.http10 tells them apart. HTTP/2. HTTP/3, carried over QUIC.

Returns the Client for the settings in b. The settings are copied, so later changes to b do not reach the client. When b has a jar from with_cookie_jar the client uses it; otherwise with_cookies gives it a new private jar, and without either it keeps no cookies. No connection is made until the first request.
fn download(b: Builder[Response], path: str) -> Response ! Error

Sends the request and writes the body to the file at path, creating it or truncating it. The returned response has an empty body. The file is written whatever the status, so call ensure_success on the result and remove the file for a status that is not wanted. When the request fails part way, the file is removed. A file that cannot be created fails with Io holding the cause, such as NotFound or Denied.
fn proxy_for(b: Builder[Client], url: str) -> str

Returns the proxy that a client built from b would use for a request to url, as scheme://host[:port] without credentials. Returns an empty string when the request goes direct: no proxy is set for the scheme, with_no_proxy matches the target, url does not parse, or the configured proxy is not a valid proxy URL.

Sends the request and returns the response with its whole body read into Response.body. Blocks until the body has arrived. Any status is a success; use ensure_success to treat other than 2xx as an error. Redirects, retries, cookies and decompression follow the settings of the builder. The response has the final url, the version it arrived on, and any trailers. A response to HEAD, 1xx, 204 or 304 has an empty body. A body over 64 MiB fails with a TooLarge cause. Failures are the variants of Error.
fn stream_to(b: Builder[Response], sink: fn([]u8) ! io.Error) -> Response ! Error

Sends the request and passes the body to sink in chunks as it arrives, without holding it in memory. The returned response has the status, headers, url, version and trailers but an empty body. sink is called after redirects have been followed and decompression applied, and its failure fails the request with Io, closing the connection. Failures are the variants of Error.
fn with_base_url(b: Builder[Client], url: str) -> Builder[Client]

Sets the URL that relative request URLs are resolved against, as resolve does, so /items with the base https://example.com/api/ becomes https://example.com/items. A request URL that has a scheme is used as it is.
fn with_basic_auth[K](b: Builder[K], user: str, password: str) -> Builder[K]

Sets the authorization header to HTTP Basic credentials for user and password. The header is dropped when a redirect leads to another origin. A URL with user information gets the same header when none is set.
fn with_bearer_token[K](b: Builder[K], token: str) -> Builder[K]
Sets the authorization header to Bearer followed by token. The header is dropped when a redirect leads to another origin.
fn with_body(b: Builder[Response], body: []u8, content_type: str) -> Builder[Response]
Sets the request body to body and the content-type header to content_type, replacing any earlier body or body reader.
fn with_body_reader(b: Builder[Response], source: *io.Reader, content_type: str) -> Builder[Response]

Sets the request body to be read from source as the request is sent, with the content-type header content_type, replacing any earlier body. The length is not known in advance, so the body is sent with chunked transfer coding on HTTP/1.1 and as DATA frames on HTTP/2. source is read once, so the request is never retried and a 307 or 308 redirect is not followed. A read error from source fails the request.

Sets a token that, once cancelled, aborts the request. The connection in use is closed and the request fails with Io(Aborted), whatever it was doing. Set it on the builder returned by request; a token set on a client builder is not carried to its requests.
fn with_connect_timeout[K](b: Builder[K], millis: i64) -> Builder[K]

Sets the time limit for the TCP connection to the target, or to the proxy, in milliseconds. A connection that is not established in time fails with Timeout. The time left under with_timeout also bounds it. Over HTTP/3 it bounds the whole QUIC handshake, which includes TLS. Name lookup and proxy negotiation are not counted. 0, the default, sets no limit of its own.
fn with_cookie_jar(b: Builder[Client], jar: CookieJar) -> Builder[Client]
Gives the client the shared jar jar, so that several clients can use the same cookies. It takes precedence over with_cookies.

Gives the client its own cookie jar, which stores the cookies from every response and sends matching ones with every request. Cookies set by a redirect response are kept for the following hop, and a cookie header set on the request is sent before the jar's cookies. with_cookie_jar takes precedence.
fn with_decompression[K](b: Builder[K], on: bool) -> Builder[K]

Sets whether the client asks for and decodes compressed responses, true by default. When on, a request without an accept-encoding header sends gzip, deflate, br, zstd, and a body with content-encoding of gzip, x-gzip, deflate, br or zstd is decoded. The response then has no content-encoding header, and send sets content-length to the decoded length. A body that cannot be decoded fails with Decode. When off, no header is added and the body is returned as received.
fn with_dialer(b: Builder[Client], d: net.Dialer) -> Builder[Client]

Sets d to open every connection the client makes, in place of resolving the host and connecting directly. d.dial receives the host name and port of the target or, when a proxy is used, of the proxy. with_resolver, with_interface and with_connect_timeout do not apply to connections it opens, and it must resolve names itself. TLS and any proxy negotiation still run over the connection it returns. A client with a dialer sends no request over HTTP/3, since a dialer opens stream connections.
Sets the request body to fields encoded as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, with that content-type.

Sets the TLS key exchange groups the client offers, as IANA named group numbers in preference order. The default is 0x11EC (X25519MLKEM768), 0x001D (X25519), 0x0017 (secp256r1) and 0x0018 (secp384r1).
fn with_header[K](b: Builder[K], name: str, value: str) -> Builder[K]

Sets the header name to value on every request, replacing any header of that name, ignoring case. The name is sent as written. On a client builder the header is a default for all its requests; on a request builder it replaces the client's header of that name for that request. A name or value that is not valid fails the request with Io(Invalid). Headers the client adds itself, user-agent, accept, accept-encoding and authorization from the URL's user information, are skipped when one of that name is set.
fn with_http_proxy(b: Builder[Client], url: str) -> Builder[Client]
Sets url as the proxy for http requests only, in the forms accepted by with_proxy. An empty string means no proxy for http.
fn with_https_proxy(b: Builder[Client], url: str) -> Builder[Client]
Sets url as the proxy for https requests only, in the forms accepted by with_proxy. An empty string means no proxy for https.
fn with_idle_timeout(b: Builder[Client], millis: i64) -> Builder[Client]

Sets how long an unused pooled connection is kept, in milliseconds, 90000 by default. A connection idle for longer is closed rather than reused, and a background sweep closes them while the client has connections.
Turns off verification of server certificates, so that any https server is accepted and the connection can be intercepted. Use it for tests only.
fn with_interface(b: Builder[Client], device: str) -> Builder[Client]

Binds every connection the client makes to the network interface named device, for example eth0. An empty name, the default, leaves the choice to the system. It does not apply to connections opened by with_dialer. HTTP/3 requests fail with Connect holding Unsupported, because a QUIC connection cannot be bound to an interface.
fn with_json[T](b: Builder[Response], value: T) -> Builder[Response]
Sets the request body to value serialized with json.serialize, with content-type set to application/json.
fn with_max_connections_per_host(b: Builder[Client], n: i64) -> Builder[Client]

Limits the open HTTP/1.1 connections the client keeps to one host to n. A request over the limit waits until a connection is free, or fails with Timeout when the request time runs out. 0, the default, sets no limit. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 requests share one connection per host and are not counted.

Sets the request body to parts encoded as multipart/form-data by multipart.Writer, with a content-type that names a random boundary. Each part is held in memory; use with_body_reader to send a large body.
fn with_no_proxy(b: Builder[Client], list: str) -> Builder[Client]

Sets the targets that bypass any proxy, from the comma-separated list, replacing an earlier list. Entries are trimmed and compared case-insensitively, and empty entries are ignored. * matches every target. A host name such as example.com matches that host and its subdomains; .example.com and *.example.com match subdomains only. host:port restricts the entry to that port. An IP address matches that address, and a CIDR range such as 10.0.0.0/8 matches IP address targets inside it. A host name is not resolved to test it against an IP address or range.
fn with_prior_knowledge[K](b: Builder[K], on: bool) -> Builder[K]

Sets whether plain http requests start HTTP/2 directly, without negotiation, false by default. Only enable it for servers known to speak HTTP/2 over cleartext. It has no effect with with_version set to Http1.
fn with_proxy(b: Builder[Client], url: str) -> Builder[Client]

Sets url as the proxy for both http and https requests. The URL can use http://, socks5://, socks5h://, socks4:// or socks4a://; a value without :// is read as http://. User name and password in the URL authenticate to the proxy: as Proxy-Authorization: Basic for an http proxy, as username and password for SOCKS5, and as the user id for SOCKS4. The SOCKS proxy resolves the target host name. An empty string means no proxy. A URL that does not parse or has another scheme is not rejected here; each request fails with InvalidUrl holding the proxy text. A URL without a port uses port 80, including for SOCKS proxies. An http proxy receives http requests in absolute form, always over HTTP/1.1, and is sent CONNECT for https requests. A CONNECT answered with 407 or 403 fails the request with Connect(Denied), and any other non-2xx answer with Connect(Refused). Targets matched by with_no_proxy bypass the proxy.

Sets the proxy and bypass list from the environment, replacing any earlier proxy settings. http_proxy, https_proxy and no_proxy are read, with the lowercase name taking precedence over the uppercase one. all_proxy supplies the proxy for a scheme whose own variable is unset. An unset or empty variable leaves that setting empty. The variables are read when this is called, not when requests are made.
fn with_query(b: Builder[Response], name: str, value: str) -> Builder[Response]
Appends name=value to the query of the request URL, percent-encoding both parts. Existing query parameters, including repeated names, are kept.
fn with_redirects[K](b: Builder[K], max: i64) -> Builder[K]

Sets how many redirects a request follows, 10 by default. Responses 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 with a location header are followed. 301, 302 and 303 turn the request into a GET with no body, except that HEAD stays HEAD; 307 and 308 repeat the method and body, but a request with a body from with_body_reader is not followed and its redirect response is returned. authorization, cookie and proxy-authorization are dropped when the target has another origin. A request that has used up the limit fails with TooManyRedirects, and a location that is not an http or https URL fails with InvalidUrl. 0 or less returns every redirect response as it is. Response.url holds the final URL.
fn with_resolver(b: Builder[Client], resolver: fn(str) -> [][]u8 ! io.Error) -> Builder[Client]

Sets the function that turns a host name into addresses, in place of net.lookup. It is called for the target host, or for the proxy host when a proxy is used, and returns the addresses to try in order. TLS still uses the host name for SNI and certificate checks. A failure from it is a connection failure. It does not apply to connections opened by with_dialer.
fn with_retries[K](b: Builder[K], n: i64) -> Builder[K]

Sets how many times a failed request is sent again, 0 by default. A request is retried only when its body can be replayed, so not with with_body_reader. A failed connection attempt is retried for any method. For GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE, a connection that resets, closes early, times out or breaks after it opened, and a response with status 429, 502, 503 or 504, are also retried. A TLS handshake failure is not. The first retry waits 100 ms and each later one doubles the wait, up to 6.4 s, or the whole seconds in a retry-after header when that is longer, up to 30 s. A retry that would not fit in the time left under with_timeout is not made, and the last failure or response is returned. Separately from this setting, a replayable request on a pooled connection that the server had already closed is sent once more on a new connection.
Sets the certificates that server certificate chains are verified against. With an empty list, the default, the system roots are used.
fn with_text(b: Builder[Response], body: str) -> Builder[Response]
Sets the request body to the bytes of body, with content-type set to text/plain; charset=utf-8.
fn with_timeout[K](b: Builder[K], millis: i64) -> Builder[K]

Sets the time limit for a request, in milliseconds. The limit covers the whole request: connecting, sending, redirects, retries and reading the whole body, including time spent in the stream_to sink. A request that exceeds it fails with Timeout and its connection is closed. 0, the default, sets no limit.
fn with_tls(b: Builder[Client], config: tls.Config) -> Builder[Client]

Sets the TLS configuration for https connections, replacing the earlier one including with_roots, with_insecure and with_groups. The client overwrites config.alpn with the protocols it negotiates, and uses the host of the request as config.server_name when that is empty.
fn with_user_agent[K](b: Builder[K], agent: str) -> Builder[K]
Sets the user-agent header. Without it the client sends lowlang-http/1.
fn with_version[K](b: Builder[K], v: Version) -> Builder[K]

Sets the HTTP version to use. Http2, the default, offers HTTP/2 and falls back to HTTP/1.1 when the server does not accept it; Http1 always uses HTTP/1.1; Http3 sends https requests over HTTP/3 on QUIC with no fallback. HTTP/2 is negotiated through ALPN on https and is not used through a forwarding proxy. Plain http uses HTTP/2 only with with_prior_knowledge. HTTP/3 offers only ALPN h3 and keeps one QUIC connection per host and port, shared by concurrent requests and replaced when it has ended or the server sent GOAWAY. A connection that cannot be made fails with Connect, Tls or Timeout and is not retried over TCP. The TLS settings, the resolver, the connect timeout, which bounds the QUIC handshake, and with_idle_timeout apply. http requests, and https requests through a proxy or a dialer, use HTTP/1.1. A client with a network interface from with_interface fails its HTTP/3 requests with Connect(Unsupported). The request is HEADERS, DATA and a FIN on a bidirectional stream, the response is read the same way, and Response.trailers holds a trailing HEADERS. A request that ran out of time or was cancelled resets only its stream. A request whose stream the server reset before the response head, or that the server refused with GOAWAY, is sent once more on a new connection when its body can be replayed.

Closes the idle pooled connections of c. HTTP/1.1 connections that are idle are closed, and an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection is closed once its in-flight requests finish. Requests in flight are not interrupted, and later requests open new connections.
Returns the cookie header value that the jar of c would send to url. Returns an empty string when c has no jar, url does not parse, or no cookie matches.
fn del(c: *Client, url: str) -> Response ! Error
Sends a DELETE request to url and returns the response, as send does.
fn get(c: *Client, url: str) -> Response ! Error
Sends a GET request to url and returns the response, as send does.
fn head(c: *Client, url: str) -> Response ! Error
Sends a HEAD request to url and returns the response, as send does. The body is empty.
fn patch(c: *Client, url: str, content_type: str, body: []u8) -> Response ! Error
Sends a PATCH request to url with body as the content of type content_type, and returns the response as send does.
fn post(c: *Client, url: str, content_type: str, body: []u8) -> Response ! Error
Sends a POST request to url with body as the content of type content_type, and returns the response as send does.
fn put(c: *Client, url: str, content_type: str, body: []u8) -> Response ! Error
Sends a PUT request to url with body as the content of type content_type, and returns the response as send does.
fn request(c: *Client, method: str, url: str) -> Builder[Response]

Returns a request builder for method and url on c. Run it with send, stream_to or download. The method is sent as given. url is resolved against the client's base URL when it has no scheme, and its scheme must be http or https; anything else fails the request with InvalidUrl when it runs. The builder starts with the client's headers, timeout, connect timeout, redirect limit, retry count, version, prior knowledge and decompression settings.
Stops c from closing its stream when released, and returns the stream. The caller becomes responsible for closing it.

Returns the value of a Set-Cookie header for c. The attributes are written in the order Path, Domain, Max-Age, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite. Domain is left out for a host-only cookie, Max-Age for a negative max_age, and SameSite for Unset. The name and value are written as given.
Removes every cookie from the jar.
Returns a copy of every unexpired cookie in the jar, in storage order. Changing the returned slice does not change the jar.
fn jar_header(j: CookieJar, url: str) -> str

Returns the value of the Cookie header for a request to url. The value is the matching name=value pairs joined by ; . A cookie matches when its domain and path match the URL and, for a Secure cookie, the scheme is https or wss. Cookies with longer paths come first, then older cookies. Returns an empty string when url does not parse or no cookie matches.
fn jar_set(j: CookieJar, url: str, set_cookie: str) -> bool

Stores the cookie described by a Set-Cookie header value, as received in a response from url. Returns true when the cookie is now in the jar. Returns false, leaving the jar unchanged, when url does not parse, when the value has no = or an empty name, when the name and value exceed 4096 bytes, when Domain does not cover the host of url, when Secure is set for a URL that is not https or wss, when a __Secure- or __Host- prefix rule is broken, or when the cookie would replace a Secure cookie from a URL that is not secure. A cookie that is already expired (Max-Age of 0 or less, or a past Expires) deletes the matching cookie and returns false.
fn multipart_form(req: Request, limits: multipart.Limits, spill: multipart.Spill?) -> multipart.Form ! multipart.Error
Reads the whole multipart body of a request into a multipart.Form. Fails with the errors of multipart_reader and multipart.read_form.
fn multipart_reader(req: Request, limits: multipart.Limits) -> *multipart.Reader ! multipart.Error
Returns a reader for the multipart body of a request. Fails with BadContentType when the request has no content-type header, and with the errors of multipart.boundary_from_content_type.
Sets the body and content-type of a request from a multipart writer. The writer is finished, so nothing can be added to it afterwards. An existing content-type header is replaced.

Writes a 101 Switching Protocols response with headers to the connection of req and returns the reader of that connection, for a handler to speak another protocol. Fails with Unsupported when req has no connection to take over, as on HTTP/2 and for a request made by new_request, and with Invalid for a header that is not valid. After using the connection, return upgraded() from the handler.
Returns resp when its status is 200 to 299, and fails with Status holding the status otherwise.
fn header_value(resp: Response, name: str) -> str?
Returns the value of the first header of resp named name, ignoring case, or none when there is none.
Deserializes the body of resp as JSON into T. Fails with Json holding the serde.Error when the body is not valid JSON or does not fit T. The status is not checked; call ensure_success first.
Returns true when resp delivers its body through stream.
Returns the body of resp as a string, taking its bytes as they are without checking the encoding.
Returns the host[:port] part of u, as sent in a host header. An IPv6 host is put in brackets, and the port is left out when it is the default for the scheme.
fn connect(u: Url, protocols: []str) -> Connection ! io.Error

Opens a connection to the host and port of u and returns it as a Connection. The scheme must be http, ws, https or wss, or the call fails with Unsupported. The host is resolved and connected with net.dial; no client settings, proxy or timeout option apply. For https and wss a TLS handshake follows, with protocols offered through ALPN, u.host as the server name and the certificate checked against the system roots; protocols is ignored for a plain connection. Blocks until the connection is ready, and fails with the error of the connection or the handshake.
Returns u as text: its origin followed by its target. The user, password and fragment are not included.
fn resolve(base: Url, reference: str) -> Url ! io.Error

Resolves reference against base, following the rules of RFC 3986. Leading and trailing whitespace and any fragment are removed from reference first. An absolute reference is parsed on its own, and one starting with // takes the scheme of base. An empty reference returns base. A reference starting with / replaces the target, one starting with ? replaces only the query, and any other reference is joined to the directory of the base path. Dot segments are resolved. The relative forms keep the host, port and userinfo of base. Fails like parse_url when the reference is absolute and does not parse.
fn with_query_pair(u: Url, name: str, value: str) -> Url
Returns u with name=value appended to its query, separated by ? or &. Both parts are percent-encoded with escape. An existing pair of the same name is kept.
Returns the protocol version of v as telemetry names it: "1.1", "2" or "3".
fn accepts_coding(accept: str, coding: str) -> bool
Returns true when the accept-encoding value accept lists coding, ignoring case, with a quality other than zero. * is not treated as a wildcard.
Returns the host of a host[:port] authority as sent in a host header, without the port and without the brackets of an IPv6 host.

Returns a Builder[Client] with the default settings. By default there is no timeout and no connect timeout, up to 10 redirects are followed, there are no retries, cookies and proxies are off, HTTP/2 is used where available, response decompression is on, certificates are verified against the system roots, connections per host are unlimited and idle connections are kept for 90 seconds.
Returns a new, empty CookieJar that reads the time from the operating system.
Returns a new, empty CookieJar that reads the time of c, which decides when its cookies expire.
fn encode_body(coding: str, body: []u8, level: i64) -> []u8?
Compresses body with coding, one of zstd, br, gzip and deflate, at level, and returns none for any other coding.
fn file_part(name: str, filename: str, content_type: str, data: []u8) -> Part
Returns a Part for the file filename sent under the field name, with content_type and the bytes data.
Returns the coding encode_body should use for the accept-encoding value accept: the first of zstd, br and gzip that it accepts, or an empty string when it accepts none.
fn new_request(method: str, target: str) -> Request

Returns a Request for method and target, splitting path and query at the first ?. The request is Http1, has no headers or body, an empty authority and remote, no connection and a fresh cancellation token. Nothing is validated until the request is written.

Parses an absolute URL of the form scheme://[user[:password]@]host[:port][/path][?query]. Any scheme is accepted. The scheme and host are lowercased, the fragment is dropped, and the target is normalised as described on Url.target. An empty or absent port uses the default for the scheme. Fails with Invalid when the scheme or the // is missing, the host is empty or contains a space, /, \ or @, the port is not a number from 1 to 65535, or a bracketed host is not an IP address. Fails with Malformed when the userinfo holds a bad percent-escape.

Reads one HTTP/1 request from r, including its whole body. Blocks until the request is complete. Blank lines before the request line are skipped. The returned request has version Http1, http10 set when the request line says HTTP/1.0, its authority taken from the host header, and connection set to r. The body is read from chunked transfer coding, or from content-length bytes; a request with neither has an empty body. When the request carries expect: 100-continue, HTTP/1.1 100 Continue is written to the stream beneath r before the body is read. Fails with Eof when the input ends before a complete request, Malformed for a request line that is not METHOD target HTTP/1.x, a header line without a valid name and :, a bad chunk size or a content-length that is not a number, Unsupported when the version is not HTTP/1.0 or HTTP/1.1, and TooLarge for more than 100 headers, a line longer than the reader's buffer, or a body over 64 MiB. Header names are lowercased.
fn read_response(r: *io.Reader, method: str) -> Response ! io.Error

Reads one HTTP/1 response from r, including its whole body. method is the method of the request being answered. Blocks until the response is complete. Interim 1xx responses other than 101 are skipped. The body is empty for a response to HEAD and for 1xx, 204 and 304; otherwise it is read from chunked transfer coding, from content-length bytes, or, when neither is present, until the peer closes the connection. Chunked trailers are returned in trailers. The returned response has version Http1 and an empty url. Fails with Eof when the input ends early, Malformed for a status line that is not HTTP/1.x and a three-digit status, a bad header, a bad chunk size or a content-length that is not a number, and TooLarge for more than 100 headers or a body over 64 MiB.

Returns the cookies sent in the cookie headers of a request as a map of names to values. Every cookie header is read. Values are kept as sent, without decoding, and a repeated name keeps its last value.
fn response(status: i64, body: str) -> Response
Returns a Response with status and the bytes of body and no headers.
Returns the wait in milliseconds that a retry-after header of whole seconds asks for, or -1 when there is none or it is not a number of seconds.
Returns true for the statuses a retry may recover from: 429, 502, 503 and 504.
fn serve(l: net.Listener, handler: fn(Request) -> Response) ! io.Error

Accepts connections from l and serves each on its own task, calling handler for every request. Blocks until accepting fails and returns that error; it never returns otherwise. The server speaks HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive and, on plain connections, HTTP/2 to a client that opens with the HTTP/2 connection preface. Requests on one HTTP/1 connection run one after another; requests on an HTTP/2 connection run concurrently. A request that cannot be parsed is answered with 400, a body or header block that is too large with 413, and an unsupported protocol version with 505; any other read or write failure ends that connection without a response. Errors on one connection never reach the caller.
fn serve_conn(c: net.Conn, handler: fn(Request) -> Response)
Serves requests from c as serve_conn_on does, and closes c when the connection ends.
fn serve_conn_on(h: net.ConnHandle, handler: fn(Request) -> Response)
Serves requests from one accepted connection until the connection ends, then closes it. Blocks for the lifetime of the connection. serve spawns this once per connection.
fn serve_on(l: net.ListenerHandle, handler: fn(Request) -> Response) ! io.Error
Serves HTTP as serve does, accepting from a ListenerHandle.
fn serve_quic(l: quic.Listener, handler: fn(Request) -> Response) ! io.Error

Accepts QUIC connections from l and serves each on its own green thread over HTTP/3, calling handler for every request. Blocks until accepting fails and returns that error, which is NotConnected once the listener is closed. The listener's config.tls.alpn should be ["h3"]; a connection that negotiated another protocol is closed with H3_GENERAL_PROTOCOL_ERROR. Each request stream runs on its own green thread, and a connection runs at most the listener's config.max_streams handlers at a time: the next request stream is not accepted until one of them has returned and written its response, so the QUIC stream credit of the peer stays held back meanwhile. A request that is malformed, or that carries a body over 64 MiB, is answered by resetting its stream with H3_MESSAGE_ERROR or H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD and the handler is not called; a field section over 64 KiB is answered with 431; a protocol violation on a connection closes that connection with the matching HTTP/3 error code. Request.token is cancelled when the response is complete, when a write of the response fails because the client stopped or reset the stream, and when the connection ends; a client that stops the stream while the handler is still running is not noticed until the handler's response is written. The server sends no push, accepts no extended CONNECT and no HTTP datagrams, and uses only the static QPACK table for the field sections it sends. Errors on one connection never reach the caller.
fn serve_quic_on(l: *quic.ListenerHandle, handler: fn(Request) -> Response) ! io.Error
Serves HTTP/3 as serve_quic does, accepting from a ListenerHandle.
fn serve_stream(s: io.Stream, handler: fn(Request) -> Response) ! io.Error

Serves requests read from s and writes the responses to it, until the peer ends the stream or a response requires the connection to close. Blocks until then. s is not closed, and Request.remote is empty. Returns the error from a failed write; a read failure or end of input ends the loop and returns normally.
fn serve_tls(l: net.Listener, config: tls.Config, handler: fn(Request) -> Response) ! io.Error

Serves HTTPS as serve does, terminating TLS on every accepted connection with config. config must hold the server certificates and key. When config.alpn is empty it is set to h2 and http/1.1. A connection whose handshake fails is closed.
fn serve_tls_on(l: net.ListenerHandle, config: tls.Config, handler: fn(Request) -> Response) ! io.Error
Serves HTTPS as serve_tls does, accepting from a ListenerHandle.
Appends a set-cookie header for c to headers, keeping any earlier cookie of the same name.
Returns the reason phrase for status, such as Not Found for 404, or an empty string for a code without a known phrase.
fn text_part(name: str, value: str) -> Part
Returns a Part for a plain form field name with the bytes of value and no file name or content type.

Returns the response a handler returns after it has taken over the connection. On an HTTP/1 request that carries an upgrade header, a handler that has run another protocol over Request.connection, as websocket.accept does, returns this response. The server then writes nothing and stops serving the connection, which serve_conn and serve_conn_on close. Over HTTP/2 the response is written as an ordinary 101.
fn write_request(s: io.Stream, req: Request) ! io.Error

Writes req to s as an HTTP/1.1 request in one write. The request line is req.method, req.target and HTTP/1.1. A host header from req.authority is added when req.headers has none. content-length is added from the body when it is absent and the body is not empty or the method is POST, PUT or PATCH. The body follows the headers. Fails with Invalid before writing anything when a header name or value is not valid, and otherwise with the error of the write.
fn write_response(s: io.Stream, method: str, resp: Response, closing: bool) ! io.Error

Writes resp to s as an HTTP/1.1 response in one write. method is the method of the request being answered. The body is left out for HEAD and for 1xx, 204 and 304 responses. content-length is added from the body when resp.headers has none, except for 1xx, 204 and 304. When closing is true, connection: close is added, except for a 101 response. The status line carries the reason phrase from status_text. resp.stream and resp.trailers are not written. Fails with Invalid before writing anything when a header name or value is not valid, and otherwise with the error of the write.
struct FileOptions { pub name: str pub content_type: str pub encoding: str pub cache_control: str }

Overrides for serve_file_with. Every field is optional and an empty string leaves the default. The file name used to pick the content type from its extension. Defaults to the path being served. The content-type to send. Overrides any detection. The content-encoding the file is stored in, for example gzip. It is sent as content-encoding together with vary: Accept-Encoding. The content type then comes from name only; when the extension is unknown it is application/octet-stream and the file is not sniffed. The cache-control header to send. Not sent when empty.
fn serve_file(req: http.Request, target: str) -> http.Response
Returns the response that serves the file at target with default options, as serve_file_with does.
fn serve_file_with(req: http.Request, target: str, o: FileOptions) -> http.Response

Returns the response that serves the regular file at the filesystem path target for req. target is used as given, so a caller that builds it from a request path must first reject or confine anything that escapes its root. The status is 404 when the path does not exist or is not a regular file, 403 when it is not accessible, and 500 for other failures. The response carries last-modified, a weak etag made from the size and modification time, and accept-ranges: bytes. It is 304 when if-none-match lists the entity tag or is *, or, if that header is absent, when if-modified-since is not older than the file. The content type is o.content_type, else the type for the extension of o.name or the path, else a guess from the first 512 bytes, else application/octet-stream. A single bytes= range in range is answered with 206 and content-range: first-last, first- and -suffix forms are accepted, and the end is clamped to the file size. A range starting past the end of the file, or a zero-length suffix, gets 416 with content-range: bytes */size. A range that is malformed, lists several ranges or is not in bytes is ignored and the whole file is sent. An if-range header that is not the date the file was last modified also sends the whole file. The body is read in 64 KiB chunks on a separate task and delivered through Response.stream, and reading stops when req.token is cancelled. A HEAD request and an empty file get the headers and content-length and no stream.

Decodes raw, a string coded with the static Huffman code of RFC 7541 appendix B, which HPACK and QPACK share, and returns the bytes it spells as a str. The result is not checked for UTF-8. Fails Malformed when a code in raw is the EOS symbol, when the final byte pads with more than 7 bits, or when the padding is not all ones. An empty raw decodes to an empty string.
Appends the Huffman code of the bytes of s to out, padding the last byte with the high bits of the EOS symbol. An empty s appends nothing. The number of bytes appended is encoded_size(s).
Returns the number of bytes encode appends for s.

The result of decoding one encoded field section. The field lines of the section, in the order the section lists them. The section needs dynamic table entries the encoder stream has not delivered yet. The stream is recorded as blocked. The caller keeps the section bytes and decodes them again after on_encoder_stream lists the stream as ready.

A QPACK decoder (RFC 9204): the dynamic table, the encoder stream parser and the decoder stream instructions owed to the peer's encoder. A decoder does no I/O and is not safe for concurrent use. The caller owns the streams. It feeds bytes read from the peer's encoder stream to on_encoder_stream, field sections read from request or response streams to decode, and writes take_decoder_stream to its own decoder stream. Failures map to HTTP/3 error codes by the function that failed. A failure of decode is QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED (decompression_failed), except TooLarge, which is a field section over the size limit and is handled as RFC 9114 section 4.2.2 describes. A failure of on_encoder_stream is QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR (encoder_stream_error). After any failure the connection is to be closed with that code, so the decoder is not used again.

A QPACK encoder (RFC 9204) that uses only the static table. It never inserts into the dynamic table and writes nothing to the encoder stream, so every field section it produces has a Required Insert Count of 0 and can be decoded at once. A peer decoder needs no SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY for it. The caller feeds the bytes it reads from the peer's decoder stream to on_decoder_stream.

Records that stream was reset or abandoned before its field sections were all decoded, and queues a Stream Cancellation for the peer's encoder. A blocked section of the stream is forgotten and no longer counts against max_blocked. When max_capacity is 0 the encoder cannot hold references and no instruction is queued.
fn decode(d: *Decoder, stream: i64, block: []u8) -> Decoded ! io.Error

Decodes one encoded field section read from stream, which is a non-negative QUIC stream ID. Returns Fields with the field lines in order. When the section's Required Insert Count is above insert_count, returns Blocked and records the stream as blocked; the caller keeps the section bytes and decodes them again once on_encoder_stream lists the stream. A blocked section is parsed only as far as its prefix, so its field lines are checked on the second call. After a section whose Required Insert Count is not zero is decoded, a Section Acknowledgment for stream is queued for take_decoder_stream. Fails Malformed, which the caller reports as QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED, for a truncated section, an integer over 2^62-1, an invalid Required Insert Count encoding, a Base below zero, an index past the static table, a dynamic reference that is evicted, at or above the Required Insert Count or relative to a Base it underflows, a string that runs past the section, invalid Huffman data, and a block that would exceed max_blocked blocked streams. Fails TooLarge when the decoded field section would exceed max_field_section_size; the decoder stops before building more than that.
Returns the number of entries the decoder has inserted into the dynamic table, counting those since evicted.

Consumes bytes of the peer's encoder stream and returns the streams that were blocked and can now be decoded. The instructions are Set Dynamic Table Capacity, Insert With Name Reference (static or dynamic), Insert With Literal Name and Duplicate. An instruction may be split across calls: the unparsed tail is kept and joined to the next call's data. The tail is never larger than 65536 bytes, and no string in an instruction may declare a longer length, so a peer cannot make the decoder buffer more. The returned stream IDs are those decode reported as Blocked whose Required Insert Count the table has now reached, in the order they became blocked. Each is returned once. The caller decodes its stored section for each stream again. Fails Malformed, which the caller reports as QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR, for a capacity above max_capacity, an entry larger than the capacity, a static index past the table, a dynamic index that was evicted or never inserted, an integer over 2^62-1, a string longer than its limit, invalid Huffman data and a tail over the buffer limit.
Returns the entries still in the dynamic table, oldest first.
Returns the size of the dynamic table in bytes: each entry counts its name length, its value length and 32.

Returns the bytes to write to the decoder stream and clears them. They are the Section Acknowledgments and Stream Cancellations queued since the last call, in order, followed by one Insert Count Increment covering the insertions the peer has not yet been told about, either by an increment or by the Required Insert Count of an acknowledged section. The result is empty when nothing is owed. Call it after on_encoder_stream, decode and cancel_stream.

Encodes fields as one field section and returns its bytes. The name of each field is lowercased. A field that equals a static table entry is written as an indexed field line, a field whose name is in the static table as a literal with a name reference, and any other as a literal with a literal name. A string is Huffman coded when that is shorter. The section starts with a Required Insert Count of 0 and a Base of 0. An empty fields gives the two prefix bytes alone.

Consumes bytes of the peer's decoder stream. An instruction may be split across calls; the unparsed tail is kept. A Stream Cancellation is accepted and has no effect, because this encoder holds no references. Any other instruction contradicts what the encoder sent: a Section Acknowledgment names a section with no dynamic table references, and an Insert Count Increment, whatever its value, exceeds the zero insertions made. Fails Malformed, which the caller reports as QPACK_DECODER_STREAM_ERROR, for a Section Acknowledgment, an Insert Count Increment, or an integer over 2^62-1.
The HTTP/3 error code QPACK_DECODER_STREAM_ERROR, 0x202. It is the code for a failure of on_decoder_stream.
The HTTP/3 error code QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED, 0x200. It is the code for a failure of decode.
The HTTP/3 error code QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR, 0x201. It is the code for a failure of on_encoder_stream.
fn decoder(max_capacity: i64, max_blocked: i64, max_field_section_size: i64) -> *Decoder

Returns a decoder with an empty dynamic table. max_capacity is the largest dynamic table capacity the peer's encoder may set, the value advertised as SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY. max_blocked is the most streams that may be blocked at once, the value of SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS. max_field_section_size is the most a decoded field section may measure, the value of SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE, where each field line counts its name length, its value length and 32. A negative argument is treated as 0.
Returns the QPACK static table of RFC 9204 appendix A: 99 field lines indexed from 0. Field lines whose value the RFC leaves empty have an empty value. The slice is built on each call.

The handle a producer uses to send events to the client. The events go to the response created by stream or stream_with. The cancellation token of the request. It is cancelled when the client disconnects.
struct Event { pub id: str? pub event: str? pub data: str pub retry: i64? }

A server-sent event. format writes it to the wire and parse and feed read it back. The event identifier a client echoes in last-event-id when it reconnects. none writes no id field. Line breaks and zero bytes are removed when written. A parsed event carries the latest identifier the stream set. The event name. none, or a name that is empty once line breaks are removed, leaves the event unnamed. The event payload. When written, each line becomes a data field, and lines may end in 
,  or 
. A parsed event joins its data lines with 
. The reconnection delay in milliseconds. Not written when none or negative.
struct Options { pub keepalive: i64 pub retry: i64 }

Settings for a server-sent events response. The milliseconds of silence after which a keepalive comment is sent so proxies keep the connection open. The default is 15000; 0 or less turns keepalives off. The reconnection delay in milliseconds sent to the client as the first thing in the stream. The default -1 sends none.

An incremental parser for a text/event-stream body. It follows the WHATWG event stream rules: lines end in \n, \r or \r\n, a leading byte order mark is skipped, lines beginning with : are comments, unknown fields are ignored, and a blank line dispatches the event. A Parser keeps partial lines and a partial event between calls to feed, so chunks may be split anywhere. The reconnection delay in milliseconds from the latest valid retry field the parser has seen, or -1 when the stream has sent none.

Sends e to the client and returns true, or returns false when the request has been cancelled. Blocks while the response is not keeping up. A false result means the client is gone and the producer should return.

Returns the wire text of e: its id, event, retry and data fields in that order, each ending in a newline, followed by a blank line. An event with empty data and no name has no fields and is only the blank line, which clients ignore. An empty-data event with a name writes an empty data field so that it is dispatched.

Parses chunk and returns the events it completes, in order. An event is returned when its terminating blank line is read, and only if it had at least one data field. Multiple data lines are joined with \n. Event.id is the latest id the stream set, which carries over to later events and is none when that id was empty, Event.event is the event field if one was given, and Event.retry is set only on the event that followed a retry field. An id containing a zero byte is ignored, and so is a retry that is not all digits. Input after the last line ending stays in the parser until more arrives.
Returns note as an event stream comment: one line beginning with : for each line of note, followed by a blank line. Clients ignore comments.
Returns the comment that keeps an idle stream open.
Returns the last-event-id header of req, which a reconnecting client sends to resume, or none when it is missing or empty.
fn listen(b: http.Builder[http.Response], on_event: fn(Event) ! io.Error) -> http.Response ! http.Error

Sends the request built by b and calls on_event for each event of the response as it arrives, until the stream ends. The request gets accept: text/event-stream and cache-control: no-cache. Returns the response, whose body is empty because it was delivered to on_event. Failures are those of stream_to; an error from on_event stops reading and is returned as Io. It does not reconnect or send last-event-id.
Parses data as a complete event stream and returns its events. An event not ended by a blank line is dropped.
Returns a new Parser that has read nothing.
fn serve_events(req: http.Request, events: chan[Event]) -> http.Response
Returns the response of serve_events_with with the default Options.
fn serve_events_with(req: http.Request, o: Options, events: chan[Event]) -> http.Response

Returns a streaming 200 response that writes each event received from events in the text/event-stream format. The response has content-type: text/event-stream, cache-control: no-cache and x-accel-buffering: no. If o.retry is not negative it is sent first, and after o.keepalive milliseconds without an event a keepalive comment is sent. The stream ends when the caller closes events or the request is cancelled. Nothing reads events after cancellation, so a sender should watch req.token.
fn stream(req: http.Request, producer: fn(*Emitter)) -> http.Response
Returns the response of stream_with with the default Options.
fn stream_with(req: http.Request, o: Options, producer: fn(*Emitter)) -> http.Response
Returns a streaming response that runs producer on a new task and sends the events it passes to send. The stream ends when producer returns. The producer should stop when send returns false.
struct Message { pub text: bool pub data: []u8 }
A complete message received from the peer. true for a text message, whose data is valid UTF-8, and false for a binary one. The message payload with fragments joined.

An open WebSocket connection that closes itself. Dropping a Socket sends a close frame with code 1000 and waits for the peer's close, unless it was detached. Use detach to keep the connection open past the end of the scope. The shared connection state, for use with the _on functions.

The state of one WebSocket connection: the reader over the connection, which side it is, and whether it has been closed. A *SocketHandle can be shared between tasks and passed to the _on functions, which exist so a connection can be used without an owning Socket.
fn close(ws: Socket, code: i64) ! io.Error

Closes the connection with the status code. Sends a close frame with code unless one has been exchanged already, then reads and discards messages until the peer's close frame or an error, and releases the connection; a client side closes its stream. Blocks until then. Normal closure is 1000. Fails with the write error when the close frame cannot be sent, and the connection is still released.
Stops s closing its connection on drop and returns its handle. The caller becomes responsible for calling close_on.
Sends a ping frame carrying data, which the protocol limits to 125 bytes. The peer's pong is skipped by receive. Fails with NotConnected once the socket is closed, or with the write error.

Blocks until a complete message arrives and returns it. Fragments are joined into one Message of at most 16 MiB. Ping frames are answered with a pong and pong frames are skipped, so neither is returned. When the peer sends a close frame the close is echoed and the call fails with Eof. A protocol violation, such as a bad frame, a text message that is not UTF-8 or a message over the size limit, sends a close frame with code 1002, 1007 or 1009 and fails with Malformed. A connection that ends fails with Eof, and any other read failure with Reset. Fails with NotConnected once the socket is closed.
Sends data as one binary frame. Fails with NotConnected once the socket is closed, or with the write error.
fn send_text(ws: Socket, message: str) ! io.Error
Sends message as one text frame. Fails with NotConnected once the socket is closed, or with the write error.
Returns a Socket that owns h and closes it on drop.
Closes ws with code as close does.
Sends a ping frame on ws as ping does.
Receives a message from ws as receive does.
Sends a binary frame on ws as send_binary does.
Sends a text frame on ws as send_text does.

Completes the server side of the WebSocket handshake for req and returns the open connection. req must be a GET that has upgrade: websocket, a connection header with the upgrade token, sec-websocket-version: 13 and a sec-websocket-key that decodes to 16 bytes. http.upgrade writes the 101 Switching Protocols response to the connection. The origin header, subprotocols and extensions are not examined. Fails with Unsupported when req has no connection to take over, as on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and with Malformed when a handshake requirement is not met. Write failures are returned as they occur. After using the socket, return upgraded() from the handler. import std/http import ws = std/http/websocket fn echo(req: http.Request) -> http.Response { using s = ws.accept(req) or return http.response(400, "bad handshake") for { let m = ws.receive(s) or break ws.send_text(s, str(m.data)) or break } http.upgraded() }

Connects to a ws or wss URL, performs the client handshake and returns the open connection. Messages the client sends are masked as the protocol requires. Fails with Unsupported for any other scheme, with the error from parse_url for a bad URL, with the connection or TLS error when connecting fails, and with Refused when the handshake cannot be completed or the server does not answer 101 with the expected sec-websocket-accept.
enum Filter { Nearest Bilinear Bicubic Lanczos3 }

The resampling filter for resize. Picks the nearest source pixel without interpolation. Linear interpolation between the two nearest pixels on each axis. Catmull-Rom cubic interpolation. A Lanczos window of radius 3, the sharpest and slowest filter.
enum Format { Gray8 GrayAlpha8 Rgb8 Rgba8 Gray16 Rgba16 }

The layout of one pixel in an Image. Samples are interleaved. Eight-bit formats use one byte per channel; 16-bit formats store each sample big-endian. One 8-bit gray channel. 8-bit gray followed by 8-bit alpha. 8-bit red, green and blue. 8-bit red, green, blue and alpha. One 16-bit gray channel. 16-bit red, green, blue and alpha.
struct Frame { pub image: Image pub delay_ms: i64 }
A decoded GIF frame. The full canvas as it looks after this frame is drawn, in Rgba8. How long the frame is shown, in milliseconds. 0 when the frame has no graphic control extension.
struct Image { pub width: i64 pub height: i64 pub format: Format pub stride: i64 pub pixels: []u8 }

A raster of pixels in row-major order from the top-left. Operations return new images and leave their argument unchanged, except set, fill_rect and blend, which write into the pixels they are given. The width in pixels. The height in pixels. The pixel layout of pixels. The number of bytes from the start of one row to the start of the next. The pixel bytes, stride * height of them.
struct Rgba { pub r: u8 pub g: u8 pub b: u8 pub a: u8 }

An 8-bit red, green, blue and alpha color, with alpha 255 fully opaque and not premultiplied. The red channel. The green channel. The blue channel. The alpha channel, 0 fully transparent and 255 fully opaque.
Returns the number of bytes one pixel of f takes: the channel count, doubled for the 16-bit formats.
Returns the number of channels in f: 1 for gray, 2 for gray with alpha, 3 for Rgb8 and 4 for Rgba8 and Rgba16.
Returns true when f has an alpha channel: GrayAlpha8, Rgba8 and Rgba16.
fn blend(dst: Image, src: Image, x: i64, y: i64)

Composites src over dst with its top-left corner at x, y, in place. Alpha is straight, not premultiplied. The part of src outside dst is ignored, and src and dst can have different formats. Where src is opaque it replaces the pixel, and where it is transparent dst is unchanged.
fn convert(img: Image, format: Format) -> Image

Returns a copy of img in format. Gray is expanded to equal red, green and blue, color to gray takes the luma, a missing alpha becomes fully opaque and alpha is dropped when the target has none (it is not composited). Converting to the same format returns a plain copy.
fn crop(img: Image, x: i64, y: i64, width: i64, height: i64) -> Image
Returns the width by height region of img whose top-left corner is x, y. The region is clipped to the image, so the result can be smaller than requested, and is empty when nothing remains.

Encodes img as an uncompressed bottom-up BMP. An image with an alpha channel is written as 32 bits per pixel with a 108-byte header and bit fields; any other image is written as 24 bits per pixel with a 40-byte header. Images are converted to Rgba8 or Rgb8 first, so 16-bit samples are reduced to 8 bits and gray becomes equal red, green and blue.

Encodes img as a single-frame GIF89a. palette is the color table; an empty palette is replaced by median_cut of the image, and a palette longer than 256 colors (255 when the image has an alpha channel) is truncated. Each pixel maps to its nearest palette color. When the image has an alpha channel, pixels with alpha below 128 become a transparent index and the rest are opaque.

Encodes img as a baseline JPEG. quality is clamped to 1 to 100 and scales the standard quantisation tables. Gray formats produce a single-component file and all others 4:2:0 YCbCr. Alpha is discarded and 16-bit samples are reduced to 8 bits.

Encodes img as a non-interlaced PNG. Every row picks whichever of the five filters has the lowest score, and the data is zlib compressed at level 6. 8-bit and 16-bit images keep their depth; Gray8, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8 and Rgba8 and the 16-bit formats map to the matching PNG color type.

Encodes img as QOI, with 4 channels when the image has an alpha channel and 3 otherwise. The image is converted to Rgba8 or Rgb8 first, so 16-bit samples are reduced to 8 bits. The color space byte is 0.
fn fill_rect(img: Image, x: i64, y: i64, width: i64, height: i64, c: Rgba)
Sets every pixel in the width by height rectangle at x, y to c, in place. The rectangle is clipped to the image. Alpha is written, not blended.
Returns img mirrored left to right.
Returns img mirrored top to bottom.
fn get(img: Image, x: i64, y: i64) -> Rgba

Returns the pixel at x, y as an 8-bit Rgba. Gray formats give equal red, green and blue, and formats without alpha give alpha 255. 16-bit samples are rounded to 8 bits. A position outside the image gives transparent black.

Returns a palette of at most count colors for img, chosen by median cut. Pixels with alpha below 128 are ignored. When the image has no more than count distinct colors, those colors are returned as they are. All returned colors are opaque.
fn orient(img: Image, orientation: i64) -> Image
Returns img transformed so that it displays upright for the EXIF orientation value 1 to 8. exif_orientation reads that value from a JPEG. 1 and any value outside 1 to 8 return img itself.
Returns a copy of img with the color channels multiplied by alpha. An image without an alpha channel is returned as a plain copy.
fn resize(img: Image, width: i64, height: i64, filter: Filter) -> Image

Returns img scaled to width by height pixels using filter. Non-nearest filters resample each axis separately on premultiplied values, so transparent pixels do not bleed color. The format is kept. When width or height is not positive, or img is empty, the result is a zeroed image of the requested size.
Returns img rotated 270 degrees clockwise (90 degrees counterclockwise), with width and height swapped.
Returns img rotated 90 degrees clockwise, with width and height swapped.
fn set(img: Image, x: i64, y: i64, c: Rgba)
Writes c at x, y, converting it to the image's format. Formats without alpha drop it, and gray formats store the luma of the color. A position outside the image is ignored.
Returns img reflected across its main diagonal, so pixel x, y moves to y, x, with width and height swapped.

Returns a copy of img with the color channels divided by alpha, the inverse of premultiply. Pixels with alpha 0 or full alpha are left as they are. An image without an alpha channel is returned as a plain copy.
fn create(width: i64, height: i64, format: Format) -> Image

Returns a zeroed image of width by height pixels in format, with stride equal to width times bytes_per_pixel(format). A negative size is treated as 0. A zeroed pixel is black, and transparent when the format has alpha.

Decodes data as PNG, GIF, JPEG, WebP, BMP or QOI, chosen by its signature. A GIF yields its first frame. Images over 2^26 pixels are rejected; decode_limited takes another limit. Fails with Unsupported when no signature matches, and otherwise with the error of the chosen codec, such as Malformed or TooLarge.

Decodes every frame of a GIF. Each Frame holds the whole canvas after the frame is composited onto the result of applying the previous frame's disposal method (leave, restore to background, restore to previous). Fails with Malformed when the data is invalid or there is no frame, and TooLarge when the canvas size times the frame count, or any frame, exceeds 2^26 pixels.
fn decode_limited(data: []u8, max_pixels: i64) -> Image ! io.Error
Decodes data like decode, rejecting images with more than max_pixels pixels. Fails with TooLarge when the image, or the total of all GIF frames, exceeds max_pixels, or a side exceeds 2^24.

Returns the EXIF orientation of a JPEG, 1 to 8. Returns 1 (upright) when data is not a JPEG, has no EXIF segment or orientation tag, the tag is out of range, or the data is malformed. Pass the result to orient.
fn from_pixels(width: i64, height: i64, format: Format, pixels: []u8) -> Image ! io.Error
Returns an image that uses pixels directly, without copying. Fails with Invalid when a size is negative or pixels.len is not width * bytes_per_pixel(format) * height.

An ordered list of sections. The first section is the unnamed one for entries before any header; it is always present. Sections are shared pointers, so a Section found with find reflects later changes to the document. The sections in order of first appearance, starting with the unnamed section.
struct Entry { pub key: str pub value: str pub line: i64 }

One key = value line of a section. The key, trimmed of surrounding whitespace. The value after escape processing when it was quoted, otherwise trimmed of surrounding whitespace. The line on which the entry starts, counting from 1, or 0 for an entry made by add or set.

The error returned when INI text is malformed. The input breaks the INI syntax at line, counting from 1. message names the problem: an unterminated or empty section header, text after a header or quoted value, a line without = or :, an empty key, or a bad escape or unterminated string in a quoted value.
Options for parse_with. Keeps every entry of a repeated key when true; when false, a repeated key within a section replaces the earlier entry in place, so the last value wins. Defaults to false.
struct Section { pub name: str pub entries: []Entry }

A named group of entries, kept in file order. The name between the brackets, or the empty string for the entries that come before the first header. The entries of the section in the order they were read or added, including repeated keys when the document was parsed with collect.
fn add(mut d: Document, section: str, key: str, value: str)
Appends the entry key and value to section, even when the key is already present. The section is created at the end of the document when it does not exist. The entry's line is 0.
Returns the section called name, or none when the document has no such section. The empty name finds the unnamed section.

Formats the document as INI text. The unnamed section is written first without a header and is skipped when it is empty; each named section follows as [name], with a blank line between sections. An entry is written as key = value, or key = for an empty value. A value is quoted, with \", \\, \n, \r, \t and \uXXXX escapes, when it starts with a space, tab or ", ends with a space, tab or \, or holds a control character; other values are written as they are. Keys and section names are not escaped. Every line ends with \n.
fn get(d: Document, section: str, key: str) -> str?
Returns the value of key in section, or none when the section or the key does not exist. When the key occurs more than once the last value is returned.
fn get_all(d: Document, section: str, key: str) -> []str
Returns every value of key in section, in order. Returns an empty slice when the section or the key does not exist. A document parsed without collect holds at most one value per key.
fn has_section(d: Document, name: str) -> bool
Returns whether the document has a section called name.
Returns the distinct keys of section in order of first appearance. Returns an empty slice when the section does not exist.
Returns the names of the named sections in order of first appearance. The unnamed section is not listed.
fn set(mut d: Document, section: str, key: str, value: str)

Sets key to value in section. Replaces the value of the last entry with that key, keeping its position and line, or appends a new entry with line 0 when there is none. The section is created at the end of the document when it does not exist.
Returns an empty document: one unnamed section with no entries.
Parses INI text into a Document, with default Options. See parse_with.
fn parse_with(source: str, options: Options) -> Document ! Error

Parses INI text into a Document. A leading UTF-8 byte order mark is dropped. Lines are split at \n; a \r before it is trimmed away. A line whose first non-blank character is ; or # is a comment, and blank lines are skipped. [name] starts a section, and a header may be followed by a comment; repeating a name continues the same section. Entries before the first header belong to the unnamed section. An entry is split at the first = or :, and key and value are trimmed. An unquoted value is taken as it is, so ; and # inside it are part of the value. A value starting with " is quoted: it understands \n, \t, \r, \0, \\, \", \', \;, \#, \=, \: and \uXXXX (not a surrogate), and may be followed by a comment. A line whose last non-blank character is an odd number of backslashes continues on the next line; the backslash is removed and the next line is trimmed before it is joined. Fails with Syntax, which carries the line, for malformed input.

enum Error { NotFound Denied Exists NotDir IsDir NotEmpty Invalid NoSpace BrokenPipe AddrInUse AddrUnavailable Unreachable Refused Reset Aborted TimedOut NotConnected WouldBlock Eof Malformed TooLarge Unsupported Os(i64) }

The error type shared by the I/O, codec and protocol modules. Operating system error numbers map onto the named variants through errno; numbers without a variant become Os. The file, directory or other named resource does not exist. The operation is not permitted. The resource already exists. A path component that must be a directory is not one. The operation does not apply to a directory. The directory still has entries. An argument or the input is not valid for the operation. The device has no space left. The peer closed the pipe or connection before the write completed. The address is already bound. The address cannot be bound on this host. The network or host cannot be reached. The peer actively refused the connection. The peer reset the connection. The connection was aborted. The operation did not finish in time. The resource is closed or was never connected. The operation would block and the resource is non-blocking. The input ended before the operation was complete. The input does not follow the expected format. The input exceeds the size the operation accepts. The operation is not supported by this resource or platform. An operating system error number that has no named variant.

Shared state that tracks the uses of a resource so a closed descriptor fails with NotConnected instead of reaching a reused one. Made by guard; each use holds a Lease from enter, and retire stops new uses.
A scope token returned by enter that keeps a Guard in use. Dropping the lease releases the use. When the guard has been retired and the last lease is dropped, the guard's release runs.
A buffered reader over a Stream or a fixed byte slice, created by reader or bytes_reader. Used through a pointer. Not safe for concurrent use.
struct Stream { pub read: fn([]u8) -> i64 ! Error pub write: fn([]u8) -> i64 ! Error pub close: fn() }

A copyable view of a readable and writable resource, made of read, write and close closures. Copies of a Stream refer to the same underlying resource. Reads up to len bytes into the slice and returns the count, or 0 at end of input. Writes a prefix of the slice and returns how many bytes were written, which can be fewer than len. Closes the resource.
Registers a use of the guarded resource and returns the lease that ends it when dropped. Fails with NotConnected once the guard has been retired, so a closed descriptor is never reached.
Closes the guard to new uses. Runs wake so that blocked operations return, then runs release immediately if no lease is held, or when the last lease is dropped. Later calls do nothing.
Returns the number of bytes buffered in the reader and available without reading the stream.

Reads more bytes from the stream into the reader's buffer and returns the count, or 0 at end of input. Blocks until the stream returns data. Buffered bytes that are not yet consumed are kept. Fails with TooLarge when the buffer is full of unconsumed bytes, and with any error the stream returns. A reader made by bytes_reader returns 0.
Reads and returns the next byte. Blocks until a byte is available. Fails with Eof at end of input.

Reads exactly n bytes and returns them in a new slice. Blocks until n bytes have been read. Fails with Eof if the input ends first, in which case the bytes already read are discarded, and with any error the stream returns.

Reads up to the next line feed and returns the line without its terminator. A \r directly before the \n is removed as well. The returned string is a copy. Blocks until a full line is available. Fails with Eof when the input ends before a line feed, including when text without a terminator remains; that text stays buffered and can be read with read_some. Fails with TooLarge when a line does not fit in the 16384-byte buffer.

Reads up to dst.len bytes into dst and returns the count, or 0 at end of input. Returns buffered bytes first. When nothing is buffered it blocks for one read of the stream, and a dst at least as long as the reader's buffer is read into directly, bypassing the buffer. Returns fewer bytes than requested when that is all that is available.

Reads into dst until it is full or the input ends, and returns the count read. The count is smaller than dst.len only at end of input. Blocks until dst is full or the input ends. Fails with any error the stream returns, in which case the bytes already read are in dst but not reported.
Returns the stream the reader reads from. Bytes already buffered by the reader are not returned by the stream.

Reads the stream until end of input and returns everything read. Blocks until the stream reports end of input. Fails with the first error read returns, discarding the bytes read so far. Does not close the stream.
Returns a buffered reader over s with a 16384-byte buffer.
Writes all of data to the stream, calling write repeatedly until every byte is accepted. Fails with the first error write returns; bytes written before the error are not reported.
fn write_str(s: Stream, text: str) ! Error
Writes the bytes of text to the stream in full, as write_all does.
Appends the bytes of src to dst, growing it as needed.
Returns the big-endian 16-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b.
Returns the big-endian 24-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b.
Returns the big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b.
Returns the big-endian 64-bit integer at offset at in b. Values of 2^63 and above wrap to negative.
Returns a zeroed byte slice of length n.
Returns a reader over the bytes in data, which reports end of input once they are consumed. The reader reads data in place without copying it. Its stream rejects writes with Unsupported.
Copies bytes from src into dst and returns the number copied, which is the smaller of the two lengths. The slices can overlap.
Returns the Error for a Linux error number. Numbers without a named variant become Os(code).

Returns a guard that coordinates use of a resource with its closing. wake runs once when the guard is retired, to unblock operations that are waiting on the resource. release runs once when the guard is retired and no leases remain, and is where the resource is freed.
Returns the little-endian 16-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b.
Returns the little-endian 24-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b.
Returns the little-endian 32-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b.
Returns the little-endian 64-bit integer at offset at in b. Values of 2^63 and above wrap to negative.
fn put_be(mut b: []u8, v: i64, size: i64)
Appends the low size bytes of v to b in big-endian order, for a size from 0 to 8.
Appends the low 16 bits of v to b in big-endian order.
Appends the low 24 bits of v to b in big-endian order.
Appends the low 32 bits of v to b in big-endian order.
Appends the 64 bits of v to b in big-endian order.
fn put_le(mut b: []u8, v: i64, size: i64)
Appends the low size bytes of v to b in little-endian order, for a size from 0 to 8.
Appends the low 16 bits of v to b in little-endian order.
Appends the low 24 bits of v to b in little-endian order.
Appends the low 32 bits of v to b in little-endian order.
Appends the 64 bits of v to b in little-endian order.
fn set_be16(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the low 16 bits of v into b at offset at in big-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
fn set_be24(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the low 24 bits of v into b at offset at in big-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
fn set_be32(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the low 32 bits of v into b at offset at in big-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
fn set_be64(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the 64 bits of v into b at offset at in big-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
fn set_le16(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the low 16 bits of v into b at offset at in little-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
fn set_le24(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the low 24 bits of v into b at offset at in little-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
fn set_le32(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the low 32 bits of v into b at offset at in little-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
fn set_le64(b: []u8, at: i64, v: i64)
Stores the 64 bits of v into b at offset at in little-endian order. Overwrites existing bytes; b must already be long enough.
Converts a raw system call return value into a result. Returns r when it is not negative. A negative r is a negated error number and fails with errno(-r).
Returns the big-endian 16-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b as a u16.
Returns the little-endian 16-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b as a u16.
fn u16_le_str(s: str, at: i64) -> u16
Returns the little-endian 16-bit unsigned integer at offset at in the bytes of s as a u16.
Returns the big-endian 32-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b as a u32.
Returns the little-endian 32-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b as a u32.
fn u32_le_str(s: str, at: i64) -> u32
Returns the little-endian 32-bit unsigned integer at offset at in the bytes of s as a u32.
Returns the big-endian 64-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b as a u64.
Returns the little-endian 64-bit unsigned integer at offset at in b as a u64.
fn u64_le_str(s: str, at: i64) -> u64
Returns the little-endian 64-bit unsigned integer at offset at in the bytes of s as a u64.
fn uint_be(b: []u8, at: i64, width: i64) -> u64
Returns the big-endian unsigned integer of width bytes, from 1 to 8, at offset at in b.
fn uint_le(b: []u8, at: i64, width: i64) -> u64
Returns the little-endian unsigned integer of width bytes, from 1 to 8, at offset at in b.
struct Member { pub name: str pub value: Value }
A name and value pair of an Object. The member name, with its escapes decoded. The member value.
enum Naming { Unchanged CamelCase SnakeCase PascalCase }

How struct field names and enum variant names are spelled in JSON. Low field names are conventionally snake_case and variant names PascalCase. serialize_with converts them to this spelling, and deserialize_with converts JSON names back: struct field names to snake_case, and variant names to PascalCase unless the naming is Unchanged. Names are written as they are in Low and matched exactly. Names are camelCase: underscores are dropped and the next letter is capitalised, and a leading capital becomes lowercase. When reading, an uppercase letter in a JSON name becomes _ and the lowercase letter. Names are snake_case: an uppercase letter becomes an underscore and its lowercase letter, with none at the start. When reading, JSON names are used as they are. Names are PascalCase: as CamelCase with the first letter uppercase. When reading, an uppercase letter in a JSON name becomes _ and the lowercase letter.
struct Options { pub indent: i64 pub naming: Naming pub max_depth: i64 pub omit_none: bool }

Settings for serialize_with and deserialize_with. The spaces per nesting level when writing; 0, the default, writes compact text. How field and variant names are spelled; defaults to Unchanged. It applies to struct field names and variant names, not to the keys of a map. The deepest nesting accepted when reading; defaults to 64. Deeper input fails with serde.Error.TooDeep. Leaves out struct fields whose value is none when writing, instead of writing null. Defaults to false. Map entries are not affected.

A pull tokenizer over one JSON text, made by reader. read advances to the next token and the get_ functions read the value of the current one. The reader checks the whole of RFC 8259 syntax, the validity of UTF-8 and the order of commas, colons and brackets, so a successful token sequence is a well-formed document. Strings, names and numbers are views of the input until a get_ function converts them.
enum Token { None StartObject EndObject StartArray EndArray PropertyName String Number True False Null }
