Sets a time to live of seconds on key. Returns true when it was set and false when the key does not exist.
fn get(c: Client, key: str) -> str? ! Error
Returns the value of key, or none when the key does not exist. Fails with Server on an error reply such as a key holding a different type.
fn hget(c: Client, key: str, field: str) -> str? ! Error
Returns the value of field in the hash at key, or none when the field or the key does not exist.
fn hgetall(c: Client, key: str) -> []Field ! Error
Returns every field and value of the hash at key. A missing key gives an empty list. Reads the RESP3 map form and the RESP2 flat list; a flat list of odd length fails with Protocol.
fn hset(c: Client, key: str, fields: []Field) -> i64 ! Error
Sets each of fields in the hash at key and returns how many were new. Fields that already existed are updated and not counted. An empty fields fails with Server.
fn incr(c: Client, key: str) -> i64 ! Error
Adds one to the integer at key and returns the new value. A missing key counts as 0. Fails with Server when the value is not an integer.
fn incrby(c: Client, key: str, n: i64) -> i64 ! Error
Adds n to the integer at key and returns the new value. A missing key counts as 0. Fails with Server when the value is not an integer.
fn lpop(c: Client, key: str) -> str? ! Error
Removes and returns the first element of the list at key, or none when the list is empty or missing.
fn lpush(c: Client, key: str, values: []str) -> i64 ! Error
Pushes values onto the head of the list at key one after another, so the last value ends up first, and returns the new length. An empty values fails with Server.
fn lrange(c: Client, key: str, start: i64, stop: i64) -> []str ! Error

Returns the elements of the list at key from index start to stop, both inclusive. Negative indexes count from the end, so -1 is the last element. A missing key or an out of range slice gives an empty list.

Starts a transaction with MULTI. Commands sent with command are then queued by the server and answer Status("QUEUED"); the typed commands such as get fail with Type meanwhile. End it with exec or discard. Fails with Server on an error reply.
Sends PING and returns when the server answers. Fails with Type on any reply other than PONG or a bulk string, so it also checks that the connection is alive.
fn psubscribe(c: Client, patterns: []str) -> Subscription ! Error
Subscribes to the glob-style patterns and returns the running Subscription. Each Message carries the matching pattern in pattern. Fails as subscribe does.
fn publish(c: Client, channel: str, message: str) -> i64 ! Error
Sends message to channel and returns how many subscribers received it.
fn rpop(c: Client, key: str) -> str? ! Error
Removes and returns the last element of the list at key, or none when the list is empty or missing.
fn rpush(c: Client, key: str, values: []str) -> i64 ! Error
Appends values to the tail of the list at key in order and returns the new length. An empty values fails with Server.

Sends commands in one write and returns the replies in the same order. Each entry is a command name followed by its arguments. An empty list returns an empty list without using the connection. An error reply appears as a Failure element and does not stop the rest. Fails as command does, and a transport failure closes the client.
fn sadd(c: Client, key: str, members: []str) -> i64 ! Error
Adds members to the set at key and returns how many were new. An empty members fails with Server.
fn set(c: Client, key: str, value: str) ! Error
Stores value at key, replacing any existing value and clearing its time to live. Fails with Server on an error reply.

Sets the read and write time limit in milliseconds for later operations, replacing Options.timeout. 0 waits indefinitely. A running subscription reads without a limit; the value applies again once it ends.
fn set_with(c: Client, key: str, value: str, o: SetOptions) -> bool ! Error
Stores value at key subject to o. Returns true when the value was stored and false when the nx or xx condition stopped it. Fails with Server on an error reply.
fn smembers(c: Client, key: str) -> []str ! Error
Returns every member of the set at key in the order the server sends them, which is unspecified. A missing key gives an empty list.
fn subscribe(c: Client, channels: []str) -> Subscription ! Error

Subscribes to channels and returns the running Subscription. Returns once the server has confirmed every channel. The connection is dedicated to the subscription until it ends; other commands fail with Subscribed. Fails with Protocol when channels is empty, Server when the server rejects the subscription, Subscribed when one is already running, and Closed when the connection ends before the confirmation.

Runs commands atomically between MULTI and EXEC, sent in one write, and returns the result of each in order. Fails with Server when the server rejects a command or MULTI while queueing, and with Aborted when EXEC returns nil because a key given to watch changed. A command that fails while EXEC runs appears as a Failure element.
fn ttl(c: Client, key: str) -> i64 ! Error
Returns the remaining time to live of key in seconds: -1 when it has none and -2 when the key does not exist.
Forgets every key watched with watch.
Watches keys so that the next exec returns Aborted if any of them changes first. The watch ends with exec, discard or unwatch. Fails with Server on an error reply, including an empty keys.
fn zadd(c: Client, key: str, members: []Scored) -> i64 ! Error
Adds members to the sorted set at key, updating the score of any that exist, and returns how many were new. An empty members fails with Server.
fn zrange(c: Client, key: str, start: i64, stop: i64) -> []str ! Error
Returns the members of the sorted set at key ranked start to stop, both inclusive, by ascending score. Negative indexes count from the end. A missing key gives an empty list.
fn zrange_scores(c: Client, key: str, start: i64, stop: i64) -> []Scored ! Error

Returns the members of the sorted set at key ranked start to stop, both inclusive, each with its score. Reads the RESP3 list of pairs and the RESP2 flat list. Ranking and negative indexes are as for zrange.
Wraps a connection handle in a Client that owns it. Dropping the returned client closes the connection. Pairs with detach.
Closes the connection behind h. Closing twice is harmless. See close_client.
Sends one command on the connection behind h and returns its reply. See command.
Deletes keys on the connection behind h. See del.
Drops the queued transaction on the connection behind h. See discard.
Runs the queued transaction on the connection behind h. See exec.
Counts the existing keys on the connection behind h. See exists.
fn expire_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, seconds: i64) -> bool ! Error
Sets a time to live on key on the connection behind h. See expire.
fn get_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str) -> str? ! Error
Returns the value of key on the connection behind h. See get.
fn hget_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, field: str) -> str? ! Error
Returns a hash field on the connection behind h. See hget.
Returns every field of the hash at key on the connection behind h. See hgetall.
fn hset_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, fields: []Field) -> i64 ! Error
Sets hash fields on the connection behind h. See hset.
fn incr_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str) -> i64 ! Error
Adds one to the integer at key on the connection behind h. See incr.
fn incrby_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, n: i64) -> i64 ! Error
Adds n to the integer at key on the connection behind h. See incrby.
fn lpop_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str) -> str? ! Error
Pops the head of a list on the connection behind h. See lpop.
fn lpush_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, values: []str) -> i64 ! Error
Pushes onto the head of a list on the connection behind h. See lpush.
fn lrange_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, start: i64, stop: i64) -> []str ! Error
Returns a slice of a list on the connection behind h. See lrange.
Starts a transaction on the connection behind h. See multi.
Pings the server on the connection behind h. See ping.
Subscribes to patterns on the connection behind h. See psubscribe.
fn publish_on(h: *ClientHandle, channel: str, message: str) -> i64 ! Error
Publishes message on the connection behind h. See publish.
fn rpop_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str) -> str? ! Error
Pops the tail of a list on the connection behind h. See rpop.
fn rpush_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, values: []str) -> i64 ! Error
Appends to the tail of a list on the connection behind h. See rpush.
Sends commands in one write on the connection behind h. See run_pipeline.
fn sadd_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, members: []str) -> i64 ! Error
Adds members to a set on the connection behind h. See sadd.
fn set_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, value: str) ! Error
Stores value at key on the connection behind h. See set.
Sets the read and write time limit in milliseconds on the connection behind h. See set_timeout.
fn set_with_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, value: str, o: SetOptions) -> bool ! Error
Stores value at key subject to o on the connection behind h. See set_with.
Returns the members of a set on the connection behind h. See smembers.
Subscribes to channels on the connection behind h. See subscribe.
Runs commands in a transaction on the connection behind h. See transaction.
fn ttl_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str) -> i64 ! Error
Returns the remaining time to live of key on the connection behind h. See ttl.
Forgets the watched keys on the connection behind h. See unwatch.
Watches keys on the connection behind h. See watch.
fn zadd_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, members: []Scored) -> i64 ! Error
Adds scored members to a sorted set on the connection behind h. See zadd.
fn zrange_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, start: i64, stop: i64) -> []str ! Error
Returns a rank range of a sorted set on the connection behind h. See zrange.
fn zrange_scores_on(h: *ClientHandle, key: str, start: i64, stop: i64) -> []Scored ! Error
Returns a rank range with scores on the connection behind h. See zrange_scores.

Opens a TCP connection to o.host and o.port and performs the handshake. The handshake sends HELLO 3 when o.protocol is 3, otherwise AUTH when o.password is set, then SELECT when o.database is not 0. Fails with Connect when the server cannot be reached, Timeout when o.connect_timeout expires, Auth when the credentials are rejected, Unsupported when HELLO 3 is rejected and no password is set, Server when SELECT is rejected, or with a transport Error from the exchange. The connection is closed when the handshake fails.
fn connect_tls(o: Options, config: tls.Config) -> Client ! Error

Opens a TCP connection and performs the handshake over TLS configured by config. When config.server_name is empty, o.host is used. Behaves as connect, and a failed TLS handshake fails with Connect, or Timeout when it times out.

Returns a single-line text form of reply for logs and tests. Nil is (nil), Status is +text, Failure is -text, Integer is :n, and Bulk is the quoted text. Arrays are [a, b], maps {k: v}, sets ~[a, b] and pushes >[a, b], with elements formatted recursively.

Asks the server to end the subscription. Drops every channel, or every pattern for a psubscribe subscription, and returns once the request is sent. Messages already in flight may still arrive; s.messages is closed when the server confirms and the client can then run commands again. Fails with Closed when the connection is closed.
fn connect_stream(s: io.Stream, o: Options) -> Client ! Error

Performs the handshake over an existing io.Stream instead of dialling. o.host, o.port, o.timeout and o.connect_timeout are not used, and set_timeout has no effect because the stream carries no time limits. Closing the client closes the stream. Fails as connect does from the handshake onwards.
Decodes the first reply in data using the default Limits. Bytes after the first reply are ignored. Fails with Protocol when data is malformed or ends before the reply is complete.
fn decode_with(data: []u8, limits: Limits) -> Reply ! Error
Decodes the first reply in data using limits. Fails as decode does, and with TooLarge when a bound is exceeded.
Returns the RESP encoding of a command as an array of bulk strings. args[0] is the command name and the rest are its arguments. Arguments are length-prefixed, so any bytes are allowed.
Appends the RESP encoding of a command to out, for batching several commands into one buffer. See encode.
fn read_reply(r: *io.Reader, limits: Limits) -> Reply ! Error

Reads one reply from r, blocking until it is complete. RESP3 attribute frames before the reply are read and discarded. Fails with Closed at end of input or on a read failure, Timeout when the read times out, Protocol when the bytes are not valid RESP, and TooLarge when a bound in limits is exceeded.

Why a pattern failed to compile. The pattern is not valid or uses an unsupported feature. at is the byte offset in the pattern and message describes the problem, such as nothing to repeat, missing ), unterminated subpattern, lookaround is not supported or repeat count too large. Lookaround, backreferences, octal escapes and named groups are not supported. A repeat count above 10000 and a pattern that assembles to more than 100000 instructions are rejected.
struct Flags { pub ignore_case: bool pub multiline: bool pub dot_all: bool }

Options that change how a pattern matches, set for the whole pattern by compile_with. The pattern can also switch them on and off with (?i), (?m), (?s) and the scoped forms such as (?i:...) and (?-s:...). Whether letters match regardless of ASCII case. Defaults to false. Only A-Z and a-z are folded. Whether ^ and $ also match at line boundaries rather than only at the start and end of the input. Defaults to false. Whether . also matches a newline. Defaults to false.
The outcome of one successful match: the matched text and the byte spans of its capture groups. Read it with start, end, text, span and group. It stays valid after further searches.

A compiled regular expression. Matching runs in time linear in the input and uses no backtracking, in the RE2 style, and the leftmost match is chosen with greedy and lazy repeats taking priority as in Perl. Patterns match code points of UTF-8 text, and all offsets are byte offsets. The syntax covers literals, ., classes [a-z] and [^a-z], \d \w \s and their negations, \x, \u and \U escapes, groups (...) and (?:...), alternation |, repeats * + ? {n} {n,} {n,m} with a lazy ? suffix, and the anchors ^ $ \A \z \b \B. A Regex may be used from several threads at once.
struct Span { pub start: i64 pub end: i64 }
A byte range start..end in the input, with end exclusive. The offset of the first byte of the range. The offset one past the last byte of the range.
Returns the byte offset one past the end of m.
fn group(m: Match, index: i64) -> str?
Returns the text of capture group index in m, where 0 is the whole match. Returns none in the cases where span does.
fn span(m: Match, group: i64) -> Span?
Returns the byte span of capture group group in m, where 0 is the whole match. Returns none when group is negative or beyond group_count, and when the group did not take part in the match.
Returns the byte offset where m begins.
Returns the text m matched, as a slice of the searched input.
fn find(re: Regex, input: str) -> Match?
Returns the leftmost match in input, or none when there is none. Group 0 of the result spans the match.

Returns every non-overlapping match in input, from left to right. After an empty match the next match may not be empty at the same offset, so the search always advances. Returns an empty slice when nothing matches.
fn full_match(re: Regex, input: str) -> Match?
Returns a match only when the pattern matches the whole of input, from its first byte to its last, and none otherwise.
Returns the number of capture groups in re, not counting group 0 for the whole match.
fn is_match(re: Regex, input: str) -> bool
Returns whether input contains a match anywhere. It does not record capture groups and is the cheapest query.
fn replace_all(re: Regex, input: str, replacement: fn(Match) -> str) -> str

Returns input with every non-overlapping match replaced by the string replacement returns for it. The closure's result is inserted as it stands, with no $1 expansion. Input between matches is copied unchanged.

Splits input around each non-overlapping match of re and returns the pieces between them. Returns a single piece, input, when nothing matches. Adjacent matches and matches at either end produce empty pieces.
fn split_n(re: Regex, input: str, max: i64) -> []str

Splits input as split does, using at most max matches. The result has at most max + 1 pieces and the last holds the unsplit rest. 0 returns input as the only piece, and a negative max splits at every match.
Compiles pattern with default Flags. Fails with Invalid when the pattern is malformed or unsupported.
fn compile_with(pattern: str, flags: Flags) -> Regex ! Error
Compiles pattern with flags. Fails with Invalid as compile does.
enum Jitter { None Full Equal Decorrelated }

How the wait before a retry is randomised. No randomisation: the wait is the policy's backoff delay. A random wait from zero up to the backoff delay. Half the backoff delay plus a random share of the other half. A random wait from the base delay up to three times the previous wait, capped at the maximum delay. It ignores the attempt number, so the growth follows the actual previous waits.
enum Outcome[T, E] { Value(T) Failed(E) GaveUp(E, Stop) Stopped(Stop) }

How run ended. An attempt returned Done with this value. An attempt returned Fatal with this error. The loop stopped with reason after attempts that returned Retry or RetryAfter; error is the last one. The loop stopped with this reason before any attempt ran, because the token was already cancelled.

struct Policy { pub attempts: i64 pub base: duration.Duration pub multiplier: f64 pub max_delay: duration.Duration pub jitter: Jitter pub deadline: duration.Duration? pub rng: rand.Rng? pub token: *cancel.Token? pub clock: clock.Clock pub observer: fn(i64, duration.Duration)? }

How a retry loop backs off, built from policy and the with_ functions. The wait before attempt n + 1 is the backoff delay(p, n), randomised by jitter. Every field has a default, so Policy {} is the same as policy(). A Policy is a copyable value; the with_ functions return a changed copy. The total number of attempts, including the first. Defaults to 5. The delay before the first retry. Defaults to 100 milliseconds. The factor the delay grows by after each attempt. Defaults to 2.0. The largest delay between attempts. Defaults to 30 seconds. How each delay is randomised. Defaults to Full. The total time the loop may take, measured from start, or none for no limit. The source of random numbers for jitter, or none to draw a fresh generator at start. A token that ends the loop and any wait when cancelled, or none for no cancellation. The clock that measures elapsed time against the deadline and performs each wait. Defaults to the system clock. A function called before each wait with the number of the attempt that just ended and the wait, or none.
struct Retrier { pub attempt: i64 pub stop: Stop pub last_delay: duration.Duration ... }

The state of a retry loop, driven by next. Read attempt inside the loop for the current attempt number. A Retrier is a pointer returned by start; it is not safe to share between green threads. The number of the current attempt, counting from 1, or 0 before the first call to next. Why the loop ended, or Running while next can still return true. The wait before the current attempt, which starts as the policy's base delay.
enum Step[T, E] { Done(T) Retry(E) RetryAfter(E, duration.Duration) Fatal(E) }

What one attempt asks run to do next. The attempt succeeded with this value. The attempt failed with this error; try again after the backoff delay. The attempt failed with this error; try again after at least wait, or the backoff delay if that is longer. The attempt failed with this error and must not be retried.
enum Stop { Running Exhausted Deadline Cancelled }

Why a Retrier stopped, or Running while it has not. The loop may still make another attempt. The policy's attempts are used up. The next wait would run past the policy's deadline. The policy's cancel token was cancelled.
fn delay(p: Policy, attempt: i64) -> duration.Duration

Returns the backoff delay after attempt number attempt, before jitter. The base delay is grown by multiplier once for every attempt after the first and capped at max_delay, so attempts 1 or lower return base, or max_delay when that is smaller.
fn jittered(p: Policy, attempt: i64, previous: duration.Duration, mut r: rand.Rng) -> duration.Duration

Returns the wait after attempt attempt with the policy's jitter applied, drawing from r. previous is the last wait, which only Decorrelated uses. With None the result is delay(p, attempt); with Full it is between zero and that delay; with Equal it is between half of it and all of it.
fn on_retry(p: Policy, f: fn(i64, duration.Duration)) -> Policy
Returns p that calls f before each wait with the number of the attempt that just ended and the wait about to start. It is not called for the first attempt or when the loop stops instead of waiting.
fn run[T, E](p: Policy, op: fn(i64) -> Step[T, E]) -> Outcome[T, E]

Calls op with the attempt number until it returns Done or Fatal or the policy stops the loop. Attempts count from 1. Retry and RetryAfter wait as next does. Returns Value for Done, Failed for Fatal, GaveUp with the last error and the Stop reason when attempts, deadline or cancellation end the loop, and Stopped only when the loop stopped before the first attempt.
Returns a retry loop for p that has made no attempts yet. Starts the deadline clock. Without a policy rng, the loop seeds its own random generator.
fn with_attempts(p: Policy, attempts: i64) -> Policy
Returns p allowing attempts attempts in total, the first included. Values below 1 become 1, which makes one attempt and no retries.
fn with_base(p: Policy, base: duration.Duration) -> Policy
Returns p with base as the delay before the first retry. A negative base becomes zero.
Returns p that stops when t is cancelled. The token is checked before each attempt and after each wait, and a wait ends early when it is cancelled.
fn with_clock(p: Policy, c: clock.Clock) -> Policy
Returns p measuring elapsed time and waiting on c.
fn with_deadline(p: Policy, total: duration.Duration) -> Policy
Returns p limited to total time from start. A retry whose wait would end past total is not made and the loop stops with Deadline. The time already spent in an attempt counts.
fn with_jitter(p: Policy, jitter: Jitter) -> Policy
Returns p using jitter to randomise each delay.
fn with_max_delay(p: Policy, max_delay: duration.Duration) -> Policy
Returns p with max_delay as the largest delay between attempts. A negative max_delay becomes zero.
fn with_multiplier(p: Policy, multiplier: f64) -> Policy
Returns p with multiplier as the factor the delay grows by after each attempt. Values below 1.0 become 1.0, which keeps the delay constant.
fn with_rng(p: Policy, r: rand.Rng) -> Policy
Returns p drawing jitter from r, which makes the waits reproducible for a seeded generator.

Raises the wait before the next attempt to at least d, for a server-requested delay such as Retry-After. The floor applies to one wait only, and the jittered delay is used if it is longer. The deadline still applies to the raised wait.

Carries out the wait planned by the last successful reserve and starts the next attempt. It calls the observer, blocks the green thread for the wait and returns true, or returns false with stop set to Cancelled when the token was cancelled during the wait. The first attempt starts at once without a wait or the observer.
Returns the time since start, on the policy's clock.

Waits and returns true when the caller should make the next attempt, or returns false once the loop has stopped. It is reserve followed by commit. The first call returns true at once. Later calls return false with stop set to Cancelled when the token is cancelled, Exhausted when the attempts are used up, or Deadline when the wait would pass the deadline. Otherwise they call the observer, block the green thread for the wait and return true, or return false with Cancelled if the token was cancelled during the wait. Once false is returned, every later call returns false.

Decides whether another attempt may follow the current one and plans its wait, without waiting. Returns false with stop set to Cancelled when the token is cancelled, Exhausted when the attempts are used up, or Deadline when the wait would pass the deadline. Otherwise it returns true and commit carries out the wait. Call at_least first to raise the planned wait. Before the first attempt reserve returns true and commit makes it; use it when the caller must check the plan, as for a deadline, before it discards work that the retry replaces.
Returns the default policy: five attempts, a 100 millisecond base delay doubling up to 30 seconds, full jitter, no deadline and no cancel token.

Why a version string was rejected. The string is empty. The string is not a valid semantic version. at is the index of the offending byte in a pre-release or build identifier, and the index where the numeric core starts (0, or 1 after a leading v) for a malformed core.
struct Version { pub major: i64 pub minor: i64 pub patch: i64 pub pre: []str pub build: []str }

A semantic version (semver.org 2.0.0): a numeric core with optional pre-release and build identifiers. The major version. The minor version. The patch version. The dot-separated pre-release identifiers after -, empty for a release. The dot-separated build identifiers after +, empty when there are none. compare ignores them.
fn compare(a: Version, b: Version) -> i64

Orders two versions by semver precedence and returns -1, 0 or 1 when a is lower than, equal to or higher than b. Major, minor and patch compare numerically. A version with a pre-release is lower than the same core without one. Pre-release identifiers compare left to right: numeric identifiers numerically at any size, others by byte value, numeric lower than non-numeric, and a shorter list lower when it is a prefix of the other. Build identifiers are ignored.
Returns v as major.minor.patch, followed by - and the pre-release identifiers and + and the build identifiers when they are not empty.
fn less(a: Version, b: Version) -> bool
Returns whether a has lower precedence than b, as ordered by compare.

Parses a version such as 1.2.3, v1.2.3-rc.1 or 1.2.3+build.5. A single leading v is accepted. The text after the first + is the build metadata and the text after the first - in the rest is the pre-release. The core must be exactly three dot-separated decimal numbers without leading zeros that fit in an i64. Pre-release and build identifiers must be non-empty and made of 0-9, a-z, A-Z and -, and a numeric pre-release identifier has no leading zero. Fails with Empty for an empty string and with Malformed for any other violation.
enum Error { Syntax(i64, str) Mismatch(str, i64) Missing(str) UnknownVariant(str) Range(i64) TooDeep TooLarge }

The error returned when reading a value through a Reader fails. at in a variant is the Reader.position at the offending value; Reader.position says what it counts. The input is not well formed for the format, or a reader was used out of sequence; message describes the problem. The next value has a different type than the one being read; expected names the expected type. A struct field or labelled variant field is absent from the input, has no default and is not optional; field is its name. The input names a variant, name, that the enum does not have. A number does not fit the integer type it is being read into. The input nests deeper than the reader allows. A string, array or map in the input is longer than the format's reader allows.
struct Field[T, F] { pub name: str pub index: i64 }

A reference to the field name of struct T, whose type is F, written T.field. It carries the name and position of the field so a function can take a field of a given struct with a given type. It needs std/serde to be imported. The field's name as written in the struct. The zero-based position of the field in the struct's declaration order.
enum Kind { Bool Int Uint Float Text Binary Seq Map Optional Struct Enum Ref }

The kind of type a Schema describes. A boolean. A signed integer; Schema.bits is its width. An unsigned integer; Schema.bits is its width. A floating point number; Schema.bits is its width. A string. A byte slice ([]u8). A sequence; Schema.items holds the element schema. A map; Schema.items holds the key schema followed by the value schema. An optional value; Schema.items holds the schema of the value. A struct; Schema.name is its name and Schema.fields its fields. An enum; Schema.name is its name and Schema.variants its variants. A struct or enum met again while it is still being described, which makes the type recursive. Schema.name names the struct or enum it refers to.
struct Member { pub key: Node pub value: Node }
An entry of a Tree.Map. The key. A tree built by to_tree has Text keys; a format's reader may have any scalar. The value for the key.
struct Node { pub tree: Tree pub at: i64 }
A Tree and where it came from. The value. The position reported in errors for this value, such as a source line. 0 has the reader report the number of values it has read so far instead.
struct Property { pub name: str pub schema: Schema pub required: bool }

A field of a struct or a variant. The field name. A positional variant field is named by its zero-based index. The schema of the field's type. Whether the field must be present when reading. It is false for an optional field and for a struct field that has a default.

struct Reader { pub null: fn() -> bool ! Error pub boolean: fn() -> bool ! Error pub integer: fn() -> i64 ! Error pub unsigned: fn() -> u64 ! Error pub float: fn() -> f64 ! Error pub text: fn() -> str ! Error pub binary: fn() -> []u8 ! Error pub begin_seq: fn() ! Error pub next_element: fn() -> bool ! Error pub begin_map: fn() ! Error pub next_field: fn() -> str? ! Error pub next_key: fn() -> str? ! Error pub begin_variant: fn() -> str ! Error pub end_variant: fn() ! Error pub skip: fn() ! Error pub position: fn() -> i64 }

The source that a value is read from, made of closures that a format implements. read calls the closures in document order and each reading closure consumes one value. Reading closures fail with Mismatch when the next value has another type, Range when a number does not fit, and Syntax when the input has no value to read. Returns whether the next value is null, consuming it when it is. Otherwise nothing is consumed. Optionals use it. Reads a boolean. Reads a signed integer. Narrower integer types read it and then check the range. Reads an unsigned integer for the u64 type. Reads a floating point number. f32 values are narrowed from it. Reads a string. Reads a byte slice ([]u8). Opens the next value as a sequence. next_element then steps through its elements. Moves to the next element of the open sequence and returns true, leaving the element to be read next, or returns false and closes the sequence once there are no more. Opens the next value as a map, or as a struct. next_key steps through the entries of a map and next_field through the fields of a struct. Returns the name of the next field of the open struct, leaving its value to be read next, or none and closes the struct once there are no more fields. It is for the names of struct fields and of labelled variant fields, which a format may spell differently from the keys of a map. Returns the key of the next entry of the open map, leaving its value to be read next, or none and closes the map once there are no more entries. Opens the next value as an enum variant and returns the variant's name. A variant without fields is a name; one with fields carries them as a map when they are labelled or as a sequence otherwise, which is read next. Closes the variant opened by begin_variant. Skips the next value, including everything nested in it. Reading a struct uses it for fields it does not know. Returns where the reader is in its input, which is the at of an Error raised by the next reading closure. Its unit is up to the format: a byte offset, a source line, the count of values read so far, or 0 when the format has no position.
struct Rebuild[V] { pub leaf: fn(Tree) -> V ! Error pub sequence: fn([]V) -> V ! Error pub mapping: fn([]V, []V) -> V ! Error }

How a format builds its own value type V from the parts of a Node in value_of. Returns the value for a Tree that has no children, or fails when the format cannot hold it. Returns the value for a sequence of already built values. Returns the value for a map whose ith entry has the key keys[i] and the value values[i].
struct Schema { pub kind: Kind pub name: str pub bits: i64 pub items: []Schema pub fields: []Property pub variants: []Variant }

A description of a type, made by schema. A pointer is described as its target. What kind of type this is. The name of a struct or enum, or of the type a Ref points to; empty for other kinds. The width in bits of an integer or float type; 0 for other kinds. The component schemas of a sequence, map or optional; empty for other kinds. The fields of a struct, in declaration order; empty for other kinds. The variants of an enum, in declaration order; empty for other kinds.
enum Shape[V] { Leaf(Tree, i64) Sequence([]V, i64) Mapping([]V, []V, i64) }

How a format's value type V presents one value to node_of. A value with no children, as the Tree that stands for it. A sequence of values. A map whose ith entry has the key keys[i] and the value values[i].
enum Tree { Null Bool(bool) Int(i64) Uint(u64) Float(f64) Text(str) Binary([]u8) Seq([]Node) Map([]Member) Overflow Opaque }

A value in the shape that tree formats such as CBOR, MessagePack, TOML and YAML share. to_tree builds one from any serialisable value, a format's reader builds one from its own value type for tree_reader, and a format converts between it and its value type. Integers are Int when they fit an i64 and Uint only above 9223372036854775807, so each integer has one form. No value. A boolean. An integer that fits an i64. An integer above 9223372036854775807. A floating point number. A string. A byte string. A sequence of values. A map of entries in order. An integer outside both i64 and u64. A reader of a format that has one produces it; reading it as a number fails with Range. A value that has no meaning to serde, such as a tagged or extension value. A reader of a format that has one produces it; reading it fails with Mismatch. to_tree never produces it.
struct Variant { pub name: str pub labelled: bool pub fields: []Property }
A variant of an enum. The variant name. Whether its fields are labelled (true) or positional (false). The fields of the variant; empty for a variant without fields.

struct Writer { pub null: fn() pub boolean: fn(bool) pub integer: fn(i64) pub unsigned: fn(u64) pub float: fn(f64) pub text: fn(str) pub binary: fn([]u8) pub begin_seq: fn() pub end_seq: fn() pub begin_map: fn() pub key: fn(str) pub end_map: fn() pub begin_struct: fn() pub field: fn(str) pub end_struct: fn() pub unit_variant: fn(str) pub begin_variant: fn(str) pub end_variant: fn() }

The sink that a value is written to, made of closures that a format implements. write calls the closures in document order. A sequence, map, struct or variant is opened by a begin_ closure and closed by the matching end_ closure, with its elements written between them by the closures for their own types. A map entry is key followed by its value, and a struct field is field followed by its value. Writes a null value, which is what a none optional becomes. Writes a boolean. Writes a signed integer. Every integer type except u64 is widened to i64 and written here. Writes an unsigned integer of type u64. Writes a floating point number. f32 values are widened to f64. Writes a string. Writes a byte slice ([]u8). Opens a sequence, whose elements follow. Closes the sequence opened by begin_seq. Opens a map, whose entries follow. Writes the key of the next map entry, as text; integer and boolean keys arrive as their decimal digits or true and false. Closes the map opened by begin_map. Opens a struct, whose fields follow. Every field is written, private and optional ones included. Names the struct field whose value follows. Closes the struct opened by begin_struct. Writes an enum variant that has no fields, given the variant's name. Opens an enum variant that has fields, given the variant's name. The fields follow as a struct when they are labelled and as a sequence otherwise, and end_variant closes the variant. Closes the variant opened by begin_variant.
fn key_text(key: Node, at: i64) -> str ! Error

Returns the text of the map key key, which is how a map key of any scalar type matches a field name or a map key of a given type. A Text is itself, an integer is its decimal digits, a boolean is true or false, a float is its default text and Null is null. Fails with Range at position at for an Overflow key and with Mismatch for a sequence, a map or an opaque value.
fn tree_reader(root: Node, base64_text: bool) -> Reader

Returns a Reader over the tree root, to pass to read. A struct is read from a Map by key, a slice from a Seq, an optional from Null, and an enum variant from a Text of its name or a Map with one member named by the variant. An integer is read from Int, and from Uint only as a u64; a u64 is read from a non-negative Int as well. A float is read from Float or an integer. A []u8 is read from Binary, and from Text holding base64 when base64_text is true. Keys are matched as key_text gives. Fails with Mismatch when a value has another type and with Range when a number does not fit. position is the at of the node last read, or the number of nodes read so far when a node has at of 0.
fn value_of[V](node: Node, rebuild: Rebuild[V]) -> V ! Error
Returns the value of a format's own type V for node, built bottom up as rebuild says. Fails with whatever rebuild fails with.

Reads a T from r. A struct is opened with begin_map and read through next_field: unknown fields are skipped, a missing field takes the field's default or none for an optional field, and any other missing field fails with Missing. Integer types narrower than i64 are range checked and fail with Range. A slice is read as a sequence. A map is read through next_key and its keys are parsed from the key text, failing with Mismatch when an integer or boolean key is not one and with Range when it does not fit. An enum is read from the variant name that begin_variant returns, failing with UnknownVariant for an unknown name; a labelled variant reads its fields like a struct, and a positional variant fails with Mismatch when the number of values is wrong. Other failures come from r.
fn node_of[V](v: V, shape: fn(V) -> Shape[V]) -> Node
Returns the Node for the value v of a format's own type, where shape says whether v is a leaf, a sequence or a map. The node and the nodes below it carry the at that shape gives.
fn parse_integer(s: str, what: str, at: i64) -> i64 ! Error
Parses s as a signed decimal integer. A single leading - or + is accepted. Fails with Mismatch naming what when s is not an integer, and with Range when it does not fit an i64, both at position at.
fn parse_unsigned(s: str, what: str, at: i64) -> u64 ! Error
Parses s as an unsigned decimal integer. Fails with Mismatch naming what when s has anything but digits, and with Range when it does not fit a u64, both at position at.
Returns the Schema of T. A struct or enum reached again while it is being described becomes a Ref to its name. A pointer is described as its target.
fn syntax_at(line: i64, column: i64, message: str) -> Error
Returns the Syntax error for a problem at line and column of a format's text. Its position is line and its message is message followed by the line and column.

Returns v as a Tree, through write. A struct and a map become a Map with Text keys, a slice a Seq, a []u8 a Binary, a none optional Null, and an enum variant without fields a Text of its name. A variant with fields becomes a Map with one member named by the variant, whose value is a Map of its labelled fields or a Seq of its positional ones. Every node has at of 0.
Returns n as a Tree: Int when it fits an i64 and Uint above 9223372036854775807.

Writes v to w. The compiler derives the code for the concrete type T: booleans, integers, floats and strings map to the Writer primitives, []u8 to binary, slices to sequences, maps to maps with keys written as text (keys must be strings, integers or booleans), optionals to null or the value, and pointers to their target, a shared pointer in full each time. A pointer reached again while its target is being written is a cycle and panics with serde: cycle through *T. A struct is written with every field, in declaration order. An enum variant without fields is written with unit_variant; one with fields with begin_variant, followed by a struct of its fields when they are labelled and a sequence otherwise. A type that cannot be derived is a compile error.
Returns true when the top bit of at least one lane of v is set. Applied to the result of a lane-wise comparison, it tells whether any lane compared true.
fn blend[V: Vector](choose: V, a: V, b: V) -> V

Returns a vector that takes each lane from a where the matching lane of choose is set and from b where it is clear. choose is normally the result of a lane-wise comparison, whose lanes are all ones or all zeros. A lane of choose with only some bits set is not defined to select either input.
fn find_byte(data: []u8, from: i64, to: i64, c: u8) -> i64

Returns the index of the first byte equal to c in data from index from up to but not including to, or -1 when there is none. Compares 32 bytes at a time while at least 32 remain. Panics when the scan reaches an index past the end of data.
fn find_byte_str(s: str, from: i64, to: i64, c: u8) -> i64

Returns the index of the first byte equal to c in s from index from up to but not including to, or -1 when there is none. Compares 32 bytes at a time while at least 32 remain. Panics when the scan reaches an index past the end of s.
fn lane[V: Vector, E](v: V, i: i64) -> E
Returns lane i of v, counting from 0. Panics when i is negative or not less than the number of lanes.
Returns a bit mask with one bit per lane of v, taken from the top bit of the lane. Lane 0 is bit 0. Applied to the result of a lane-wise comparison, bit i is set when the comparison held in lane i.
fn max[V: Vector](a: V, b: V) -> V
Returns the lane-wise maximum of a and b.
fn min[V: Vector](a: V, b: V) -> V
Returns the lane-wise minimum of a and b.
fn read[V: Vector, E](data: []E, at: i64) -> V

Returns the vector of type V whose lanes are the elements of data starting at index at. at counts elements of data, not bytes, and the read is bounds-checked, so it panics when the vector would extend past the end of data.
fn read_str[V: Vector](s: str, at: i64) -> V
Returns the vector of type V whose lanes are the bytes of s starting at byte index at. The read is bounds-checked and panics when the vector would extend past the end of s.
fn shuffle(table: u8x32, indices: u8x32) -> u8x32

Looks up the bytes of indices in table, 16 bytes at a time, and returns the 32 bytes found. Within each 16-byte half, result byte i is the byte of the same half of table at position indices[i] & 15, or zero when the top bit of indices[i] is set. The lookup never crosses between the two halves.
fn shuffle16(table: u8x16, indices: u8x16) -> u8x16
Looks up the bytes of indices in table and returns the 16 bytes found. Result byte i is table[indices[i] & 15], or zero when the top bit of indices[i] is set.
fn splat[V: Vector, E](x: E) -> V
Returns a vector of type V with every lane set to x.
fn with_lane[V: Vector, E](v: V, i: i64, x: E) -> V
Returns a copy of v with lane i set to x. Panics when i is negative or not less than the number of lanes. v does not change.
fn write[V: Vector, E](data: []E, at: i64, v: V)
Stores the lanes of v into data starting at index at. at counts elements of data, not bytes, and the write is bounds-checked, so it panics when the vector would extend past the end of data.

A value that is refreshed on demand and reused until its time to live runs out. When the value is stale, the first fetch runs the refresh and concurrent callers wait for that one result, so the refresh runs at most once per interval at a time. An Expiring is a handle: copies share one state, and every operation is safe to call from several green threads.

A set of calls in flight, keyed by K, that runs at most one call per key at a time. While a call for a key is running, other callers with the same key wait for its value instead of running their own. A Group is a handle: copies share one state, and every operation is safe to call from several green threads. The group keeps nothing once a call finishes, so it does not cache.

A success or failure value, for a Group whose calls can fail. do returns V only, so a call that can fail uses Result[T, E] as V and every caller sharing the flight receives the same outcome. The call succeeded with this value. The call failed with this error.
struct Shared[V] { pub value: V pub shared: bool }
The outcome of do_shared. The value the call produced. true if the value was produced for more than one caller, whether this caller waited for it or led the call and others joined.
Returns the value if one is stored and fresh, or none otherwise. Never refreshes and never blocks on a refresh in progress.

Returns the value, refreshing it first if there is none or it is older than the time to live. When a refresh is already running, waits for it and returns its value. Otherwise the caller runs refresh on its own green thread, outside the lock, and stores the value with the time the call started. refresh cannot fail; encode failure in V. A refresh finishing after invalidate is returned to its callers but not stored.
Discards the stored value so the next fetch refreshes. A refresh already running still returns its value to the callers waiting for it, but does not store it.
Returns the number of refreshes that have finished.
fn do[K: Hash, V](g: Group[K, V], key: K, f: fn() -> V) -> V
Runs f for key once across concurrent callers and returns the value. Behaves as do_shared without the shared flag.
fn do_shared[K: Hash, V](g: Group[K, V], key: K, f: fn() -> V) -> Shared[V]

Runs f for key unless a call for key is already in flight, in which case waits for that call and returns its value. The first caller for a key runs f on its own green thread; later callers block until it returns and receive the same value. f runs outside the group's lock. The result's shared field is true for every caller when any caller joined the flight. If f panics, the key stays in flight until forget is called and joined callers wait indefinitely.
fn followers[K: Hash, V](g: Group[K, V], key: K) -> i64

Returns how many callers have joined the in-flight call for key, not counting the one running it. Returns 0 when no call is in flight. The count includes callers that have joined and are still waiting for the call to return.
fn forget[K: Hash, V](g: Group[K, V], key: K)

Stops treating the in-flight call for key as current, so the next do for key starts a new call. Callers already waiting still receive the value of the call they joined. Does nothing when no call is in flight.
fn in_flight[K: Hash, V](g: Group[K, V], key: K) -> bool
Returns true if a call for key is in flight and has not been forgotten.
fn pending[K: Hash, V](g: Group[K, V]) -> i64
Returns the number of keys with a call in flight.
fn expiring[V](ttl: duration.Duration, c: clock.Clock, refresh: fn() -> V) -> Expiring[V]

Returns an Expiring that calls refresh to produce its value and keeps the value for ttl, measured on c's monotonic clock. Nothing is fetched until the first fetch. A ttl of zero or less never counts the value as fresh, so every fetch that is not joining a refresh runs refresh. A ttl too large to represent in nanoseconds never expires.
fn group[K: Hash, V]() -> Group[K, V]
struct Pair[A, B] { pub first: A pub second: B }
A pair of values of two types, returned by partition and zip. The first value. The second value.
fn all[T](xs: []T, test: fn(T) -> bool) -> bool
Returns true when test returns true for every element of xs. Stops at the first failure. Returns true for an empty slice.
fn any[T](xs: []T, test: fn(T) -> bool) -> bool
Returns true when test returns true for at least one element of xs. Stops at the first match. Returns false for an empty slice.
fn binary_search[T: Ord](xs: []T, x: T) -> i64?
Returns the index of the first element of the sorted slice xs equal to x, or none when there is none. The slice must be sorted in ascending order. Takes logarithmic time.
fn binary_search_by[T](xs: []T, order: fn(T) -> i64) -> i64?

Searches xs with a three-way comparison function and returns the index of an element for which order returns 0, or none. order(item) returns a negative number when item is before the target, a positive number when it is after the target and 0 for the target. The slice must be partitioned in that order. When several elements match, any of their indexes can be returned. Takes logarithmic time.

Splits xs into consecutive slices of size elements. The last slice is shorter when size does not divide xs.len, and the result is empty for an empty xs. The slices share storage with xs. Panics when size is less than 1.
Returns a new slice with a copy of the elements of xs. The result does not share storage with xs.
Compares xs with ys element by element and returns -1, 0 or 1. The first differing pair decides. When one slice is a prefix of the other, the shorter one is less.
Returns a new slice holding the elements of xs followed by those of ys. The result does not share storage with either argument.
fn contains[T: Eq](xs: []T, x: T) -> bool
Returns true when xs has an element equal to x. Scans xs from the start, so it takes linear time.
fn count[T](xs: []T, test: fn(T) -> bool) -> i64
Returns the number of elements of xs for which test returns true.
Returns true when the last elements of xs equal suffix. An empty suffix always matches.
Returns true when xs and ys have the same length and equal elements at every index.
Sets every element of xs to value.
Returns a new slice of the elements of xs for which keep returns true, in their original order.
fn find[T](xs: []T, test: fn(T) -> bool) -> T?
Returns the first element of xs for which test returns true, or none when there is none.
fn find_index[T](xs: []T, test: fn(T) -> bool) -> i64?
Returns the index of the first element of xs for which test returns true, or none when there is none.
Returns the first element of xs, or none when it is empty.
Returns the concatenation of f applied to each element of xs, in order.
Returns a new slice of the elements of each slice in xss, in order.
fn fold[T, A](xs: []T, initial: A, f: fn(A, T) -> A) -> A
Combines the elements of xs from the first to the last into one value. Starts with initial and sets the accumulator to f(accumulator, element) for each element. Returns initial when xs is empty.
fn index[T: Eq](xs: []T, x: T) -> i64?
Returns the index of the first element of xs equal to x, or none when there is none.
fn insert[T](mut xs: []T, at: i64, value: T)

Inserts value into xs so that it ends up at index at, moving later elements one place right. at may equal xs.len to append. Takes linear time in the number of elements moved. Panics when at is negative or greater than xs.len.
Returns the last element of xs, or none when it is empty.
fn lower_bound[T: Ord](xs: []T, x: T) -> i64

Returns the index of the first element of the sorted slice xs that is not less than x. Returns xs.len when every element is less than x. The slice must be sorted in ascending order. Takes logarithmic time.
fn map[T, U](xs: []T, f: fn(T) -> U) -> []U
Returns a new slice of f applied to each element of xs, in order.
Returns the largest element of xs, or none when it is empty. When several elements are equal and largest, the first is returned.
Returns the smallest element of xs, or none when it is empty. When several elements are equal and smallest, the first is returned.
fn partition[T](xs: []T, test: fn(T) -> bool) -> Pair[[]T, []T]
Splits xs into the elements for which test returns true and the rest. first holds the matches and second the others, each in their original order.
fn reduce[T](xs: []T, f: fn(T, T) -> T) -> T?
Combines the elements of xs from the first to the last with f, starting from the first element. Returns none when xs is empty and the only element, without calling f, when it has one.
fn remove[T](mut xs: []T, at: i64) -> T
Removes the element at index at from xs and returns it, moving later elements one place left. Takes linear time in the number of elements moved. Panics when at is out of range.
Returns a new slice holding xs repeated times times. The result is empty when times is zero or negative.
Reverses the elements of xs in place.
Rotates the elements of xs left by by places in place, so the element at index by moves to index 0. A negative by rotates right. by is taken modulo xs.len. Takes linear time and no extra storage.
fn scan[T, A](xs: []T, initial: A, f: fn(A, T) -> A) -> []A
Returns every accumulator value fold passes through, in order, without initial. Element i of the result is fold over the first i + 1 elements of xs, so the result is as long as xs.
Returns xs without its first n elements. The result shares storage with xs. It is xs itself when n is zero or negative and empty when n is at least xs.len.

Sorts xs in ascending order in place. The sort is not stable. It is a quicksort with a median-of-three pivot that finishes small ranges with insertion sort, taking O(n log n) time on typical input and O(n^2) in the worst case, with logarithmic stack use.
fn sort_by[T](mut xs: []T, less: fn(T, T) -> bool)

Sorts xs in place so that no element is preceded by one for which less returns true. less(a, b) returns true when a must come before b and must be a strict weak ordering. The sort is not stable and has the cost of sort.
fn sort_by_key[T, K: Ord](mut xs: []T, key: fn(T) -> K)
Sorts xs in place by the ascending value of key for each element, keeping elements with equal keys in their original order. key runs on every comparison, not once per element, so it should be cheap.
Sorts xs in ascending order in place, keeping equal elements in their original order. A merge sort that takes O(n log n) time and a temporary buffer of half the slice.
fn sort_stable_by[T](mut xs: []T, less: fn(T, T) -> bool)

Sorts xs in place by less, keeping elements that compare equal in their original order. less(a, b) returns true when a must come before b and must be a strict weak ordering. A merge sort that takes O(n log n) time and a temporary buffer of half the slice.
Returns true when xs is in ascending order, which includes equal neighbours. Slices with fewer than two elements are sorted.
Returns true when the first elements of xs equal prefix. An empty prefix always matches.
Returns the sum of the elements of xs, which is 0 for an empty slice. The addition has the overflow behaviour of T.
fn swap[T](mut xs: []T, i: i64, j: i64)
Exchanges the elements of xs at indexes i and j. Panics when either index is out of range.
Returns the first n elements of xs, or all of xs when it is shorter. The result shares storage with xs. It is empty when n is zero or negative.
Returns a new slice of xs with each run of consecutive equal elements reduced to one. Only neighbours are compared, so equal elements that are apart both stay. Sort xs first to remove all duplicates.

Returns every run of size consecutive elements of xs, starting at each index in turn. The result is empty when xs has fewer than size elements. The slices share storage with xs. Panics when size is less than 1.
Returns a slice of pairs of the elements of xs and ys at the same index. The result has the length of the shorter slice.
An owned SMTP connection. Dropping a Client closes the connection without sending QUIT, unless it was passed to detach. Call quit for an orderly close. The shared handle of the connection.
struct ClientHandle { pub timeout: i64 pub encrypted: bool pub extensions: Extensions ... }

A shared reference to an SMTP connection, for use from several tasks. Commands on one handle are serialised, so only one runs at a time. The current read and write timeout in milliseconds. Change it with set_timeout_on. Whether the connection is encrypted with TLS. The extensions the server announced in its most recent EHLO reply. After a HELO fallback only the greeting is set.
struct Envelope { pub from: str pub to: []str pub eight_bit: bool pub utf8: bool }

The sender and recipients of one message as given to the SMTP commands, separate from the message headers. The reverse path sent in MAIL FROM. Empty sends the null sender <>, used for bounces. The forward paths sent in RCPT TO. At least one is required. Declares the data as 8BITMIME, which the server must advertise. Declares SMTPUTF8 for internationalised addresses, which the server must advertise.
enum Error { Connect Closed Timeout Protocol TooLarge Insecure MessageTooLarge Unsupported(str) Transient(i64, str) Permanent(i64, str) Auth(str) Invalid(mail.Error) }

The error type of the SMTP client. The connection could not be made, or the TLS handshake failed. The connection is closed, or reading or writing failed. The server did not respond within the configured timeout. The server sent a reply that is malformed or not valid at that point of the dialogue. A reply exceeded Limits.lines or the reader's line length limit. The chosen mechanism would send the password over an unencrypted connection and Options.insecure_auth is not set. The message is larger than the size the server announced. The server does not offer feature, such as STARTTLS, AUTH, a named mechanism, SMTPUTF8 or 8BITMIME. The server replied with a 4xx code. The same request can succeed later. The server replied with a 5xx code. Repeating the request will fail again. The server rejected the credentials. message is the server's text. The message or envelope failed validation before anything was sent.

struct Extensions { pub greeting: str pub names: []str pub mechanisms: []str pub size: i64 pub starttls: bool pub eight_bit_mime: bool pub smtputf8: bool pub pipelining: bool pub enhanced_codes: bool }

The capabilities a server announced in reply to EHLO. The text of the first line of the reply, which carries the server's greeting. The keyword of every announced extension in uppercase, in order, including those with their own fields. The authentication mechanisms in uppercase, collected from AUTH lines and AUTH= lines without duplicates. The largest message size in bytes the server accepts, or 0 when it announces no limit or none that parses. The server supports STARTTLS. The server supports 8BITMIME. The server supports SMTPUTF8. The server supports PIPELINING. The server supports ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES.
Bounds applied while reading replies. The most lines accepted in one reply. A longer reply fails with TooLarge. Defaults to 1024.
enum Mechanism { Auto Plain Login XOAuth2 CramMd5 }

An SMTP authentication mechanism. Picks a mechanism the server advertises. choose defines the order, and XOAuth2 is never picked. PLAIN: sends the user name and password in one step. LOGIN: sends the user name and the password in two steps. XOAUTH2: authenticates with an OAuth 2 bearer token passed as the password. CRAM-MD5: answers a server challenge with an HMAC-MD5 digest, so the password is not sent.

struct Options { pub host: str pub port: i64 pub hello: str pub username: str pub password: str pub mechanism: Mechanism pub insecure_auth: bool pub timeout: i64 pub connect_timeout: i64 pub limits: Limits }

Settings for connecting to an SMTP server. The server host name or address. Also the TLS server name when the TLS configuration has none. Defaults to 127.0.0.1. The server port. Defaults to 25; submission with STARTTLS usually uses 587 and implicit TLS 465. The name sent in EHLO, or in HELO when the server rejects EHLO. Must not contain a line break or NUL; otherwise connecting fails with Invalid. Defaults to localhost. The user name. When non-empty, connecting also authenticates with username and password. The password, or the bearer token for XOAuth2. The authentication mechanism. Defaults to Auto. Allows Plain, Login and XOAuth2 to send credentials over an unencrypted connection. Without it they fail with Insecure. Defaults to false. Milliseconds a read or write on the established connection may take before it fails with Timeout. 0 means no limit. Milliseconds the TCP connection may take before connect fails with Timeout. 0 means no limit. The bounds applied when reading replies.
struct Receipt { pub accepted: []str pub refused: []Refusal pub code: i64 pub message: str }

The outcome of a delivery the server accepted. The recipients the server accepted. The recipients the server refused. The message was still delivered to accepted. The reply code the server gave after the data. The text of the reply the server gave after the data, which commonly carries a queue identifier.
struct Refusal { pub address: str pub code: i64 pub message: str }
A recipient the server refused. The recipient address. The reply code of the refusal. The text of the refusal.
struct Reply { pub code: i64 pub lines: []str }
A server reply: a three digit code and its text. The reply code, from 100 to 599. The text of each reply line, after the code and the separator. A single line reply has one entry.
fn authenticate(c: Client, username: str, password: str, mechanism: Mechanism) ! Error
Authenticates with the server. See authenticate_on.
Releases c from closing the connection when dropped and returns its handle. The caller becomes responsible for calling close_client_on or quit_on.
Sends NOOP, which keeps the connection alive. See noop_on.
Ends the session and closes the connection. See quit_on.
Abandons the current mail transaction. See reset_on.
fn send(c: Client, m: mail.Message) -> Receipt ! Error
Renders and sends a message. See send_on.
fn send_raw(c: Client, e: Envelope, data: []u8) -> Receipt ! Error
Sends already rendered message data. See send_raw_on.
Sets the read and write timeout of the connection. See set_timeout_on.
fn start_tls(c: Client, config: tls.Config) ! Error
Upgrades the connection to TLS. See start_tls_on.
Wraps a handle in a Client that closes the connection when dropped.
fn authenticate_on(h: *ClientHandle, username: str, password: str, mechanism: Mechanism) ! Error

Authenticates with username and password using mechanism. Auto picks the first of the mechanisms the server advertises that choose prefers. Fails with Unsupported when the server advertises no usable mechanism or not the requested one, Insecure when a password mechanism would run over an unencrypted connection without insecure_auth, Auth(message) when the server rejects the credentials, Transient for a 4xx reply and Protocol for an unexpected reply. Waits for any command in progress.
Closes the connection without sending QUIT. Later commands fail with Closed. Safe to call more than once and from several tasks. Use quit_on for an orderly close.
Sends NOOP and waits for the reply. Fails with Closed when the client is closed, Transient or Permanent when the server refuses, and with a transport error that also closes the connection.
Sends QUIT and closes the connection. Errors while sending are ignored, and the connection is closed in every case. Safe to call more than once.
Sends RSET, which abandons any mail transaction in progress, and waits for the reply. Fails like noop_on.
fn send_on(h: *ClientHandle, m: mail.Message) -> Receipt ! Error

Renders m with mail.render and sends it to the recipients from mail.recipients, which include bcc. The envelope sender is m.from.email, and 8BITMIME and SMTPUTF8 are requested when mail.needs_8bit and mail.needs_utf8 report that the message needs them. Fails with Invalid when the message cannot be rendered or has no valid recipients, and with the errors of send_raw_on.
fn send_raw_on(h: *ClientHandle, e: Envelope, data: []u8) -> Receipt ! Error

Sends data, a complete RFC 5322 message, with the given envelope. The data is dot stuffed and terminated here. The transaction is MAIL FROM, one RCPT TO per recipient and DATA; when the server advertises PIPELINING the first two are sent together. SIZE is declared when the server announces a limit. A recipient the server refuses is listed in Receipt.refused and does not fail the call. The call fails with Transient or Permanent when the sender, every recipient, the DATA command or the final reply is refused; RSET is sent when every recipient or the DATA command is refused. It fails with Invalid for an invalid address or no recipients, Unsupported when the envelope needs 8BITMIME or SMTPUTF8 and the server lacks it, MessageTooLarge when the data exceeds the announced size, and Closed, Timeout or Protocol on transport failures, which close the connection. Waits for any command in progress.
Sets how many milliseconds each read and write on the connection may take before failing with Timeout. 0 removes the limit. Applies to later operations.

Sends STARTTLS, performs the TLS handshake and repeats EHLO over the encrypted channel, refreshing extensions. Does nothing when the connection is already encrypted. Fails with Unsupported("STARTTLS") when the server does not advertise it, Closed when the client is closed, Transient or Permanent when the server refuses, and Connect, Timeout or Protocol when the handshake fails or the server sent data before it, which closes the connection. config.server_name defaults to the host of the connection. Waits for any command in progress.
Returns the name a server advertises for m: AUTO, PLAIN, LOGIN, XOAUTH2 or CRAM-MD5.

Connects to the server in plain text, reads the greeting, sends EHLO and authenticates when o.username is set. If the server rejects EHLO with a 5xx code, HELO is tried. Fails with Connect or Timeout while connecting, Transient or Permanent when the server refuses the greeting or the hello, and with the errors of authenticate, which includes Insecure for password mechanisms unless o.insecure_auth is set. A failure after the connection is made closes it.
fn connect_starttls(o: Options, config: tls.Config) -> Client ! Error

Connects like connect but upgrades to TLS with STARTTLS after the first EHLO, repeats EHLO over the encrypted channel and then authenticates. Fails with Unsupported("STARTTLS") when the server does not offer it, and with the errors of connect otherwise. config.server_name defaults to o.host.
fn connect_tls(o: Options, config: tls.Config) -> Client ! Error

Connects with TLS from the first byte, as on port 465, then reads the greeting, sends EHLO and authenticates when o.username is set. Fails with Connect or Timeout when the connection or handshake fails, and with the errors of connect after that. config.server_name defaults to o.host.
Returns the first digit of the reply code: 2 success, 3 more input needed, 4 transient failure, 5 permanent failure.

Builds an Extensions from the reply to EHLO. The first line becomes greeting and each further line is read as an extension keyword with parameters. Keywords are matched ignoring case, and unknown ones are only added to names.
Returns whether the reply is a success, a 2xx code.
Returns the lines of r joined with \n.

Returns the preferred mechanism the server advertises, or none when it advertises none of them. On an encrypted connection the order is Plain, Login, CramMd5. On an unencrypted one CramMd5 comes first, because it does not send the password. XOAuth2 and Auto are never returned.
fn connect_stream(s: io.Stream, o: Options) -> Client ! Error

Runs the SMTP session over an already open stream instead of dialling. The stream is treated as unencrypted, so password mechanisms need o.insecure_auth. o.timeout and set_timeout have no effect, because the client holds no socket of its own to apply them to. Fails like connect, and closes the stream on failure.
fn cram_md5_digest(password: str, challenge: str) -> str
Returns the lowercase hexadecimal HMAC-MD5 of challenge, keyed with password. challenge is the decoded server challenge.
fn cram_md5_response(user: str, password: str, challenge: str) -> str
Returns the base64 CRAM-MD5 response: user, a space and cram_md5_digest(password, challenge). challenge is the decoded server challenge.
Decodes a base64 server challenge, ignoring surrounding whitespace. Fails with base64.DecodeError when encoded is not valid base64.

Returns data framed for the SMTP DATA command. Every line break (
, 
 or a lone ) becomes 
, a . at the start of a line is doubled, a missing final line break is added, and the terminator .
 is appended. Empty input gives only the terminator.
Returns the base64 encoding of value, the response to each LOGIN prompt. Use it once for the user name and once for the password.
Parses the first reply in data, with the default Limits. See parse_reply_with.
fn parse_reply_with(data: []u8, limits: Limits) -> Reply ! Error

Parses the first reply in data, which may span several lines such as 250-first and 250 last. Data after the reply is ignored. Fails with Protocol when a code is not three digits from 100 to 599, the codes of the lines differ, a separator is not a space or -, or the data ends before the last line, and with TooLarge when the reply has more than limits.lines lines.
fn plain_response(user: str, password: str) -> str
Returns the base64 initial response of PLAIN: an empty authorization identity, user and password, each preceded by a NUL byte.
fn read_reply(r: *io.Reader, limits: Limits) -> Reply ! Error

Reads one reply from r, which may span several lines. Blocks until the last line arrives. Fails with Protocol for a malformed or inconsistent reply, TooLarge when it has more than limits.lines lines or a line over the reader's limit, Timeout when the stream times out, and Closed when the stream ends or fails first.
Returns whether the authentication mechanism mechanism is in advertised, ignoring case in mechanism. advertised must hold uppercase names, as Extensions.mechanisms does.
Maps an I/O error onto the SMTP error type: TimedOut becomes Timeout, TooLarge stays TooLarge, Malformed becomes Protocol and everything else becomes Closed.
fn xoauth2_response(user: str, token: str) -> str
Returns the base64 initial response of XOAUTH2 for user and the bearer token.
struct Auth { pub user: str pub password: str }
A username and password for a SOCKS5 proxy (RFC 1929). The username, 1 to 255 bytes. The password, up to 255 bytes.
fn dial(proxy: net.Addr, host: str, port: i64, auth: Auth?) -> net.Conn ! io.Error

Connects to the SOCKS5 proxy at proxy and asks it to connect to host and port. Returns the connection to the proxy, which then carries the traffic to the target. Parks the green thread while connecting and negotiating. The connection is closed if the proxy refuses. Fails as net.connect and tunnel do.
fn dial4a(proxy: net.Addr, host: str, port: i64, user: str) -> net.Conn ! io.Error

Connects to the SOCKS4a proxy at proxy and asks it to connect to host and port, identifying the caller as user. Returns the connection to the proxy, which then carries the traffic to the target. Parks the green thread while connecting and negotiating. The connection is closed if the proxy refuses. Fails as net.connect and tunnel4a do.
fn dial4a_handle(proxy: net.Addr, host: str, port: i64, user: str) -> net.ConnHandle ! io.Error
Does what dial4a does and returns the view of the connection. The caller owns the connection and must close it with net.close_on.
fn dial_handle(proxy: net.Addr, host: str, port: i64, auth: Auth?) -> net.ConnHandle ! io.Error
Does what dial does and returns the view of the connection. The caller owns the connection and must close it with net.close_on.
fn dialer(proxy: net.Addr, auth: Auth?) -> net.Dialer

Returns a net.Dialer that reaches every target through the SOCKS5 proxy at proxy using auth. Each call of the dialer connects to the proxy and passes the host name to it unresolved, so the proxy resolves it.
fn dialer4a(proxy: net.Addr, user: str) -> net.Dialer

Returns a net.Dialer that reaches every target through the SOCKS4a proxy at proxy, identifying the caller as user. Each call of the dialer connects to the proxy and passes the host name to it unresolved, so the proxy resolves it.
fn tunnel(c: net.Conn, host: str, port: i64, auth: Auth?) ! io.Error
Asks the SOCKS5 proxy at the other end of c to connect to host and port. Does the same as tunnel_on on the connection's handle.
fn tunnel4a(c: net.Conn, host: str, port: i64, user: str) ! io.Error
Asks the SOCKS4a proxy at the other end of c to connect to host and port. Does the same as tunnel4a_on on the connection's handle.
fn tunnel4a_on(h: net.ConnHandle, host: str, port: i64, user: str) ! io.Error

Asks the SOCKS4a proxy at the other end of the connection h to connect to host and port, identifying the caller as user, so that h then carries the traffic to the target. host is an IPv4 literal or a name of up to 255 bytes that the proxy resolves. Parks the green thread during the exchange and is limited by the connection's timeouts. Fails with Invalid for a port outside 1 to 65535, with Unsupported for an IPv6 literal or an unusable host, with Refused if the proxy rejects the request, with Denied for any other failure reply and with Malformed for a reply that does not follow the protocol.
fn tunnel_on(h: net.ConnHandle, host: str, port: i64, auth: Auth?) ! io.Error

Asks the SOCKS5 proxy at the other end of the connection h to connect to host and port, so that h then carries the traffic to the target. host is an IP literal, optionally in square brackets, or a name of up to 255 bytes that the proxy resolves. With auth set, offers no authentication and username and password; with none, only no authentication. Parks the green thread during the exchange and is limited by the connection's timeouts. Fails with Invalid for a port outside 1 to 65535, an unusable host or credentials, and with Denied if the proxy refuses every method or the credentials, or requires authentication and auth is none. A proxy reply code of 2 gives Denied, 3 and 4 Unreachable, 5 Refused, 6 TimedOut, 7 and 8 Unsupported, and another code Os(code). A reply that does not follow the protocol gives Malformed, and a proxy that closes early gives Eof.
struct Column { pub name: str pub kind: str }
A column of a result set. The column name or alias as the database reports it. The database's name for the column type, empty when the database reports none.

struct ColumnTypes { pub boolean: str pub small: str pub medium: str pub large: str pub unsigned_large: str pub single: str pub double: str pub text: str pub short_text: str pub binary: str pub enumeration: str pub document: str pub identity: str }

The column types a dialect uses for the shapes of data std/orm and std/sql/migrate store. A boolean. An integer of at most 16 bits. An integer of at most 32 bits. A 64-bit integer. A 64-bit unsigned integer. A 32-bit float. A 64-bit float. A text string of any length. A text string short enough to be a key. A binary string. A value drawn from a fixed set of names. A structured value stored as JSON. A 64-bit integer key the database generates, without the PRIMARY KEY clause.

An owned database connection that closes the underlying connection when dropped. Its handle is the copyable view that std/orm and std/sql/pool work in terms of; adopt builds a Connection from one. The copyable view of the connection.

struct ConnectionHandle { pub dialect: Dialect pub query: fn(str, []Value) -> Rows ! Error pub each: fn(str, []Value, fn([]Column, []Value) -> bool) ! Error pub execute: fn(str, []Value) -> i64 ! Error pub begin: fn() ! Error pub commit: fn() ! Error pub rollback: fn() ! Error pub close: fn() }

A copyable view of a database connection, made of closures. Copies refer to the same connection and none of them owns it: close closes the connection for all of them. std/orm and std/sql/pool work in terms of this view. The handle field of a Connection is one. The dialect the connection speaks. Runs the statement with the parameters and returns all rows. Runs the statement with the parameters and calls the callback for each row in turn, with the columns and the row. The callback returns false to stop early. Runs the statement with the parameters, discards any rows and returns the number of rows affected. Starts a transaction. Commits the current transaction. Rolls back the current transaction. Closes the connection. A second call has no effect.

struct Dialect { pub system: str pub default_port: i64 pub placeholder_prefix: str pub open_quote: u8 pub close_quote: u8 pub key_return: KeyReturn pub paging: Paging pub types: ColumnTypes pub table_guard: TableGuard pub lock: Lock pub begin_write: str }

Everything that differs between the databases the drivers speak to: placeholders, identifier quotes, column types, generated keys, paging, DDL, locks, the OpenTelemetry system name and the default port. postgres, sqlserver and sqlite build the three dialects. Every connection carries its own, and std/orm and std/sql/migrate read it. The db.system.name that OpenTelemetry reports for the database. The port a driver connects to when Options.port is 0; 0 for a database with no port. The text before the one-based parameter number in a placeholder. The character that opens a quoted identifier. The character that closes a quoted identifier, doubled when it occurs in the name. How an insert reports the generated key. How a SELECT is paged. The column types. How CREATE TABLE is made conditional. The session lock statements. The statement that starts a transaction holding the write lock, or empty when begin already does.
enum Error { Connect Authentication Closed Timeout Protocol Unsupported Conversion Busy Server(str, str) }

The error the SQL drivers return, which std/sql/pool wraps in pool.Error.Sql. The connection could not be established. The server rejected the login or the authentication exchange failed. The connection is closed. Connecting, reading or writing did not finish within Options.timeout. The server sent data the driver does not understand. The driver abandons the connection. The server or the statement needs a feature the driver does not support, such as an unsupported authentication method or TLS negotiation. A value cannot be converted to or from its database representation, or the parameter count does not match the statement. The connection is in use by another call, or the SQLite database is locked. The server reported an error. code is the SQLSTATE on PostgreSQL, the error number on SQL Server and the extended result code on SQLite; message is the server's text.
How an insert reports the key the database generated. The insert reports no key. A RETURNING clause after the values. An OUTPUT INSERTED clause before the values.
struct Lock { pub key: LockKey pub acquire: str pub release: str }

The statements that take and release a session lock. What the statements take as their resource.
