The statement that waits for the lock, with the resource as its first parameter and, when it reports a status, a negative first column for a lock that was not granted. Empty when key is Absent. The statement that releases the lock, with the resource as its first parameter. Empty when key is Absent.
What a lock statement takes as its resource. The dialect has no session lock. A 64-bit integer. A text name.
struct Options { pub host: str pub port: i64 pub user: str pub password: str pub database: str pub application: str pub timeout: i64 }

The settings a driver's connect function takes. The server host name or address. Defaults to "localhost". The server port. 0, the default, selects the dialect's default_port: 5432 for PostgreSQL and 1433 for SQL Server. The user name. Defaults to empty. The password. Defaults to empty. The database to use. Defaults to empty, which leaves the choice to the server. std/sql/sqlite reads it as the file path and ignores the other fields. The application name reported to the server. Defaults to "lowlang". The timeout in milliseconds for connecting and for socket reads and writes. Defaults to 15000. A timeout fails with Error.Timeout.

How a SELECT limits and skips rows. LIMIT n and OFFSET n, each written only when it applies. LIMIT n OFFSET n, written together, so an unlimited page is LIMIT -1. OFFSET n ROWS and FETCH NEXT n ROWS ONLY, which need an ORDER BY.
struct Rows { pub columns: []Column pub rows: [][]Value }
A fully buffered result set. The columns of the result. A query that returns no rows still reports them. The rows in the order the database returned them; each row has one Value per column.
How CREATE TABLE is made to do nothing when the table exists. CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. An IF OBJECT_ID(...) IS NULL test before CREATE TABLE.
enum Value { Null Bool(bool) Int(i64) Float(f64) Decimal(str) Text(str) Bytes([]u8) Uuid([]u8) Date(i64) Time(i64) Timestamp(i64) TimestampTz(i64) }

A database value, used both as a statement parameter and as a cell in a result row. Which variants a driver returns depends on the database: SQLite only produces Null, Int, Float, Text and Bytes, and stores the other variants as integers, text or blobs when they are bound. A driver fails with Error.Conversion when it cannot represent a parameter. SQL NULL. A boolean. A 64-bit signed integer. A 64-bit floating point number. An exact decimal number as its decimal digits in text form, for example "12.50". A text string. A binary string. A UUID as its 16 raw bytes. A calendar date as the number of days since 1970-01-01. A time of day as the number of microseconds since midnight. A date and time without a zone as the number of microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00. A date and time in UTC as the number of microseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.
Returns a Connection that owns the connection behind the handle, so that dropping it calls the handle's close.
fn rolled_back(h: ConnectionHandle, cause: Error) -> Error

Rolls back the current transaction of h after cause and returns the error to report. That is cause when the rollback succeeds and the rollback's own error when it fails, because the transaction may then still be open.
fn create_table_if_missing(d: Dialect, name: str, columns: str) -> str
Returns the statement that creates the table name with columns unless it exists. columns is the text between the parentheses, and name is quoted for the dialect.
fn placeholder(d: Dialect, index: i64) -> str
Returns the placeholder for the parameter at the zero-based index: $1 for PostgreSQL, @p1 for SQL Server and ?1 for SQLite when index is 0.
fn quote_identifier(d: Dialect, name: str) -> str
Returns the identifier quoted for the dialect, with each closing quote character in the name doubled.
Returns the PostgreSQL dialect, with $1 placeholders and "name" identifiers.
Returns the SQLite dialect, with ?1 placeholders and "name" identifiers.
Returns the Microsoft SQL Server dialect, with @p1 placeholders and [name] identifiers.
struct Session { pub busy: bool pub closed: bool }

The state of one driver connection that every call checks: whether a call is running and whether the connection is closed. Whether a call is running on the connection. Whether the connection is closed.
fn connection(s: *Session, fatal: fn(sql.Error) -> bool, abandon: fn(), scope: str, o: sql.Options, raw: sql.ConnectionHandle) -> sql.Connection
Returns the owning sql.Connection for a driver's raw handle: guarded by the session, traced under scope and closed when dropped.
fn establish(s: *Session, fatal: fn(sql.Error) -> bool, abandon: fn(), terminate: fn(), handshake: fn() ! sql.Error) ! sql.Error
Runs the login exchange handshake as a call on the session and, when it fails, calls terminate before returning the error.
The number of microseconds in a day, the unit of sql.Value.Time, Timestamp and TimestampTz.
fn collect(run: fn(fn([]sql.Column), fn([]sql.Column, []sql.Value) -> bool) ! sql.Error) -> sql.Rows ! sql.Error
Runs run with a column callback and a row callback that buffer the result, and returns it. A second column callback call, as for a later result set, discards the rows buffered so far.
fn dial(o: sql.Options, d: sql.Dialect) -> net.Conn ! sql.Error
Opens a TCP connection to o.host at the dialect's port within o.timeout. Fails with sql.Error.Timeout when the dial times out and sql.Error.Connect otherwise.
A column callback that ignores the columns.
A row callback that ignores the row and continues.
Returns a session for a connection that is open and idle.
fn traced(raw: sql.ConnectionHandle, scope: str, o: sql.Options) -> sql.ConnectionHandle

Returns raw with every query, each and execute recorded as an OpenTelemetry database call under scope, tagged with the database o.database, the server o.host and the server's port, o.port or the dialect's default when o.port is 0. Every driver applies it once to the handle it returns, so a connection from any driver is traced the same way.
struct Entry { pub version: i64 pub name: str pub state: State pub expected: str pub recorded: str pub applied_at: timestamp.Timestamp? }

The state of one version, as reported by status. The version. The name from the plan, or the recorded name for an Unknown entry. Whether the version is applied, pending, drifted or unknown. The checksum of the plan's migration, or an empty string for an Unknown entry. The checksum stored in the table, or an empty string for a Pending entry. When the migration was applied, or none for a pending entry or a time that cannot be represented.
enum Error { Sql(sql.Error) Failed(i64, sql.Error) Duplicate(i64) OutOfOrder(i64) Invalid(i64) Drift(i64) Unknown(i64) NoDown(i64) Locked Syntax(i64) BadName(str) Io(io.Error) }

Why a migration operation failed. A statement outside any migration failed: creating or reading the migration table, or taking or releasing the lock. The migration with this version failed, so its transaction was rolled back and earlier migrations stay applied. cause is the database error, or the rollback's error when the rollback failed too. Two migrations share this version. This migration is below the previous one in the plan, or below a version that is already applied. This migration has a version below 1. The checksum recorded for this applied version differs from the plan's, so the migration was edited after it was applied. This version is recorded as applied but is not in the plan, so it cannot be reverted. This version has no down statements, so it cannot be reverted. Another session holds the migration lock. The migration text is malformed at this one-based line: a statement before -- +up, a missing -- +up, a -- +begin or -- +end out of place, or a block left open. This file name does not have the form NNN_name.sql. Reading the migration directory or a file failed.
struct Migration { pub version: i64 pub name: str pub up: []str pub down: []str }

One schema change: statements that apply it and statements that revert it. The position in the plan. Versions are at least 1 and ascending through the plan. A label for the migration, recorded when it is applied. The statements that apply the migration, run in order inside one transaction. The statements that revert the migration, run in order inside one transaction. Empty when it cannot be reverted.
struct Plan { pub migrations: []Migration pub table: str pub clock: clock.Clock }

An ordered list of migrations and the table that records which have been applied. Build one with plan. A Plan is a copyable value; with_table and with_clock return a changed copy. The migrations, in ascending version order. The table that records applied versions. Defaults to schema_migrations. It is created on first use with version, name, applied_at (Unix milliseconds) and checksum columns. The clock that supplies applied_at for newly applied migrations. Defaults to the system clock.
enum State { Applied Pending Drifted Unknown }

Where a migration stands against the migration table. Recorded in the table, with a checksum that matches the plan. In the plan but not recorded in the table. Recorded in the table, but the plan's checksum differs, so the migration changed after it was applied. Recorded in the table but absent from the plan.

Returns the SHA-256 digest of the migration's up statements as lower-case hexadecimal. Each statement is hashed with its length, so moving text between statements changes the result. The version, name and down statements are not covered.

Checks that the plan's versions are at least 1, unique and ascending. Fails with Invalid for a version below 1, Duplicate for a repeated version, or OutOfOrder for a version below its predecessor. Every operation that takes a plan calls it first.
fn with_clock(p: Plan, c: clock.Clock) -> Plan
Returns p that stamps applied_at with c.
fn with_table(p: Plan, table: str) -> Plan

Returns p recording applied versions in table. The table name is quoted for the connection's dialect. The migration lock is derived from the name, so plans with different tables do not block each other.
fn down(c: sql.Connection, p: Plan, steps: i64) -> []i64 ! Error
Reverts the latest steps applied migrations on c and returns the versions reverted. See down_on.
fn down_on(h: sql.ConnectionHandle, p: Plan, steps: i64) -> []i64 ! Error

Reverts the latest steps applied migrations of p through h and returns the versions it reverted, highest first. Validates the plan, takes the migration lock and creates the migration table as up_to_on does. Before reverting anything it fails with Unknown for an applied version missing from the plan and NoDown for one without down statements. Each migration is reverted in its own transaction together with the removal of its record, so a failure returns Failed and leaves the earlier reversions in place. Reverts nothing when steps is 0 or less or nothing is applied.
fn from_text(version: i64, name: str, source: str) -> Migration ! Error

Parses migration text into a Migration with the given version and name. The text has an -- +up section and an optional -- +down section. Statements end at a line that ends in ;, and may span lines. A statement containing semicolons, such as a function body, goes between -- +begin and -- +end lines, which makes everything between them one statement. Blank lines and comments between statements are dropped, and a final statement without ; is kept. Fails with Syntax at the offending line for text before -- +up, a missing -- +up, a misplaced -- +begin or -- +end, a section change inside a block, or a block left open.

Reads every NNN_name.sql file in dir as a migration and returns them in ascending version order. NNN is the version and name the label, split at the first underscore. Files without the .sql suffix are ignored and subdirectories are not searched. Fails with BadName for a file that does not fit the pattern, Duplicate for a repeated version, Syntax for malformed text and Io when the directory or a file cannot be read.
Returns a plan of migrations, which must be in ascending version order, using the table schema_migrations and the system clock.
fn status(c: sql.Connection, p: Plan) -> []Entry ! Error
Reports the state of every migration on c. See status_on.
fn status_on(h: sql.ConnectionHandle, p: Plan) -> []Entry ! Error

Returns one Entry per version of the plan and per recorded version missing from it, in ascending version order, through h. Creates the migration table if it is missing, takes no lock and changes no migration. Fails with the errors of validate, or Sql when the table cannot be read.
fn up(c: sql.Connection, p: Plan) -> []i64 ! Error
Applies every pending migration on c and returns the versions applied. See up_to_on.
fn up_on(h: sql.ConnectionHandle, p: Plan) -> []i64 ! Error
Applies every pending migration of p through h and returns the versions it applied, in order. Calls up_to_on with no upper limit.
fn up_to(c: sql.Connection, p: Plan, version: i64) -> []i64 ! Error
Applies the pending migrations up to and including version on c and returns the versions applied. See up_to_on.
fn up_to_on(h: sql.ConnectionHandle, p: Plan, version: i64) -> []i64 ! Error

Applies the pending migrations of p up to and including version through h and returns the versions it applied, in order. Validates the plan, takes the migration lock, creates the migration table if it is missing, and releases the lock before returning; a failed release fails with Sql unless an earlier error is returned instead. The lock is a session advisory lock on Postgres, an application lock on SQL Server that waits for the holder, and absent on SQLite. Fails with Drift if an applied migration's checksum no longer matches and OutOfOrder if a pending migration is below the highest applied version. Each migration runs in its own transaction with its record, and is skipped if another session recorded it first, so a failure leaves earlier migrations applied and returns Failed for the failing one. Returns an empty list when nothing is pending.

struct Config { pub max: i64 pub max_idle: i64 pub idle_timeout: duration.Duration pub max_lifetime: duration.Duration pub wait_timeout: duration.Duration pub ping_after: duration.Duration pub ping: fn(sql.ConnectionHandle) ! sql.Error pub clock: clock.Clock }

How a pool sizes itself and how it keeps its connections healthy. A duration of zero turns the matching limit off. The most connections the pool keeps open at once, idle and leased together. Defaults to 4; a value below 1 becomes 1. The most connections kept idle for reuse. Defaults to -1, and a negative value or one above max means max. A connection returned while this many are idle is closed. How long a connection may sit idle before the pool closes it instead of handing it out. Defaults to zero, which keeps idle connections indefinitely. How long after it was opened a connection may be reused. An older connection is closed when it is returned or found idle. Defaults to zero, which has no limit. How long acquire waits for a connection when all of them are in use before it fails with Error.Timeout. Defaults to zero, which waits until a connection or the cancel token ends the wait. How long a connection must have been idle before ping checks it as it leaves the pool. Defaults to zero, which never pings. Checks an idle connection that has passed ping_after; a connection for which it fails is closed and replaced by another. Defaults to running SELECT 1. The source of the monotonic time behind the lifetime, idle and ping limits. Defaults to the system clock.
enum Error { Closed Timeout Cancelled Sql(sql.Error) }

The error acquire, acquire_until and with return. The pool has been shut down, including while the call was waiting for a connection. No connection became available within the wait time. The cancel token was cancelled before or while the call waited for a connection. The opener failed to make a connection, or the callback of with returned an error. cause is the underlying sql.Error.

A connection leased from a pool, returned to the pool when dropped. Use conn or connection to run statements on it. Dropping the lease rolls back an open transaction and returns the connection, or closes it when the lease was discarded or a call failed with a connection-level error. The copyable LeaseHandle for the lease.

The copyable state of a lease: the pool, the leased connection and whether the lease is released, broken or inside a transaction. release_on and discard_on act on it. Every copy refers to the same lease.

A pool of connections made on demand by an opener. A Pool is a copyable handle; copies share one pool. It opens a connection when none is idle and max is not reached, and otherwise queues the caller in first-in first-out order. It is safe to use from several green threads.
struct Stats { pub open: i64 pub idle: i64 pub in_use: i64 pub waiting: i64 pub acquires: i64 pub waits: i64 pub timeouts: i64 pub cancelled: i64 pub discarded: i64 pub opened: i64 }

A snapshot of the counters and sizes of a pool. The connections open, idle and leased together, counting those being opened. The idle connections kept in the pool. The connections currently leased. The calls waiting for a connection. The leases handed out in total. The calls that had to queue because every connection was in use. The waits that ended in Error.Timeout. The calls that ended in Error.Cancelled. The connections the pool closed because they were broken, past their lifetime or idle for too long. The connections the opener has made successfully in total.

Returns the leased connection as an sql.ConnectionHandle. Its calls fail with sql.Error.Closed once the lease is released or broken, and calling its close discards the lease instead of closing the connection directly. A call that fails with Connect, Authentication, Closed, Timeout or Protocol, or with a Server error whose code starts with 08 or 57P, marks the connection broken so that the pool closes it on release.
Returns the leased connection as an sql.Connection whose close does nothing, so that dropping it leaves the connection with the lease. Its calls behave as those of conn.
Marks the connection broken so that the pool closes it instead of reusing it when the lease is released. Statements on the lease then fail with sql.Error.Closed.

Returns the connection to the pool. Releasing a released lease has no effect. An open transaction is rolled back first, and the connection is closed instead of reused when the rollback fails or the lease was discarded. Dropping the Lease calls it.
Returns the connection view for the lease behind the handle; see conn.
Returns the connection for the lease behind the handle; see connection.
Marks the connection behind the handle broken; see discard.
Returns the connection behind the handle to the pool; see release.
Leases a connection, waiting up to Config.wait_timeout when every connection is in use. It is acquire_until with a token that is never cancelled.
fn acquire_until(p: Pool, t: *cancel.Token, wait: duration.Duration) -> Lease ! Error

Leases a connection, waiting at most wait for one; a zero wait waits without a time limit. An idle connection is reused first, failing that a new one is opened while fewer than max are open, and failing that the call queues in first-in first-out order. Idle connections past their limits are closed first, and one idle longer than ping_after is pinged and replaced when the ping fails. Returns Error.Closed when the pool is shut down, Error.Cancelled when t is cancelled, Error.Timeout when wait runs out and Error.Sql when the opener fails. Dropping the returned Lease returns the connection.
Closes the idle connections that are past max_lifetime or idle_timeout and returns how many it closed. Leased connections are not touched.

Shuts the pool down: closes every idle connection, fails the queued callers with Error.Closed and refuses later calls to acquire. Blocks the calling green thread until every outstanding lease is returned; each connection returned after the shutdown is closed.
Returns a snapshot of the pool's sizes and counters.
fn with(p: Pool, work: fn(sql.ConnectionHandle) ! sql.Error) ! Error
Leases a connection, passes it to work and returns it to the pool when work finishes. Fails like acquire; an error from work is returned as Error.Sql.
Returns the copyable view of an owned connection and turns the connection's own close into a no-op, so that dropping c no longer closes it. An opener uses it to give a connection to the pool.
fn open(opener: fn() -> sql.Connection ! sql.Error, config: Config) -> Pool

Returns a pool that calls opener to make connections as callers need them. No connection is opened until the first acquire. The config is normalized: max below 1 becomes 1 and max_idle below 0 or above max becomes max.
The state of one SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication exchange: the password, the client nonce, the client-first-message body and the server signature scram_final computes for scram_verify.
fn scram_final(s: *Scram, server_first: str) -> str ! sql.Error

Computes the client-final-message, with the proof, from the server-first-message server_first. Returns sql.Error.Protocol when server_first lacks the r, s or i attribute, when the server nonce does not extend the client nonce, or when the salt or iteration count is invalid, and sql.Error.Unsupported when the server demands an extension. It records the signature scram_verify expects.
Returns the client-first-message to send to the server, n,,n=<user>,r=<nonce>.

Checks the server-final-message server_final against the signature scram_final computed. Returns sql.Error.Authentication when the server reports an e= error or the signature differs, and sql.Error.Protocol when the message has no v attribute or it is not valid base64.

Connects to a PostgreSQL server over plain TCP, using o.host and o.port (5432 by default), and authenticates as o.user to o.database. A call that times out closes the connection and sends a cancel request to the server over a new connection. Passwords are sent in cleartext, as an MD5 hash or through SCRAM-SHA-256, as the server requests. Returns sql.Error.Connect when the connection cannot be made, sql.Error.Timeout when it exceeds o.timeout, sql.Error.Authentication when the login fails, sql.Error.Unsupported for an authentication method the driver lacks and sql.Error.Server when the server rejects the startup. Dropping the returned sql.Connection closes the socket.
fn connect_stream(s: io.Stream, o: sql.Options) -> sql.Connection ! sql.Error

Connects over a stream that is already connected, such as a Unix socket or a tunnel, and authenticates as connect does. o.host, o.port and o.timeout are not used to dial. A timed out call closes the stream without sending the cancel request that connect sends. Fails like connect after the dial.
fn connect_tls(o: sql.Options, config: tls.Config) -> sql.Connection ! sql.Error

Connects to a PostgreSQL server and upgrades the connection to TLS with the SSLRequest exchange before authenticating. config sets the TLS options; an empty server_name is replaced with o.host. Returns sql.Error.Unsupported when the server answers that it does not do TLS and sql.Error.Protocol for any other answer. Otherwise fails like connect.
fn scram(user: str, password: str, nonce: str) -> *Scram
Starts a SCRAM-SHA-256 exchange for user and password with the client nonce. The , and = characters in user are escaped as =2C and =3D.
struct Config { pub read_only: bool pub create: bool pub busy_timeout: i64 }

How open_with opens a database. Opens the database read-only. Defaults to false; a read-only open never creates the file. Creates the file when it does not exist. Defaults to true; it has no effect when read_only is set. How long in milliseconds SQLite retries a locked database before the call fails with sql.Error.Busy. Defaults to 5000.

An open SQLite database that closes itself when dropped. Calls block the calling OS thread. Statements are prepared once per distinct text and cached until the database is closed. The copyable DatabaseHandle for the database.

The copyable state of an open database: the native handle, the file path and the cache of prepared statements. close_on closes it. Every copy refers to the same database, so a closed handle makes calls through any copy fail with sql.Error.Closed.
fn backup(d: Database, path: str) ! sql.Error

Copies the whole database into the file at path with the online backup API, creating the file when needed. The copy runs in one step and retries every 10 milliseconds while the source or the target is locked. Returns sql.Error.Closed when the database is closed and sql.Error.Server or sql.Error.Busy when the target cannot be opened or the copy fails.
Starts a deferred transaction with BEGIN.
Starts a transaction with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, which takes the write lock at once instead of at the first write.
Closes the database. Closing a closed database has no effect.
Returns the database as an sql.Connection whose close does nothing, so the Database stays responsible for closing it.
fn each(d: Database, text: str, values: []sql.Value, visit: fn([]sql.Column, []sql.Value) -> bool) ! sql.Error

Runs one statement with values bound to its ? or ?N parameters and calls visit with the columns and the row for each row it returns. visit returns false to stop early. Returns sql.Error.Conversion when values does not match the statement's parameter count, sql.Error.Closed when the database is closed, sql.Error.Busy when it is locked and sql.Error.Server for any other failure. Rows hold Null, Int, Float, Text or Bytes values.
fn exec(d: Database, script: str) ! sql.Error

Runs the SQL script, which may hold several statements separated by ;, without parameters and discards any rows. Returns sql.Error.Closed when the database is closed, sql.Error.Busy when it is locked and sql.Error.Server for any other failure.
fn execute(d: Database, text: str, values: []sql.Value) -> i64 ! sql.Error

Runs one statement with values bound to its parameters and returns the number of rows changed by the database's most recent INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. Any rows the statement returns are discarded. Fails like each.
Returns the row id of the most recent successful INSERT on this database, or 0 when the database is closed.
fn query(d: Database, text: str, values: []sql.Value) -> sql.Rows ! sql.Error
Runs one statement with values bound to its parameters and returns all rows. A statement that returns no rows still reports its columns, with each column's declared type as kind. Fails like each.
Finalizes the cached statements and closes the database behind the handle. Closing a closed database has no effect.
Opens the file named by o.database with the default Config and returns it as an sql.Connection whose close closes the database. The other fields of o are ignored. Fails like open.
Opens the database file at path for reading and writing, creating it when it does not exist, with a busy timeout of 5000 milliseconds.
fn open_with(path: str, c: Config) -> Database ! sql.Error

Opens the database file at path using the settings in c. Returns sql.Error.Server when SQLite cannot open it and sql.Error.Busy when it is locked. path is passed to SQLite unchanged, so ":memory:" opens a private in-memory database.

Connects to a SQL Server over plain TCP, using o.host and o.port (1433 by default), and logs in as o.user to o.database. Returns sql.Error.Connect when the connection cannot be made, sql.Error.Timeout when it exceeds o.timeout, sql.Error.Authentication when the login fails and sql.Error.Unsupported when the server requires encryption, which needs connect_tls. Dropping the returned sql.Connection closes the socket.
fn connect_stream(s: io.Stream, o: sql.Options) -> sql.Connection ! sql.Error
Connects over a stream that is already connected, without TLS, and logs in as connect does. Fails like connect after the dial.
fn connect_tls(o: sql.Options, config: tls.Config) -> sql.Connection ! sql.Error

Connects to a SQL Server and negotiates TLS during the TDS pre-login exchange using config, then logs in. Returns sql.Error.Unsupported when the server does not offer encryption. Otherwise fails like connect.
A rendezvous point where a fixed number of green threads wait for each other. The barrier is reusable: once the last party arrives it resets for the next round. Copies of a Barrier share its state.
A condition variable tied to a Mutex. Green threads park in wait_cond until another calls signal or broadcast. Copies of a Cond share the same waiters.
A set of tasks that run concurrently on green threads, with a limit on how many run at once and a record of the first error. Copies of an ErrorGroup share its state.

A mutual exclusion lock shared by its copies. A mutex is not reentrant: locking it again from the green thread that holds it parks forever. Waiting for a lock parks the green thread rather than blocking the OS thread.
A guard that lets a function run a single time. Copies of a Once share its state.
A value computed by a function the first time it is requested and then reused. Copies of an OnceValue share the cached value.

A lock that admits many readers or one writer. Requests are granted in arrival order: a reader that arrives while a writer is waiting queues behind it, so writers are not starved. Waiting parks the green thread. The lock is not reentrant, and copies of an RwLock refer to the same lock.
A counting semaphore that limits how many green threads use a resource at once. Waiters are served in arrival order. Copies of a Semaphore share the count.
A counter of outstanding tasks that wait parks on until it reaches zero. Copies of a WaitGroup share the counter.
Parks the green thread until parties green threads have called wait_barrier on b. Returns true to the call that completed the round, which releases the others, and false to the rest.
Wakes every green thread parked in wait_cond.
Wakes the longest-waiting green thread parked in wait_cond, and does nothing if there is none. A call that happens before the waiter has parked is not remembered.

Unlocks the owner of c, parks the green thread until signal or broadcast wakes it, and locks the owner again before returning. The caller must hold the owner. A wakeup does not guarantee the awaited condition still holds, so check it in a loop.
fn go[E](g: ErrorGroup[E], f: fn() -> E?)

Runs f on a new green thread as a task of g. Parks the green thread while limit tasks are already running. When f returns some(e), e is recorded unless an earlier task has already recorded an error; the other tasks are not stopped.
Parks the green thread until every task started with go has finished, and returns the first recorded error, or none if no task failed.
Returns a Cond that is used with the lock owner.
Locks m, parking the green thread until it is available.
fn locked[T](m: Mutex, f: fn() -> T) -> T
Locks m, runs f, unlocks m and returns the result of f.
Locks m if it is free and returns whether it did, without parking.
Unlocks m. m must be locked. Unlocking an unlocked mutex is a bug and parks the green thread until another green thread locks the mutex, then releases that lock.

Runs f if no call to run on o has run a function before, and does nothing otherwise. Calls from other green threads that arrive while f runs park until it finishes, so when run returns, f has completed.

Returns the value of o, calling its function if this is the first request. Callers that arrive while the function runs park until it finishes, so the function runs once and every caller receives the same result.
Takes a shared lock, parking the green thread while a writer holds the lock or any request is queued.
Releases a shared lock taken with read_lock or try_read_lock. Panics with sync: read_unlock of an unlocked RwLock if no shared lock is held.
fn reading[T](l: RwLock, f: fn() -> T) -> T
Takes a shared lock, runs f, releases the lock and returns the result of f.
Takes a shared lock if one is available immediately and returns whether it did, without parking.
Takes the exclusive lock if it is available immediately and returns whether it did, without parking.
Takes the exclusive lock, parking the green thread while any reader or writer holds the lock or any request is queued.
Releases the exclusive lock. Panics with sync: write_unlock of an unlocked RwLock if the lock is not held for writing.
fn writing[T](l: RwLock, f: fn() -> T) -> T
Takes the exclusive lock, runs f, releases the lock and returns the result of f.
Takes a permit, parking the green thread until one is available.
Returns the number of permits that can be taken without waiting.

Returns a permit. Hands it to the longest-waiting acquire if there is one, and otherwise increases the available count. The count has no upper bound, so releasing more than was acquired grows the capacity.
Takes a permit if one is available and returns whether it did, without parking.
Adds n to the count of w, which can be negative. Wakes every green thread parked in wait when the count reaches zero. Panics with sync: negative wait group count if the count would go below zero.
Subtracts one from the count of w. Panics if the count is already zero.
Parks the green thread until the count of w is zero, and returns at once if it already is.
Returns a Barrier that releases once parties green threads are waiting.
Returns an ErrorGroup that runs at most limit tasks at a time. limit must be at least 1: with a smaller limit go parks forever.

Pins the calling green thread to the OS thread it is running on. Until a matching unlock_thread, the green thread runs only on this OS thread, and the OS thread runs no other green thread: while the green thread waits, its OS thread sleeps and the scheduler starts another for the rest. Code that calls a C library whose state belongs to one OS thread, such as a Win32 window, locks first. Calls nest, and each lock_thread needs its own unlock_thread.
Returns a Once that has not run.
Returns an OnceValue that calls compute on the first get_once.
Returns a Semaphore with permits permits available.
Releases one lock_thread of the calling green thread. Once every lock is released the green thread may move between OS threads again.
Returns a WaitGroup with a count of zero.
struct Accepted { pub fd: i64 pub address: []u8 }
A connection taken from a listening socket by accept. The descriptor of the connection, non-blocking and closed on exec. The address of the peer in the system's socket address layout.
What access tests for. The path is present. The path is present and the caller may execute it.
struct Action { pub handler: i64 pub flags: i64 pub restorer: i64 pub mask: i64 }

A signal action, as the kernel stores it for each signal. The address of the handler, or 0 for the default and 1 for ignore. The action flags. The address of the code that returns from the handler. The set of signals blocked while the handler runs.
struct Credentials { pub pid: i64 pub uid: i64 pub gid: i64 }
The identity of the process at the other end of a Unix socket. The process id. The user id. The group id.
struct DirEntry { pub name: str pub kind: Kind? }
An entry of a directory as list_dir reports it. The entry's name. The kind of the entry itself, or none when the file system does not record it.
The disposition of a signal that set_disposition installs. The system default for the signal. The signal is ignored.

An owned descriptor that closes itself when dropped. handle is the copyable view for passing the descriptor to other green threads, and detach hands the descriptor over so that dropping the owner leaves it open. The copyable view of the descriptor.

A copyable view of an open descriptor and the guard that coordinates its closing. Copies of an FdHandle refer to the same descriptor. Once any copy is closed, every operation on the view fails with NotConnected, so a closed descriptor is never reached after the kernel reuses its number. Reads and writes park the green thread while the descriptor is non-blocking and not ready. The operating system file descriptor.
enum Kind { Regular Dir Symlink Other }
The kind of a file system object. A regular file. A directory. A symbolic link. Anything else, such as a socket or a device.
The advisory lock lock takes or releases. A lock no other descriptor may share. A lock other shared holders may hold too. Releases the lock this descriptor holds.
enum Open { Read Truncate Append Update Directory Locate Fresh FreshNoFollow ReadWrite Terminal }

How open opens a path. Every mode closes the descriptor on exec. Read only. Write only, creating the file with the given mode or truncating it to zero length. Write only at the end, creating the file with the given mode. Read and write, creating the file with the given mode and keeping its content. Read only, and the path must be a directory. A descriptor that only names the path, usable for readlink of /proc/self/fd/N and for nothing else. Read and write a file that must not exist, created with the given mode. Write only a file that must not exist and is not a symbolic link, created with the given mode. Read and write an existing file or device. Read and write a terminal device without making it the controlling terminal.
struct Pair { pub first: i64 pub second: i64 }
A pair of descriptor numbers made by pipe or socketpair. The read end of a pipe, or the first socket. The write end of a pipe, or the second socket.
struct PtyPair { pub master: i64 pub slave: i64 pub path: str }
The two sides of a pseudoterminal. The descriptor of the master side. The descriptor of the slave side. The device path of the slave side, such as /dev/pts/3.
struct Reaped { pub exited: bool pub value: i64 }
How a child process ended, as reap reports it. Whether the process ended by itself, as opposed to by a signal. The exit status when exited is true, and the signal number otherwise.
struct Received { pub size: i64 pub address: []u8 }
A datagram received by recv_from. The number of bytes written into the buffer. The address of the sender in the system's socket address layout.
The position an offset given to seek is measured from. The beginning of the file. The current position. The end of the file.
Which direction shutdown closes. The sending direction; the peer reads end of input once it has the data sent so far. Both directions; operations waiting on the socket return.
The kind of socket socket makes. A reliable byte stream, as TCP and Unix stream sockets provide. Unreliable datagrams, as UDP provides.

enum SocketOption { ReuseAddr ReusePort KeepAlive ReceiveBuffer SendBuffer NoDelay KeepIdle KeepInterval KeepCount MulticastTtl4 MulticastLoop4 MulticastTtl6 MulticastLoop6 MulticastInterface6 Error }

A socket option with an integer value, for set_option and get_option. Lets a restarted program bind a port still in TIME_WAIT. Lets several sockets bind the same port. Whether keep-alive probes are sent on a TCP connection. The receive buffer size in bytes. The send buffer size in bytes. Whether a TCP connection sends small writes at once. The idle seconds before the first keep-alive probe. The seconds between keep-alive probes. The number of unanswered probes after which a connection is dropped. The time to live of outgoing IPv4 multicast datagrams. Whether outgoing IPv4 multicast datagrams are delivered to this host too. The hop limit of outgoing IPv6 multicast datagrams. Whether outgoing IPv6 multicast datagrams are delivered to this host too. The interface index outgoing IPv6 multicast datagrams leave through. The error number pending on the socket, which reading clears. Read it with get_option; setting it fails.
struct Spawned { pub pid: i64 pub pidfd: FdHandle pub failure: io.Error? }

The outcome of fork_exec. The process id of the child. The process descriptor of the child, which becomes readable when the child ends. The error the child met while changing directory or executing the program, or none when the program started. The child has exited with status 127 when this is set, and the caller must still reap it.
struct Stat { pub kind: Kind pub size: i64 pub mode: i64 pub uid: i64 pub gid: i64 pub device: i64 pub inode: i64 pub accessed: i64 pub modified: i64 }

The attributes of a file as fstat and stat report them. The kind of object. The size in bytes. The permission bits, including setuid, setgid and sticky, without the file type bits. The numeric ID of the owning user. The numeric ID of the owning group. The ID of the device that holds the file. The inode number. The access time in whole seconds since the Unix epoch. The modification time in whole seconds since the Unix epoch.
A snapshot of the settings of a terminal, as termios reads them and set_termios applies them.
struct Usage { pub total: i64 pub free: i64 pub available: i64 pub files: i64 pub files_free: i64 }

The capacity figures of a file system, as statfs reports them. The size of the file system in bytes. The unused space in bytes, including space reserved for the superuser. The unused space in bytes that an unprivileged process can use. The total number of inodes. The number of unused inodes.
struct WindowSize { pub columns: i64 pub rows: i64 }
The dimensions of a terminal window in character cells. The number of columns. The number of rows.
Closes the descriptor owned by f. Does the same as close_on on its handle.
Stops f from closing the descriptor when dropped, and returns its view. The caller must close the descriptor with close_on.
Returns the Fd that owns the descriptor behind h, which closes it when dropped.

Closes the descriptor that h views. Later operations on h or its copies fail with NotConnected. The descriptor is released immediately, or when the last operation in flight returns. Closing twice does nothing.

Registers a use of the descriptor behind h and returns the lease that ends it when dropped. Fails with NotConnected once the descriptor has been closed, so a closed descriptor is never reached. Operations on the descriptor number h.fd that other sys functions perform hold a lease for their duration.
fn read_on(h: FdHandle, buf: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Reads from the descriptor that h views, as read does. Fails with NotConnected when the descriptor has been closed.
Returns an io.Stream over the descriptor that h views. Closing the stream closes the descriptor. The stream is safe to copy and use from other green threads.
Writes all of data to the descriptor that h views, as write_all does. Fails with NotConnected when the descriptor has been closed.
fn write_on(h: FdHandle, data: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Writes to the descriptor that h views, as write does. Fails with NotConnected when the descriptor has been closed.
Returns whether t has line buffering and echo both turned off.

Returns a copy of t in raw mode. Raw mode turns off line buffering, echo, signal-generating keys, flow control and input and output translation, uses 8-bit characters, and makes reads return after one byte.
The path of the device that discards what is written and reads as empty.
The offset in handler_code of the code that returns from the handler.
Takes the next waiting connection from the listening socket fd. Fails with WouldBlock when none is waiting. An interrupted call and a connection reset before it was accepted are skipped.
fn access(path: str, how: Access) -> bool
Returns whether the caller can how the path. Follows symbolic links. Any error gives false.
Returns the command-line arguments the program started with, the program name first.
Binds the socket fd to address, given in the system's socket address layout.
fn bind_device(fd: i64, device: str) ! io.Error
Binds the socket fd to the network interface device.
fn catch_signal(n: i64, handler: i64, restorer: i64) -> Action ! io.Error
Installs the handler at handler for signal number n, which returns through restorer, and returns the action it replaces. The handler runs on the alternate signal stack and interrupted calls restart.
fn change_membership(fd: i64, group: []u8, index: i64, join: bool) ! io.Error
Joins or leaves the multicast group on the UDP socket fd. group is 4 bytes for IPv4 or 16 for IPv6. index is the interface index, or 0 to let the system choose.
Changes the working directory of the whole process to path.
fn chmod(path: str, mode: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the permission bits of the file at path to mode, following symbolic links.
fn chown(path: str, uid: i64, gid: i64, follow: bool) ! io.Error
Sets the owner and group of the file at path. A final symbolic link is followed when follow is true and changed itself otherwise.
Closes the descriptor number fd. A negative number stands for no descriptor and is ignored. Errors from the kernel are ignored, because nothing can be done about a descriptor that failed to close.
fn connect(fd: i64, address: []u8) -> bool ! io.Error

Starts connecting the socket fd to address and returns whether the connection is complete. Returns false while the connection is in progress; wait for fd to become writable and call finish_connect. Fails with WouldBlock when a Unix socket's listener has a full queue, which no later event announces, so the caller tries again.
Returns the number of CPUs the process may run on, according to its affinity mask. Fails with Invalid when the mask is empty and with the system error when it cannot be read.
Returns the environment the program started with, as name=value entries.
Returns the path of the running executable. Reads /proc/self/exe on Linux, which fails with NotFound when /proc is not mounted.
Ends the process at once with the status code, stopping every thread.
Reports how a connection started by connect ended. Fails with the error the connection met, such as Refused.
fn fork_exec(path: str, argv: []str, envp: []str, dir: str, group: bool, stdin: i64, stdout: i64, stderr: i64) -> Spawned ! io.Error

Starts the program at path in a new process and returns once the program has been executed. argv is the whole argument vector, program name first, and envp is the complete environment as name=value entries. A dir that is not empty becomes the working directory of the child. With group the child starts its own process group. stdin, stdout and stderr are descriptors the child receives as standard streams, and a negative one leaves that stream as the parent's. On Linux the parent waits for the child to report on a pipe that closes when the program is executed, so the call parks the green thread until then. Fails with the system error when the pipe or the fork fails, and on Windows when the program cannot be started. On Linux an error of chdir or execve in the child comes back in Spawned.failure; on Windows Spawned.failure is always none.
Returns the attributes of the open descriptor fd.
Flushes the data and metadata of the descriptor fd to the storage device.
fn ftruncate(fd: i64, size: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the size of the file behind fd to size bytes.
fn get_option(fd: i64, option: SocketOption) -> i64 ! io.Error
Returns the integer socket option option of the socket fd.
Returns the absolute path of the current working directory. Fails with NotFound if the directory has been removed and with TooLarge if the path exceeds 1 MiB.

Returns x86-64 machine code for a signal handler that writes the signal number as one byte to the descriptor fd. The code ends with a restorer at restorer_offset that returns from the handler. A negative fd makes the write fail, which turns the handler into a no-op.
Returns the address of the handler installed for signal number n.
Returns the host name of the machine.
fn inotify_add(fd: i64, path: str, mask: i64) -> i64 ! io.Error

Adds path to the inotify instance fd for the events in the bit set mask and returns the watch number. Watching a path that is already watched replaces its mask and returns the same watch number. Fails with NotFound when path does not exist.
Creates an inotify instance and returns its descriptor, which is non-blocking and closed on exec.
fn inotify_remove(fd: i64, wd: i64) ! io.Error
Removes the watch wd from the inotify instance fd.

Returns the kernel index of the network interface name. Fails with Invalid if name is empty or, on Linux, longer than 15 bytes; Windows has no length limit. Fails with NotFound if there is no such interface.
Returns whether the page at address is mapped.
Returns whether the descriptor fd refers to a terminal.
fn kill(pid: i64, signal: i64) ! io.Error
Sends signal number signal to the process pid, or to the process group -pid when pid is negative.
fn link(existing: str, new_path: str) ! io.Error
Creates new_path as a hard link to the file existing.
Returns the entries of the directory path, without . and .., in the order the file system returns them.
fn listen(fd: i64, backlog: i64) ! io.Error
Marks the socket fd as listening with a queue of backlog waiting connections.
Returns the address the socket fd is bound to, in the system's socket address layout.
fn lock(fd: i64, kind: LockKind) -> bool ! io.Error
Takes or releases the advisory lock on the open descriptor fd. Returns false without waiting when another descriptor holds a conflicting lock.
fn map_anonymous_at(address: i64, size: i64) -> i64 ! io.Error

Maps size bytes of zeroed, readable and writable memory at exactly address and returns the address of the mapping. Fails with Exists when something is already mapped there. A kernel that ignores the placement can return another address, which the caller must check and unmap.
Maps size bytes of zeroed memory that can be read, written and executed, and returns its address.
fn mkdir(path: str, mode: i64) ! io.Error
Creates the directory path with permission bits mode, filtered by the process umask.
fn open(path: str, how: Open, mode: i64) -> FdHandle ! io.Error

Opens the file at path as how says and returns a view of the descriptor, which the caller closes. mode gives the permission bits of a file that is created, filtered by the process umask, and is otherwise ignored. An interrupted call is repeated. Fails with NotFound when the path does not exist, Exists for a Fresh mode when it does, and Denied when the caller lacks permission.
Opens a new pseudoterminal and returns its master and slave sides. The caller closes both descriptors. Fails with the system error if /dev/ptmx or the slave device cannot be opened.
Returns an Fd that owns the open descriptor number fd and closes it when dropped.
Returns the absolute path of the open descriptor fd, with every symbolic link resolved.
Returns the process id, user id and group id of the peer of the Unix socket fd, as recorded when the connection was made.
fn pidfd_send_signal(pidfd: i64, signal: i64) ! io.Error
Sends signal number signal to the process behind the process descriptor pidfd.
Returns the read end and the write end of a new pipe, both closed on exec. On Linux the ends are non-blocking when nonblocking is true and blocking otherwise. On Windows they are always blocking.
Returns the process id of the parent.
Sends signal number signal to the calling thread.

Returns n bytes from the operating system's cryptographically secure random generator. Blocks until the kernel pool is initialised. A short or interrupted read is repeated. Fails with the system error when the generator cannot be read.
fn read(fd: i64, buf: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Reads up to buf.len bytes from the descriptor number fd and returns the count, or 0 at end of input. Parks the green thread while fd is non-blocking and has no data. An interrupted read is repeated.
Returns whether the descriptor number fd has data to read or has reached end of input, without waiting.
Returns the target text of the symbolic link path. Fails with Invalid when path is not a symbolic link and TooLarge when the target is 1 MiB or longer.
Waits for the child behind the process descriptor pidfd to end, reaps it and returns how it ended. Blocks the OS thread, so wait for the descriptor to become readable first.
fn recv(fd: i64, buf: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Receives up to buf.len bytes from the socket fd and returns the count, or 0 at end of input. Fails with WouldBlock when nothing has arrived. An interrupted call is repeated.
fn recv_from(fd: i64, buf: []u8) -> Received ! io.Error
Receives one datagram into buf from the socket fd. A datagram longer than buf is truncated. Fails with WouldBlock when nothing has arrived. An interrupted call is repeated.
fn rename(from: str, to: str) ! io.Error
Renames the entry from to to, replacing an existing to.
fn restore_action(n: i64, saved: Action) ! io.Error
Sets the action of signal number n to saved.
Removes the empty directory at path.
fn seek(fd: i64, offset: i64, from: Seek) -> i64 ! io.Error
Moves the position of the descriptor fd by offset bytes relative to from and returns the new position.
fn send(fd: i64, data: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error

Sends a prefix of data on the connected socket fd and returns how many bytes were sent. A peer that has closed the connection gives BrokenPipe or Reset and never raises SIGPIPE. Fails with WouldBlock when the send buffer is full. An interrupted call is repeated.
fn send_to(fd: i64, data: []u8, address: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Sends data as one datagram from the socket fd to address and returns the number of bytes sent. Fails with WouldBlock when the send buffer is full. An interrupted call is repeated.
fn set_disposition(n: i64, how: Disposition) ! io.Error
Sets the disposition of signal number n to how.
fn set_multicast_interface4(fd: i64, index: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the interface IPv4 multicast datagrams from the socket fd leave through to the interface with kernel index index, or to the system's choice when index is 0.
Makes the descriptor number fd non-blocking. On Windows only a socket becomes non-blocking; a pipe or file stays blocking, and a read from it holds an OS thread until it returns.
fn set_option(fd: i64, option: SocketOption, value: i64) ! io.Error
Sets the integer socket option option of the socket fd to value.
fn set_termios(fd: i64, t: Termios, drain: bool) ! io.Error
Applies t to the terminal on fd. With drain set the change waits until pending output has been sent. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
fn set_times(path: str, accessed: i64?, modified: i64?, follow: bool) ! io.Error

Sets the access and modification times of the file at path, in whole seconds since the Unix epoch. A time that is none is left unchanged. A final symbolic link is followed when follow is true and stamped itself otherwise.
fn set_window_size(fd: i64, size: WindowSize) ! io.Error
Sets the size of the terminal on fd to size. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
fn shutdown(fd: i64, how: Shutdown) ! io.Error
Shuts down the socket fd in the direction how.
fn socket(family: i64, kind: SocketKind) -> i64 ! io.Error
Makes a non-blocking socket closed on exec and returns its descriptor. family is the address family number of the addresses the socket will use.
Returns two connected, unnamed stream sockets, non-blocking and closed on exec. They are Unix stream sockets on Linux and a pair of loopback TCP sockets on Windows.
fn stat(path: str, follow: bool) -> Stat ! io.Error
Returns the attributes of the file at path. A final symbolic link is followed when follow is true and described itself otherwise.
Returns the capacity figures of the file system that holds path.
Returns an io.Stream over the descriptor number fd. Closing the stream does nothing; the owner of fd closes it.
fn symlink(target: str, link_path: str) ! io.Error
Creates the symbolic link link_path that holds the text target.
Returns the settings of the terminal on fd. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
fn try_read(fd: i64, buf: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Reads once from the descriptor number fd without waiting. Fails with WouldBlock when fd is non-blocking and has no data. An interrupted read is repeated.
fn try_write(fd: i64, data: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error
Writes once to the descriptor number fd without waiting. Fails with WouldBlock when fd is non-blocking and cannot take output. An interrupted write is repeated.
Sets the file creation mask to mask & 0o777 and returns the previous mask.
Removes the file or symbolic link at path.
Returns the number of seconds the machine has been running.
Parks the green thread until the descriptor number fd may have input or has reached end of input. Can return before input arrives, so the caller reads and waits again.

Parks the green thread until the socket fd may be ready to read, or to write when writable is set. Can return before the socket is ready, and returns when another green thread shuts the socket down, so the caller repeats its operation and waits again.
Returns the size of the terminal on fd. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
Returns a view of the open descriptor fd, which the view's owner closes. A negative fd makes a view whose closing does nothing.
fn wrap_with(fd: i64, wake: fn()) -> FdHandle
Returns a view of the open descriptor fd whose closing first runs wake. wake unblocks operations that are waiting on the descriptor, for example by shutting a socket down.
fn write(fd: i64, data: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error

Writes a prefix of data to the descriptor number fd and returns how many bytes were written, which can be fewer than data.len. Parks the green thread while fd is non-blocking and cannot take more output. An interrupted write is repeated.
Writes all of data to the descriptor number fd, repeating write until nothing remains. Fails with the first error a write returns, after which part of data may have been written.

Returns a second descriptor for the socket fd, closed on exec, that carries writes so a writer waits for buffer space while a reader waits on fd. On Linux it is a duplicate of fd. On Windows it is a duplicate of the socket with its own event. The caller closes it with close_fd.
enum Data { Null Bool(bool) Int(i64) Float(f64) Str(str) Safe(str) List([]Data) Map([str: Data]) }

A value that a template reads: null, a scalar, a list or a map with string keys. Build one with the variants, with list and map, from JSON with from_json, or from any serialisable value with to_data. No value. Outputs nothing, is false in conditions and is what a missing name gives when strict is off. A boolean. Output as true or false. A 64-bit integer. A 64-bit float. Text that is escaped on output according to Options.escape. Text that is already safe and is written unescaped. The raw filter produces it, and upper, lower and trim keep it. A list of values, indexed from 0. A map from string keys to values.
enum Error { Parse(str, i64, i64, str) Render(str, i64, i64, str) NotFound(str, i64, i64, str) TooDeep(str, i64, i64) TooLarge Write(io.Error) }

Why compiling or rendering a template failed. template names the template where the problem is, and line and column count from 1, with the column in bytes. describe formats an error as one line. The template source is not valid: an unclosed tag, an unknown or unbalanced statement, or a bad expression. message says which. Rendering failed: a value has the wrong type for an operation or a filter, an unknown filter is used, or, with Options.strict, a name, key or index is missing. message says which. An include, extends or render names a template that is not in the Set. name is the missing template. line and column are 0 when the name came directly from render or render_to. The include and extends chain is deeper than Options.max_depth. The output would be longer than Options.max_output bytes. Writing to the stream given to render_to failed with cause.

How the value of an {{ expression }} is escaped before it is written. Escapes &, <, >, " and ' as HTML entities. A Data.Safe value and the output of the raw filter are written unchanged. Writes values as they are.
Why a filter registered with add_filter rejected its input. The filter cannot work with its subject or arguments. message is reported in a Render error as filter name: message.
struct Options { pub escape: Escape pub strict: bool pub max_depth: i64 pub max_output: i64 }

Settings of a Set. How values are escaped on output. Defaults to Html. Whether a missing value is an error. When true, an undefined variable, a missing map key or list index, and a member read of null fail with Error.Render. When false, the default, they give null. The subject of the default filter is always lenient. The deepest nesting of include and extends allowed. Defaults to 32. The most output a single render may produce, in bytes. Defaults to 16 MiB.

A collection of named templates and filters that render together. A Set is only read while rendering, so green threads may share one once it is built. include and extends look templates up by name in the same Set.
Returns e as a one-line message, template:line:column: message. A NotFound for a name given to render has no position and reads template NAME not found.
Returns an empty Set with options.
fn add(mut s: Set, name: str, source: str) ! Error
Compiles source and adds it to s under name, replacing any template of that name. Fails with Error.Parse when the source is not a valid template.
fn add_filter(mut s: Set, name: str, f: fn(Data, []Data) -> Data ! FilterError)

Registers the filter function f under name for use as value | name(arguments). f receives the subject and the argument list. It takes precedence over a built-in filter of the same name, and a FilterError it returns becomes an Error.Render.
fn has(s: Set, name: str) -> bool
Returns whether s has a template named name.
fn render(s: Set, name: str, data: Data) -> str ! Error

Renders the template name of s with data and returns the output. data is the root scope: names in the template are looked up in it when it is a Data.Map. Fails with NotFound when name is not in s, and with Render, TooDeep or TooLarge while rendering.
fn render_to(s: Set, name: str, data: Data, out: io.Stream) ! Error

Renders the template name of s with data and writes the output to out. Output is written in chunks as it is produced, so part of it may already be written when an error is returned. Fails as render does and with Write when out fails.
fn compile(name: str, source: str) -> Template ! Error

Compiles source into a Template named name without adding it to a Set. name is used in the errors. Fails with Error.Parse for a syntax error such as an unclosed tag, an unbalanced if, for or block, a repeated extends or block name, or nesting deeper than 100 levels.
Parses the JSON text source into Data. Objects become Map, arrays List and numbers Int or Float. Fails with a serde.Error when source is not valid JSON.
Returns the Data list of items.
Returns the Data map of entries.
fn render_source(source: str, data: Data) -> str ! Error
Compiles source and renders it once with data, with default Options.

Converts any serialisable value v into Data. Structs and maps become Map, sequences become List, an enum variant without a payload becomes the Str of its name and one with a payload becomes a Map with the variant name as its only key. Byte strings become base64 Str and an unsigned integer above the i64 range becomes a Float.

enum Colour { Black = 0 Red = 1 Green = 2 Yellow = 3 Blue = 4 Magenta = 5 Cyan = 6 White = 7 BrightBlack = 8 BrightRed = 9 BrightGreen = 10 BrightYellow = 11 BrightBlue = 12 BrightMagenta = 13 BrightCyan = 14 BrightWhite = 15 Indexed(u8) = -1 Rgb(u8, u8, u8) = -1 }

A terminal colour for fg and bg. Standard black. Standard red. Standard green. Standard yellow. Standard blue. Standard magenta. Standard cyan. Standard white. Bright black, usually shown as grey. Bright red. Bright green. Bright yellow. Bright blue. Bright magenta. Bright cyan. Bright white. An entry n of the 256-colour palette. A 24-bit colour with the given red, green and blue levels.
enum Key { Char(u32) Ctrl(u32) Alt(u32) Function(i64) Enter Tab BackTab Backspace Escape Up Down Left Right Home End PageUp PageDown Insert Delete Unknown }

A key press decoded from terminal input. A printable character, given as its code point. A control combination. c is the lowercase letter, so Ctrl+A is Ctrl('a'); Ctrl+Space is Ctrl(' '), and the codes 28 to 31 give \, ], ^ and _. Alt with a key, reported as an escape followed by one byte c. A function key, n from 1 to 12. The Enter key, sent as carriage return or line feed. The Tab key. Shift+Tab. The Backspace key, sent as byte 8 or 127. The Escape key, a lone escape byte with nothing following within the timeout. The up arrow. The down arrow. The left arrow. The right arrow. The Home key. The End key. The Page Up key. The Page Down key. The Insert key. The Delete key. An escape sequence that is not recognised or was cut short.
The owner of a pseudoterminal pair. Dropping it closes both descriptors. The copyable view of the pseudoterminal.
struct PtyHandle { pub master: i64 pub slave: i64 pub path: str ... }
A copyable view of a pseudoterminal pair, used to close it. The descriptor of the master side. The descriptor of the slave side. The device path of the slave side, such as /dev/pts/3.
The owner of a terminal that was put in raw mode. Dropping it restores the saved terminal settings. The copyable view of the raw terminal.
A copyable view of a terminal in raw mode, used to restore it. The descriptor of the terminal.
struct Size { pub columns: i64 pub rows: i64 }
The dimensions of a terminal window in character cells. The number of columns. The number of rows.
fn bg(c: Colour, s: str) -> str
Returns s wrapped in the escape sequences that set the background colour to c and then back to the default.
fn fg(c: Colour, s: str) -> str
Returns s wrapped in the escape sequences that set the foreground colour to c and then back to the default.
Closes both sides of the pseudoterminal owned by p. Does the same as close_pty_on on its handle.
Closes both sides of the pseudoterminal behind h. Later calls do nothing.
Restores the terminal settings saved by enter_raw. Does the same as restore_on on its handle.
Restores the terminal settings saved by enter_raw, after pending output has been sent. Later calls do nothing, and a failure to restore is ignored.
Returns s wrapped in the escape sequences that turn bold on and off.
Returns the escape sequence that erases the whole current line without moving the cursor.
Returns the escape sequences that erase the whole screen and move the cursor to the top left corner.
Returns the escape sequence that erases from the cursor to the end of the line.

Returns whether coloured output is appropriate for the descriptor fd. NO_COLOR set to a non-empty value turns colour off. Otherwise CLICOLOR_FORCE set to a non-empty value other than 0 turns it on, TERM=dumb turns it off, and the answer is then whether fd is a terminal.
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor left n columns, or an empty string if n is less than 1.
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor to the 1-based column on the current row.
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor down n rows, or an empty string if n is less than 1.
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor right n columns, or an empty string if n is less than 1.
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor to the top left corner.
fn cursor_to(row: i64, column: i64) -> str
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor to the 1-based row and column.
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor up n rows, or an empty string if n is less than 1.
Returns s wrapped in the escape sequences that turn dim on and off.
Returns the escape sequence that switches to the alternate screen buffer.

Puts the terminal on fd in raw mode and returns the owner that restores it. Raw mode turns off line buffering, echo, signal-generating keys, flow control and input and output translation, uses 8-bit characters, and makes reads return after one byte. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
Returns the escape sequence that hides the cursor.
Returns whether the terminal on fd has line buffering and echo both turned off. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
Returns whether the descriptor fd refers to a terminal.
Returns the escape sequence that switches back to the main screen buffer.
Opens a new pseudoterminal and returns its master and slave sides. Fails with the system error if /dev/ptmx or the slave device cannot be opened.

Decodes the key presses in data, which holds bytes already read from a terminal. Does not wait: a sequence cut short by the end of data gives Unknown, and a lone escape byte at the end gives Escape. Never fails.
Reads one key press from the descriptor fd, waiting 50 milliseconds after an escape byte to tell an Escape key from a longer sequence. Does the same as read_key_with with that timeout.
fn read_key_with(fd: i64, escape_ms: i64) -> Key ! io.Error

Reads one key press from the descriptor fd. Parks the green thread until the first byte arrives. After an escape byte, and while it reads the rest of a sequence, it waits at most escape_ms milliseconds for each following byte and reports Escape when none comes. A multi-byte UTF-8 character is decoded to Char, and a malformed one gives Char(0xFFFD). The terminal should be in raw mode, or input arrives only after Enter. Fails with Eof at end of input and with the system error otherwise.
Returns the escape sequence that turns off every text attribute and colour.
Returns the escape sequence that moves the cursor to the position saved by save_cursor.
Returns the escape sequence that saves the cursor position.
fn set_size(fd: i64, s: Size) ! io.Error
Sets the size of the terminal on fd to s. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
Returns the escape sequence that shows the cursor.
Returns the size of the terminal on fd. Fails with Unsupported if fd is not a terminal.
Returns s without its escape sequences. Removes CSI sequences such as colours and cursor movement, string sequences ended by BEL or ESC \, and other short escapes. Text outside escapes is kept.
Returns s wrapped in the escape sequences that turn underline on and off.
Returns the number of Unicode code points in s once its escape sequences are removed. Wide and combining characters are counted as one each.
fn write_all(fd: i64, s: str) ! io.Error
Writes all of s to the descriptor fd. Parks the green thread while fd is non-blocking and cannot take more output. Fails with the system error if a write fails.
struct Bench { pub name: str pub iterations: i64 pub nanos: i64 pub ns_per_op: f64 }

The result of a benchmark. The benchmark name. The number of iterations the measured run made. The time the measured run took, in nanoseconds. The mean time of one iteration, in nanoseconds: nanos divided by iterations.
struct Settings { pub filter: str pub verbose: bool pub timing: bool pub timeout_ms: i64 pub golden_dir: str pub update_golden: bool }

Options for a test run. settings_from builds one from command-line flags. Every field has a default, so Settings {} is valid. Selects the tests to run through selected: the text a test name must contain, with / separating the levels of subtest names. The empty default selects every test. Whether to report every test, passing and skipped included, instead of only the failures. The default is false. Whether the reports carry elapsed times. The default is true. The number of milliseconds a test, or a subtest, may run before it is failed as hung. The default is 30000. The directory that golden reads and writes its files in. The default is testdata. Whether golden rewrites its files instead of comparing them. The default is false.

The state of one running test or subtest, passed to its body as a *T. Records, assertions and subtests all go through it. The recording functions are safe to call from several green threads at once. The test's full name: the name of a top-level test, or its parent's name and the subtest names joined with /.
struct Test { pub name: str pub run: fn(*T) }
A named test for run and run_with. The test name, which -run filters on. The test body. It runs on its own green thread and receives the T that records its result.
Returns a one-line report of b: its name, its iteration count and its time per iteration in nanoseconds with two decimals.
fn check_ints(t: *T, runs: i64, seed: u64, low: i64, high: i64, prop: fn(i64) -> bool) -> bool

Checks that prop holds for runs integers drawn uniformly from low through high, both inclusive. Seeding and the error are those of check_shrunk. Failing inputs are shrunk with shrink_int, keeping only candidates within the range.
fn check_property[V](t: *T, runs: i64, seed: u64, gen: fn(mut rand.Rng) -> V, prop: fn(V) -> bool) -> bool

Checks that prop holds for runs inputs made by gen. gen draws each input from the random generator. A seed of 0 picks one from the clock. The first failing input stops the check: the error records the run number, the seed, which reproduces the failure, and the input. Returns true when every run passes. The input is not shrunk; see check_shrunk.
fn check_shrunk[V](t: *T, runs: i64, seed: u64, gen: fn(mut rand.Rng) -> V, prop: fn(V) -> bool, shrink: fn(V) -> []V) -> bool

Checks that prop holds for runs inputs made by gen, and shrinks a failing input. Behaves like check_property, and the error also shows the smallest failing input found. After a failure, shrink lists simpler candidates for the current input; the first candidate that still fails replaces it, and this repeats until no candidate fails or 10000 rounds have passed.
fn close_to(t: *T, got: f64, want: f64, tolerance: f64) -> bool
Checks that got is within tolerance of want. Passes when the absolute difference is at most tolerance. A got or want that is not a number never passes.
fn contains(t: *T, whole: str, part: str) -> bool
Checks that the text part occurs in whole. An empty part is always found.
fn contains_item[V: Eq](t: *T, items: []V, item: V) -> bool
Checks that items has an element equal to item.
fn equal[V: Eq](t: *T, got: V, want: V) -> bool

Checks that got equals want. Returns true when they are equal. Otherwise records an error that shows both values rendered with format and returns false; the test keeps running. Every assertion in this module reports the same way.
fn equal_slice[V: Eq](t: *T, got: []V, want: []V) -> bool

Checks that the slices got and want have the same length and equal elements. Returns true when they do. Otherwise records an error that shows both slices and either the index of the first differing element or the two lengths, and returns false.
Records message on t and marks the test failed. The test body keeps running, so later checks still report.
fn error_if(t: *T, condition: bool, message: str) -> bool
Calls error with message when condition is true. Returns condition, so the result is true when a failure was recorded.
fn expect_error[E: Eq, V](t: *T, e: E, want: E, fallback: V) -> V

Checks that the error e equals want and returns fallback. Meant for the handler of a catch around a call that is expected to fail. Records an error that shows both when they differ. The test keeps running.
Returns true when t has recorded a failure. A failed subtest also fails its parent, and a timeout counts as a failure.
Records message on t, marks the test failed and ends it. The calling green thread never continues after this call.
fn fatal_if(t: *T, condition: bool, message: str)
Calls fatal with message when condition is true.
fn golden(t: *T, name: str, actual: str) -> bool

Checks actual against the golden file name in the directory Settings.golden_dir of t. The file is name with .golden appended. See golden_in; the files are rewritten when Settings.update_golden is true, which the -update flag sets.
fn golden_in(t: *T, dir: str, name: str, actual: str, update: bool) -> bool

Checks actual against the file dir/name.golden, or rewrites that file when update is true. When updating, creates the directory if needed, writes actual and returns true; an error creating or writing is recorded on t and gives false. Otherwise returns true when the file's text equals actual. A file that cannot be read, such as a missing one, and a difference are both recorded as errors that name -update, and the difference shows the first line that differs, or the two line counts.
Checks that the optional value is none. The recorded error shows the value that was found.
Checks that the optional value holds a value.
Records message on t without failing the test. The run prints the notes of a test that fails, or of every test with -v.
fn must[E, V](t: *T, e: E, fallback: V) -> V
Records e as an unexpected error, ends the test and never returns fallback. Meant for the handler of a catch like unexpected, but stops the test as fatal does.
fn not_equal[V: Eq](t: *T, got: V, other: V) -> bool
Checks that got and other differ. Returns true when they are not equal, and otherwise records an error that shows the value and returns false.

Ends the test when ok is false, without recording a failure. The calling green thread never continues in that case. Use it to stop after a check that already reported through error or an assertion, when the rest of the test cannot run.

Records reason on t, marks the test skipped and ends it. The calling green thread never continues after this call. A skipped test is reported as SKIP with -v and is counted apart from passes and failures, unless it also recorded a failure.
fn sub(t: *T, name: str, body: fn(*T)) -> bool

Runs body as a subtest of t named name, and waits for it to finish. The subtest's full name is t.name and name joined with /. It has its own green thread and timeout. It is not run when the run's filter does not select its full name, which counts as a pass. A subtest that fails also fails t. Returns true when the subtest recorded no failure.
fn table[C](t: *T, cases: [str: C], body: fn(*T, C)) -> bool
Runs body as a subtest of t for each entry of cases, named by its key. Cases run in the map's insertion order. Returns true when every subtest passed. See sub.
fn table_of[C](t: *T, cases: []C, name: fn(C) -> str, body: fn(*T, C)) -> bool
Runs body as a subtest of t for each element of cases, named by name applied to the element. Cases run in order. Returns true when every subtest passed. See sub.
fn unexpected[E, V](t: *T, e: E, fallback: V) -> V

Records e as an unexpected error and returns fallback. Meant for the handler of a catch, where the expression still needs a value of the right type: parse(text) catch { e => testing.unexpected(t, e, 0) }. The test keeps running.
fn bench(name: str, body: fn(i64)) -> Bench
Benchmarks body for about one second, prints the result line and returns it. This is bench_for with a target of 1000 milliseconds followed by printing describe of the result.
fn bench_for(name: str, body: fn(i64), target_ms: i64) -> Bench

Benchmarks body until one run takes at least target_ms milliseconds, and returns that run. body(n) must do the measured work n times. It is first called with 1, then with a larger n estimated from the previous run, growing at most 100 times per step, until a run reaches the target or n reaches one billion. Only the last run is reported. Nothing is printed.
Consumes value so a benchmarked computation is not optimised away. It does nothing observable, apart from printing a fixed word when value converts to one specific unlikely integer.
Consumes value so a benchmarked computation is not optimised away. It uses the length of value and its last byte.

Returns a readable rendering of v for test messages, for a value of any type. Structs print as Name{field: value}, slices as [a, b], maps as {key: value}, a variant with positional fields as Name(a, b), one with labelled fields as Name{label: value} and one without fields as its name.
