Text, including map keys and a top-level str, is quoted with ", \, newline and tab escaped, and []u8 is 0x and hex digits. An absent optional is none and a present one is its value. A pointer renders its target, and a pointer reached again while it is being rendered is <cycle>. Integers and floats use their default text. The rules are those of print for a value nested in a composite.

Runs tests using the flags in the process arguments and returns the number of failed tests. Reads the flags with settings_from after the program name. A bad flag prints the usage and exits with status 2. Otherwise it runs the tests as run_with does and exits with status 1 when any test failed; it returns only when none did.

Runs each test of tests selected by settings.filter and returns the number of failed tests. Each test runs on its own green thread and is failed when it exceeds settings.timeout_ms. It prints a report for each failed test, or each test with settings.verbose, then a final line with the verdict and the counts of failed, passed and skipped tests. It does not exit the process.
fn selected(filter: str, name: str) -> bool

Returns true when the test name is selected by filter. An empty filter selects every name. Otherwise the filter and the name are split at /, and each level of the name must contain the filter's text at the same level. Levels of the name beyond the filter's depth match anything, and so does a name with fewer levels than the filter, so a top-level test is selected while its first level matches and its subtests are then filtered by the remaining levels.

Builds Settings from command-line flag arguments. Reads -run for the filter, -v for verbose output, -notime to leave timings out, -update to rewrite golden files and -timeout for the milliseconds a test may take. Fails with the flag.Error for an unknown flag, a flag without its value, or a -timeout that is not an integer.

Returns candidate smaller values for shrinking the integer n. Zero has none. Any other value yields 0, and for a negative n also its absolute value, then n / 2 and n + 1; for a positive n it yields n / 2 and n - 1.
struct Cut { pub before: str pub after: str pub found: bool }

The result of splitting a string once at a separator. The text before the separator, or the whole input when the separator was not found. The text after the separator, or an empty string when the separator was not found. Whether the separator was found.
Why parsing a number, boolean or hex string failed. The input is empty. A byte is not a valid digit. at is its index in the input. The value does not fit in the integer type being parsed.
struct Position { pub line: i64 pub column: i64 }
A place in a text, counted from 1. The line, which a \n ends. The byte offset from the start of the line, plus 1.

Why unquoting a string failed. The input does not start and end with a double quote, or has an unescaped double quote between them. An escape sequence is unknown, incomplete or has a non-hex digit. at is the index of the backslash, or of the bad digit. A \u or \U escape names a surrogate or a value above 0x10FFFF. at is the index of the backslash.
Appends the bytes of s to out.
Appends the UTF-8 encoding of the code point c to out. The value is not validated: surrogates are encoded as they stand, and a value above 0x1FFFFF gives a malformed sequence.
fn append_hex(mut out: []u8, n: i64, width: i64, upper: bool)
Appends the low width hexadecimal digits of n to out, padded with leading zeros. upper selects A to F over a to f. n must not be negative.
Returns the number of code points in s. A byte that is not part of a valid UTF-8 sequence counts as one.
Returns the number of bytes the UTF-8 encoding of c takes, from 1 to 4. The value is not validated: a surrogate takes 3 bytes and a value from 0x10000 up takes 4.
Returns the code points of s as one-character strings. A byte that is not part of a valid UTF-8 sequence becomes a piece of its own. The pieces are slices of s.
fn contains(s: str, sub: str) -> bool
Returns whether sub occurs in s. An empty sub always occurs.
fn count(s: str, sub: str) -> i64
Returns the number of non-overlapping occurrences of sub in s. An empty sub counts the positions between code points, which is char_count(s) + 1.
fn cut(s: str, sep: str) -> Cut
Splits s at the first occurrence of sep. When sep is not found the result has before set to s, an empty after and found set to false. An empty sep is found at index 0. Both parts are slices of s.

Decodes a hexadecimal string into bytes, accepting upper- and lowercase digits. Fails with BadDigit at the index of the start of the first pair that holds a non-hex digit, and at s.len when the length is odd. An empty string gives empty data.
fn digit(c: u8, base: i64) -> i64
Returns the value of the digit byte c in base, 2 to 36, where 0 to 9 then a to z and A to Z count from 0 and 10, or -1 when c is not a digit of base.
Returns the lowercase digit byte for the value d, 0 to 9 and then a to z. d must be 0 to 35.
fn edit_distance(a: str, b: str) -> i64
Returns the Levenshtein distance between a and b over code points. Insertion, deletion and substitution of one code point each cost 1. Time is proportional to the product of the two lengths.
Returns the bytes of data as lowercase hexadecimal, two digits per byte.
fn ends_with(s: str, suffix: str) -> bool
Returns whether s ends with suffix. An empty suffix always matches.
fn equal_fold(a: str, b: str) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are equal when ASCII letters are compared without regard to case. Other bytes must match exactly. Allocates nothing.
Splits s around runs of ASCII whitespace, as defined by space, and returns the non-empty pieces. An empty or all-whitespace s gives an empty slice.
fn fixed(x: f64, places: i64) -> str

Returns x as a decimal string with exactly places digits after the decimal point. The digits come from the exact binary value of x and are rounded half to even, so fixed(0.125, 2) gives 0.12 and fixed(2.5, 0) gives 2. The result has no point when places is 0. The sign is kept when the rounded value is zero, so a small negative number gives -0.00. Returns NaN, inf or -inf for those values.
Returns the IEEE 754 binary32 bit pattern of v.
Returns the f32 with the IEEE 754 binary32 bit pattern bits.
Returns the IEEE 754 binary64 bit pattern of v.

Returns x as decimal text that reads back as a float, which always has a . or an exponent. A finite x that prints as an integer gets .0 before any exponent, so 2 is 2.0 and 1e+30 is 1.0e+30. An infinity or a NaN prints as inf, -inf or NaN.
Returns x as the diagnostic text of CBOR, MessagePack and BSON: NaN, Infinity or -Infinity when not finite, and otherwise float_decimal.
Returns the f64 with the IEEE 754 binary64 bit pattern bits.
Returns the UTF-8 encoding of the code point c as a string.
fn has_token(list: str, token: str) -> bool
Returns whether the comma-separated list contains token. Each item is trimmed of ASCII whitespace and compared without regard to ASCII case, as for the value of an HTTP header such as Connection.
Returns the lowercase hexadecimal form of the 64 bits of n, without prefix or leading zeros. A negative n gives its sixteen-digit two's complement form. 0 gives 0.
Returns the value 0 to 15 of the hexadecimal digit byte c, accepting both cases, or -1 when c is not a hexadecimal digit.
fn index(s: str, sub: str) -> i64
Returns the byte index of the first occurrence of sub in s, or -1 when it is absent. An empty sub is found at index 0.
fn index_byte(s: str, c: u8) -> i64
Returns the index of the first byte c in s, or -1 when it is absent.
Returns whether every byte of s is below 0x80. An empty string is ASCII.
Returns whether s is not empty and holds only the ASCII digits 0 to 9.
Returns whether c is a Unicode scalar value: not a surrogate and not above 0x10FFFF.
Returns the strings in parts joined with sep between them. An empty parts gives an empty string.
fn last_cut(s: str, sep: str) -> Cut
Splits s at the last occurrence of sep. When sep is not found the result has before set to s, an empty after and found set to false. An empty sep is found at the end of s. Both parts are slices of s.
fn last_index(s: str, sub: str) -> i64
Returns the byte index of the last occurrence of sub in s, or -1 when it is absent. An empty sub is found at index s.len.
fn last_index_byte(s: str, c: u8) -> i64
Returns the index of the last byte c in s, or -1 when it is absent.
Returns the length in bytes of the UTF-8 sequence that begins with the byte lead, from 1 to 4. An ASCII byte or a continuation byte gives 1.

Splits s into lines at 
 and removes a  before each 
. A final line without a newline is included, but an empty piece after a trailing newline is not, so a
 gives one line. A  that ends the last line is also removed. Empty lines in the middle are kept.
Returns s with ASCII letters lowercased. Other bytes, including non-ASCII UTF-8, are unchanged. Returns s itself when no byte changes. For full Unicode case mapping use std/unicode.
Returns the ASCII lowercase form of c, or c when it is not A to Z.
fn pad_left(s: str, width: i64, fill: u32) -> str
Returns s padded on the left with the code point fill until it is width code points wide. Widths count code points, not bytes or display columns. A string already width or wider is returned as it is.
fn pad_right(s: str, width: i64, fill: u32) -> str

Returns s padded on the right with the code point fill until it is width code points wide. Widths count code points, not bytes or display columns. A string already width or wider is returned as it is.
Parses true or false. Fails with Empty for an empty string and with BadDigit at index 0 for anything else, including True and 1.

Parses a decimal floating-point number and returns the nearest f64. The form is an optional + or -, digits with an optional ., and an optional exponent e or E with its own sign, as in -12.5e-3, .5 and 5.. inf, infinity and nan are accepted in any case after the optional sign. Underscores, whitespace, prefixes and hexadecimal forms are not. The result is correctly rounded for any number of digits. A value beyond the f64 range gives infinity and one below it gives zero, neither is an error. Fails with Empty for an empty string and with BadDigit at the first byte that does not fit the form, or at the end of the text when digits are missing.
fn parse_hex_at(s: str, at: i64, width: i64) -> i64 ! ParseError

Parses width hexadecimal digits of either case that start at index at of s and returns their value. width is 1 to 15. Fails with BadDigit at the index of the first byte that is not a hexadecimal digit, or at s.len when the digits run past the end of s.
Parses a signed decimal integer. Behaves as parse_radix with base 10.
fn parse_radix(s: str, base: i64) -> i64 ! ParseError

Parses a signed integer written in base. A single leading - or + is accepted and base is 2 to 36. The smallest i64 parses. Fails with Empty for an empty string, with BadDigit at the first byte that is not a digit (a lone sign fails at index 1), and with Overflow when the value does not fit in an i64.
fn parse_u64(s: str, base: i64) -> u64 ! ParseError

Parses an unsigned integer written in base and returns it as a u64. base is 2 to 36 and letters of either case give the digits from 10. No sign, prefix, underscore or whitespace is accepted. Fails with Empty for an empty string, BadDigit at the first byte that is not a digit of base, and Overflow when the value exceeds the largest u64.
fn parse_uint(s: str, base: i64) -> i64 ! ParseError

Parses an unsigned integer written in base and returns it as an i64. base is 2 to 36 and letters of either case give the digits from 10. No sign, prefix, underscore or whitespace is accepted. Fails with Empty for an empty string, BadDigit at the first byte that is not a digit of base, and Overflow when the value exceeds the largest i64.
fn position(s: str, at: i64) -> Position
Returns the line and column of the byte offset at in s. An offset beyond the end of s is taken as the end.
fn put_char(out: []u8, at: i64, c: u32)
Writes the UTF-8 encoding of the code point c into out starting at index at. out must hold char_len(c) bytes from at. The value is not validated, as for append_char.

Returns s as a double-quoted literal. " and \ are backslash-escaped, newline, tab and carriage return become \n, \t and \r, and other control bytes below 0x20 and 0x7F become \xNN. Valid multi-byte UTF-8 is kept as it is and a byte that is not part of a valid sequence becomes \xNN, so unquote restores the original bytes.

Returns s as a double-quoted literal that is printable ASCII. " and \ are backslash-escaped and every character outside 0x20 to 0x7E is written as \uXXXX in lowercase hexadecimal, with a surrogate pair for a character above U+FFFF.
fn radix(n: i64, base: i64) -> str
Returns n written in base using lowercase digits, with a leading - when negative. base is 2 to 36. 0 gives 0.
fn repeat(s: str, n: i64) -> str
Returns s repeated n times. n of 0 or below gives an empty string.
fn replace(s: str, old: str, new: str) -> str
Returns s with every non-overlapping occurrence of old replaced by new. Returns s unchanged when old is empty.
Returns s with its code points in reverse order. Combining marks and other grapheme clusters are not kept together. A byte that is not part of a valid UTF-8 sequence is moved as a unit of its own.
Returns whether c is ASCII whitespace: space, tab, carriage return or newline. Vertical tab and form feed are not included.

Splits s at every byte equal to sep and returns the pieces. Always returns at least one piece: an empty s gives one empty string, and adjacent separators give empty pieces. The separator is not included. The pieces are slices of s.
fn split_n(s: str, sep: str, n: i64) -> []str

Splits s around sep into at most n pieces. The last piece holds the unsplit rest of s. n of 0 gives an empty slice and a negative n splits at every occurrence. An empty sep splits into code points, with the last piece holding the rest.
Splits s at every non-overlapping occurrence of sep and returns the pieces. Behaves as split for a string separator. An empty sep splits s into its code points, as chars does.
fn starts_with(s: str, prefix: str) -> bool
Returns whether s begins with prefix. An empty prefix always matches.
fn starts_with_fold(s: str, prefix: str) -> bool
Returns whether s begins with prefix, comparing ASCII letters without regard to case. Allocates nothing.
fn strip_prefix(s: str, prefix: str) -> str?
Returns s without its leading prefix, or none when s does not begin with it.
fn strip_suffix(s: str, suffix: str) -> str?
Returns s without its trailing suffix, or none when s does not end with it.

Returns s with the first letter of each word uppercased. A word starts after any byte that is not an ASCII letter, a digit, ' or part of a multi-byte character, so o'neil gives O'neil and a-b gives A-B. Only ASCII letters change, and the other letters of a word are left as they are, not lowercased.
Returns the number of backslashes that end s, as a line continuation counts them: an odd number escapes the line break.
Returns s without leading and trailing ASCII whitespace, as defined by space.
Returns s without trailing ASCII whitespace, as defined by space.
fn trim_prefix(s: str, prefix: str) -> str
Returns s without a leading prefix, or s unchanged when it does not begin with it. Only one occurrence is removed.
Returns s without leading ASCII whitespace, as defined by space.
fn trim_suffix(s: str, suffix: str) -> str
Returns s without a trailing suffix, or s unchanged when it does not end with it. Only one occurrence is removed.

Parses a double-quoted literal and returns the string it denotes. The escapes are \n, \t, \r, \a, \b, \f, \v, \\, \", \', \xNN for one byte, \uNNNN and \UNNNNNNNN for a code point. All other bytes are copied as they stand. Fails with NotQuoted when the quotes are missing or a bare " occurs inside, with BadEscape for an unknown or truncated escape, and with BadCodePoint for a \u or \U escape that is a surrogate or above 0x10FFFF.
Returns s with ASCII letters uppercased. Other bytes, including non-ASCII UTF-8, are unchanged. Returns s itself when no byte changes. For full Unicode case mapping use std/unicode.
Returns the ASCII uppercase form of c, or c when it is not a to z.
fn wrap(s: str, width: i64) -> str

Wraps s so that no line is wider than width code points where possible. Each line of s is wrapped on its own: words are separated by ASCII whitespace, runs of whitespace become a single space, and leading and trailing whitespace is dropped. A word wider than width stays whole on a line of its own. Empty lines are kept. The lines are joined with \n with no trailing newline.
struct Edit { pub op: Op pub old_at: i64 pub new_at: i64 }

One step of an edit script. What the step does. The index in the old sequence: of the element for Equal and Delete, and the position where an Insert happens. The index in the new sequence: of the element for Equal and Insert, and the position where a Delete happens.
struct Hunk { pub old_start: i64 pub old_count: i64 pub new_start: i64 pub new_count: i64 pub edits: []Edit }

A group of nearby changes with their surrounding context lines, as one @@ section of a unified diff. The zero-based index in the old text of the hunk's first line. The number of old lines the hunk covers: its Equal and Delete edits. The zero-based index in the new text of the hunk's first line. The number of new lines the hunk covers: its Equal and Insert edits. The edits of the hunk, including its context.

What an Edit does to turn the old sequence into the new one. The element is in both sequences and is kept. The element is in the new sequence only and is added. The element is in the old sequence only and is removed.

Why a patch could not be applied. The patch is not a valid unified diff. line is the line of the patch where the problem was found, counting from 1. A hunk's context and removed lines were not found in the text. hunk is the number of the hunk, counting from 1.
struct Span { pub op: Op pub text: str }
A run of text in an inline diff, all inserted, all deleted or unchanged. Whether the text is unchanged, deleted or inserted. The text of the run.
struct Stats { pub added: i64 pub removed: i64 pub unchanged: i64 }
Counts of the edits in a script, as stats_of returns them. The number of Insert edits. The number of Delete edits. The number of Equal edits.

Returns the @@ -a,b +c,d @@ header line of h, without a newline. Line numbers count from 1. A range of one line omits the count, and a range of no lines is written with the line before it and a count of 0.
Returns the edit script that turns before into after, with elements compared by ==. The script has the properties described for diff_by.
fn diff_by[T](before: []T, after: []T, same: fn(T, T) -> bool) -> []Edit

Returns the edit script that turns before into after, with elements compared by same. The script is minimal in the number of insertions and deletions, found by Myers' algorithm in linear space. It walks both sequences in order and has one Equal, Insert or Delete for every element, with the deletions of a changed region before its insertions. Two empty sequences give an empty script.
Returns the line-level edit script that turns before into after. Lines are split with lines, so a line that differs only in its missing final newline counts as changed.
Returns the edit script that turns the rows before into the rows after. Rows are compared as whole strings.
Returns the number of insertions and deletions in edits.

Groups edits into hunks with context unchanged edits around each change. Changes closer than twice context edits share one hunk. A negative context counts as 0. A script with no changes gives no hunks.

Returns a word-level diff of before and after as a list of spans. Neighbouring tokens with the same operation, as split by words, are merged into one span. Unchanged and deleted text comes from before and inserted text from after.
Returns a diff of before and after over grapheme clusters as a list of spans. Spans are merged as for inline.
Renders spans with deleted text as [-deleted-] and inserted text as {+inserted+}.
fn inline_with(spans: []Span, delete_open: str, delete_close: str, insert_open: str, insert_close: str) -> str
Renders spans as a single string, wrapping each deleted span in delete_open and delete_close and each inserted span in insert_open and insert_close. Unchanged text is copied as it is.
Splits s into lines that keep their \n terminators. The last line has no terminator when s does not end in a newline, and an empty s gives no lines. Joining the lines gives s back.
fn patch(before: str, patch_text: str) -> str ! PatchError
Applies a unified diff to before and returns the result. Behaves as patch_within with a window of 1000 lines.
fn patch_within(before: str, patch_text: str, window: i64) -> str ! PatchError

Applies a unified diff to before and returns the result, searching up to window lines from where each hunk is expected. Lines before the first @@ header, such as --- and +++, are ignored. A hunk is expected where the previous hunk's shift leaves its stated start and is searched for outward in both directions, never before the end of the previous hunk, and its context and removed lines must match exactly. \ No newline at end of file markers are honoured. Fails with Malformed when a header or hunk line cannot be read or a hunk has fewer lines than it declares, and with Mismatch when a hunk is not found within window lines.
fn render(before: []str, after: []str, edits: []Edit, context: i64, before_name: str, after_name: str) -> str

Renders edits as a unified diff, with --- and +++ lines naming before_name and after_name. before and after are the line lists the edits were computed from, as lines returns them, and context is the number of unchanged lines kept around each change. A line without a newline is followed by \ No newline at end of file. Returns an empty string when there are no changes.
fn similarity(before: str, after: str) -> f64
Returns how alike before and after are by lines, from 0.0 to 1.0. The value is twice the number of unchanged lines divided by the total number of lines in both texts. Two empty texts give 1.0.
fn stats(before: str, after: str) -> Stats
Returns the line-level Stats of changing before into after.
Returns the number of Insert, Delete and Equal edits in edits.
fn unified(before: str, after: str, context: i64, before_name: str, after_name: str) -> str
Returns the unified diff that turns before into after. Both texts are split into lines, diffed and rendered as render does, so an empty string means no difference.
Splits s into the tokens that inline compares. A token is a run of letters, digits, marks and _, a run of whitespace, or a single other character. Joining the tokens gives s back.
struct SlugOptions { pub separator: str pub max_len: i64 }

Options for slug_with. The text placed between words. Defaults to -. The greatest length of the slug in bytes. 0, the default, means no limit. Whole words are kept while they fit, and when the first word alone exceeds the limit it is cut at the limit.
Returns s in camelCase: the first word lowercase and each later word capitalised, joined without a separator.
fn delimited(s: str, sep: str) -> str
Returns the words of s lowercased and joined with sep.
Returns s as lowercase words joined with ..
Returns whether s is in camelCase. s must start with a lowercase letter, hold only letters, digits and marks, and have no two uppercase letters in a row. parseHttp qualifies and parseHTTP does not.
Returns whether s is in kebab-case. s must be non-empty and made of lowercase letters, digits and marks in groups separated by single -, with no leading, trailing or doubled -.
Returns whether s is in PascalCase. s must start with an uppercase letter, hold only letters, digits and marks, and have no two uppercase letters in a row. ParseHttp qualifies and ParseHTTP does not.
Returns whether s is in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE. s must be non-empty and made of uppercase letters, digits and marks in groups separated by single _, with no leading, trailing or doubled _.
Returns whether s is in snake_case. s must be non-empty and made of lowercase letters, digits and marks in groups separated by single _, with no leading, trailing or doubled _.
Returns whether s is non-empty and unchanged by title.
Returns s in kebab-case: lowercase words joined with -.

Splits an identifier or phrase into its words, keeping their original case. Words break at any character that is not a letter, number or mark, at a change from a lowercase to an uppercase letter, and between letters and digits. An uppercase run followed by a lowercase letter ends before that letter, and a plural s stays with the run before it. Apostrophes are dropped and combining marks stay with the letter before them. So parseHTTPResponse gives parse, HTTP, Response, user_id2 gives user, id, 2, and APIs stays whole. Text with no letters or digits gives an empty slice.
Returns s in PascalCase: each word capitalised and joined without a separator. A capitalised word has its first letter in title case and the rest lowercased.
Returns s in SCREAMING-KEBAB-CASE: uppercase words joined with -.
Returns s in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE: uppercase words joined with _.
Returns s as a sentence: the first word capitalised, the rest lowercase, joined with spaces.
Returns s as a lowercase ASCII slug with words joined by - and no length limit. Behaves as slug_with with default SlugOptions.
fn slug_with(s: str, o: SlugOptions) -> str

Returns s as a lowercase ASCII slug made of its words joined by o.separator. The text is decomposed with NFKD and combining marks, apostrophes and quotes inside words are dropped, so Café gives cafe. Letters with no decomposition are spelled out where there is a convention, such as ß as ss, æ as ae, ø as o, đ as d, þ as th and ŋ as ng. Every other character, including letters of scripts that have no ASCII form, ends the current word, and runs of them do not repeat the separator. Returns an empty string when no ASCII letter or digit remains.
Returns s in snake_case: lowercase words joined with _.
Returns s as Title Case: each word capitalised and joined with a space.
Splits s as parts does and returns the words lowercased by Unicode case mapping.
enum NumberError { Empty Malformed(i64) UnknownUnit(str) TooPrecise OutOfRange }

Why a number could not be parsed or converted. The input is empty or only whitespace. The input is not shaped as a number. offset is the byte offset of the offending byte. The unit suffix is not recognised. unit is the unit text, trimmed. The fraction has more digits than the parser can hold exactly. The value is outside the range the conversion accepts.

Returns n abbreviated with a suffix for thousands, such as 999, 1.5K or 12M. The suffixes are K, M, B, T, Qa and Qi, with no space before them. A value below 10 of its unit shows one decimal, dropped when it is 0, and a larger value is rounded to an integer. A negative n has a leading -.
fn format_bytes(n: i64, binary: bool) -> str

Returns n as a human-readable byte size such as 1.5 KiB or 999 B. binary selects the units: true uses powers of 1024 named KiB to EiB, false uses powers of 1000 named kB to EB. The unit is the largest that keeps the value at 1 or above. A value below 10 of its unit shows one decimal, dropped when it is 0, and a larger value is rounded to an integer. A negative n has a leading -.
fn grouped(n: i64, sep: str) -> str
Returns n in decimal with sep between each group of three digits, and a leading - when negative.
Returns n in decimal followed by its English ordinal suffix, such as 1st, 22nd, 103rd and 11th.

Parses a byte size such as 1.5 KiB, 10MB or 512 and returns the number of bytes. The text is an optional sign, digits with an optional . and fraction digits, optional whitespace and a unit. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored. The unit is matched without regard to case and is empty or B for bytes, K, M, G, T, P or E optionally followed by B for powers of 1000, or followed by i or iB for powers of 1024. A fractional result is rounded to the nearest byte. Fails with Empty for blank input, Malformed at the offset where digits were expected, UnknownUnit for any other unit, TooPrecise when the fraction has more than 18 digits after trailing zeros, and OutOfRange when the result does not fit in an i64.

Parses a Roman numeral and returns its value. Letters may be either case. Only the canonical form that roman produces is accepted, so IV parses and IIII and IC do not. Fails with Empty for an empty string, with Malformed at the index of the first byte that is not a Roman letter or that departs from the canonical form, and with OutOfRange when the value exceeds 3999.
fn percent(ratio: f64, digits: i64) -> str
Returns ratio as a percentage with digits digits after the decimal point, so percent(0.256, 1) gives 25.6%. A negative digits is treated as 0. Rounding is that of text.fixed.
fn percent_of(part: i64, whole: i64, digits: i64) -> str
Returns part as a percentage of whole with digits digits after the decimal point. A whole of 0 gives NaN% or inf%, as the division produces.
Returns n as an uppercase Roman numeral. Fails with OutOfRange when n is outside 1 to 3999.
fn si(v: f64, unit: str) -> str
Returns v scaled to an SI prefix with three significant digits, followed by unit. Behaves as si_digits with digits of 3.
fn si_digits(v: f64, unit: str, digits: i64) -> str

Returns v scaled to an SI prefix with digits significant digits, followed by unit, such as 1.5 kHz or 47 µF. The prefix runs from y (10^-24) to Y (10^24), and a magnitude beyond that range keeps the nearest prefix and shows more integer digits. The number is rounded half to even from the exact value of v and trailing zeros are removed. The integer part is never cut, so a digits below the number of integer digits still shows all of them. A space separates the number from the prefix and unit, and is omitted when both are empty. A zero is shown as 0 with no prefix. NaN, inf and -inf are shown as such.

Returns n spelled out in English, such as forty-two or one thousand two hundred. Tens and units are joined by a hyphen, no and is used, a negative n starts with minus, and 0 is zero. Every i64 is supported.

How a cell's text is positioned within a wider column. The text starts at the left edge and the padding follows it. The text is centred. When the padding is odd, the extra blank goes after the text. The text ends at the right edge and the padding precedes it.
enum Border { None Ascii Unicode Markdown Tabs }

The line style render draws around and between cells. No lines. Columns are padded and separated by blanks, and trailing blanks are removed from each line. A grid drawn with +, - and |, with a rule below the header. A grid drawn with box-drawing characters, with a rule below the header. A GitHub-flavoured Markdown pipe table. The first row is always the header, empty when header is empty, followed by the delimiter row that carries each column's alignment. Columns are at least 3 wide, | and \ in cells are escaped with a backslash and line breaks become
. Tab-separated values with no padding or widths. Backslash, tab, newline and carriage return in cells are written as \\, \t, \n and \r.
struct Column { pub align: Align pub min_width: i64 pub max_width: i64 }

The layout of one column of a Table. How cell text is positioned within the column. Defaults to Left. The least width of the column in display columns. Defaults to 0. The greatest width of the column in display columns, beyond which cells are wrapped or truncated. 0, the default, means no limit. The minimum width wins when it is larger.
struct Table { pub header: []str pub rows: [][]str pub columns: []Column pub border: Border pub padding: i64 pub wrap: bool pub ellipsis: str }

A table of text cells that render lays out as a string. Fill header and rows and optionally columns, then call render. Widths are measured in display columns as cell.width does. The header cells. Empty, the default, means the table has no header. The body rows, each a slice of cells. Rows may have different lengths and missing cells are drawn empty. Per-column settings by index. Columns beyond the end of the slice use the defaults of Column. The line style. Defaults to Ascii. The number of blanks on each side of every cell. Defaults to 1. With None the columns are separated by twice this many blanks. Whether a cell wider than its column wraps onto further lines. When false, the default, it is truncated. The text that ends a truncated cell. Defaults to …. It is left out for a column narrower than itself.
Appends row to the body rows of t.

Returns t laid out as text in the style of t.border. Every column is as wide as its widest cell, limited by its Column settings. Cells longer than their column are wrapped or truncated according to wrap and ellipsis, and a wrapped cell makes its row several lines tall. A Border of Ascii or Unicode puts a rule below the header only when header is not empty. The lines are joined with \n with no trailing newline, and a table with no header and no rows gives an empty string.
fn set_align(mut t: Table, index: i64, a: Align)
Sets the alignment of column index to a and leaves its limits as they are, adding default columns up to it as needed.
fn set_column(mut t: Table, index: i64, c: Column)
Replaces the settings of column index with c, adding default columns up to it as needed.
fn set_limits(mut t: Table, index: i64, min_width: i64, max_width: i64)
Sets the minimum and maximum width of column index and leaves its alignment as it is, adding default columns up to it as needed. A max_width of 0 means no maximum.

Pads the cells of rows into columns and returns the lines joined with \n. gap is the number of blank columns between a column and the next. A cell is padded to the width of the widest cell above or below it in the same column, measured by cell.width, so wide characters and ANSI escape sequences align. A block of consecutive rows share a column width only while each has another cell after it, and the last cell of a row is not padded, so lines carry no trailing blanks. Rows may have different numbers of cells.
fn align_tabbed(s: str, gap: i64) -> str
Splits each line of s into cells at tabs and aligns them as align does with gap.
fn fit(cell: str, limit: i64, wrap: bool, ellipsis: str) -> []str

Fits cell to a column limit columns wide and returns its lines. cell is split at \n, carriage returns are removed and tabs become four spaces. A line within limit is returned unchanged. A longer line is wrapped at spaces and tabs when wrap is true, with each run of them becoming one space and breaking inside a word only when the word alone is wider than limit, and is cut and ended with ellipsis when wrap is false. The ellipsis is left out when it is itself wider than limit. ANSI colour and style sequences take no width, are carried onto each following line and are closed with a reset at the end of every line they are active on.
Returns the width in columns of the widest line of cell once tabs are expanded to four spaces and carriage returns removed. This is the width at which fit leaves cell unchanged.
fn pad(s: str, limit: i64, a: Align) -> str
Returns s padded with spaces to limit columns, positioned by a. The width is measured by width. A string already limit columns or wider is returned unchanged.

Returns the display width of s in terminal columns. Printable ASCII counts one column per byte. Otherwise each grapheme cluster counts its unicode.text_width, at most 2, and ANSI escape sequences count 0.
A starting point on the monotonic clock, made by start, from which elapsed measures. Copies of a Stopwatch share the same starting point.

A repeating timer made by ticker that sends on its ticks channel once per period until stop_ticker is called. Copies of a Ticker refer to the same ticker. The channel that receives true on each tick. It holds one value, so a tick that finds the channel full is dropped and a slow receiver sees fewer ticks rather than a backlog. It is never closed and can be used in select.

A one-shot timer made by timer that sends on its fired channel when its duration has passed. Copies of a Timer refer to the same timer. stop_timer cancels a pending firing and reset_timer arms it again. The channel that receives true when the timer fires. It holds one value, so a firing that finds the channel full is dropped. It is never closed and can be used in select.
Returns the time since w was started. Each call measures from the original start, so repeated calls keep growing and the stopwatch is never stopped.
Stops the ticker. Its green thread exits the next time it wakes, so a tick already in ticks stays readable and the channel is not closed.
Stops the timer, discards any value waiting in fired and arms it again to fire after d.
Cancels a pending firing and returns true, or returns false if the timer already fired or was already stopped. A value already sent to fired stays in the channel.
Returns the channel of a new timer that fires once after d. The timer cannot be stopped or reset. Use timer when it must be.

Returns a reading of the monotonic clock in nanoseconds. The origin is unspecified, so only the difference between two readings is meaningful. The reading never goes backwards when the wall clock is adjusted.
Returns the wall clock as whole seconds since the Unix epoch. The fractional second is dropped. Use now_millis or now_nanos for finer resolution.
Returns the wall clock as whole milliseconds since the Unix epoch.
Returns the wall clock as nanoseconds since the Unix epoch.

Pauses the calling green thread for at least d. The duration is rounded up to whole milliseconds. A zero or negative duration returns immediately, and a duration beyond the range of i64 nanoseconds sleeps for that maximum.
Returns a Stopwatch that begins at the current monotonic reading.

Returns a Ticker that ticks every d. The first tick comes one period after the call. A period under one millisecond is raised to one millisecond. Ticks stay on the original schedule: a late tick does not delay the next one, and periods missed while the thread was late are skipped.

Returns a Timer that fires once after d. The duration is rounded up to whole milliseconds. A zero or negative duration fires as soon as the timer's green thread runs. The timer sleeps on its own green thread and does not block the caller.
struct Civil { pub year: i64 pub month: i64 pub day: i64 }
A year, month and day of the proleptic Gregorian calendar. The year, which can be zero or negative. The month, from 1 for January to 12 for December. The day of the month, from 1.
Returns the date that is days days after 1970-01-01, or before it when days is negative.
fn days_from_civil(year: i64, month: i64, day: i64) -> i64
Returns the number of days from 1970-01-01 to the given date, negative before it. The month and day are not range checked.
fn days_in_month(year: i64, month: i64) -> i64
Returns the number of days in month month, from 1 for January, of year.
Returns whether year is a leap year in the proleptic Gregorian calendar.
Returns the English month names, from January.
Returns the three-letter English month names, from January.
Returns the three-letter English weekday names, from Monday.
Returns the position of the weekday of day number days counted from 1970-01-01, from 0 for Monday to 6 for Sunday.
Returns the English weekday names, from Monday.
struct Clock { pub read: fn() -> timestamp.Timestamp pub monotonic: fn() -> duration.Duration pub sleep: fn(*cancel.Token?, duration.Duration) }

A source of the current time made of a wall reading, a monotonic reading and a sleep, which lets code that asks for the time and waits be tested without sleeping. system reads the operating system, fixed never moves and manual is moved by the caller. Returns the current wall-clock time. Returns the monotonic reading as a duration from an origin the clock chooses. Only differences between readings of the same clock are meaningful. Waits for the given duration on this clock, or returns as soon as the token is cancelled. A zero or negative duration returns at once. With no token the wait cannot be interrupted.
A clock under the caller's control, made by manual and turned into a Clock by clock. Copies of a Manual and the clocks made from it share one state, so advance and set are seen by all of them.
fn elapsed_since(c: Clock, start: duration.Duration) -> duration.Duration
Returns the monotonic time that has passed on c since start. start is an earlier reading of c.monotonic.
Returns the wall-clock time of c.

Moves the wall and monotonic readings of m forward by d. A negative d moves both backwards. Panics with clock: advance overflows when either reading would leave its range, and leaves the clock unchanged.

Returns a Clock that reads the current state of m. Its sleep records the duration, then moves m forward by it without waiting. A sleep whose token is already cancelled is recorded and does not move m.
Replaces the wall reading of m with ts. The monotonic reading is unchanged.
Returns the durations passed to the sleeps of the clocks made from m, in the order they were requested. Zero and negative sleeps are not recorded.
Returns a clock whose wall reading is always ts and whose monotonic reading is always zero. Its sleep waits in real time and moves neither reading.
Returns a Manual clock whose wall reading starts at start and whose monotonic reading starts at zero.
Returns a clock that reads the operating system's wall and monotonic clocks.

A calendar date in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, from -9999-01-01 to 9999-12-31, with no time of day or zone. Year 0 is 1 BC. A Date is always valid: the constructors reject a day that does not exist.
struct IsoWeek { pub year: i64 pub week: i64 }

An ISO 8601 week-numbering year and week. Week 1 is the week with the year's first Thursday, so the first days of January can belong to the last week of the previous year and the last days of December to week 1 of the next. The week-numbering year, which can differ from the calendar year near its ends. The week of that year, from 1 to 53.
enum Month { January February March April May June July August September October November December }

A month of the year, in calendar order. The first month, 1, with 31 days. The second month, 2, with 28 days, or 29 in a leap year. The third month, 3, with 31 days. The fourth month, 4, with 30 days. The fifth month, 5, with 31 days. The sixth month, 6, with 30 days. The seventh month, 7, with 31 days. The eighth month, 8, with 31 days. The ninth month, 9, with 30 days. The tenth month, 10, with 31 days. The eleventh month, 11, with 30 days. The twelfth month, 12, with 31 days.
enum Weekday { Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday }

A day of the week, in ISO 8601 order from Monday. The first day of the ISO week, 1. The second day of the ISO week, 2. The third day of the ISO week, 3. The fourth day of the ISO week, 4. The fifth day of the ISO week, 5. The sixth day of the ISO week, 6. The last day of the ISO week, 7.
fn after(a: Date, b: Date) -> bool
Returns whether a is later than b.
fn before(a: Date, b: Date) -> bool
Returns whether a is earlier than b.
fn compare(a: Date, b: Date) -> i64
Returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is earlier than, the same as or later than b.
Returns the day of the month of d, from 1 to 31.
Returns the day of the year of d, from 1 for January 1 to 365 or 366.
Returns the number of days in the month of d.
Returns 366 when the year of d is a leap year and 365 otherwise.
fn days_until(a: Date, b: Date) -> i64
Returns the number of days from a to b, negative when b is earlier.
Returns the number of days from 1970-01-01 to d, negative for an earlier date.
fn equal(a: Date, b: Date) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are the same date.
Returns the first day of the month of d.
Returns January 1 of the year of d.
fn format(d: Date, layout: str) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns d printed through the layout layout, such as %d %B %Y or %a, %d %b. Fails with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout, as pattern.compile does, and otherwise as format_names does.
fn format_names(d: Date, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns d printed through the compiled pattern p with the month and weekday words of names. Fails with Invalid when p needs a value a date does not have, such as a time of day or an offset.
fn format_with(d: Date, p: pattern.Pattern) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns d printed through the compiled pattern p with English names. Fails as format_names does.
Returns whether the year of d is a leap year. A leap year is divisible by 4, except for years divisible by 100 that are not divisible by 400.
Returns the ISO 8601 week-numbering year and week that contain d.
Returns the last day of the month of d.
Returns December 31 of the year of d.
fn max(a: Date, b: Date) -> Date
Returns the later of the two dates, or a when they are equal.
fn min(a: Date, b: Date) -> Date
Returns the earlier of the two dates, or a when they are equal.
fn minus(d: Date, s: span.Span) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns d moved back by the span s. Fails as plus does.
Returns the month of d as a number from 1 to 12.
fn next_weekday(d: Date, w: Weekday) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the first date after d that falls on w. When d is already on w, the result is seven days later. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn on_or_next(d: Date, w: Weekday) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns d when it falls on w and otherwise the next date that does. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn on_or_previous(d: Date, w: Weekday) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns d when it falls on w and otherwise the previous date that does. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn plus(d: Date, s: span.Span) -> Date ! fault.Fault

Returns d moved forward by the span s. Years and months are added first, with the day moved back to the last day of a shorter month, and then weeks and days. A negative span moves backwards. Fails with Invalid when s has hours, minutes, seconds or smaller units, and with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn plus_days(d: Date, n: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the date n days after d, which can be negative. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn plus_months(d: Date, n: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault

Returns the date n months after d, which can be negative. The day of the month is kept, or moved back to the last day of the month when that month is shorter. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years or n is beyond about a trillion months.
fn plus_weeks(d: Date, n: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the date n weeks after d, which can be negative. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn plus_years(d: Date, n: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the date n years after d, which can be negative. A February 29 that lands in a year that is not a leap year becomes February 28. Fails with OutOfRange as plus_months does.
fn previous_weekday(d: Date, w: Weekday) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the last date before d that falls on w. When d is already on w, the result is seven days earlier. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
Returns the quarter of the year of d, from 1 for January to March to 4.
fn range(a: Date, b: Date) -> []Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the dates from a up to but not including b, in order. The result is empty when b is not later than a. Fails with OutOfRange when it would hold more than a million dates.
fn range_inclusive(a: Date, b: Date) -> []Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the dates from a up to and including b, in order. Fails with OutOfRange when it would hold more than a million dates.
fn since(a: Date, b: Date, diff: span.Diff) -> span.Span ! fault.Fault
Returns the span from b to a, measured and rounded as diff says. Fails as until does.
Returns the date of d as pattern Fields, with year, month, day, day of year, weekday, ISO year and ISO week.
Returns d as YYYY-MM-DD. A negative year is written with a leading - and four digits, such as -0044-03-15.
fn until(a: Date, b: Date, diff: span.Diff) -> span.Span ! fault.Fault

Returns the span from a to b, measured and rounded as diff says. The span is negative when b is earlier. Years and months are counted on the calendar from a, while weeks and days are exact. diff.largest must be a calendar unit and its default is Days. A smallest below days is treated as Days, and then only with an increment of 1. Fails with Invalid when the options are inconsistent and with OutOfRange or Overflow where the result cannot be represented.
fn until_with_time(a: Date, b: Date, extra: duration.Duration, diff: span.Diff) -> span.Span ! fault.Fault

Returns the span from the start of a to b plus the time of day extra, measured and rounded as diff says. It serves the date-time types, which pass the difference of their times of day as extra. extra must be less than a day in magnitude and must not point the opposite way from the days between a and b. Years and months are counted on the calendar from a, while weeks, days and the time units are exact. Fails with Invalid when largest is not a calendar unit, when extra is out of bounds, or when the options are inconsistent as span.check_diff and span.check_time_increment state, and with OutOfRange or Overflow where rounding cannot represent the result.
Returns the day of the week of d.
fn with_day(d: Date, n: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns d with its day of the month replaced by n. Fails with OutOfRange when n is outside 1 to 31 and with Invalid when the month has no day n.
fn with_month(d: Date, m: Month) -> Date
Returns d in the month m, with the day moved back to the last day of m when d's day is past it. This never fails.
fn with_year(d: Date, y: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns d in the year y, with February 29 becoming February 28 when y is not a leap year. Fails with OutOfRange when y is outside -9999 to 9999.
fn month_days(m: Month, year: i64) -> i64
Returns the number of days in m in the year year. It is 29 for February in a leap year.
Returns the English name of m, such as March.
Returns the month after m, with December followed by January.
Returns the month before m, with January preceded by December.
Returns the three-letter English name of m, such as Mar.
Returns the number of m, from 1 for January to 12.
fn weekday_days_until(a: Weekday, b: Weekday) -> i64
Returns the number of days from a forward to the next b, from 0 to 6. It is 0 when the two weekdays are the same.
Returns the English name of w, such as Monday.
Returns the weekday after w, with Sunday followed by Monday.
Returns the weekday before w, with Monday preceded by Sunday.
Returns the three-letter English name of w, such as Mon.
Returns the number of w, from 1 for Monday to 7 for Sunday.
fn clamped(year: i64, month: i64, day: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the date with the year year and month number month, using the last day of the month when day is past it. Fails with OutOfRange when the year or month is out of range or day is below 1.
Returns the date n days after 1970-01-01, which can be negative. Fails with OutOfRange when the date is outside -9999-01-01 to 9999-12-31.

Returns the date in f. The date comes from year, month and day, or else from year and day of year, or else from ISO year, ISO week and weekday. Other fields that are present, such as weekday or century, must agree with the date. Fails with Invalid when the fields do not name a date or conflict, and otherwise as of, from_ordinal and from_iso_week do.
fn from_iso_week(year: i64, week: i64, day: Weekday) -> Date ! fault.Fault

Returns the date on weekday day of ISO week week in the ISO year year. Fails with OutOfRange when week is outside 1 to 53, when the year is outside -10000 to 10000 or when the date is outside the supported years, and with Invalid when the year has no week week.
fn from_month(year: i64, month: Month, day: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Returns the date with the year year, month month and day day. Fails as of does.
fn from_ordinal(year: i64, doy: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault

Returns the date that is day doy of the year year, counting 1 for January 1. Fails with OutOfRange when the year is out of range or doy is outside 1 to 366, and with Invalid when doy is 366 in a year that is not a leap year.
fn from_weekday_in_month(year: i64, month: Month, day: Weekday, n: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault

Returns the nth day of month in year, such as the second Tuesday, or the last one when n is -1. n is from 1 to 5 or -1. Fails with OutOfRange when n is not one of those or the year is out of range, and with Invalid when the month has no nth such weekday.
Returns the month numbered n, from 1 for January to 12. Fails with OutOfRange when n is outside 1 to 12.
fn of(year: i64, month: i64, day: i64) -> Date ! fault.Fault

Returns the date with the year year, month number month and day day. Fails with OutOfRange naming the field when the year is outside -9999 to 9999, the month is outside 1 to 12 or the day is outside 1 to 31, and with Invalid when the day is past the end of the month.

Parses a date in the ISO 8601 forms YYYY-MM-DD, YYYYMMDD, ordinal YYYY-DDD and YYYYDDD, and week dates YYYY-Www-D and YYYYWwwD. The year has four digits and can start with -. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte, with OutOfRange when a field is out of range and with Invalid when the day or week does not exist.
fn parse_names(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> Date ! fault.Fault

Parses s with the compiled pattern p and the words of names. Fails with Invalid when p uses a time, offset, zone or Unix-time verb, with Syntax or OutOfRange when s does not match, and with Invalid when the fields do not give a date or conflict.
fn parse_pattern(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the compiled pattern p and English names. Fails as parse_names does.
fn parse_with(s: str, layout: str) -> Date ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the layout layout and English names. Fails as parse_names does and with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout.
Returns the date of the clock c in UTC.
Returns the weekday numbered n, from 1 for Monday to 7 for Sunday. Fails with OutOfRange when n is outside 1 to 7.
Returns the number of ISO weeks in the ISO year year, which is 52 or 53.

A date and a time of day on a wall clock, with no offset or zone. It names a local time, not an instant. Arithmetic treats every day as exactly 24 hours, so it never accounts for daylight saving changes. Use zoned for that. A DateTime is a date.Date from -9999-01-01 to 9999-12-31 with a timeofday.TimeOfDay.
fn after(a: DateTime, b: DateTime) -> bool
Returns whether a is later than b.
fn before(a: DateTime, b: DateTime) -> bool
Returns whether a is earlier than b.
Returns the whole seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00 to dt, counting the local time as if it were UTC. The fraction of a second is dropped, and the result is negative before the epoch.
fn compare(a: DateTime, b: DateTime) -> i64
Returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is earlier than, the same as or later than b.
Returns the date part of dt.
Returns the day of the month of dt.
Returns the day of the year of dt, from 1.
fn duration_until(a: DateTime, b: DateTime) -> duration.Duration
Returns the exact length of time from a to b, counting every day as 24 hours, which is negative when b is earlier.
fn equal(a: DateTime, b: DateTime) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are the same date and time of day.
fn format(dt: DateTime, layout: str) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns dt printed through the layout layout, such as %Y-%m-%d %H:%M. Fails with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout, as pattern.compile does, and otherwise as format_names does.
fn format_names(dt: DateTime, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> str ! fault.Fault

Returns dt printed through the compiled pattern p with the month, weekday and period words of names. Fails with Invalid when p needs a value a date-time does not have, such as an offset or a zone name.
fn format_with(dt: DateTime, p: pattern.Pattern) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns dt printed through the compiled pattern p with English names. Fails as format_names does.
Returns the hour of dt, from 0 to 23.
fn max(a: DateTime, b: DateTime) -> DateTime
Returns the later of the two date-times, or a when they are equal.
fn min(a: DateTime, b: DateTime) -> DateTime
Returns the earlier of the two date-times, or a when they are equal.
fn minus(dt: DateTime, s: span.Span) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault
Returns dt moved back by the span s. Fails as plus does.
fn minus_duration(dt: DateTime, d: duration.Duration) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault
Returns the date-time d before dt. Fails as plus_duration does.
Returns the minute of dt, from 0 to 59.
Returns the month of dt as a number from 1 to 12.
Returns the nanosecond within the second of dt, from 0 to 999999999.
fn plus(dt: DateTime, s: span.Span) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault

Returns dt moved forward by the span s. The years, months, weeks and days are added to the date as date.plus does, with the day moved back to the last day of a shorter month. The time units are then added as an exact duration, carrying into the date. A negative span moves backwards. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years and with Overflow when the time units do not fit in a Duration.
fn plus_duration(dt: DateTime, d: duration.Duration) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault

Returns the date-time d after dt, counting every day as 24 hours. A negative d moves backwards. Fails with Overflow when the sum does not fit in a Duration and with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn round(dt: DateTime, unit: span.Unit, increment: i64, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault

Returns dt with its time of day rounded to a multiple of increment units since midnight using mode. unit can be Days, which needs an increment of 1 and rounds to a midnight. A result that reaches the end of the day becomes 00:00 on the next day. Fails with Invalid when unit is a larger calendar unit or the increment does not divide the next larger unit as timeofday.rounded_nanos states, and with OutOfRange when rounding up passes the last supported date.
Returns the second of dt, from 0 to 59.
fn since(a: DateTime, b: DateTime, diff: span.Diff) -> span.Span ! fault.Fault
Returns the span from b to a, measured and rounded as diff says. Fails as until does.
Returns the time-of-day part of dt.
Returns the date and time of dt as pattern Fields.
Returns dt as YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss, with a fraction after the seconds when the nanosecond is not zero.
fn truncate(dt: DateTime, unit: span.Unit) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault
Returns dt with everything below unit set to zero. Fails as round does.
fn until(a: DateTime, b: DateTime, diff: span.Diff) -> span.Span ! fault.Fault

Returns the span from a to b, measured and rounded as diff says. The span is negative when b is earlier. When diff.largest is a calendar unit, years and months are counted on the calendar from a and the remainder is split into weeks, days and time units. Otherwise the span is the exact duration split into time units from largest down. Fails with Invalid when the options are inconsistent as span.check_diff and span.check_time_increment state, and with OutOfRange or Overflow where the result cannot be represented.
Returns the day of the week of dt.
fn with_date(dt: DateTime, d: date.Date) -> DateTime
Returns dt with its date replaced by d.
fn with_time(dt: DateTime, t: timeofday.TimeOfDay) -> DateTime
Returns dt with its time of day replaced by t.
Returns the date-time at 23:59:59.999999999 on d.
fn from_civil_seconds(secs: i64, nanos: i64) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault

Returns the date-time secs seconds and nanos nanoseconds after 1970-01-01T00:00:00, counting as if the local time were UTC. Fails with OutOfRange when nanos is outside 0 to 999999999 or the date-time is outside the supported years.
Returns the date-time in f. Fails as date.from_fields and timeofday.from_fields do.
fn from_parts(d: date.Date, t: timeofday.TimeOfDay) -> DateTime
Returns the date-time made of the date d and the time of day t.
fn of(y: i64, mo: i64, d: i64, h: i64, mi: i64, s: i64, ns: i64) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault
Returns the date-time with the given year y, month number mo, day d, hour h, minute mi, second s and nanosecond ns. Fails with OutOfRange or Invalid as date.of and timeofday.of do.

Parses a date and a time of day separated by T, t or a space, such as 2024-03-01T12:30:00. The date accepts the forms of date.parse and the time the forms of timeofday.parse. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte, including when there is no separator, and otherwise as those do.
fn parse_names(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault

Parses s with the compiled pattern p and the words of names. Fails with Invalid when p uses an offset, zone or Unix-time verb, with Syntax or OutOfRange when s does not match, and with Invalid when the fields do not give a date and a time or conflict.
fn parse_pattern(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the compiled pattern p and English names. Fails as parse_names does.
fn parse_with(s: str, layout: str) -> DateTime ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the layout layout and English names. Fails as parse_names does and with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout.
Returns the date-time at 00:00 on d.

An exact signed length of time with nanosecond precision. It is held as whole seconds and a nanosecond part that always share a sign, with at most 999999999 nanoseconds. The seconds can be any i64 except the minimum. The plain arithmetic functions panic with duration: overflow when the result does not fit, and the try_ forms return none instead.
Returns the length of d without its sign.
fn after(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> bool
Returns whether a is longer than b.
Returns d as a count of nanoseconds, or none when it does not fit in an i64. An i64 holds about 292 years of nanoseconds.
Returns d as fractional seconds. The result is the nearest f64, so a long duration can lose nanosecond precision.
fn before(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> bool
Returns whether a is shorter than b.
Returns d as a count of milliseconds, rounded up. A zero or negative duration returns 0, and a duration beyond the range of i64 nanoseconds returns the count for that maximum.
fn compare(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> i64
Returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is shorter than, equal to or longer than b. Negative durations are shorter than positive ones.
fn divide(d: Duration, n: i64) -> Duration
Returns d divided by n, truncated toward zero to a whole nanosecond. Panics with duration: divide by zero when n is 0. The result is negative when exactly one of d and n is.
fn equal(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are the same length.
Returns the nanoseconds that remain after floor_seconds, from 0 to 999999999.
Returns the seconds of d rounded toward negative infinity. Together with floor_nanos, it splits d into whole seconds and a nanosecond part that is never negative.

Returns d in a short readable form, such as 1h 30m, 2.5s or 250us. Zero is 0s and a negative duration starts with -. A duration under one second uses a single unit of ns, us or ms. Longer ones list h, m and s parts separated by spaces and omit a part that is zero. parse reads the result back.
Returns whether d is below zero.
Returns whether d has no length.
fn max(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> Duration
Returns the longer of the two durations, or a when they are equal.
fn min(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> Duration
Returns the shorter of the two durations, or a when they are equal.
fn minus(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> Duration
Returns a less b. Panics with duration: overflow on overflow.
Returns d with its sign reversed. This never overflows.
fn plus(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> Duration
Returns the sum of a and b. Panics with duration: overflow on overflow.
fn ratio(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> f64
Returns how many times b fits in a as an f64. A zero b follows floating-point division and gives an infinity or NaN.
fn round(d: Duration, unit: Duration, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> Duration ! fault.Fault

Returns d rounded to a multiple of unit using mode. Multiples are counted from zero. Fails with Invalid when unit is zero or negative, with OutOfRange when unit is longer than about 146 years (2^62 - 1 nanoseconds), and with Overflow when the rounded result does not fit.

Returns d as a count of nanoseconds, clamped to the range of an i64. A duration beyond about 292 years in either direction returns the largest count, or its negation. The minimum i64 is never returned, so the result can be negated.
Returns the nanoseconds left after the whole seconds of d. The result has the sign of d and is under one second in magnitude.
fn times(d: Duration, n: i64) -> Duration
Returns d multiplied by n. Panics with duration: overflow on overflow.

Returns d in the ISO 8601 time form, such as PT1H30M or PT0.25S. Zero is PT0S and a negative duration starts with -. Hours are not folded into days, and the seconds carry up to nine fraction digits with trailing zeros removed. parse reads the result back.
fn truncate(d: Duration, unit: Duration) -> Duration ! fault.Fault
Returns d rounded toward zero to a multiple of unit. Fails in the same cases as round.
fn try_minus(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> Duration?
Returns a less b, or none on overflow.
fn try_plus(a: Duration, b: Duration) -> Duration?
Returns the sum of a and b, or none on overflow.
fn try_times(d: Duration, n: i64) -> Duration?
Returns d multiplied by n, or none on overflow.
Returns the whole hours in d, truncated toward zero.
Returns the whole microseconds in d, truncated toward zero. Panics with duration: overflow when the count does not fit in an i64.
Returns the whole milliseconds in d, truncated toward zero. Panics with duration: overflow when the count does not fit in an i64.
Returns the whole minutes in d, truncated toward zero.
Returns the whole seconds in d, truncated toward zero.
fn from_parts(secs: i64, nanos: i64) -> Duration
Returns the duration of secs seconds plus nanos nanoseconds. Panics with duration: overflow where try_from_parts returns none.

Returns the duration nearest to f seconds. The fraction is rounded to the nearest nanosecond, with a half rounded away from zero. Fails with Invalid for NaN or an infinity and with Overflow when f is about 9.2e18 seconds or more in magnitude.
Returns a duration of n hours. Panics with duration: overflow when the count of seconds does not fit in an i64.
Returns a duration of n microseconds. n can be any i64; this never overflows.
Returns a duration of n milliseconds. n can be any i64; this never overflows.
Returns a duration of n minutes. Panics with duration: overflow when the count of seconds does not fit in an i64.
Returns a duration of n nanoseconds. n can be any i64; this never overflows.

Parses a duration written in either the ISO 8601 form or the friendly form. Both forms can start with + or -. The ISO form is PT followed by nH, nM and nS in that order, in either case, with a fraction allowed on the seconds only and at least one part present. The friendly form is one or more numbers each followed by a unit, ns, us, µs, ms, s, m or h, with optional spaces, such as 1h 30m or 1.5s. A fraction must be exactly representable in nanoseconds and have at most nine digits. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte and with Overflow when the total does not fit.
Returns a duration of n seconds. Panics with duration: overflow when n is the minimum i64.
fn try_from_parts(secs: i64, nanos: i64) -> Duration?
Returns the duration of secs seconds plus nanos nanoseconds, or none on overflow. nanos can be any value and can differ in sign from secs; whole seconds in it carry into secs.
Returns the duration of zero length.
enum Fault { OutOfRange(str) Invalid(str) Syntax(i64) Overflow UnknownZone(str) Malformed(str) Unsupported(str) Skipped Ambiguous OffsetConflict }

The error type returned by every fallible function in the time modules. to_string renders a fault as a message. A value for what is outside the range the type can hold, such as month 13 or a timestamp after year 9999. A value for what is in range but not valid in context, such as day 30 of February or a rounding unit that is not positive. The text does not match the expected format. at is the byte offset where it stopped matching. The result cannot be represented. No time zone is named name. Zone data or a zone file is corrupt or unreadable. what names the part that is bad. The input is well formed but names a feature that is not supported, such as a calendar other than ISO 8601 or a locale format verb. what names it. The local time falls in a gap that a zone transition skips, so it does not exist in the zone, and the disambiguation asked for a failure. The local time occurs twice in the zone because a transition repeats it, and the disambiguation asked for a failure. The offset given with a local time does not match any offset the zone has at that time.
Returns the message for f, such as syntax error at byte 5 or unknown time zone Mars/Base.
struct Words { pub just_now: str pub under_second: str pub past: str pub future: str pub about: str pub quantity: str pub singular: []str pub plural: []str pub short: []str }

The wording that ago, in_words and compact use, so that a program can print another language. A template marks where its text goes with %s, and quantity also uses %d for the count. The unit lists have six entries in order: second, minute, hour, day, month and year. A month counts as 30 days and a year as 365 days. The _with functions fail with Invalid when a unit list does not have six entries. The text for an elapsed time under five seconds. The text for in_words of a nonzero duration under one second. The template for a time in the past, with the quantity at %s. The template for a time in the future, with the quantity at %s. The template that marks a quantity as approximate, with the quantity at %s. The template that joins a count and a unit name, with the count at %d and the name at %s. The unit names used for a count of exactly one, from second to year. The unit names used for any other count, from second to year. The abbreviated unit names that compact uses, from second to year.

Returns how long ago d was in English, such as 3 hours ago. d is the time elapsed since the event. It is counted in its largest whole unit, rounded down, so 90 minutes reads 1 hour ago. Under five seconds the result is just now. A negative d reads as a future time, such as in 2 days.
fn ago_with(d: duration.Duration, w: Words) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns how long ago d was, worded by w. Fails with Invalid when w does not have six names in each unit list. Otherwise it is ago with different words.
Returns d as a single count in its largest whole unit, such as 5m or -3d. The count is rounded down, a negative duration has a leading -, and a duration under one second is 0s.
fn compact_with(d: duration.Duration, w: Words) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns d as a single count in its largest whole unit, using the short names of w. Fails as ago_with does.
Returns the English Words: just now, less than a second, %s ago, in %s, about %s, %d %s, and the names second to year, with s, m, h, d, mo and y as the short forms.

Returns an approximate English description of the length of d, such as about 2 hours or 3 days. The sign is ignored. The duration is rounded to the nearest whole unit of the largest unit that fits, and the result is prefixed about unless it is exact. A nonzero duration under one second is less than a second and zero is 0 seconds.
fn in_words_with(d: duration.Duration, w: Words) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns an approximate description of the length of d, worded by w. Fails as ago_with does.
fn relative(ts: timestamp.Timestamp, now: timestamp.Timestamp) -> str
Returns when ts is compared with now in English, such as 2 days ago or in 3 hours. It is ago of the time from ts to now, so a ts before now reads as the past.
fn relative_with(ts: timestamp.Timestamp, now: timestamp.Timestamp, w: Words) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns when ts is compared with now, worded by w. Fails as ago_with does.
fn round_to(d: duration.Duration, units: i64) -> duration.Duration ! fault.Fault

Returns d rounded to its units most significant units. The units are years, 30-day months, days, hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds, so 1h 30m 20s rounded to two units is 1h 30m and to one unit is 2h. A half rounds away from zero. Fails with Invalid when units is below 1 and with OutOfRange or Overflow where duration.round does. More units than the ladder has keep full precision.
A fixed difference from UTC in whole seconds, positive to the east, from -25:59:59 to +25:59:59.
struct Reading { pub offset: Offset pub end: i64 }
An offset read by read and the position just past it. The offset that was read. The byte position after the last byte of the offset.
fn after(a: Offset, b: Offset) -> bool
Returns whether a is east of b.
fn before(a: Offset, b: Offset) -> bool
Returns whether a is west of b.
fn compare(a: Offset, b: Offset) -> i64
Returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is west of, equal to or east of b.
fn equal(a: Offset, b: Offset) -> bool
Returns whether the two offsets are the same.
Returns whether the offset is zero.
fn max(a: Offset, b: Offset) -> Offset
Returns the more eastern of the two offsets.
fn min(a: Offset, b: Offset) -> Offset
Returns the more western of the two offsets.
Returns the offset with its sign reversed.
Returns the offset as signed seconds from UTC.
Returns the offset as +hh:mm, or +hh:mm:ss when it has a seconds part. Zero renders as +00:00.
Returns Z for a zero offset and the to_string form otherwise.
fn hm(h: i64, m: i64) -> Offset ! fault.Fault

Returns the offset of h hours and m minutes. The sign of h applies to the minutes as well, so hm(-3, 30) is -03:30. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is beyond 25:59:59 and with Invalid when m is not from 0 to 59.
Returns the offset of h whole hours. Fails with OutOfRange when h is below -25 or above 25.
Returns the offset of n seconds from UTC. Fails with OutOfRange when n is beyond 25:59:59 in either direction.

Parses an offset written as Z, z, +hh, +hhmm, +hh:mm, +hhmmss or +hh:mm:ss, with - accepted for the sign. Z must stand alone. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first byte that does not fit, and with OutOfRange when an hour is above 25, a minute or second is above 59 or the result is out of range.
fn read(s: str, from: i64) -> Reading ! fault.Fault

Reads an offset written as Z, z, +hh, +hhmm, +hh:mm, +hhmmss or +hh:mm:ss, with - accepted for the sign, starting at byte from of s. Reading stops at the first byte that is not part of the offset. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first byte that does not fit, and with OutOfRange when an hour is above 25, a minute or second is above 59 or the result is out of range.

struct Fields { pub year: i64? pub month: i64? pub day: i64? pub day_of_year: i64? pub weekday: i64? pub iso_year: i64? pub iso_week: i64? pub week_sunday: i64? pub week_monday: i64? pub century: i64? pub year_of_century: i64? pub hour: i64? pub hour12: i64? pub period: i64? pub minute: i64? pub second: i64? pub nanosecond: i64? pub offset_seconds: i64? pub zone_abbreviation: str? pub unix_seconds: i64? }

The calendar and clock values a pattern reads or writes, each optional so that a pattern can fill in only the parts it names. render takes the values to print from it and scan returns the values it found in it. The date and time types convert to and from Fields with to_fields and from_fields. The year, which can be negative. The month, from 1 for January to 12. The day of the month, from 1 to 31. The day of the year, from 1 to 366. The ISO weekday, from 1 for Monday to 7 for Sunday. The ISO 8601 week-numbering year. The ISO 8601 week number, from 1 to 53. The week of the year counting from the first Sunday, from 0 to 53. The week of the year counting from the first Monday, from 0 to 53. The century, which is the year divided by 100, from 0 to 99. The year within its century, from 0 to 99. The hour on the 24-hour clock, from 0 to 23. The hour on the 12-hour clock, from 1 to 12. The half of the day: 0 for before noon and 1 for after. The minute, from 0 to 59. The second, from 0 to 59. A 60 is read as 59 when scanning. The nanosecond within the second, from 0 to 999999999. The offset from UTC in seconds, positive to the east. The zone abbreviation, such as UTC or CEST. The seconds since the Unix epoch.
struct Names { pub months: []str pub short_months: []str pub weekdays: []str pub short_weekdays: []str pub am: str pub pm: str }

The words a pattern prints and recognises for months, weekdays and the halves of the day. Month lists have twelve entries from January and weekday lists have seven entries from Monday. A list of any other length is rejected with Invalid by render, scan and check_names. The full month names, from January. The abbreviated month names, from January. The full weekday names, from Monday. The abbreviated weekday names, from Monday. The text for before noon. The text for after noon.
A layout compiled by compile, ready for render and scan.
enum Plan { Calendar(i64, i64, i64) Ordinal(i64, i64) IsoWeek(i64, i64, i64) }
The way a set of Fields names a date. A date given by year, month and day of the month. A date given by year and day of the year. A date given by ISO year, ISO week and weekday from 1 for Monday.
struct Uses { pub date: bool pub time: bool pub offset: bool pub zone: bool pub unix: bool }

Which kinds of value a pattern touches, as returned by uses. The pattern uses a year, month, day, weekday or week verb. The pattern uses an hour, minute, second, fraction or am/pm verb. The pattern uses the UTC offset verb %z. The pattern uses the zone abbreviation verb %Z. The pattern uses the Unix seconds verb %s.
struct Wall { pub hour: i64 pub minute: i64 pub second: i64 pub nanosecond: i64 }
The time of day found by wall. The hour, from 0 to 23. The minute, from 0 to 59. The second, from 0 to 59. The nanosecond, from 0 to 999999999.
fn check_date(parsed: Fields, actual: Fields) ! fault.Fault

Checks that the fields in parsed agree with actual, the fields of the date they resolved to. A field missing from either side is not compared. Fails with Invalid when a weekday, week, century or other field differs.

Returns how f names a date, trying year with month and day first, then year with day of year, then ISO year with week and weekday. A year of century without a century becomes 19xx for 69 to 99 and 20xx otherwise. Fails with Invalid when none of the three is complete.

Returns the time of day in f. The hour comes from hour, or from hour12 with period. Minute, second and nanosecond default to 0. Fails with Invalid when there is no hour, when hour12 has no period, or when hour, hour12 and period disagree.
Checks that n has twelve month names, twelve short month names, seven weekday names and seven short weekday names. Fails with Invalid otherwise.
fn render(p: Pattern, f: Fields, names: Names) -> str ! fault.Fault

Returns f printed through p using names. Fails with Invalid when names has the wrong number of entries, when a value that p needs is missing from f and when a two-digit year is asked of a negative year.
