fn restrict(p: Pattern, date: bool, time: bool) ! fault.Fault

Checks that p uses only the kinds of value the caller supplies, where date and time say whether date and time-of-day values are available. Fails with Invalid when p needs a date or a time of day that is not available, and always when it needs an offset, a zone name or Unix time.
fn scan(p: Pattern, input: str, names: Names) -> Fields ! fault.Fault

Reads input through p using names and returns the values it found. Names are matched without regard to case, taking the longest match. A field that appears twice must have the same value both times. A zone abbreviation is a run of letters. Fails with Syntax at the offset where the input stops matching or where input is left over, with OutOfRange naming a field whose value is outside its range, and with Invalid when two fields conflict or names has the wrong number of entries.
Returns which kinds of value p reads or writes.

Compiles a layout into a Pattern. Text is copied as written and a % starts a verb. The verbs are: Date: %Y year, %y year of century, %C century, %m month, %d day, %e day padded with a space, %j day of year, %u weekday from 1 for Monday, %w weekday from 0 for Sunday, %U and %W week of the year from Sunday or Monday, %V ISO week and %G ISO year. Names: %a and %A short and full weekday, %b and %B short and full month, %p AM or PM and %P the same in lower case, %Z the zone abbreviation. Time: %H hour, %I hour on the 12-hour clock, %M minute, %S second and %s Unix seconds. Fraction: %f six digits when formatting and one to nine when parsing, %3f, %6f and %9f an exact digit count, and %N nine digits. Offset: %z as +hhmm, %:z as +hh:mm and %::z as +hh:mm:ss. Shorthand: %F for %Y-%m-%d, %T for %H:%M:%S, %R for %H:%M and %D for %m/%d/%y. Literal: %%, %n for a newline and %t for a tab. Numeric verbs take a padding flag after the %: - for none, _ for spaces and 0 for zeros. Name verbs take ^ to print in upper case. Numbers are zero padded by default, except %e. A run of spaces in the layout prints that many spaces and matches that many or more when scanning. Fails with Syntax at the offset of an unknown verb, a flag the verb does not accept or an incomplete verb, and with Unsupported for the locale verbs %c, %x and %X.
Returns the English Names: full and abbreviated months and weekdays, AM and PM.
enum Rounding { Trunc Ceil Floor Expand HalfExpand HalfEven HalfTrunc HalfCeil HalfFloor }

How a value that lies between two multiples of a unit is rounded to one of them. A value that is exactly a multiple is never changed. The first four modes ignore the position of the value between the multiples. The Half modes round to the nearer multiple and differ only in which way an exact midpoint goes. Rounds toward zero. Rounds toward positive infinity. Rounds toward negative infinity. Rounds away from zero. Rounds to the nearest multiple and an exact midpoint away from zero. Rounds to the nearest multiple and an exact midpoint to the even multiple. Rounds to the nearest multiple and an exact midpoint toward zero. Rounds to the nearest multiple and an exact midpoint toward positive infinity. Rounds to the nearest multiple and an exact midpoint toward negative infinity.
fn up(mode: Rounding, negative: bool, even: bool, r: i64, divisor: i64) -> bool

Returns whether mode takes the upper of the two multiples around a value. r is how far the value is above the lower multiple, from 0 to divisor exclusive, and divisor is the distance between the multiples. negative says the value is below zero and even says the lower multiple is an even multiple of the unit. An exact multiple (r of 0) returns false.
fn apply(q: i64, r: i64, divisor: i64, mode: Rounding) -> i64

Returns q or q + 1, whichever mode selects for a quotient q with remainder r of a division by divisor. q is the floored quotient and r is in 0 to divisor exclusive. A quotient below zero counts as a negative value for the modes that depend on the sign.
fn remainder(secs: i64, nanos: i64, m: i64) -> i64

Returns the remainder of secs * 1000000000 + nanos divided by m, from 0 to m exclusive. The sum is never formed, so the result is exact where it would overflow i64. nanos is expected to be from 0 to 999999999, and m must be positive.
struct Scan { pub s: str pub at: i64 }

A read position in a string, shared by the time parsers. The take_ and expect functions advance at as they read and fail with Syntax at the position of the first byte that does not fit. The string being read. The byte position of the next byte to read.
fn accept(mut p: Scan, c: u8) -> bool
Reads c and returns true, or returns false and reads nothing.
fn at_byte(p: Scan, c: u8) -> bool
Returns whether the next byte is c.
Returns whether the next byte is an ASCII digit.
Returns the number of digits that start at the read position, without reading them.
fn digits(mut p: Scan, count: i64) -> i64 ! fault.Fault
Reads exactly count digits as one number. Fails with Syntax when fewer are there.
fn digits_between(mut p: Scan, least: i64, most: i64) -> i64 ! fault.Fault
Reads between least and most digits as one number. Fails with Syntax when fewer than least are there.
fn expect(mut p: Scan, c: u8) ! fault.Fault
Reads c. Fails with Syntax when the next byte is another one.
fn expect_text(mut p: Scan, word: str) ! fault.Fault
Reads exactly the bytes of word. Fails with Syntax at the first byte that differs.
Returns the position after a . at the read position and the digits that follow it, without reading them.
fn take_fraction(mut p: Scan, unit_nanos: i64) -> i64 ! fault.Fault

Reads a . and the fraction digits after it, and returns the fraction as a count of nanoseconds when the whole number before it was counted in units of unit_nanos nanoseconds. At most nine digits are read, and the fraction must be exactly representable in nanoseconds. Fails with Syntax when no digit follows the dot, when a tenth digit follows, or when a digit that cannot be represented is not zero.
fn take_whole(mut p: Scan, overflow: fault.Fault) -> i64 ! fault.Fault
Reads a run of digits as one number. Fails with Syntax when there is none and with overflow when the number does not fit in an i64.
fn fraction_text(value: i64, width: i64) -> str
Returns value as a . and width digits with trailing zeros removed, or an empty string for zero.
Returns a count of nanoseconds below a second in the largest of ms, us and ns that keeps the number whole, with a trimmed fraction.
struct Diff { pub largest: Unit pub smallest: Unit pub increment: i64 pub mode: rounding.Rounding }

The options for measuring the difference between two dates or date-times as a Span. A Diff with no fields set measures in days, keeps full precision and truncates. until and since on the date types check the options and fail with Invalid or OutOfRange when they are inconsistent. The largest unit the result uses; an amount larger than it is counted in it, so Days gives 40 days and Weeks gives 5 weeks and 5 days. The default is Days. The smallest unit the result keeps; anything below it is rounded. It cannot be larger than largest. The default is Nanoseconds. The result is rounded to a multiple of this many smallest units, from 1 to 1000000000. The default is 1. How the result is rounded to smallest and increment. The default is Trunc.

A length of time held as a separate count for each Unit, from years to nanoseconds. The counts are kept as given and never carried into each other, so 90 minutes stays 90 minutes and 1 month stays a month until it is added to a date. All counts share one sign. Each count is limited to a bound: 19999 years, 239999 months, 1043999 weeks, 7304999 days, 175319999 hours, and larger bounds for the smaller units up to the range of i64 for nanoseconds. A Span can be compared with ==.
enum Unit { Years Months Weeks Days Hours Minutes Seconds Milliseconds Microseconds Nanoseconds }

A unit of time that a Span counts, from the largest, Years, to the smallest, Nanoseconds. Years, Months, Weeks and Days are calendar units, whose length depends on the date they are applied to. The others are time units of a fixed length. Calendar years. Calendar months. Weeks of seven days. Calendar days. Hours of 3600 seconds. Minutes of 60 seconds. Seconds. Thousandths of a second. Millionths of a second. Billionths of a second.
Checks the increment and unit order of diff. Fails with OutOfRange when the increment is below 1 or above 1000000000 and with Invalid when smallest is a larger unit than largest.
Returns s with every count made non-negative.
Returns s with its time units set to 0.
fn count(s: Span, u: Unit) -> i64
Returns the count of u in s.
Returns the ten counts of s in order from years to nanoseconds.
Returns the count of days in s.
fn equal(a: Span, b: Span) -> bool
Returns whether a and b have the same count for every unit. 1 day and 24 hours are not equal.

Returns s in a short readable form, such as 1y 2mo 3d 4h 5m 6.5s. Zero is 0s and a negative span starts with -. Only the nonzero counts are written, using y, mo, w, d, h, m and s, and the sub-second units are folded into fractional seconds. A span of only sub-second units is a single ms, us or ns count. parse reads the result back.
Returns whether s has a nonzero count of years, months, weeks or days.
Returns whether s has a nonzero count of hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds.
Returns the count of hours in s.
Returns whether any count of s is below zero. All nonzero counts share a sign, so this is the sign of the span.
Returns whether every count of s is 0.
Returns the count of microseconds in s.
Returns the count of milliseconds in s.
fn minus(a: Span, b: Span) -> Span ! fault.Fault
Returns the span whose count for each unit is the count of a less the count of b. Fails in the same cases as plus.
Returns the count of minutes in s.
Returns the count of months in s.
Returns the count of nanoseconds in s.
Returns s with every count's sign reversed.
fn plus(a: Span, b: Span) -> Span ! fault.Fault

Returns the span whose count for each unit is the sum of the counts of a and b. Units are not carried into each other. Fails with OutOfRange naming the unit when a sum is beyond its bound and with Invalid when the result would mix positive and negative counts.
fn round_time(s: Span, smallest: Unit, increment: i64, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> Span ! fault.Fault

Returns s with its time units rounded to a multiple of increment of smallest, using mode, and its calendar units unchanged. The rounded time part is re-expressed from the larger of its largest unit in use and smallest, down to nanoseconds, and never carries into days. Fails with Invalid when smallest is a calendar unit or increment is below 1, and with OutOfRange or Overflow where duration.round does.
Returns the count of seconds in s.
Returns the Duration made by the time units of s. The calendar units are ignored.
Returns s with its calendar units set to 0.
Returns the Duration of s. Fails with Invalid when s has years, months, weeks or days, whose length depends on a date.

Returns s in the ISO 8601 duration form, such as P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.5S. Zero is P0D and a negative span starts with -. Only the nonzero counts are written, weeks are W, and the smaller units are folded into fractional seconds. parse reads the result back.
Returns the count of weeks in s.
fn with_unit(s: Span, u: Unit, n: i64) -> Span ! fault.Fault
Returns s with its count of u set to n. Fails in the same cases as from_counts.
Returns the count of years in s.
fn check_time_increment(smallest: Unit, increment: i64, largest: Unit) ! fault.Fault

Checks that increment of smallest rounds evenly within the next larger unit. For hours the increment must divide 24, for minutes and seconds 60, and for milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds 1000, and it must be smaller than that. Fails with Invalid otherwise. The check passes for calendar units and when largest is the same unit as smallest.
Returns whether u is Years, Months, Weeks or Days.
Returns the number of nanoseconds in one u. Fails with Invalid when u is a calendar unit, which has no fixed length.
Returns the position of u from 0 for Years to 9 for Nanoseconds. A smaller rank is a larger unit.
fn step_of(smallest: Unit, increment: i64) -> duration.Duration ! fault.Fault
Returns the length of increment of the time unit smallest. Fails with Invalid when smallest is a calendar unit or increment is below 1, and with OutOfRange when the length does not fit in a Duration.
Returns the plural lower-case name of u, such as days.
Returns a span of n days. Panics with span: days out of range when n is beyond the bound for days.

Returns the span with the ten counts in c, ordered from years to nanoseconds. Fails with Invalid when c does not have ten counts or when the counts have both positive and negative values, and with OutOfRange naming the unit when a count is beyond its bound.
fn from_duration(d: duration.Duration, largest: Unit) -> Span ! fault.Fault

Returns d as a span whose largest unit is largest, with the rest split into the smaller time units. Fails with Invalid when largest is a calendar unit and with OutOfRange when a count is beyond its bound. A negative d gives a negative span.
Returns a span of n hours. Panics with span: hours out of range when n is beyond the bound for hours.
Returns a span of n microseconds. Panics with span: microseconds out of range when n is beyond the bound for microseconds.
Returns a span of n milliseconds. Panics with span: milliseconds out of range when n is beyond the bound for milliseconds.
Returns a span of n minutes. Panics with span: minutes out of range when n is beyond the bound for minutes.
Returns a span of n months. Panics with span: months out of range when n is beyond the bound for months.
Returns a span of n nanoseconds. Panics with span: nanoseconds out of range when n is beyond the bound for nanoseconds.
fn of_calendar(years: i64, months: i64, weeks: i64, days: i64, time: duration.Duration) -> Span ! fault.Fault

Returns the span of years, months, weeks and days together with the time units of time, which are counted from hours down. Fails in the same cases as from_counts, and with Overflow or OutOfRange where from_duration does.
fn of_elapsed(elapsed: duration.Duration, diff: Diff) -> Span ! fault.Fault

Returns the exact length of time elapsed rounded as diff says and split into time units from diff.largest down. Fails with Invalid when diff.smallest or diff.largest is a calendar unit, and with OutOfRange or Overflow where duration.round and from_duration do.
fn of_unit(n: i64, u: Unit) -> Span ! fault.Fault
Returns the span of n of u. Fails in the same cases as from_counts.

Parses a span written in the ISO 8601 form or the friendly form. Both forms can start with + or -. The ISO form is P followed by nY, nM, nW and nD, then an optional T and nH, nM and nS, in that order, in either case. The friendly form is one or more counts each followed by y, mo, w, d, h, m, s, ms, us, µs or ns, with optional spaces. Each unit appears at most once and in descending order. A fraction is allowed on a time unit only, ends the span, must be exact in nanoseconds and has at most nine digits. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte and with OutOfRange or Invalid when a count is beyond its bound.
fn round_fraction(q: i64, num: duration.Duration, den: duration.Duration, negative: bool, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> i64

Returns the count q rounded to q or q + 1 using mode, given the fraction num over den that follows it. q is a non-negative magnitude and negative says the value it stands for is below zero, so Floor and Ceil act on the signed value. num and den are non-negative durations with den positive. A num of zero returns q.
Returns a span of n seconds. Panics with span: seconds out of range when n is beyond the bound for seconds.
Returns the unit at position rank, the inverse of rank. A rank outside 0 to 9 panics.
Returns a span of n weeks. Panics with span: weeks out of range when n is beyond the bound for weeks.
Returns a span of n years. Panics with span: years out of range when n is beyond the bound for years.
Returns the span with every count 0.
A time on a 24-hour clock with nanosecond precision, from 00:00 to 23:59:59.999999999. It has no date, offset or zone and is held as nanoseconds since midnight.
fn after(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> bool
Returns whether a is later in the day than b.
fn before(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> bool
Returns whether a is earlier in the day than b.
fn compare(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> i64
Returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is earlier than, the same as or later than b in the day.
fn equal(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are the same time of day.
fn format(t: TimeOfDay, layout: str) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns t printed through the layout layout, such as %H:%M or %I:%M %p. Fails with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout, as pattern.compile does, and otherwise as format_names does.
fn format_names(t: TimeOfDay, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns t printed through the compiled pattern p with the month, weekday and period words of names. Fails with Invalid when p needs a value a time of day does not have, such as a date or an offset.
fn format_with(t: TimeOfDay, p: pattern.Pattern) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns t printed through the compiled pattern p with English names. Fails as format_names does.
fn max(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> TimeOfDay
Returns the later of the two times, or a when they are equal.
Returns the whole microseconds within the second, from 0 to 999999.
Returns the whole milliseconds within the second, from 0 to 999.
fn min(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> TimeOfDay
Returns the earlier of the two times, or a when they are equal.
fn minus(t: TimeOfDay, d: duration.Duration) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns the time d before t. Fails with Overflow when the result is before midnight or on a later day. Use minus_wrapping to wrap around midnight instead.
fn minus_wrapping(t: TimeOfDay, d: duration.Duration) -> TimeOfDay
Returns the time d before t, wrapping around midnight in either direction. This never fails and discards whole days.
Returns the nanosecond within the second, from 0 to 999999999.
fn plus(t: TimeOfDay, d: duration.Duration) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns the time d after t. Fails with Overflow when the result is before midnight or on a later day. Use plus_wrapping to wrap around midnight instead.
fn plus_wrapping(t: TimeOfDay, d: duration.Duration) -> TimeOfDay
Returns the time d after t, wrapping around midnight in either direction. This never fails and discards whole days.
fn round(t: TimeOfDay, unit: span.Unit, increment: i64, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault

Returns t rounded to a multiple of increment units since midnight using mode. Fails with Overflow when the result is a full day, and otherwise as rounded_nanos does. Use round_wrapping to get midnight in that case.
fn round_wrapping(t: TimeOfDay, unit: span.Unit, increment: i64, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns t rounded like round, with a result of a full day wrapping to 00:00. Fails as rounded_nanos does.
fn rounded_nanos(t: TimeOfDay, unit: span.Unit, increment: i64, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> i64 ! fault.Fault

Returns t rounded to a multiple of increment units since midnight, as nanoseconds since midnight. The result can equal a full day when t rounds up past the end of the day. Fails with Invalid when unit is a calendar unit or increment is below 1 or does not divide the next larger unit evenly (24 for hours, 60 for minutes and seconds, 1000 for the smaller units), as span.check_time_increment states.
fn since(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> duration.Duration
Returns the duration from b to a, which is negative when a is earlier in the day. It does not wrap around midnight.
Returns the hour, minute, second and nanosecond of t as pattern Fields.
Returns t as hh:mm when the seconds and nanoseconds are zero and otherwise as hh:mm:ss with the fraction as to_string_seconds writes it.
Returns t as hh:mm:ss.nnnnnnnnn with all nine fraction digits.
Returns t as hh:mm:ss, followed by a fraction with trailing zeros removed when the nanosecond is not zero.
fn truncate(t: TimeOfDay, unit: span.Unit) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns t with everything below unit set to zero. Fails as round does.
fn until(a: TimeOfDay, b: TimeOfDay) -> duration.Duration
Returns the duration from a to b, which is negative when b is earlier in the day. It does not wrap around midnight.
fn with_hour(t: TimeOfDay, h: i64) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns t with the hour replaced by h. Fails with OutOfRange as of does.
fn with_minute(t: TimeOfDay, m: i64) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns t with the minute replaced by m. Fails with OutOfRange as of does.
fn with_nanosecond(t: TimeOfDay, ns: i64) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns t with the nanosecond replaced by ns. Fails with OutOfRange as of does.
fn with_second(t: TimeOfDay, s: i64) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns t with the second replaced by s. Fails with OutOfRange as of does.

Returns the time of day in f. The hour comes from hour or from hour12 with period, and the minute, second and nanosecond default to 0. Fails with Invalid when the fields do not give an hour or contradict each other, and with OutOfRange when a value is out of range.
Returns the time of day n nanoseconds after midnight. Fails with OutOfRange when n is negative or at least one day.
fn hm(h: i64, m: i64) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Returns the time of day at hour h and minute m. Fails with OutOfRange as of does.
Returns the last instant of the day, 23:59:59.999999999.
fn of(h: i64, m: i64, s: i64, ns: i64) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault

Returns the time of day with the hour h, minute m, second s and nanosecond ns. Fails with OutOfRange naming the field when h is outside 0 to 23, m or s is outside 0 to 59, or ns is outside 0 to 999999999. There is no leap second.

Parses a time written as hh, hh:mm, hh:mm:ss, hhmm or hhmmss, with an optional fraction of at most nine digits after the seconds. The text can start with T or t. A second of 60 is read as 59. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte and with OutOfRange when a field is out of range.
fn parse_names(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault

Parses s with the compiled pattern p and the words of names. Fails with Invalid when p uses a date, offset, zone or Unix-time verb, with Syntax or OutOfRange when s does not match, and with Invalid when the fields conflict or give no hour.
fn parse_pattern(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the compiled pattern p and English names. Fails as parse_names does.
fn parse_with(s: str, layout: str) -> TimeOfDay ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the layout layout and English names. Fails as parse_names does and with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout.

A point on the UTC timeline with nanosecond precision, from 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z to 9999-12-31T23:59:59.999999999Z. It is held as seconds since the Unix epoch and a nanosecond part that is never negative, so instants before the epoch also have a nanosecond part counted forward.
fn after(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> bool
Returns whether a is later than b.
fn before(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> bool
Returns whether a is earlier than b.
fn compare(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> i64
Returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is earlier than, the same as or later than b.
fn equal(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are the same instant.
fn max(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> Timestamp
Returns the later of the two instants, or a when they are equal.
fn min(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> Timestamp
Returns the earlier of the two instants, or a when they are equal.
fn minus(ts: Timestamp, d: duration.Duration) -> Timestamp ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant d before ts. Fails with Overflow where try_minus returns none.
fn plus(ts: Timestamp, d: duration.Duration) -> Timestamp ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant d after ts. Fails with Overflow where try_plus returns none.
fn round(ts: Timestamp, unit: duration.Duration, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> Timestamp ! fault.Fault

Returns ts rounded to a multiple of unit counted from the Unix epoch, using mode. Fails with Invalid when unit is zero or negative, with OutOfRange when unit is longer than about 146 years, and with Overflow when the rounded result leaves the supported years.
fn since(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> duration.Duration
Returns the duration from b to a, which is negative when a is earlier.
Returns the nanoseconds after the whole second, from 0 to 999999999.
Returns ts in the HTTP date form, such as Fri, 01 Mar 2024 12:30:00 GMT. A fraction of a second is dropped.
Returns ts in RFC 3339 form in UTC, such as 2024-03-01T12:30:00Z. The fraction is left out when it is zero and otherwise has 3, 6 or 9 digits, whichever is the fewest that is exact.
fn truncate(ts: Timestamp, unit: duration.Duration) -> Timestamp ! fault.Fault
Returns ts rounded toward zero to a multiple of unit counted from the Unix epoch. For an instant before the epoch this rounds toward the epoch, which is later. Fails in the same cases as round.
fn try_minus(ts: Timestamp, d: duration.Duration) -> Timestamp?
Returns the instant d before ts, or none when the result overflows or leaves the supported years.
fn try_plus(ts: Timestamp, d: duration.Duration) -> Timestamp?
Returns the instant d after ts, or none when the result overflows or leaves the supported years. A negative d moves backwards.
Returns the whole milliseconds since the Unix epoch, rounded toward negative infinity.
Returns the nanoseconds since the Unix epoch, or none when the count does not fit in an i64.
Returns the whole seconds since the Unix epoch, rounded toward negative infinity.
fn until(a: Timestamp, b: Timestamp) -> duration.Duration
Returns the duration from a to b, which is negative when b is earlier.
fn from_parts(secs: i64, nanos: i64) -> Timestamp ! fault.Fault

Returns the timestamp secs seconds and nanos nanoseconds after the Unix epoch. nanos can be any value, including a negative one or one beyond a second, and is carried into the seconds. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
Returns the timestamp secs seconds after the Unix epoch. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
Returns the timestamp ms milliseconds after the Unix epoch. Fails with OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
Returns the timestamp n nanoseconds after the Unix epoch. This never fails, because an i64 of nanoseconds covers only the years 1677 to 2262.

Parses an RFC 3339 date and time into a Timestamp. The form is YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss, an optional fraction of at most nine digits, and a required offset that is Z, z or a sign followed by hh, hh:mm or hh:mm:ss. The T can also be t or a space. A second of 60 is read as 59. The result is converted to UTC. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte, with OutOfRange when a field or the offset is out of range or the result is outside the supported years, and with Invalid when the day does not exist in the month.

Parses an HTTP date in the IMF-fixdate form (Fri, 01 Mar 2024 12:30:00 GMT), the RFC 850 form (Friday, 01-Mar-24 12:30:00 GMT) or the asctime form (Fri Mar 1 12:30:00 2024). The zone must be GMT where the form has one. A two-digit RFC 850 year of 69 to 99 is in the 1900s and any other is in the 2000s. Fails with Invalid when the weekday does not match the date, with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte, and with OutOfRange when a field is out of range.
Returns the names of all embedded zones in index order.
Returns a function that gives the embedded TZif data for a zone name, or none for an unknown name. It is the source argument for zone.load_from.
Returns the version label of the IANA time zone database embedded in the program.
enum Candidates { One(offset.Offset) Overlap(offset.Offset, offset.Offset) Gap(offset.Offset, offset.Offset) }

The offsets a zone allows for one local date and time, which a local time needs because daylight saving changes can repeat it or skip it. The local time occurs once, at only. The local time occurs twice because the clocks go back. earlier is the offset of the first occurrence and later is the offset of the second. The local time does not occur because the clocks go forward. before is the offset in force before the change and after is the offset after it.
struct Info { pub offset: offset.Offset pub abbreviation: str pub dst: bool }
The offset, abbreviation and daylight saving flag in force in a zone over some period. The offset from UTC. The zone abbreviation, such as CET or PDT. Whether daylight saving time is in effect.
struct Transition { pub at: timestamp.Timestamp pub before: Info pub after: Info }
A change in a zone's Info at one instant. The instant the change takes effect. The Info in force just before at. The Info in force from at.
A time zone: a name and the rules that give the UTC offset at each instant. Copies of a Zone share the same rules. A zone is made by named, local, load_from, from_posix, fixed or utc.
fn candidates(z: Zone, local_seconds: i64) -> Candidates

Returns the offsets z allows for a local time given as seconds since the Unix epoch counted as if the local clock were UTC. The result is One for a time that occurs once, Overlap for one that occurs twice and Gap for one that does not occur.

Returns the offset of z when z is the zone fixed makes for it, and none for every other zone. A zone from from_posix, decode or a database file is not such a zone, even when its offset never changes, because fixed also decides the name.
fn info_at(z: Zone, ts: timestamp.Timestamp) -> Info
Returns the Info in force in z at ts.
fn is_dst_at(z: Zone, ts: timestamp.Timestamp) -> bool
Returns whether daylight saving time is in effect in z at ts.
Returns whether z has a single offset for all time, with no recorded transitions and no daylight saving rule.
fn next_transition(z: Zone, ts: timestamp.Timestamp) -> Transition?

Returns the first change of offset, abbreviation or daylight saving flag after ts, or none when the zone has none after it. A fraction of a second in ts is ignored. A transition outside the supported timestamp years is not returned.
fn offset_at(z: Zone, ts: timestamp.Timestamp) -> offset.Offset
Returns the UTC offset in force in z at ts.
fn previous_transition(z: Zone, ts: timestamp.Timestamp) -> Transition?
Returns the latest change of offset, abbreviation or daylight saving flag before ts, or none when the zone has none before it.
fn transitions(z: Zone, from: timestamp.Timestamp, to: timestamp.Timestamp) -> []Transition
Returns the changes of z from from up to but not including to, in time order. At most 10000 are returned.
fn decode(name: str, data: []u8) -> Zone ! fault.Fault

Returns the zone name decoded from the TZif data data. It reads the 64-bit block of a version 2 or later file and its POSIX rule footer, which continues the zone past the last stored transition, and reads the 32-bit block of a version 1 file. Fails with Malformed when the header, a transition type, an offset, an abbreviation or the footer is not valid.
Returns a zone that always has the offset o. It is named UTC for a zero offset and otherwise by the offset text, such as +05:30, and that is also its abbreviation.
fn from_posix(rule: str, name: str) -> Zone ! fault.Fault

Returns a zone described by the POSIX TZ rule rule, named name. A rule such as CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3 has standard and daylight names, offsets and the dates the daylight period starts and ends. A rule without daylight saving gives a fixed zone. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first byte of the rule that does not fit.
fn load_from(name: str, source: fn(str) -> []u8?) -> Zone ! fault.Fault

Returns the zone with the name name, with its TZif data supplied by source. source returns the data for a name, or none when it has none. Use tzdata.source() to read the embedded database. Fails with Invalid for a bad name as named does, with UnknownZone when source returns none, and with Malformed when the data is not valid.

Returns the system's local time zone. The TZ environment variable is used when it is set. A leading : is dropped, an empty value is UTC, a value starting with / is a zone file, and other values are tried as a zone name and then as a POSIX rule. Failing all of those gives UnknownZone. Without TZ the zone comes from /etc/localtime, named from the link target after zoneinfo/ or Local, then from the name in /etc/timezone, and falls back to UTC.

Returns the zone with the IANA name name, such as Europe/Paris. The name is read from the directory in the ZONEINFO environment variable when it is set and has the file, and then from /usr/share/zoneinfo. Fails with Invalid when the name is empty, starts with /, or contains .., a backslash or a NUL byte. Fails with UnknownZone when no file has the name, except that UTC then returns utc(). Fails with Malformed when the file is unreadable or is not valid TZif data.
Returns the zone with a zero offset, named UTC.
enum Disambiguation { Compatible Earlier Later Reject }

How a local date-time that a zone's daylight saving change makes ambiguous or nonexistent is turned into an instant. A local time occurs twice when the clocks go back, an overlap, and not at all when they go forward, a gap. Takes the first occurrence in an overlap and, in a gap, moves the time forward by the length of the gap. A local 02:30 that does not exist becomes 03:30. Takes the first occurrence in an overlap and, in a gap, moves the time back by the length of the gap. A local 02:30 that does not exist becomes 01:30. Takes the second occurrence in an overlap and, in a gap, moves the time forward as Compatible does. Fails with Ambiguous in an overlap and with Skipped in a gap.
enum OffsetPolicy { Reject PreferOffset UseOffset UseZone }

What parse and its variants do with an offset written next to a zone. An offset is valid when the zone has it at the written local time. Uses a valid offset and fails with OffsetConflict for any other. Uses a valid offset, and for any other resolves the local time by the zone's rules, as Disambiguation.Compatible does. Always uses the written offset. The instant is the one the offset gives, shown in the zone, so the local time can differ from the one written. Ignores the written offset and resolves the local time by the zone's rules, as Disambiguation.Compatible does.

An instant in a time zone: the moment, the zone, and the local date-time and offset the zone has at that moment. It is the type for human-facing times. Arithmetic on the calendar fields follows the zone's wall clock, so adding a day keeps the local time across a daylight saving change, while adding a duration adds exact elapsed time. Comparison looks at the instant only. Copies share the zone's rules.
Returns the zone abbreviation at the instant of z, such as CEST.
fn after(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> bool
Returns whether the instant of a is later than that of b.
fn before(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> bool
Returns whether the instant of a is earlier than that of b.
fn compare(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> i64
Returns -1, 0 or 1 as the instant of a is earlier than, the same as or later than that of b. The zones are ignored.
Returns the local date of z.
Returns the local date and time of z.
Returns the local day of the month of z.
Returns the local day of the year of z, from 1.
fn duration_until(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> duration.Duration
Returns the exact elapsed time from a to b, which is negative when b is earlier.
Returns the last nanosecond of the local date of z, one nanosecond before the start of the next day. Fails with OutOfRange when that instant is outside the supported years.
fn equal(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are the same instant, whatever their zones.
fn format(z: Zoned, layout: str) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns z printed through the layout layout, such as %Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z. Fails with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout, as pattern.compile does.
fn format_names(z: Zoned, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns z printed through the compiled pattern p with the month, weekday and period words of names. All verbs are available, including %z, %Z and %s.
fn format_with(z: Zoned, p: pattern.Pattern) -> str ! fault.Fault
Returns z printed through the compiled pattern p with English names. Fails as format_names does.
Returns the local hour of z, from 0 to 23.
Returns the length of the local date of z as a duration. It is 24 hours except on a day that a daylight saving change shortens or lengthens.
fn in_zone(z: Zoned, other: zone.Zone) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the same instant of z shown in the zone other. Fails with OutOfRange when the local date-time in other falls outside the supported years.
Returns the offset, abbreviation and daylight saving flag of the zone at the instant of z.
Returns whether daylight saving time is in effect at the instant of z.
fn max(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> Zoned
Returns the later of the two, or a when they are the same instant.
fn min(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> Zoned
Returns the earlier of the two, or a when they are the same instant.
fn minus(z: Zoned, s: span.Span, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns z moved back by the span s. Fails as plus does.
fn minus_duration(z: Zoned, d: duration.Duration) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant d of elapsed time before z, in the same zone. Fails as plus_duration does.
Returns the local minute of z, from 0 to 59.
Returns the local month of z.
Returns the local month of z as a number from 1 to 12.
Returns the local nanosecond within the second of z.
Returns the zone's next change of offset after the instant of z, or none when there is none.
Returns the UTC offset of z at its instant.
fn plus(z: Zoned, s: span.Span, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault

Returns z moved forward by the span s. The years, months, weeks and days move the local date as date.plus does and keep the local time, with how deciding what happens when that time is an overlap or a gap. The time units are then added as exact elapsed time. A negative span moves backwards. Fails with Ambiguous or Skipped when how is Reject, with Overflow or OutOfRange when the result is outside the supported years.
fn plus_duration(z: Zoned, d: duration.Duration) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant d of elapsed time after z, in the same zone. The local time can jump across a daylight saving change. Fails with Overflow when the result is outside the supported years.
Returns the zone's latest change of offset before the instant of z, or none when there is none.
fn round(z: Zoned, unit: span.Unit, increment: i64, mode: rounding.Rounding) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault

Returns z rounded to a multiple of increment units of local time using mode. unit can be Days, which needs an increment of 1 and rounds to the start of this or the next day by the actual length of the day. A smaller unit rounds the local wall time. When the result is in an overlap it takes the later occurrence only if z is already on it, and when it is in a gap it uses the offset before the change. Fails with Invalid when unit is a larger calendar unit or the increment does not divide the next larger unit as timeofday.rounded_nanos states, and with OutOfRange or Overflow when the result is outside the supported years.
fn same_instant_and_zone(a: Zoned, b: Zoned) -> bool
Returns whether a and b are the same instant in zones with the same name.
Returns the local second of z, from 0 to 59.
fn series(start: Zoned, step: span.Span, count: i64, how: Disambiguation) -> []Zoned ! fault.Fault

Returns count instants starting at start, each one step after the one before, with how deciding what happens in an overlap or a gap. Item k is start plus k steps in one move, so a month-end clamp in one item does not carry into the next. Fails with Invalid when count is negative, with OutOfRange when it is above a million, and otherwise as plus does.
fn since(a: Zoned, b: Zoned, diff: span.Diff) -> span.Span ! fault.Fault
Returns the span from b to a, measured and rounded as diff says. Fails as until does.

Returns the first instant of the local date of z. It is usually midnight, but when a gap skips midnight it is the first instant after the gap. Fails with OutOfRange when that instant is outside the supported years.
Returns the local time of day of z.
Returns the local date and time, the offset, the zone abbreviation and the Unix seconds of z as pattern Fields.
Returns z in the RFC 2822 form, such as Fri, 01 Mar 2024 12:30:00 +0100. A fraction of a second is dropped.
Returns z in RFC 3339 form with its offset, such as 2024-03-01T12:30:00+01:00. The offset is written Z when the zone is UTC. A fraction of a second is written when it is not zero.

Returns z in the RFC 3339 form followed by the zone name in brackets, such as 2024-03-01T12:30:00+01:00[Europe/Paris]. The annotation is [UTC] for UTC and is left out for a fixed-offset zone named by its offset. parse reads the result back.
fn truncate(z: Zoned, unit: span.Unit) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns z with everything below unit set to zero in local time. Fails as round does.
fn until(a: Zoned, b: Zoned, diff: span.Diff) -> span.Span ! fault.Fault

Returns the span from a to b, measured and rounded as diff says. When diff.largest is a calendar unit, b is moved into the zone of a and years, months, weeks and days are counted on its wall clock, so a day can be 23 or 25 hours long, and the remainder is split into time units. Otherwise the span is the exact elapsed time split into time units from largest down. Rounding is relative to a. The span is negative when b is earlier. Fails with Invalid when the options are inconsistent as span.check_diff and span.check_time_increment state, and with OutOfRange or Overflow where the result cannot be represented.
Returns the local day of the week of z.
fn with_date(z: Zoned, d: date.Date, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns z with its local date replaced by d and its local time of day kept, with how deciding what happens in an overlap or a gap. The instant changes. Fails as from_civil does.
fn with_datetime(z: Zoned, dt: datetime.DateTime, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant at which the zone of z shows dt, with how deciding what happens in an overlap or a gap. Fails as from_civil does.
fn with_time(z: Zoned, t: timeofday.TimeOfDay, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns z with its local time of day replaced by t and its local date kept, with how deciding what happens in an overlap or a gap. The instant changes. Fails as from_civil does.
Returns the local year of z.
fn from_civil(dt: datetime.DateTime, tz: zone.Zone, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault

Returns the instant at which the zone tz shows the local date-time dt, with how deciding what happens in an overlap or a gap. Fails with Ambiguous or Skipped when how is Reject and the time is an overlap or a gap, and with OutOfRange when the instant is outside the supported years.
fn from_parts(d: date.Date, t: timeofday.TimeOfDay, tz: zone.Zone, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant at which the zone tz shows the date d and the time of day t, with how deciding what happens in an overlap or a gap. Fails as from_civil does.
Returns the current time in the zone tz. Fails with OutOfRange as of does.
fn now_in(c: clock.Clock, tz: zone.Zone) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the time shown by the clock c in the zone tz. Fails with OutOfRange as of does.
fn of(ts: timestamp.Timestamp, tz: zone.Zone) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant ts seen in the zone tz. Fails with OutOfRange when the local date-time in the zone falls outside the supported years.
Parses a zoned date-time such as 2024-03-01T12:30:00+01:00[Europe/Paris], with zones loaded by zone.named and an offset that disagrees with the zone rejected. Fails as parse_using_options does.
fn parse_names(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault

Parses s with the compiled pattern p and the words of names into a time in a fixed-offset zone. The pattern must either give the Unix time with %s, or give a full date, a time of day and an offset with %z. A Z or z is read as a zero offset. The zone is a fixed zone of the written offset, or UTC when only %s is given. Other fields that are present must agree with the instant. Fails with Invalid when the fields do not give an instant or conflict, with Syntax or OutOfRange when s does not match, and with OutOfRange for an offset that is too large.
fn parse_names_zone(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern, names: pattern.Names, tz: zone.Zone, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault

Parses s with the compiled pattern p and the words of names into a time in the zone tz, with how deciding what happens when the local time is an overlap or a gap. The pattern gives either a date and a time of day or the Unix time with %s. An offset written with %z must be one that tz has at that local time or the parse fails with OffsetConflict. A zone abbreviation written with %Z must match the one the zone has at that instant or the parse fails with Invalid. Also fails as from_civil does.
fn parse_pattern(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the compiled pattern p and English names. Fails as parse_names does.
fn parse_pattern_zone(s: str, p: pattern.Pattern, tz: zone.Zone, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the compiled pattern p and English names into a time in the zone tz. Fails as parse_names_zone does.
fn parse_using(s: str, loader: fn(str) -> zone.Zone ! fault.Fault) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Parses a zoned date-time as parse_using_options does with the policy Reject.
fn parse_using_options(s: str, policy: OffsetPolicy, loader: fn(str) -> zone.Zone ! fault.Fault) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault

Parses a zoned date-time such as 2024-03-01T12:30:00+01:00[Europe/Paris], with policy deciding what happens when the offset disagrees with the zone and loader supplying the zone for a name. The text is a date-time as datetime.parse reads it, then an optional Z or offset, then bracketed annotations. A name in brackets such as [Europe/Paris] is passed to loader, and [+01:00] is a fixed offset. A [u-ca=iso8601] calendar annotation is accepted, and another calendar fails with Unsupported. A ! in front of an annotation marks it critical, and an unknown critical annotation fails with Unsupported. Unknown annotations that are not critical are ignored. Without a zone annotation the offset or Z is required and the result has a fixed-offset zone. With a zone annotation the offset is optional, and without it the local time is resolved as Disambiguation.Compatible does. Fails with Syntax at the offset of the first bad byte, with OffsetConflict under Reject, and with the fault loader returns for an unknown name.
fn parse_with(s: str, layout: str) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the layout layout and English names. Fails as parse_names does and with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout.
fn parse_with_options(s: str, policy: OffsetPolicy) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Parses a zoned date-time as parse_using_options does, with zones loaded by zone.named.
fn parse_with_zone(s: str, layout: str, tz: zone.Zone, how: Disambiguation) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Parses s with the layout layout and English names into a time in the zone tz. Fails as parse_names_zone does and with Syntax or Unsupported for a bad layout.
fn strict(dt: datetime.DateTime, tz: zone.Zone) -> Zoned ! fault.Fault
Returns the instant at which the zone tz shows dt, failing when dt is not exactly one instant. It is from_civil with Reject.

struct Config { pub server_name: str pub alpn: []str pub roots: []x509.Certificate pub verify: bool pub groups: []i64 pub cipher_suites: []i64 pub min_version: i64 pub max_version: i64 pub certificates: [][]u8 pub key: x509.PrivateKey? }

The settings of a TLS client or server, shared by client, server and dial. The defaults give a verifying client for TLS 1.2 and 1.3. A server also needs certificates and key. The host name the client sends as the SNI (RFC 6066) and verifies the certificate against. An IP address is not sent as SNI. The empty string, the default, sends no name and, with verify on, accepts any certificate name. The application protocols for ALPN (RFC 7301), such as ["h2", "http/1.1"]. A client offers them and fails with Malformed when the server selects one not listed. A server selects the first of its own that the client offers, or none. Empty by default. The trust anchors a client verifies the server chain against. When empty, the default, the system roots from x509.system_roots are used. Whether a client verifies the server certificate chain and name. Defaults to true; false accepts any certificate and removes the protection against an active attacker. The named group codes for key exchange in order of preference, from x25519_mlkem768, group_x25519, group_p256 and group_p384. The default is all four in that order. A client sends a key share for the first one, and also for X25519 when the first is the hybrid. The cipher suite codes in order of preference. The default is 0x1301, 0x1303 and 0x1302 for TLS 1.3 and for TLS 1.2 the ECDHE suites with AES-128-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-256-GCM, for ECDSA (0xC02B, 0xCCA9, 0xC02C) and RSA (0xC02F, 0xCCA8, 0xC030) certificates. The lowest protocol version accepted, as tls12 or tls13. Defaults to TLS 1.2. A range outside TLS 1.2 to 1.3 makes the handshake fail with Invalid. The highest protocol version accepted, as tls12 or tls13. Defaults to TLS 1.3. For a server, the DER encoded certificate chain it presents, leaf first; see x509.pem_certificates. Unused by a client. For a server, the private key of the leaf certificate; see x509.pem_private_key. Unused by a client.

The QUIC encryption level a handshake message or traffic secret belongs to (RFC 9001 section 4.1.4). The level of the packets protected with the keys derived from the destination connection ID, which carry the ClientHello and ServerHello. The level of the packets protected with the handshake traffic secrets, which carry the rest of the handshake. The level of the 1-RTT packets protected with the application traffic secrets.
struct QuicData { pub level: Level pub data: []u8 }

Handshake bytes received in QUIC CRYPTO frames, with the level of the packets that carried them. The level of the packets that carried data. The contiguous CRYPTO stream bytes, which may end inside a handshake message.
struct QuicResult { pub protocol: str pub group: i64 pub suite: Suite pub peer_certificates: []x509.Certificate pub peer_parameters: []u8 }

The outcome of a QUIC handshake. The ALPN protocol that was negotiated. Never empty. The named group code of the key exchange. The authenticated cipher in use. The certificate chain the server presented, leaf first. Empty on the server side, which does not request client certificates. The body of the peer's quic_transport_parameters extension, as received.
struct QuicSecret { pub level: Level pub writing: bool pub suite: Suite pub secret: []u8 }

A traffic secret the handshake hands to QUIC. The level whose packets the secret protects. Whether the secret protects the packets this endpoint sends. false means the packets it receives. The AEAD and hash of the negotiated cipher suite, which QUIC uses to derive the packet protection keys. The traffic secret, as long as the hash output of suite.
struct QuicTransport { pub parameters: []u8 pub send: fn(Level, []u8) ! io.Error pub receive: fn() -> QuicData ! io.Error pub install: fn(QuicSecret) ! io.Error pub alert: fn(i64) }

The QUIC side of a handshake run by quic_client or quic_server. The handshake calls these functions from the green thread that runs it, so they may block. The encoded QUIC transport parameters of this endpoint, sent in the quic_transport_parameters extension (0x39) of the ClientHello or EncryptedExtensions. Sends handshake bytes in CRYPTO frames at a level. Called with a whole handshake message, or several, at the level that was current when the handshake wrote them. An error aborts the handshake and is returned by it. Blocks for the next handshake bytes received in CRYPTO frames. An error, such as Eof or TimedOut for a connection that failed, aborts the handshake and is returned by it. Installs a traffic secret. Called in the order the handshake derives the secrets. An error aborts the handshake and is returned by it. Reports a fatal TLS alert, which QUIC sends as a connection error with code 0x100 plus the alert description.

An established TLS connection that closes itself when dropped. Dropping it sends a close_notify alert and closes the underlying stream. handle is the copyable view used by read_on, write_on, close_on and stream_on. The copyable view of this connection.
struct SessionHandle { pub protocol: str pub version: i64 pub group: i64 pub suite: Suite pub cipher_suite: i64 pub peer_certificates: []x509.Certificate ... }

A copyable view of an established TLS connection. Copies refer to the same connection. Closing through any copy closes it for all of them. The ALPN protocol that was negotiated, or the empty string when none was. The negotiated protocol version: 0x0303 for TLS 1.2 or 0x0304 for TLS 1.3. The named group code of the key exchange. The authenticated cipher in use. The negotiated cipher suite as its code on the wire. The certificate chain the server presented, leaf first. Empty on the server side, which does not request client certificates.

The authenticated cipher of a negotiated cipher suite. The TLS 1.3 key schedule uses SHA-384 with Aes256Gcm and SHA-256 with the others. The TLS 1.2 suites map onto the same values by their cipher. AES-128-GCM with a 16-byte key, TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 in TLS 1.3. AES-256-GCM with a 32-byte key, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 in TLS 1.3. ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439) with a 32-byte key, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 in TLS 1.3.
fn quic_client(t: QuicTransport, config: Config) -> QuicResult ! io.Error

Performs the client side of a QUIC TLS 1.3 handshake (RFC 9001) through t and returns the outcome. Only TLS 1.3 is used, whatever config.min_version says, and only the TLS 1.3 suites of config.cipher_suites are offered. The ClientHello carries an empty legacy_session_id, the ALPN list config.alpn and t.parameters as extension 0x39. The server certificate is verified as client does. Handshake messages go out through t.send, come in through t.receive and the traffic secrets go to t.install: Handshake read, Handshake write, Application write and Application read, in that order. Returns after the client Finished has been sent and reads no post-handshake messages. Fails with Invalid when config.max_version is below TLS 1.3, when t.parameters is longer than 16384 bytes, when config.alpn is empty, when no usable suite or group remains or when verification fails, with Unsupported when the server selects nothing the client offered or no application protocol, with TooLarge for a handshake message longer than 65536 bytes (alert 22) and with Malformed for other protocol violations: an EncryptedExtensions without transport parameters (alert 109) or with more than 16384 bytes of them (alert 47), handshake data received at a level other than the current one and bytes left in the handshake buffer when a key changes (alert 10), and messages that do not parse (alert 50). A fatal failure is reported once through t.alert. Errors of t.send, t.receive and t.install are returned unchanged.
fn quic_server(t: QuicTransport, config: Config) -> QuicResult ! io.Error

Performs the server side of a QUIC TLS 1.3 handshake (RFC 9001) through t and returns the outcome. Requires config.certificates and config.key. Only TLS 1.3 is used, whatever config.min_version says, and only the TLS 1.3 suites of config.cipher_suites are chosen. Suite, group and signature scheme are chosen as server does, with a HelloRetryRequest when the client sent no share for the chosen group. The first protocol in config.alpn that the client also offers is selected and t.parameters goes out as extension 0x39 of the EncryptedExtensions. Handshake messages go out through t.send, come in through t.receive and the traffic secrets go to t.install: Handshake write, Handshake read, then after the client Finished, Application write and Application read. Returns after the client Finished has been verified and reads no post-handshake messages. Fails with Invalid for missing certificates or key, when config.max_version is below TLS 1.3 or when t.parameters is longer than 16384 bytes, with Unsupported when no version, suite, group, scheme or application protocol is shared (alert 120, no_application_protocol, for the last), with TooLarge for a handshake message longer than 65536 bytes (alert 22) and with Malformed for other protocol violations: a ClientHello with a non-empty legacy_session_id (alert 47), without transport parameters (alert 109) or with more than 16384 bytes of them (alert 47), handshake data received at a level other than the current one and bytes left in the handshake buffer when a key changes (alert 10), and messages that do not parse (alert 50). A fatal failure is reported once through t.alert. Errors of t.send, t.receive and t.install are returned unchanged.

Sends a close_notify alert and closes the underlying stream. Closing an already closed session does nothing. The alert is best effort and its failure is ignored. Later reads and writes fail with NotConnected.
fn read(t: Session, buf: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error

Reads up to buf.len decrypted bytes into buf and returns the count, or 0 when the peer has sent close_notify. Blocks the green thread until application data arrives. Handshake messages that arrive in between are handled: a TLS 1.3 key update is applied, session tickets are ignored, and a TLS 1.2 renegotiation request is refused with a no_renegotiation alert. Fails with NotConnected after close, with Refused when the peer sends a fatal alert and with Malformed for an unexpected record.
Returns an io.Stream over t whose read, write and close are read, write and close.
fn update_keys(t: Session, request_peer: bool) ! io.Error

Rotates the sending keys with a TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate (RFC 8446 section 4.6.3). With request_peer set, the peer is asked to rotate its sending keys too. Fails with Unsupported on a TLS 1.2 connection and with NotConnected after close.
fn write(t: Session, data: []u8) -> i64 ! io.Error

Encrypts and writes all of data and returns data.len. Data is sent in records of at most 16384 bytes. Blocks the green thread until the bytes are handed to the underlying stream. Fails with NotConnected after close, with Aborted after a fatal error on the connection and otherwise with the stream's error.
Sends a close_notify alert and closes the underlying stream through the view t. See close.
Reads up to buf.len decrypted bytes through the view t. See read.
Returns an io.Stream over the view t. Streams made from the same view share the connection, and closing one closes it for all.
Encrypts and writes all of data through the view t. See write.
fn cipher(s: Suite, key: []u8) -> aead.Aead ! io.Error
Returns the AEAD of s keyed with key. Fails with Invalid for a key length the cipher does not take: 16 or 32 bytes for AES-GCM, 32 for ChaCha20-Poly1305.
Returns the key length of s in bytes: 16 for Aes128Gcm and 32 for the others.
Returns the TLS 1.3 cipher suite code of s: 0x1301, 0x1302 or 0x1303 for Aes128Gcm, Aes256Gcm and ChaCha20Poly1305.
Returns the hash of the TLS 1.3 key schedule for s: SHA-384 for Aes256Gcm and SHA-256 for the others.
The TLS named group code 0x0017 for secp256r1, the NIST P-256 curve.
The TLS named group code 0x0018 for secp384r1, the NIST P-384 curve.
The TLS named group code 0x001D for x25519 (RFC 7748, RFC 8446 section 4.2.7).

The TLS named group code 0x11EC, the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid of X25519 and ML-KEM-768. The client share is the 1184-byte ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key followed by the 32-byte X25519 public key, and the server share is the 1088-byte ML-KEM ciphertext followed by the 32-byte X25519 public key. The shared secret is the 32-byte ML-KEM secret followed by the 32-byte X25519 secret. It is offered with TLS 1.3 only.
fn client(s: io.Stream, config: Config) -> Session ! io.Error

Performs a TLS client handshake over s and returns the established session. Offers the versions, cipher suites and groups of config (TLS 1.3, RFC 8446, and TLS 1.2, RFC 5246 with ECDHE key exchange and AEAD suites) and blocks the green thread until the handshake completes. Unless config.verify is false, the server certificate chain is verified with x509.verify_chain against config.roots, or the system roots when that list is empty, for the host config.server_name. A certificate failure sends a bad_certificate alert and fails with Invalid. A client certificate is never sent; a certificate request is answered with an empty certificate list. Fails with Invalid for an unusable config (a version range outside TLS 1.2 to 1.3, no usable cipher suite or group) or a failed verification, with Unsupported when the server selects nothing the client offered, with Malformed for protocol violations and with Eof, Refused or the stream's error when the connection ends. A failed handshake does not close s. When it succeeds, closing or dropping the Session also closes s.
fn client_handle(s: io.Stream, config: Config) -> *SessionHandle ! io.Error

Performs a TLS client handshake over s and returns the copyable SessionHandle. Behaves as client, but the result is not dropped automatically: the caller closes it with close_on. Use it to move a session between green threads.
fn dial(host: str, port: i64, config: Config) -> Session ! io.Error

Connects to host and port over TCP and performs a TLS client handshake. config.server_name defaults to host when empty, which sets both the SNI sent and the name the certificate is checked against. The TCP connection is closed if the handshake fails. Fails as client does for a failed handshake, and with the error of net.dial when the connection cannot be made. Blocks the green thread.
fn expand_label(h: hash.Algorithm, secret: []u8, label: str, context: []u8, length: i64) -> []u8

Returns length bytes of HKDF-Expand-Label (RFC 8446 section 7.1) over secret with label, which gets the tls13 prefix, and context. QUIC derives its packet protection keys with it (RFC 9001 section 5.1).
fn server(s: io.Stream, config: Config) -> Session ! io.Error

Performs a TLS server handshake over s and returns the established session. Requires config.certificates and config.key. Accepts TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 within the version range of config. The cipher suite is the first in config.cipher_suites that the client also offers and that suits the key; the group is the first in config.groups the client supports, with a HelloRetryRequest when the client sent no share for it; the signature scheme must be one the client offers and the key allows (RSA keys sign with PSS in TLS 1.3). The first protocol in config.alpn that the client also offers is selected. Client certificates are not requested. Blocks the green thread until the handshake completes. Fails with Invalid when the key or certificates are missing or the version range is unusable, with Unsupported when no version, suite, group or scheme is shared and with Malformed or Invalid for protocol violations. A failed handshake does not close s. When it succeeds, closing or dropping the Session also closes s.
fn server_handle(s: io.Stream, config: Config) -> *SessionHandle ! io.Error

Performs a TLS server handshake over s and returns the copyable SessionHandle. Behaves as server, but the result is not dropped automatically: the caller closes it with close_on. Use it to hand a session to a green thread.
struct DateTime { pub year: i64 pub month: i64 pub day: i64 pub hour: i64 pub minute: i64 pub second: i64 pub nanosecond: i64 pub offset: i64 }

A TOML date, a time, or both, as the fields of a calendar date and a clock time. Which fields hold data depends on the Value variant that carries it: LocalDate uses year, month and day, LocalTime uses hour, minute, second and nanosecond, and LocalDateTime and OffsetDateTime use all of them. The other fields are 0. datetime_text formats it as RFC 3339 text. The year, 0 to 9999. The month, 1 to 12. The day of the month, 1 to 31, valid for the month. The hour, 0 to 23. The minute, 0 to 59. The second, 0 to 59; a leap second is not accepted. The fraction of a second in nanoseconds, 0 to 999999999. Digits beyond nine are truncated by the parser. The offset from UTC in minutes, east positive; 0 for Z. It is only meaningful for an OffsetDateTime.
The error returned when parsing TOML fails. The document is not valid TOML. line and column count from 1, with the column in bytes from the start of the line, and message describes the problem.
struct Table { pub keys: []str pub values: [str: Value] }
An ordered table of keys and values. The keys in the order they were first inserted or appeared in the document, each once. The value of each key in keys.
enum Value { Str(str) Int(i64) Float(f64) Bool(bool) OffsetDateTime(DateTime) LocalDateTime(DateTime) LocalDate(DateTime) LocalTime(DateTime) Array([]Value) Table(*Table) }

A TOML value (TOML 1.0.0). A string. A 64-bit signed integer. The parser rejects a literal outside that range. A 64-bit float, including inf, -inf and nan. A boolean. A date and time with an offset from UTC, such as 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z. A date and time without an offset, such as 1979-05-27T07:32:00. A date without a time, such as 1979-05-27. A time without a date, such as 07:32:00. An array of values. Elements may have different types. A table, which a Value holds by pointer; inline tables and [table] sections both produce one.
Returns the array at path, or none when the path does not exist or the value is not an array. An array of tables is an array of Table values. See get for path.
Returns the boolean at path, or none when the path does not exist or the value is not a boolean. See get for path.

Returns the DateTime at path for any of the four date and time kinds, or none when the path does not exist or the value is none of them. The kind is lost, so use get to tell them apart. See get for path.

Returns the TOML text for the table t. Keys that hold plain values are written first, as key = value, then each sub-table as a [table] section and each non-empty array whose elements are all tables as repeated [[array]] sections, all in key order and separated by blank lines. Other arrays are written inline as [1, 2], and tables inside them as { a = 1 }. Keys are bare when they hold only letters, digits, _ and -, and quoted otherwise. Strings are written as basic strings with the escapes \", \\, \n, \t and \r, and other control characters as \u00XX; other characters are written as they are. A float always shows a . or exponent, so it reads back as a float, and NaN is written as nan. Dates and times use datetime_text.
Returns the float at path, or none when the path does not exist or the value is not a float; an integer is not converted. See get for path.

Converts the table t into a T through std/serde. A struct is read from the table's keys: unknown keys are skipped, a missing key takes the field's default or none for an optional, and any other missing key fails with Missing. Integers are read from Int, floats from Float or Int, a []u8 from a base64 string, and a str from a string or from a date or time, which becomes its RFC 3339 text. An enum variant is a string, or a table with one key that names the variant. Fails with serde.Error.Mismatch when a value has another type and with Range for a negative integer read as unsigned. In errors, at counts the values consumed so far.

Returns the value at path in t, or none when there is none. path is a TOML key, with dots for nesting and quotes for a part that contains a dot or other characters outside letters, digits, _ and -, for example server.http or a."b.c". Only tables are entered, never arrays. It returns none for a path that is not a valid key, a missing part, or a part that is not a table.
fn insert(t: *Table, key: str, v: Value)
Sets key to v in t. A new key is appended to keys; an existing key keeps its position and takes the new value.
Returns the integer at path, or none when the path does not exist or the value is not an integer. See get for path.
Returns the table at path, or none when the path does not exist or the value is not a table. See get for path.
Returns the string at path, or none when the path does not exist or the value is not a string. See get for path.

Returns the RFC 3339 text of a date or time value, or none for any other value. An OffsetDateTime is YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS followed by Z for a zero offset or +HH:MM or -HH:MM; a LocalDateTime is the same without the offset, a LocalDate is YYYY-MM-DD and a LocalTime is HH:MM:SS. A fraction of a second is written after a . with trailing zeros removed, and left out when it is zero.

Parses the TOML text source into a T. Equivalent to parse followed by from_table. A syntax error becomes serde.Error.Syntax whose line is the line of the error and whose message includes the line and column.

Parses the TOML document source into its root table. The text must be valid UTF-8 and follow TOML 1.0.0, including every restriction on redefining tables and keys through headers, dotted keys, inline tables and arrays of tables. A leading byte order mark is skipped, and \r\n is read as a newline. Keys keep their document order. Values nested deeper than 128 levels are rejected. Fails with Syntax, which carries the line and column of the problem.
Returns v as TOML text. Equivalent to to_table followed by encode; fails like to_table.

Converts v into a table through std/serde. v must be a struct or a map, which becomes the table, since TOML documents are tables. A none field is left out. A []u8 becomes a base64 string and a u64 above 9223372036854775807 fails with serde.Error.Range. Fails with Mismatch when v is not a table, or an array holds none. An enum variant without fields is a string and a variant with fields a table with one key, the variant's name.
struct Bitmap { pub width: i64 pub height: i64 pub left: i64 pub top: i64 pub coverage: []u8 }

A glyph's coverage at one size, one byte per pixel from 0 to 255, rows from the top. The number of columns. The number of rows. The distance in pixels from the pen position to the left edge of the first column. The distance in pixels from the baseline down to the top edge of the first row, negative for rows above the baseline. The coverage of each pixel, width * height bytes.

A closed loop of points: lines between consecutive on-curve points, and a quadratic curve through each run of off-curve points. Between two consecutive off-curve points the curve passes through their midpoint, which the list leaves out. The points in file order.

Why a font was rejected. A table or offset runs past the end of the data, or a count, length or index disagrees with another. table names the table, or header or directory. The data is a well-formed font that holds something this module does not read: CFF outlines, a font collection or no usable character map. table names it.
struct Font { pub units_per_em: i64 pub ascent: i64 pub descent: i64 pub line_gap: i64 pub glyph_count: i64 ... }

A TrueType font with glyf outlines, held as the bytes it was parsed from. Metrics are in font units, units_per_em to the em square, with y up. The number of font units in the em square. The distance from the baseline to the top of a line, in font units. The distance from the baseline to the bottom of a line in font units, negative below the baseline. The extra space between one line's descent and the next line's ascent, in font units. The number of glyphs, which are numbered from 0, the glyph drawn for a missing character.
The shape of a glyph, in font units. The closed loops, which fill by the non-zero winding rule.
struct Point { pub x: f32 pub y: f32 pub on_curve: bool }

A point of a glyph outline, in font units with y up. The distance right of the glyph's origin. The distance above the baseline. Whether the point is on the curve, or a control point of a quadratic curve.
fn advance(f: Font, glyph: i64) -> i64
Returns the distance in font units from the pen position of glyph to the next one, or 0 for a glyph the font does not have.
fn glyph_index(f: Font, code_point: u32) -> i64
Returns the glyph that draws code_point, or 0 when the font has none.
fn kern(f: Font, left: i64, right: i64) -> i64
Returns the font units to add to the pen position between the glyphs left and right, negative to bring them closer, or 0 when the font has no kern pair for them.
fn outline(f: Font, glyph: i64) -> Outline

Returns the outline of glyph, with each component of a composite glyph placed by its offset and scale. A component placed by matching points instead of an offset is supported; SCALED_COMPONENT_OFFSET is not, so offsets are never scaled. A composite nests at most 6 deep and holds at most 64 components in all. A space, a glyph the font does not have and a glyph whose data is truncated or inconsistent give an outline with no contours.
fn rasterize(f: Font, glyph: i64, pixel_size: f32) -> Bitmap

Returns the coverage of glyph with the em square pixel_size pixels tall, the pen at the origin of an integer pixel grid. The outline is flattened into lines, each of which adds its signed area and cover to the pixels it crosses; a running sum along each row then gives the winding coverage, clamped to full. A glyph with no outline, a pixel_size that is not positive and a glyph more than 2048 pixels wide or tall give an empty bitmap.
fn scale(f: Font, pixel_size: f32) -> f32
Returns the number of pixels one font unit covers when the em square is pixel_size pixels.
Returns Go Regular, the font embedded in the standard library.

Reads the TrueType font in data. The head, hhea, maxp, cmap, hmtx, loca and glyf tables are required and kern is optional. A cmap subtable of format 12 or 4 is used, preferring a Unicode one that covers every plane. Only the first horizontal kern subtable of format 0 is read. Every table in the directory, and the loca offsets, are checked here. Glyph data and lookup tables are read when used, and a malformed one gives glyph 0, an empty outline or a zero metric instead of an error.
extern pub struct Color { pub r: f32 pub g: f32 pub b: f32 pub a: f32 }
An sRGB-encoded colour with straight alpha, each channel from 0.0 to 1.0. The red channel. The green channel. The blue channel. The alpha channel, 0.0 transparent and 1.0 opaque.
extern pub struct Corners { pub top_left: f32 pub top_right: f32 pub bottom_right: f32 pub bottom_left: f32 }
One radius per corner, clockwise from the top left. The top-left corner. The top-right corner. The bottom-right corner. The bottom-left corner.
extern pub struct Edges { pub top: f32 pub right: f32 pub bottom: f32 pub left: f32 }
One length per side, in the order top, right, bottom, left. The top side. The right side. The bottom side. The left side.
extern pub struct Point { pub x: f32 pub y: f32 }
A position in pixels from the top left, x to the right and y down. The distance to the right. The distance down.
extern pub struct Rect { pub x: f32 pub y: f32 pub width: f32 pub height: f32 }

An axis-aligned rectangle: its top-left corner and its size. Its fields are laid out as four f32s, the order the shaders read a rectangle in. The left edge. The top edge. The width, never negative in a rectangle this module returns. The height, never negative in a rectangle this module returns.
extern pub struct Size { pub width: f32 pub height: f32 }
A width and a height in pixels. The horizontal extent. The vertical extent.
fn with_alpha(c: Color, a: f32) -> Color
Returns c with its alpha replaced by a.
fn scale_corners(c: Corners, factor: f32) -> Corners
Returns c with every radius multiplied by factor.
Returns the sum of the left and right edges of e.
fn scale_edges(e: Edges, factor: f32) -> Edges
Returns e with every edge multiplied by factor.
Returns the sum of the top and bottom edges of e.
Returns the y coordinate of the bottom edge of r.

The ways opening a GPU, drawing or reading back can fail. A Vulkan call returned a failing result. call names the function and result is its VkResult. No memory type of the device has the property flags a resource needs. allowed is the bit set of types the resource accepts and flags the property flags wanted. A target was asked for with a width or height below one pixel. present was called on a Gpu that open made, which has no window surface.

A Vulkan 1.3 instance and device with the pipelines, glyph atlas texture and frame resources that draw a scene.Scene. Releasing a Gpu waits for the device to go idle and destroys everything it created. Every Target made from it must be released first, which using does when the targets are bound after the Gpu.

An offscreen image that scenes are drawn into and read back from, R8G8B8A8_UNORM with width by height pixels. A Target must be released before the Gpu it was made from. Releasing it waits for the device to go idle. The width in pixels. The height in pixels.
Returns a one-line description of e, naming the Vulkan call and result when there is one.
fn present(g: Gpu, s: scene.Scene, mut atlas: scene.Atlas) ! Error

Draws s into the next image of the window's swapchain and presents it, and uploads the rows of atlas that changed since the last call. The swapchain is made on the first call, at the size of s in device pixels, and is made again when the size of s changes or when presentation reports that it is out of date or suboptimal. A scene of no pixels presents nothing. The call returns once the frame is queued for presentation. The Gpu keeps one atlas texture that mirrors the atlas it was last given. After the call atlas is marked clean. Fails with NoSurface on a Gpu that open made.
fn read(g: Gpu, t: Target) -> []u8 ! Error

Waits for every submitted frame and returns the pixels of t as rows from the top of four bytes each, red, green, blue and alpha, width * height * 4 bytes in all. The bytes are unspecified until render has drawn into t.
fn render(g: Gpu, t: Target, s: scene.Scene, mut atlas: scene.Atlas) ! Error

Draws s into t, clearing it to the scene's background first, and uploads the rows of atlas that changed since the last call. Positions in s are device pixels of t; the scene's own width and height are not read. The call returns once the work is submitted, and read waits for it. The Gpu keeps one atlas texture that mirrors the atlas it was last given, so a Gpu draws with one Atlas. After the call atlas is marked clean.
fn target(g: Gpu, width: i64, height: i64) -> Target ! Error
Makes a target of width by height pixels on g. Fails with InvalidSize when either is below one.

Opens the first Vulkan 1.3 device that offers dynamic rendering, synchronization2 and the swapchain extension, and has a graphics queue that can present to s, for drawing into the window with present. The Gpu owns the Vulkan surface it makes from s and destroys it on release, so the window must outlive the Gpu. Offscreen targets work on it as on one from open. Fails with NoDevice when no device qualifies, and with Vulkan when a call fails, including VK_ERROR_EXTENSION_NOT_PRESENT when the instance lacks the windowing extension.
